c: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
The earth was shapeless and empty, with darkness over the face of the deep, and the Spirit of God moving over the surface of the waters.
God said, "Light, be!" And light came to be.
God saw that the light was good, and he set the light apart from the darkness.
God named the light Day and the darkness Night. Evening came, and morning came: one day.
God said, "Let there be a dome in the midst of the waters, dividing water from water."
God made the dome and separated the waters beneath it from the waters above it. So it was.
God named the dome Sky. Evening came, and morning came: a second day.
God said, "Let the waters beneath the sky be gathered into a single place, and let dry ground appear." So it was.
God named the dry ground Earth, and the gathered waters he named Seas. God saw that it was good.
God said, "Let the earth sprout vegetation: seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees that bear fruit with their seed in it, each after its own kind." So it was.
The earth brought forth vegetation: plants bearing seed after their kinds, and trees bearing fruit with seed in it, after their kinds. God saw that it was good.
Evening came, and morning came: a third day.
God said, "Let there be lights in the dome of the sky to separate day from night, and let them mark the festivals, the days and the years.
Let them be lights in the dome of the sky, giving light to the earth." So it was.
God made the two great lights, the greater to rule the day and the lesser to rule the night, and he made the stars as well.
God set them in the dome of the sky to give light to the earth,
to rule over day and night, and to divide light from darkness. God saw that it was good.
Evening came, and morning came: a fourth day.
God said, "Let the waters teem with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly over the earth, across the dome of the sky."
God created the great sea monsters and every living creature that glides and swarms in the waters, after their kinds, and every winged bird after its kind. God saw that it was good.
God blessed them: "Bear young and multiply. Fill the waters of the seas, and let the birds multiply on the earth."
Evening came, and morning came: a fifth day.
God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures after their kinds: cattle, crawling things and wild animals of the earth, each after its kind." So it was.
God made the wild animals of the earth after their kinds, the cattle after their kinds, and all the crawling things of the ground after their kinds. God saw that it was good.

God said, "Let us make humankind in our image, as our likeness, and let them have charge of the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, the cattle, the whole earth, and every crawling thing that crawls on the earth."
God created humankind in his own image; in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.

God blessed them and said to them, "Bear children and multiply. Fill the earth and subdue it. Have charge of the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and every living thing that moves on the earth."
God said, "Look, I have given you every seed-bearing plant on the face of all the earth, and every tree whose fruit bears seed. These shall be your food.
To every animal of the earth, every bird of the sky, and every creature that crawls on the earth, everything that has the breath of life in it, I give every green plant as food." So it was.
God looked at everything he had made, and it was very good. Evening came, and morning came: the sixth day.
So the heavens and the earth were completed, with everything that fills them.
On the seventh day God finished the work he had been doing, and on the seventh day he rested from all the work he had done.
God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on that day he rested from all the work that God had created and made.
This is the story of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made earth and heaven.
No wild shrub had yet appeared on the earth, and no field plant had yet sprung up, for the LORD God had not sent rain on the earth, and there was no human being to farm the ground.
Instead, a stream would rise from the earth and water the whole face of the ground.
Then the LORD God shaped the man out of the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being.
The LORD God planted a garden in Eden, to the east, and set there the man he had shaped.

Out of the ground the LORD God caused to grow every tree that is lovely to look at and good for food, with the tree of life in the middle of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and beyond the garden it divided into four headwaters.
The name of the first is the Pishon; it flows around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold.
The gold of that land is excellent; there is also bdellium and carnelian.
The name of the second river is the Gihon; it flows around the whole land of Cush.
The name of the third river is the Tigris; it runs east of Asshur. The fourth river is the Euphrates.
The LORD God took the man and placed him in the garden of Eden to farm it and take care of it.
The LORD God gave the man this command: "From every tree in the garden you may eat as much as you like,
but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; for on the day you eat from it, you will surely die."
The LORD God said, "It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make a companion to stand beside him."

Out of the ground the LORD God had shaped every wild animal and every bird of the sky, and he brought them to the man to see what he would name them. Whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name.
The man gave names to all the cattle, to the birds of the sky and to every wild animal; but for the man himself no companion was found to stand beside him.
So the LORD God cast a deep sleep over the man, and while he slept, God took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh in its place.
From the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man he fashioned a woman, and he brought her to the man.
The man said, "This one, at last, is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh! She shall be called Woman, because from Man she was taken."
For this reason a man leaves his father and mother and clings to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
The man and his wife were both naked, and they felt no shame before each other.
The serpent was the most cunning of all the wild animals the LORD God had made. It said to the woman, "Is it true that God said, 'You must not eat from any tree in the garden'?"
The woman said to the serpent, "We may eat the fruit of the garden's trees.
It is only the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden about which God said, 'Do not eat from it, and do not touch it, or you will die.'"
The serpent said to the woman, "You will certainly not die!
God knows that on the day you eat from it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil."

The woman saw that the tree was good to eat, delightful to look at, and desirable for making one wise. She took some of its fruit and ate; she also gave some to her husband, who was beside her, and he ate.
Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. They stitched fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.
They heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden at the breezy time of day, and the man and his wife hid from the LORD God among the trees of the garden.
The LORD God called to the man: "Where are you?"
He said, "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid."
He said, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I told you not to eat from?"
The man said, "The woman you placed beside me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate."
The LORD God said to the woman, "What have you done?" The woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."
The LORD God said to the serpent: "Because you have done this, you are cursed beyond all cattle and beyond every wild animal. You shall crawl on your belly, and eat dust all the days of your life.
I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike at your head, and you will strike at his heel."
To the woman he said: "I will make your labour in childbearing very hard; in pain you will give birth to children. Your desire will be for your husband, yet he will rule over you."

To the man he said: "Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat from it,' the ground is cursed because of you; by hard labour you will eat from it all the days of your life.
It will grow thorns and thistles for you, and you will eat the plants of the field.
By the sweat of your face you will eat bread, until you return to the ground, for from it you were taken. You are dust, and to dust you will return."
The man named his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all who live.
The LORD God made clothing of skins for the man and his wife, and dressed them.

The LORD God said, "Now the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil. He must not be allowed to reach out his hand and take fruit from the tree of life also, and eat, and live for ever."
So the LORD God sent him out of the garden of Eden to farm the ground from which he was taken.
He drove the man out, and east of the garden of Eden he stationed the cherubim and the whirling flame of a sword, to guard the way to the tree of life.
The man lay with his wife Eve; she conceived and gave birth to Cain, and said, "I have gained a man with the help of the LORD."
She went on to bear his brother Abel. Abel became a shepherd, and Cain became a tiller of the soil.
After a time, Cain brought some of the fruit of the soil as an offering to the LORD,
and Abel also brought an offering, some of the firstborn of his flock, the fat portions. The LORD regarded Abel and his offering with favour,
but he did not regard Cain and his offering with favour. Cain was furious, and his face fell.
The LORD said to Cain, "Why are you furious? Why has your face fallen?
If you do well, will you not hold your head high? But if you do not do well, sin lies in wait at the door. Its desire is for you, but you can master it."
Cain said to his brother Abel, "Let us go out into the field." And when they were in the field, Cain turned on his brother Abel and killed him.
The LORD said to Cain, "Where is your brother Abel?" He said, "I don't know. Am I my brother's guardian?"
He said, "What have you done? Listen! Your brother's blood is crying out to me from the ground.
Now you are under a curse, banished from the ground that opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand.
When you farm the ground, it will no longer yield its strength for you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth."
Cain said to the LORD, "My guilt is too great to bear.
You have driven me today from the face of the ground, and I shall be hidden from your face. I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and anyone who meets me will kill me."
The LORD said to him, "Not so! Anyone who kills Cain will suffer vengeance seven times over." And the LORD set a sign on Cain, so that no one who met him would strike him down.
Cain left the LORD's presence and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
Cain lay with his wife; she conceived and gave birth to Enoch. He was building a city, and he named the city after his son Enoch.
To Enoch was born Irad; Irad fathered Mehujael; Mehujael fathered Methushael; Methushael fathered Lamech.
Lamech took two wives: one was named Adah, the other Zillah.
Adah gave birth to Jabal; he was the ancestor of those who live in tents and raise livestock.
His brother's name was Jubal; he was the ancestor of all who play the lyre and the pipe.
Zillah, for her part, gave birth to Tubal-cain, who forged all kinds of tools of bronze and iron. Tubal-cain's sister was Naamah.
Lamech said to his wives: "Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; wives of Lamech, listen to my words: I have killed a man for wounding me, a youth for striking me.
If Cain is avenged seven times over, then Lamech seventy-seven times."
Adam lay with his wife again, and she gave birth to a son and named him Seth, "for God has set another child in place of Abel," she said, "since Cain killed him."
To Seth also a son was born, and he named him Enosh. At that time people began to call on the name of the LORD.
This is the written record of the descendants of Adam. When God created humankind, he made them in the likeness of God;
male and female he created them. He blessed them and gave them the name Humankind on the day they were created.
When Adam had lived 130 years, he became the father of a son in his own likeness, after his own image, and he named him Seth.
After Seth's birth Adam lived another 800 years, and had other sons and daughters.
All the days of Adam's life came to 930 years, and then he died.
When Seth had lived 105 years, he became the father of Enosh.
After Enosh's birth Seth lived another 807 years, and had other sons and daughters.
All the days of Seth came to 912 years, and then he died.
When Enosh had lived 90 years, he became the father of Kenan.
After Kenan's birth Enosh lived another 815 years, and had other sons and daughters.
All the days of Enosh came to 905 years, and then he died.
When Kenan had lived 70 years, he became the father of Mahalalel.
After Mahalalel's birth Kenan lived another 840 years, and had other sons and daughters.
All the days of Kenan came to 910 years, and then he died.
When Mahalalel had lived 65 years, he became the father of Jared.
After Jared's birth Mahalalel lived another 830 years, and had other sons and daughters.
All the days of Mahalalel came to 895 years, and then he died.
When Jared had lived 162 years, he became the father of Enoch.
After Enoch's birth Jared lived another 800 years, and had other sons and daughters.
All the days of Jared came to 962 years, and then he died.
When Enoch had lived 65 years, he became the father of Methuselah.
After Methuselah's birth Enoch walked with God for 300 years, and had other sons and daughters.
All the days of Enoch came to 365 years.
Enoch walked with God, and then he was gone, for God took him.
When Methuselah had lived 187 years, he became the father of Lamech.
After Lamech's birth Methuselah lived another 782 years, and had other sons and daughters.
All the days of Methuselah came to 969 years, and then he died.
When Lamech had lived 182 years, he became the father of a son.
He named him Noah, saying, "This one will give us rest from our work, from the hard labour of our hands, on the ground that the LORD has cursed."
After Noah's birth Lamech lived another 595 years, and had other sons and daughters.
All the days of Lamech came to 777 years, and then he died.
When Noah was 500 years old, he became the father of Shem, Ham and Japheth.
When people began to grow in number on the face of the earth, and daughters were born to them,
the sons of God saw that the daughters of humankind were beautiful, and they took wives for themselves from any they chose.
The LORD said, "My spirit will not stay in humankind for ever, since they are flesh. Their days will be 120 years."

The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and afterwards too, when the sons of God went in to the daughters of humankind and they bore children to them. These were the warriors of old, the famous men.
The LORD saw that human wickedness on the earth was great, and that every thought formed in the human heart was nothing but evil all the time.
The LORD regretted that he had made humankind on the earth, and his heart was deeply pained.
The LORD said, "I will wipe humankind, whom I created, from the face of the ground, and with them the animals, the crawling things and the birds of the sky, for I regret that I made them."
But Noah found favour with the LORD.
This is the story of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, whole-hearted among his contemporaries. Noah walked with God.
Noah became the father of three sons: Shem, Ham and Japheth.
The earth was ruined in God's sight, and filled with violence.
God looked at the earth, and it was ruined, for all flesh on the earth had ruined its way.
God said to Noah, "I have decided to put an end to all flesh, for the earth is full of violence because of them. I am about to destroy them along with the earth.
Make yourself an ark of gopher wood. Make compartments in the ark, and seal it inside and out with pitch.
This is how you are to build it: the length of the ark, 300 cubits; its width, 50 cubits; its height, 30 cubits.
Make a roof for the ark, and finish it to within a cubit of the top. Set the door of the ark in its side. Build it with a lower, a second and a third deck.
I am about to bring a flood of waters over the earth, to destroy every living thing under heaven that has the breath of life in it. Everything on the earth will perish.
But with you I will establish my covenant. You will enter the ark, you and your sons, your wife and your sons' wives with you.
From every living thing, from all flesh, you are to bring two of each into the ark to keep them alive with you; they are to be male and female.
From the birds after their kinds, the animals after their kinds, and every crawling thing of the ground after its kind, two of each will come to you, to be kept alive.
As for you, take every kind of food that is eaten and gather it, and it will serve as food for you and for them."
Noah did this. He did all that God commanded him.
The LORD said to Noah, "Go into the ark, you and all your household, for in this generation I have seen that you are righteous before me.
Take with you seven pairs of every clean animal, male and female, and one pair of every animal that is not clean, male and female;
also seven pairs of every kind of bird of the sky, male and female, to keep their offspring alive over all the earth.
In seven days' time I will make it rain on the earth for forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe from the face of the ground every living thing I have made."
Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him.
Noah was 600 years old when the flood came, with its waters over the earth.
Noah went into the ark, together with his sons, his wife and his sons' wives, to escape the waters of the flood.
Clean animals and animals that are not clean, birds and everything that crawls on the ground,
came in pairs to Noah into the ark, male and female, as God had commanded Noah.
After the seven days, the waters of the flood came over the earth.

In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that very day all the fountains of the great deep burst open and the windows of the heavens were opened.
The rain fell on the earth for forty days and forty nights.
On that very day Noah went into the ark, with Noah's sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, and Noah's wife and his sons' three wives.

They had with them every wild animal after its kind, all the cattle after their kinds, every crawling thing that crawls on the earth after its kind, and every bird after its kind, every winged creature.
They came to Noah into the ark in pairs, of all flesh that has the breath of life in it.
Those that came were male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him. Then the LORD shut him in.
The flood came upon the earth for forty days. The waters rose and lifted the ark, so that it rose high above the earth.
The waters surged and grew greatly on the earth, and the ark floated on the face of the waters.
The waters surged ever higher on the earth, and all the high mountains under all the heavens were covered.
The waters rose fifteen cubits higher, and the mountains were covered.
All flesh that moved on the earth perished: birds, cattle, wild animals, every swarming creature that swarms on the earth, and all humankind.
Everything on dry land that had the breath of the spirit of life in its nostrils died.

He wiped out every living thing on the face of the ground: human beings and animals, crawling things and birds of the sky. They were wiped from the earth, and only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark.
The waters surged over the earth for 150 days.
God remembered Noah, and all the wild animals and all the cattle that were with him in the ark. God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to go down.
The fountains of the deep and the windows of the heavens were closed, and the rain from the sky was held back.
The waters flowed back from the earth, receding steadily. At the end of 150 days the waters had decreased,
and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.
The waters kept on decreasing until the tenth month. In the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains became visible.
After forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made,
and sent out a raven; it went back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth.
Then he sent out a dove, to see whether the waters had gone down from the surface of the ground.

But the dove found nowhere to set its foot, and it returned to him in the ark, for there was water over the whole face of the earth. He reached out his hand, took it and brought it in to him in the ark.
He waited another seven days, and again he sent out the dove from the ark.
The dove came back to him at evening, and there, in its beak, was a fresh olive leaf! So Noah knew that the waters had gone down from the earth.
He waited another seven days and sent out the dove, but it did not return to him again.

In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the waters dried up from the earth. Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and the surface of the ground was dry.
In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry.
Then God spoke to Noah:
"Go out of the ark, you and your wife, your sons and your sons' wives with you.

Bring out with you every living thing that is with you, of all flesh, birds, animals and every crawling thing that crawls on the earth, so that they may swarm over the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on it."
So Noah went out, with his sons, his wife and his sons' wives.
Every animal, every crawling thing, every bird, everything that moves on the earth, went out of the ark by their families.
Noah built an altar to the LORD, and took some of every clean animal and every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar.

The LORD smelled the soothing aroma, and the LORD said in his heart, "I will never again curse the ground because of humankind, for the plans of the human heart are evil from youth; and I will never again strike down every living creature as I have done.
As long as the earth lasts, planting and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will never cease."
God blessed Noah and his sons, saying to them, "Bear children and multiply, and fill the earth.
The fear and terror of you will rest on every animal of the earth, on every bird of the sky, on everything that crawls on the ground, and on all the fish of the sea. They are placed in your hands.
Every creature that moves and lives will be food for you. As I gave you the green plants, I now give you all of them.
Only, you must not eat flesh with its life in it, that is, its blood.
For your own lifeblood, too, I will demand an account: from every animal I will demand it, and from every human being, from each one's fellow, I will demand an account for the life of a human being.
Whoever sheds the blood of a human being, by a human being shall that person's blood be shed; for God made humankind in his own image.
As for you, bear children and multiply; teem over the earth and multiply in it."
God said to Noah and to his sons with him,
"See, I am establishing my covenant with you and with your descendants after you,
and with every living creature that is with you: the birds, the cattle and all the wild animals with you, all that came out of the ark, every animal of the earth.
I establish my covenant with you: never again will all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood, and never again will a flood destroy the earth."
God said, "This is the sign of the covenant that I am making between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations:
I have set my bow in the clouds, and it will be the sign of the covenant between me and the earth.
When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow appears in the clouds,
I will remember my covenant between me and you and every living creature of all flesh: the waters will never again become a flood to destroy all flesh.
When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh on the earth."
God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh on the earth."
The sons of Noah who went out of the ark were Shem, Ham and Japheth. (Ham was the father of Canaan.)
These three were Noah's sons, and from them the whole earth was spread with people.
Noah, a farmer, was the first to plant a vineyard.
He drank some of the wine, became drunk, and lay uncovered inside his tent.
Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers outside.
Shem and Japheth took a cloak, laid it across both their shoulders, and walked backwards to cover their father's nakedness. Their faces were turned away, so that they did not see their father naked.
When Noah woke from his wine and learned what his youngest son had done to him,
he said, "Cursed be Canaan! He will be the lowest slave to his brothers."
He said also, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem, and let Canaan be his slave.
May God make room for Japheth, and may he live in the tents of Shem; and let Canaan be his slave."
After the flood Noah lived 350 years.
All the days of Noah came to 950 years, and then he died.
This is the record of the descendants of Noah's sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood.
The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras.
The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath and Togarmah.
The sons of Javan were Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim.
From these the peoples of the coasts spread out in their lands, each with its own language, by clan, within their nations.
The sons of Ham were Cush, Egypt, Put and Canaan.
The sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah were Sheba and Dedan.
Cush was the father of Nimrod, who was the first to be a mighty man on the earth.
He was a mighty hunter before the LORD; hence the saying, "Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD."
The first centres of his kingdom were Babylon, Uruk, Akkad and Kalneh, in the land of Shinar.
From that land he went out into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-ir, Calah
and Resen, between Nineveh and Calah; this is the great city.
Egypt was the father of the Ludites, the Anamites, the Lehabites, the Naphtuhites,
the Pathrusites, the Casluhites (from whom the Philistines came) and the Caphtorites.
Canaan was the father of Sidon, his firstborn, and of Heth,
and of the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites,
the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites,
the Arvadites, the Zemarites and the Hamathites. Later the clans of the Canaanites spread out,
and the Canaanite border ran from Sidon in the direction of Gerar as far as Gaza, then in the direction of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.
These are the sons of Ham, by their clans and languages, in their lands and nations.
Children were also born to Shem, ancestor of all the sons of Eber, and elder brother of Japheth.
The sons of Shem were Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud and Aram.
The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether and Mash.
Arpachshad was the father of Shelah, and Shelah was the father of Eber.
Two sons were born to Eber: one was named Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided; his brother's name was Joktan.
Joktan was the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,
Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,
Obal, Abimael, Sheba,
Ophir, Havilah and Jobab; all these were sons of Joktan.
Their settlements ran from Mesha towards Sephar, the eastern hill country.
These are the sons of Shem, by their clans and languages, in their lands and nations.
These are the clans of Noah's sons, by their family lines, in their nations; from these the nations spread over the earth after the flood.
The whole earth had one language and one set of words.
As people journeyed from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there.
They said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks and fire them hard." They used brick for stone, and bitumen for mortar.
Then they said, "Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, so that we will not be scattered over the face of the whole earth."
The LORD came down to look at the city and the tower that the people had built.
The LORD said, "Look, they are one people with one language, and this is just the start of what they will do. From now on, nothing they set out to do will be impossible for them.
Come, let us go down and confuse their language there, so that they will not understand each other's speech."
So the LORD scattered them from there over the face of the whole earth, and they stopped building the city.
That is why it was named Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of the whole earth; and from there the LORD scattered them over the face of the whole earth.
This is the record of Shem's family line. Shem was 100 years old when he became the father of Arpachshad, two years after the flood.
After Arpachshad's birth Shem lived another 500 years, and had other sons and daughters.
When Arpachshad had lived 35 years, he became the father of Shelah.
After Shelah's birth Arpachshad lived another 403 years, and had other sons and daughters.
When Shelah had lived 30 years, he became the father of Eber.
After Eber's birth Shelah lived another 403 years, and had other sons and daughters.
When Eber had lived 34 years, he became the father of Peleg.
After Peleg's birth Eber lived another 430 years, and had other sons and daughters.
When Peleg had lived 30 years, he became the father of Reu.
After Reu's birth Peleg lived another 209 years, and had other sons and daughters.
When Reu had lived 32 years, he became the father of Serug.
After Serug's birth Reu lived another 207 years, and had other sons and daughters.
When Serug had lived 30 years, he became the father of Nahor.
After Nahor's birth Serug lived another 200 years, and had other sons and daughters.
When Nahor had lived 29 years, he became the father of Terah.
After Terah's birth Nahor lived another 119 years, and had other sons and daughters.
When Terah had lived 70 years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran.
This is the record of Terah's family. Terah was the father of Abram, Nahor and Haran, and Haran was the father of Lot.
Haran died in the lifetime of his father Terah, in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans.
Abram and Nahor both took wives. Abram's wife was named Sarai, and Nahor's wife was named Milcah, daughter of Haran, who was the father of Milcah and of Iscah.
Sarai was unable to have children; she had none.

Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai, his son Abram's wife, and they set out together from Ur of the Chaldeans for the land of Canaan; but when they reached Haran, they settled there.
Terah lived 205 years, and he died in Haran.
The LORD said to Abram, "Go from your land, from your kindred and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you.
I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, and you will be a blessing.
I will bless those who bless you, and the one who treats you lightly I will curse; and through you every family on earth will find blessing."
So Abram went, as the LORD had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran.

Abram took his wife Sarai, his brother's son Lot, all the possessions they had acquired and the people they had gained in Haran, and they set out for the land of Canaan, and into the land of Canaan they came.
Abram travelled through the land as far as the sacred place at Shechem, the oak of Moreh. The Canaanites were in the land at that time.
The LORD appeared to Abram and said, "To your descendants I will give this land." So there he built an altar to the LORD, who had appeared to him.
From there he moved on to the hills east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. There he built an altar to the LORD and called on the name of the LORD.
Then Abram journeyed on, moving by stages towards the Negev.
A famine struck the land, and Abram went down into Egypt to live there for a while, for the famine was severe in the land.
As he was about to enter Egypt, he said to his wife Sarai, "I know that you are a woman beautiful to look at.
When the Egyptians see you, they will say, 'This is his wife,' and they will kill me, but they will let you live.
Say that you are my sister, so that it may go well for me because of you, and my life may be spared for your sake."
When Abram came to Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful.
Pharaoh's officials saw her and praised her to Pharaoh, and the woman was taken into Pharaoh's palace.
He treated Abram well because of her, and Abram acquired sheep and cattle, donkeys, male and female servants, female donkeys and camels.
But the LORD struck Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Abram's wife Sarai.
So Pharaoh summoned Abram and said, "What have you done to me? Why did you not tell me she was your wife?
Why did you say, 'She is my sister', so that I took her as my wife? Now here is your wife. Take her and go."
Pharaoh gave his men orders concerning Abram, and they escorted him out, with his wife and all that he had.
So Abram went up from Egypt to the Negev, he and his wife, with everything he had, and Lot with him.
Abram was very wealthy in livestock, in silver and in gold.
He travelled by stages from the Negev to Bethel, to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai,
to the place where he had first built the altar. There Abram called on the name of the LORD.
Lot, who went with Abram, also had flocks and herds and tents.
The land could not support them living side by side, because their possessions were so great that they could not live together.
Strife broke out between Abram's herders and Lot's herders. The Canaanites and the Perizzites were then living in the land.
Abram said to Lot, "Let there be no strife between you and me, or between my herders and yours, for we are kinsmen.
Is not the whole land before you? Separate from me, I ask. If you take the left, I will go right; if you take the right, I will go left."

Lot looked up and saw that the whole plain of the Jordan was well watered, all the way to Zoar, like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt. (This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.)
Lot chose for himself the whole plain of the Jordan and travelled east, and so they parted from each other.
Abram settled in the land of Canaan, while Lot settled among the cities of the plain and moved his tent as far as Sodom.
The people of Sodom were wicked, great sinners against the LORD.
The LORD said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him, "Lift up your eyes and look from where you are, north and south, east and west.
All the land that you see I will give to you and to your descendants for ever.
I will make your descendants like the dust of the earth, so that if anyone could count the dust of the earth, your descendants too could be counted.
Get up and walk through the land, through its length and its breadth, for I will give it to you."
So Abram moved his tent and came to settle by the oaks of Mamre, at Hebron, and there he built an altar to the LORD.
In the days when Amraphel was king of Shinar, with Arioch king of Ellasar, Kedorlaomer king of Elam and Tidal king of Goiim,
these kings fought a war against Bera of Sodom, Birsha of Gomorrah, Shinab of Admah, Shemeber of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is also called Zoar.
These five rulers gathered their armies in the Valley of Siddim, where the Salt Sea now lies.
For twelve years they had paid tribute to Kedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they rose against him.
In the fourteenth year Kedorlaomer came with the kings allied to him and struck down the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim at Ham, the Emim on the plain of Kiriathaim,
and the Horites in the mountains of Seir, as far as El-paran at the edge of the wilderness.
Turning back, they came to En-mishpat, that is Kadesh, and overran the whole territory of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar.
Then the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela (that is, Zoar) marched out and took their positions in the Valley of Siddim
to meet Kedorlaomer of Elam, Tidal of Goiim, Amraphel of Shinar and Arioch of Ellasar: four kings facing five.
The Valley of Siddim was riddled with tar pits. As the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some of their men fell into them, and the rest escaped to the hills.
The conquerors seized all the wealth and provisions of Sodom and Gomorrah and departed.
They took Lot as well, the son of Abram's brother, together with his belongings, for he was living in Sodom.
A survivor came and brought the news to Abram the Hebrew. Abram was camped by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and of Aner, and these men were bound to Abram by treaty.
When Abram heard that his kinsman had been taken prisoner, he called out the 318 trained fighters born in his own household and chased the invaders as far as Dan.
In the night he divided his men into groups and fell on them, he and his servants. He routed them and drove them on to Hobah, north of Damascus.
He recovered all the stolen goods, and brought back his kinsman Lot with his belongings, as well as the women and the other captives.
When Abram returned from his victory over Kedorlaomer and the kings with him, the king of Sodom came out to meet him in the Valley of Shaveh, which is the King's Valley.
Then Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine. He was a priest of God Most High.
He pronounced a blessing over Abram: "May Abram be blessed by God Most High, who made heaven and earth.
And blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand." And Abram gave him a tenth of everything he had.
The king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the people; the goods you may keep."
Abram answered the king of Sodom, "I have raised my hand in an oath to the LORD, God Most High, who made heaven and earth:
I will not take anything of yours, not so much as a thread or a sandal-strap, so that you can never say, 'It was I who made Abram rich.'
I will take nothing for myself except what my young men have eaten. But let Aner, Eshcol and Mamre, who went with me, take their share."
After these events the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: "Have no fear, Abram. I am a shield for you; your reward will be beyond measure."
Abram replied, "Lord GOD, what will you give me? I go on without a child, and the one who will inherit my house is Eliezer of Damascus."
Abram went on, "You have given me no child, so a man born in my household will be my heir."
But the word of the LORD came to him again: "That man will not be your heir. Your heir will be your own child."
He led Abram outside and said, "Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you can." Then he said to him, "That is how many your descendants will be."
Abram trusted the LORD, who reckoned it to him as righteousness.
Then he said to him, "I am the LORD, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land as your own."
Abram said, "Lord GOD, how can I be sure that it will be mine?"
He answered, "Bring me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old goat, a three-year-old ram, a turtledove and a young pigeon."
Abram brought all of these. He cut the animals in half and laid each half opposite the other; the birds he did not cut.
Vultures swooped down onto the carcasses, but Abram drove them off.
As the sun was sinking, Abram fell into a deep sleep, and a great dread, a darkness, came over him.
Then God said to Abram, "Be sure of this: your descendants will live as strangers in a land that is not theirs. They will be enslaved and ill-treated for four hundred years.
But I will bring judgement on the nation that enslaves them, and afterwards they will leave with great wealth.
You yourself will join your ancestors in peace, and you will be buried after a long and good life.
In the fourth generation your people will return here, for the guilt of the Amorites has not yet run its full course."
When the sun had set and deep darkness had come, a smoking oven and a flaming torch passed between the halves of the animals.
On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram: "To your descendants I give this land, from the stream of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates:
the Kenites, the Kenizzites and the Kadmonites,
the Hittites, the Perizzites and the Rephaim,
the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites and the Jebusites."
Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children. But she had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar.
Sarai said to Abram, "The LORD has closed my womb. Take my maidservant; perhaps through her I may have a family." Abram agreed to what Sarai said.
So after Abram had lived ten years in Canaan, Sarai his wife took Hagar the Egyptian, her maidservant, and gave her to Abram as a wife.
He lay with Hagar, and she conceived. Once she knew she was pregnant, she began to look down on her mistress.

Sarai said to Abram, "This wrong done to me is your doing. I put my maidservant in your arms, and now that she knows she is pregnant, she treats me with scorn. Let the LORD decide between you and me."
Abram said to Sarai, "Your maidservant is in your hands. Do with her what you think right." Sarai treated her harshly, and Hagar ran away from her.
The angel of the LORD found Hagar by a spring in the wilderness, the spring on the road to Shur.
He said, "Hagar, Sarai's maidservant, where have you come from, and where are you going?" She said, "I am running away from my mistress Sarai."
The angel of the LORD said to her, "Go back to your mistress and submit to her authority."
The angel of the LORD added, "I will make your descendants so many that they cannot be counted."
And the angel of the LORD said to her: "You are pregnant, and you will bear a son. You are to name him Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your suffering.
He will be a man untamed as the wild donkey, with his fist raised against everyone and everyone's fist raised against him. He will make his home in defiance of all his kin."
She gave a name to the LORD who had spoken to her: "You are El Roi," for she said, "Have I really seen the one who sees me, and lived?"
That is why the well is called Beer-lahai-roi. It lies between Kadesh and Bered.
Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram named the son she bore Ishmael.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael.
When Abram was ninety-nine years old, the LORD appeared to him and said, "I am God Almighty. Live in my presence and be whole-hearted.
I will set up my covenant between you and me, and I will make your descendants very many."
Abram bowed with his face to the ground, and God said to him,
"This is my side of the covenant with you: you will be the father of a multitude of nations.
You will no longer be called Abram. Your name will be Abraham, because I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.
I will make you extremely fruitful. Nations will come from you, and kings will be among your descendants.
I will keep my covenant with you and with your descendants after you, generation after generation, a covenant that has no end: I will be your God and the God of your descendants.
To you and to your descendants I will give the land where you now live as a stranger, the whole land of Canaan, as a possession for ever, and I will be their God."
God said to Abraham, "You, for your part, must keep my covenant, you and your descendants after you, through all their generations.
This is the covenant you must keep, between me and you and your descendants: every male among you is to be circumcised.
You are to cut away the flesh of your foreskin. This will be the sign of the covenant between me and you.
Every male among you, generation after generation, is to be circumcised at eight days old, whether born in your household or bought with money from a foreigner who is no part of your family.
Those born in your household and those you have bought must be circumcised. My covenant will be in your flesh, a covenant for all time.
Any male who is not circumcised, whose foreskin is not cut away, will be cut off from his people. He has broken my covenant."
God said to Abraham, "As for your wife Sarai, do not call her Sarai any longer. Her name is Sarah.
I will bless her, and I will give you a son through her. I will bless her, and she will become the mother of nations; rulers of peoples will come from her."
Abraham bowed to the ground and laughed. He thought, "Can a man of a hundred years have a child? Can Sarah, at ninety, give birth?"
Abraham said to God, "If only Ishmael might live before you!"
God said, "No. Your wife Sarah will bear you a son, and you are to name him Isaac. I will keep my covenant with him, a covenant for all time, for his descendants after him.
As for Ishmael, I have heard you. I will bless him; I will make him fruitful and give him very many descendants. He will father twelve chieftains, and I will make him a great nation.
But my covenant I will keep with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear to you at this time next year."
When God had finished speaking with Abraham, he went up from him.
That same day Abraham took his son Ishmael, and all those born in his household or bought with his money, every male in Abraham's household, and circumcised them, as God had told him.
Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised.
His son Ishmael was thirteen years old when he was circumcised.
On that same day Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised,
and with them all the men of his household, those born in the house and those bought from foreigners.
The LORD appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day.
He looked up and saw three men standing nearby. As soon as he saw them, he ran from the tent entrance to meet them and bowed to the ground.
"My lord," he said, "if I have found favour with you, please do not pass your servant by.
Let some water be brought so that you can wash your feet, and rest under the tree.
I will fetch a little bread so that you can refresh yourselves before you go on, now that you have come to your servant." They answered, "Do as you have said."
Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah. "Quick," he said, "take three measures of fine flour, knead it, and bake some bread."
Then Abraham ran to the herd, chose a calf, tender and fine, and gave it to a young servant, who hurried to prepare it.
He took curds and milk and the calf that had been prepared, and set them before the men. He stood beside them under the tree while they ate.
They asked him, "Where is your wife Sarah?" "There," he said, "in the tent."
One of them said, "I will certainly come back to you when the season comes round again, and your wife Sarah will have a son." Sarah was listening at the tent entrance, just behind him.
Abraham and Sarah were old, far advanced in years, and Sarah was past the age of bearing children.
So Sarah laughed to herself. "Now that I am worn out," she thought, "am I to know such joy, and with my husband so old?"
The LORD said to Abraham, "Why did Sarah laugh and say, 'Can I really bear a child, old as I am?'
Is anything too hard for the LORD? When the season comes round again, I will return to you, and Sarah will have a son."
Sarah was frightened, and she denied it: "I did not laugh." But he said, "Yes, you did laugh."
The men got up and looked down towards Sodom, and Abraham walked with them to send them on their way.
The LORD said, "Should I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?
Abraham is to become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth will find blessing through him.

I have chosen him so that he will instruct his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD, by practising righteousness and justice, so that the LORD may bring about for Abraham all that he has promised him."
Then the LORD said, "The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and their sin is very heavy.
I will go down to see whether they have done all that the outcry reaching me says. If not, I will know."
The men turned away and went towards Sodom, but Abraham remained standing before the LORD.
Abraham stepped forward and said, "Will you sweep away the righteous together with the wicked?
Suppose there are fifty righteous people in the city. Will you sweep it away, and not spare the place for the sake of the fifty righteous people in it?

It is unthinkable that you would do such a thing, to kill the righteous along with the wicked, so that the righteous fare as the wicked do. It is unthinkable! Will the Judge of all the earth not act justly?"
The LORD said, "If I find fifty righteous people in the city of Sodom, I will spare the whole place for their sake."
Abraham answered, "See how boldly I speak to the Lord, I who am nothing but dust and ashes.
Suppose the fifty righteous lack five. Will you destroy the whole city because of five?" He said, "I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there."
Abraham spoke to him again: "Suppose forty are found there." He said, "For the sake of forty I will not do it."
Then he said, "Please do not be angry, Lord, if I go on. Suppose thirty are found there." He said, "I will not do it if I find thirty there."
He said, "See how boldly I speak to the Lord. Suppose twenty are found there." He said, "For the sake of twenty I will not destroy it."
Then he said, "Please do not be angry, Lord, if I speak just once more. Suppose ten are found there." He said, "For the sake of ten I will not destroy it."
When the LORD had finished speaking with Abraham, he went on his way, and Abraham returned home.
The two angels reached Sodom at evening. Lot was sitting at the city gate, and when he saw them he got up to meet them and bowed low, his face to the ground.

"My lords," he said, "please come into your servant's house to spend the night and wash your feet. You can rise early and continue your journey." But they answered, "No, we will spend the night in the open square."
He pressed them so earnestly that they went with him and came into his house. He prepared a meal for them, baking flat bread, and they ate.
They had not yet lain down when the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, young and old, everyone without exception.
They shouted to Lot, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, so that we can have our way with them."
Lot went out to them at the doorway and pulled the door shut behind him.
"My brothers," he said, "please, do not do this wicked thing.

Listen, I have two daughters who have never slept with a man. Let me bring them out to you, and you may treat them as you like. But do nothing to these men, for they have come under the protection of my roof."
"Get back!" they shouted. "This one came here as an outsider, and now he wants to be our judge! We will treat you worse than them." They pushed hard against Lot and moved in to break down the door.
But the men inside reached out, pulled Lot back into the house, and shut the door.
Then they struck the men at the doorway, young and old, with blindness, so that they wore themselves out groping for the entrance.
The men said to Lot, "Who else do you have here: sons-in-law, sons, daughters, anyone belonging to you in the city? Get them out of this place,
because we are about to destroy it. The outcry against this city has grown great before the LORD, and he has sent us to destroy it."

Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, the men pledged to marry his daughters. "Get up and leave this place," he said, "for the LORD is about to destroy the city." But his sons-in-law thought he was joking.
When dawn came, the angels urged Lot on: "Hurry! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, or you will be swept away when the city is punished."
When he hesitated, the men took hold of his hand, and the hands of his wife and his two daughters, because the LORD had compassion on him. They led him out and left him outside the city.
As they brought them out, one of them said, "Escape for your life! Do not look behind you, and do not stop anywhere on the plain. Run to the hills, or you will be swept away."
Lot said to them, "No, my lords, please!
You have shown your servant favour and great kindness in saving my life, but I cannot run to the hills; the disaster will overtake me and I will die.
Look, there is a town close enough to run to, and it is small. Let me escape there. It is only a small place, is it not? Then my life will be saved."
He said to him, "Very well, I will grant you this also: I will not overthrow the town you speak of.
Hurry, escape there, for I can do nothing until you arrive." That is why the town was called Zoar.
The sun was rising over the land as Lot reached Zoar.
Then the LORD rained down burning sulphur on Sodom and Gomorrah; it came from the LORD, out of the sky.
He overthrew those cities and the whole plain, with all who lived in the cities and everything that grew on the ground.
Lot's wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
Early in the morning Abraham went to the place where he had stood before the LORD,
and looked out towards Sodom and Gomorrah and over all the land of the plain. He saw smoke rising from the land like the smoke of a furnace.
So when God destroyed the cities of the plain, he remembered Abraham, and he brought Lot out from the middle of the catastrophe that overthrew the cities where Lot had lived.
Lot went up from Zoar and settled in the hills with his two daughters, because he was afraid to stay in Zoar. He lived in a cave with his two daughters.
The elder said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is no man in the land to marry us, as is the custom everywhere.
Come, let us get our father drunk with wine and lie with him, so that through our father we may keep our family line alive."
That night they got their father drunk with wine, and the elder went in and lay with her father. He was not aware of her lying down or getting up.

The next day the elder said to the younger, "Last night I lay with my father. Let us get him drunk with wine again tonight, and you go in and lie with him, so that through our father we may keep our family line alive."
So that night also they got their father drunk with wine, and the younger got up and lay with him. He was not aware of her lying down or getting up.
So both of Lot's daughters became pregnant by their father.
The elder gave birth to a son and named him Moab; he is the ancestor of the Moabites to this day.
The younger also gave birth to a son and named him Ben-ammi; he is the ancestor of the Ammonites to this day.
Abraham moved on from there into the region of the Negev and lived between Kadesh and Shur. While he was staying in Gerar,
Abraham said of his wife Sarah, "She is my sister." So Abimelech king of Gerar sent for Sarah and took her.
But God came to Abimelech in a dream one night and said to him, "You are as good as dead because of the woman you have taken, for she is a married woman."
Abimelech had not gone near her. He said, "Lord, will you kill an innocent people?
Did he not tell me himself, 'She is my sister'? And she herself said, 'He is my brother.' I did this with a clear conscience and clean hands."
God said to him in the dream, "Yes, I know that you did this with a clear conscience, and that is why I kept you from sinning against me. That is why I did not let you touch her.
Now give the man's wife back. He is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live. But if you do not give her back, know that you and all who are yours will certainly die."
Early the next morning Abimelech called all his servants together and told them all that had happened, and the men were terrified.

Then Abimelech called Abraham and said to him, "What have you done to us? How did I wrong you, that you have brought so great a guilt on me and on my kingdom? You have done to me what should never be done."
Abimelech asked Abraham, "What did you have in mind, that you did this?"
Abraham said, "I thought, 'There is surely no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me on account of my wife.'
Besides, she is in fact my sister, the daughter of my father but not of my mother, and she became my wife.
When God made me wander away from my father's house, I said to her, 'This is the loyalty you can show me: in every place we go to, say of me, "He is my brother."'"
Then Abimelech took sheep and cattle and male and female servants and gave them to Abraham, and he gave his wife Sarah back to him.
Abimelech said, "My land is open before you; live wherever you like."
To Sarah he said, "I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver. This is to clear your name before all who are with you; you are vindicated before everyone."
Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, his wife and his female servants, so that they could have children again,
for the LORD had closed up every womb in Abimelech's household because of Sarah, Abraham's wife.
The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did for Sarah what he had promised.
Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the very time God had spoken of.
Abraham named the son born to him, whom Sarah bore him, Isaac.
When his son Isaac was eight days old, Abraham circumcised him, as God had commanded.
Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born.
Sarah said, "God has given me laughter, and everyone who hears of it will laugh with me."
She said, "Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age."
The child grew and was weaned, and on the day Isaac was weaned Abraham gave a great feast.
Sarah saw the son whom Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham mocking.
She said to Abraham, "Drive out this slave woman with her son, for the son of this slave woman will not share the inheritance with my son Isaac."
The matter was very painful to Abraham, because it concerned his son.
But God said to Abraham, "Do not let this distress you, over the boy or over your slave woman. Whatever Sarah tells you, listen to her, for it is through Isaac that your descendants will be called.
As for the son of the slave woman, I will make a nation of him also, for he is your offspring."

Early the next morning Abraham took bread and a skin of water and gave them to Hagar. He put them over her shoulder, and with the boy he sent her away. She set out and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.
When the water in the skin was used up, she put the boy under one of the bushes.
Then she went and sat down some distance away, about a bowshot off, for she said, "I cannot watch the boy die." She sat there and wept aloud.
God heard the boy crying, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, "What is wrong, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard the boy where he lies.
Get up, lift the boy up and take him by the hand, for I will make him into a great nation."
Then God opened her eyes and she saw a well of water. She went and filled the skin with water and gave the boy a drink.
God was with the boy as he grew up. He lived in the wilderness and became a skilled archer.
He lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother found a wife for him from the land of Egypt.
At that time Abimelech, together with Phicol the commander of his army, said to Abraham, "God is with you in everything you do.

Now swear to me here before God that you will not deal falsely with me, my children or my descendants. As I have shown loyalty to you, show the same to me and to the land where you have lived as a foreigner."
Abraham said, "I swear it."
Then Abraham complained to Abimelech about a well that Abimelech's servants had seized.
Abimelech said, "I do not know who did this. You did not tell me, and I heard nothing of it until today."
So Abraham took sheep and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and the two men made a covenant.
Abraham set apart seven ewe lambs from the flock.
Abimelech asked Abraham, "What are these seven ewe lambs that you have set apart?"
He said, "Accept these seven lambs from my hand as a witness that I dug this well."
That is why the place was called Beersheba, because the two of them swore an oath there.
When they had made the covenant at Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army left and returned to the land of the Philistines.
Abraham planted a tamarisk tree at Beersheba, and there he called on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God.
And Abraham lived as a foreigner in the land of the Philistines for a long time.
Some time after these events, God tested Abraham. He said to him, "Abraham!" and he answered, "Here I am."
He said, "Take your son, your only son, the one you love, Isaac, and go to the land of Moriah. There offer him as a burnt offering on one of the mountains that I will show you."

Early in the morning Abraham got up, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac. He split wood for the burnt offering, and set out for the place God had told him about.
On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance.
Abraham said to his young men, "Stay here with the donkey. The boy and I will go over there, and we will worship, and then we will come back to you."
Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and laid it on his son Isaac, and he himself carried the fire and the knife. And the two of them walked on together.
Isaac said to his father Abraham, "Father?" "Here I am, my son," he said. Isaac said, "The fire and the wood are here, but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?"
Abraham answered, "God himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son." And the two of them walked on together.
When they came to the place God had told him about, Abraham built an altar there and arranged the wood on it. He bound his son Isaac and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood.
Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to kill his son.
But the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven: "Abraham! Abraham!" He said, "Here I am."
The angel said, "Do not lay a hand on the boy. Do nothing to him, for now I know that you fear God, since you have not held back your son, your only son, from me."
Abraham looked up and saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. He went and took the ram and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son.
Abraham named that place "The LORD Will Provide." To this day it is said, "On the mountain of the LORD it shall be provided."
The angel of the LORD called to Abraham from heaven a second time
and said, "I swear by myself, declares the LORD: because you have done this and have not held back your son, your only son,
I will bless you richly, and I will make your descendants as many as the stars of the sky and the sand on the seashore. Your descendants will take possession of the gates of their enemies,
and through your descendants all the nations of the earth will find blessing, because you have obeyed my voice."
Abraham returned to his young men, and they set out together for Beersheba. And Abraham lived at Beersheba.
Some time later Abraham was told, "Milcah too has borne children to your brother Nahor:
Uz his firstborn, his brother Buz, Kemuel the father of Aram,
Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel."
Bethuel became the father of Rebekah. These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother.
His concubine, whose name was Reumah, also bore children: Tebah, Gaham, Tahash and Maacah.
Sarah lived to the age of 127. These were the years of Sarah's life.
She died at Kiriath-arba, that is Hebron, in the land of Canaan, and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah and to weep over her.
Then Abraham rose from beside his dead wife and spoke to the Hittites:
"I am a stranger and a settler among you. Give me a burial place among you, so that I may bury my dead and remove her from my sight."
The Hittites answered Abraham,
"Hear us, my lord. You are a mighty prince among us. Bury your dead in the best of our tombs. None of us will refuse you his tomb for burying your dead."
Abraham rose and bowed low before the people of the land, the Hittites,
and said to them, "If you are willing for me to bury my dead out of my sight, then hear me, and ask Ephron son of Zohar on my behalf
to give me the cave of Machpelah that belongs to him, at the edge of his field. Let him give it to me in your presence, for the full price, as a burial place of my own."
Ephron was sitting among the Hittites. Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of all the Hittites who had come to the gate of his city:
"No, my lord, listen to me. I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. I give it to you in the presence of my people. Bury your dead."
Abraham bowed low before the people of the land,
and said to Ephron in their hearing, "If you will, please listen to me. I will pay the price of the field. Accept it from me, so that I may bury my dead there."
Ephron answered Abraham,
"My lord, listen to me. A piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver: what is that between you and me? Bury your dead."
Abraham agreed to Ephron's price, and he weighed out for Ephron the silver he had named in the hearing of the Hittites: four hundred shekels of silver, by the standard of the merchants.
So Ephron's field at Machpelah, east of Mamre, the field with its cave and all the trees within its borders, became
Abraham's property, in the presence of the Hittites and all who had come to the gate of the city.
After this, Abraham buried his wife Sarah in the cave of the field at Machpelah, east of Mamre, that is Hebron, in the land of Canaan.
So the field and the cave in it passed from the Hittites to Abraham as a burial place of his own.
Abraham was now old, advanced in years, and the LORD had blessed him in everything.
He said to the senior servant of his household, the man who managed all that he owned, "Place your hand under my thigh.
I want you to swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and the God of earth, that you will not choose a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I live,
but will go to my own country, to my own relatives, and choose a wife for my son Isaac."
The servant asked him, "What if the woman is unwilling to come with me to this land? Should I take your son back to the country you came from?"
Abraham said, "Take care that you never take my son back there.

The LORD, the God of heaven, took me from my father's house and from my native land. He spoke to me and swore to me, 'I will give this land to your descendants.' He will send his angel ahead of you, and you will find a wife there for my son.
If the woman is unwilling to follow you, you are released from this oath of mine. Only, do not take my son back there."
The servant placed his hand under the thigh of his master Abraham and swore to him about this matter.
Then the servant took ten of his master's camels, loaded with all kinds of fine gifts from his master, and set out for Aram-naharaim, to the city of Nahor.
Towards evening, when the women go out to draw water, he made the camels kneel by the well outside the city.
He prayed, "LORD, God of my master Abraham, give me success today, and show faithful love to my master Abraham.
Here I am, standing by the spring, while the young women of the town come out to draw water.

Let it happen like this: I will say to a young woman, 'Please tip your jar so that I may drink,' and if she answers, 'Drink, and I will water your camels too,' let her be the one you have chosen for your servant Isaac. By this I will know that you have shown faithful love to my master."
Before he had finished praying, Rebekah came out with her jar on her shoulder. She was the daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Abraham's brother Nahor.
The young woman was very beautiful, a virgin; no man had been with her. She went down to the spring, filled her jar and came back up.
The servant hurried to meet her and said, "Please give me a little water from your jar."
"Drink, my lord," she said, and she quickly lowered the jar into her hands and gave him a drink.
When she had given him enough, she said, "I will draw water for your camels too, until they have drunk their fill."
She quickly emptied her jar into the trough and ran back to the well to draw more, and she drew water for all his camels.
The man watched her in silence, wondering whether the LORD had made his journey a success or not.
When the camels had finished drinking, the man took out a gold ring weighing half a shekel and two gold bracelets weighing ten shekels for her wrists,
and asked, "Whose daughter are you? Please tell me. Is there room in your father's house for us to spend the night?"
She said, "I am the daughter of Bethuel, the son that Milcah bore to Nahor."
She added, "We have plenty of straw and fodder, and room for you to stay."
The man bowed down and worshipped the LORD,

saying, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not withdrawn his faithful love and truth from my master. The LORD has led me on the journey to the house of my master's relatives."
The young woman ran and told her mother's household what had happened.
Rebekah had a brother named Laban, and he hurried out to the man at the spring.
He had seen the ring and the bracelets on his sister's wrists, and had heard Rebekah say, "This is what the man said to me." So he went to the man, who was still standing by the camels at the spring.
"Come in, you who are blessed by the LORD," he said. "Why are you standing outside? I have prepared the house, and a place for the camels."
So the man came into the house, and Laban unloaded the camels, gave them straw and fodder, and brought water to wash the feet of the man and of the men with him.
Food was set before him, but he said, "I will not eat until I have told you my business." "Speak," Laban said.
"I am Abraham's servant," he said.
"The LORD has blessed my master greatly, and he has become wealthy. He has given him flocks and herds, silver and gold, male and female servants, camels and donkeys.
My master's wife Sarah bore him a son in her old age, and my master has given him everything he owns.
My master made me swear an oath: 'Do not choose a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I live,
but go to my father's house, to my own clan, and choose a wife for my son.'
I said to my master, 'What if the woman will not come with me?'
He answered, 'The LORD, in whose presence I have walked, will send his angel with you and make your journey a success, and you will find a wife for my son from my clan, from my father's house.
You will be released from my oath if you go to my clan and they refuse you; then you will be free from my oath.'
Today I came to the spring and said, 'LORD, God of my master Abraham, if you will make my journey a success,
here I stand by the spring. Let the young woman who comes out to draw water, to whom I say, "Please let me drink a little water from your jar,"
and who replies, "Drink, and I will draw for your camels too," be the woman the LORD has chosen for my master's son.'
Before I had finished praying silently, Rebekah came out with her jar on her shoulder. She went down to the spring and drew water, and I said to her, 'Please give me a drink.'
She quickly lowered her jar from her shoulder and said, 'Drink, and I will water your camels too.' So I drank, and she watered the camels also.
I asked her, 'Whose daughter are you?' and she said, 'Bethuel's daughter, the son of Nahor and Milcah.' Then I put the ring in her nose and the bracelets on her wrists.
I bowed down and worshipped the LORD, and I blessed the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who had led me by the right road to find my master's kinsman's daughter for his son.
Now tell me whether you will show faithful love and loyalty to my master. If not, tell me, so that I may know which way to turn."
Laban and Bethuel answered, "This comes from the LORD; we can say nothing to you, either bad or good.
Here is Rebekah. Take her and go, and let her become the wife of your master's son, as the LORD has said."
When Abraham's servant heard what they said, he bowed to the ground before the LORD.
Then the servant brought out articles of silver and gold, and clothing, and gave them to Rebekah. He also gave costly gifts to her brother and her mother.
He and the men with him ate and drank and stayed the night. When they got up in the morning, he said, "Send me back to my master."
Her brother and her mother said, "Let the girl stay with us a while, ten days or so; then she may go."
But he said, "Do not delay me, now that the LORD has made my journey a success. Send me on my way, so that I may go to my master."
They said, "Let us call the girl and ask her."
They called Rebekah and asked her, "Will you go with this man?" "I will go," she said.
So they sent their sister Rebekah on her way, with her nurse, and Abraham's servant and his men.
They blessed Rebekah and said to her, "Our sister, may you become thousands upon ten thousands; may your descendants possess the gates of those who hate them."
Then Rebekah and her young women got up, mounted the camels and followed the man. So the servant took Rebekah and went on his way.
Isaac had come from Beer-lahai-roi, for he was living in the Negev.
One evening Isaac went out into the field to walk and think. He looked up, and there were camels approaching.
Rebekah looked up and saw Isaac, and she slipped down from her camel
and asked the servant, "Who is that man walking in the field to meet us?" "That is my master," the servant said. So she took her veil and covered herself.
The servant told Isaac everything he had done.
Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah. He took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.
Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah.
She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah.
Jokshan was the father of Sheba and Dedan. The descendants of Dedan were the Asshurim, the Letushim and the Leummim.
The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida and Eldaah. All these were descendants of Keturah.
Abraham gave all he owned to Isaac.
But to the sons of his concubines Abraham gave gifts, and while he was still alive he sent them away from his son Isaac, eastward to the land of the east.
This is the length of Abraham's life: 175 years.
Abraham breathed his last and died at a good old age, old and full of years, and was gathered to his people.
His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, east of Mamre,
the field that Abraham had bought from the Hittites. There Abraham was buried with his wife Sarah.
After Abraham's death, God blessed his son Isaac, and Isaac lived near Beer-lahai-roi.
This is the record of the descendants of Ishmael, Abraham's son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's servant, bore to Abraham.
These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, in the order of their birth: Nebaioth, the firstborn of Ishmael, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
Mishma, Dumah, Massa,
Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish and Kedemah.
These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their settlements and camps: twelve chieftains of as many tribes.
This is the length of Ishmael's life: 137 years. He breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people.
His descendants settled from Havilah to Shur, which is east of Egypt in the direction of Asshur. They lived in hostility towards all their kin.
This is the record of the family of Isaac, Abraham's son. Abraham was the father of Isaac.
Isaac was forty years old when he married Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram, and sister of Laban the Aramean.
Isaac prayed to the LORD for his wife, because she was childless, and the LORD answered his prayer, and his wife Rebekah conceived.
The children struggled against each other inside her, and she said, "If this is how it is, why do I live?" She went to ask the LORD.
The LORD said to her: "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will be separated from within you. One people will be stronger than the other, and the elder will serve the younger."
When the time came for her to give birth, there were twins in her womb.
The first came out red, covered all over like a hairy cloak, and they named him Esau.
Afterwards his brother came out, with his hand gripping Esau's heel, and he was named Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when they were born.
The boys grew up. Esau became a skilful hunter, a man of the open country, while Jacob was a quiet man who stayed among the tents.
Isaac loved Esau, because he had a taste for game, but Rebekah loved Jacob.
One day, when Jacob was cooking a stew, Esau came in from the open country, exhausted.
Esau said to Jacob, "Quick, let me gulp down some of that red stuff, that red stew, for I am exhausted." That is why he was named Edom.
Jacob said, "First sell me your birthright."
Esau said, "Look, I am about to die. What use is a birthright to me?"
Jacob said, "Swear to me first." So he swore an oath to him and sold his birthright to Jacob.
Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew. He ate and drank, got up and left. So Esau showed how little he valued his birthright.
There was a famine in the land, apart from the earlier famine in Abraham's time, and Isaac went to Gerar, to Abimelech king of the Philistines.
The LORD appeared to him and said, "Do not go down to Egypt. Live in the land I will tell you of.
Stay in this land as a foreigner, and I will be with you and bless you. To you and your descendants I will give all these lands, and I will keep the oath I swore to your father Abraham.
I will make your descendants as many as the stars of the sky and give them all these lands, and through your descendants all the nations of the earth will find blessing,
because Abraham obeyed me and kept my requirements, my commands, my decrees and my laws."
So Isaac stayed in Gerar.

When the men of the place asked about his wife, he said, "She is my sister." He was afraid to say, "She is my wife," for he thought, "The men of this place might kill me because of Rebekah, since she is beautiful."
After Isaac had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked down from a window and saw Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah.
Abimelech sent for Isaac and said, "She is clearly your wife! Why did you say, 'She is my sister'?" Isaac answered, "Because I thought I might be killed on her account."
