Abimelech said, "What have you done to us? One of my people might easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt on us."
So Abimelech issued an order to all his people: "Anyone who harms this man or his wife will be put to death."
Isaac sowed crops in that land and in that year reaped a hundred times what he had sown, because the LORD blessed him.
He grew rich, and his wealth increased until he became very wealthy.
He owned flocks and herds and a great household, and the Philistines envied him.
So the Philistines filled with earth all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham.
Abimelech said to Isaac, "Leave us. You have become far too powerful for us."
So Isaac left that place, camped in the valley of Gerar, and settled there.
Isaac dug out again the wells that had been dug in the days of his father Abraham, and that the Philistines had blocked after Abraham died, and he gave them the same names his father had given them.
But when Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found a spring of flowing water there,
the herders of Gerar quarrelled with Isaac's herders and said, "The water is ours." So he named the well Esek, because they had contended with him.
They dug another well, and they quarrelled over that one too, so he named it Sitnah.
He moved on from there and dug another well, and no one quarrelled over it. He named it Rehoboth and said, "Now the LORD has given us room, and we will prosper in the land."
From there he went up to Beersheba.

That night the LORD appeared to him and said, "I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of my servant Abraham."
Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD. He pitched his tent there, and his servants dug a well.
Then Abimelech came to him from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army.
Isaac asked them, "Why have you come to me, when you hated me and sent me away from you?"
They answered, "We could see plainly that the LORD was with you. So we said, 'Let there be a sworn agreement between us, between you and us. Let us make a covenant with you:
you will do us no harm, just as we did not touch you, but did only good to you and sent you away in peace. And now you are blessed by the LORD.'"
Isaac prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank.
Early the next morning the men swore an oath to each other. Isaac sent them on their way, and they left him in peace.
That same day Isaac's servants came and told him about the well they had dug. "We have found water," they said.
He named it Shibah, and to this day the city is called Beersheba.
When Esau was forty years old, he married Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite.
They made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
When Isaac was old and his eyes had grown too weak to see, he called his elder son Esau and said, "My son!" "Here I am," Esau replied.
"Listen," Isaac said, "I am old, and I do not know when I will die.
So take your gear, your quiver and bow, go out into the countryside, and bring me some game.
Then make me the savoury dish I love, and bring it to me to eat, so that I may give you my blessing before I die."
Rebekah had been listening while Isaac spoke to his son Esau. As soon as Esau left for the countryside to hunt game for his father,
Rebekah said to her son Jacob, "I have just heard your father say to your brother Esau,
'Bring me some game and make me a savoury dish to eat, so that I may bless you in the LORD's presence before I die.'
Now, my son, listen to me and do exactly as I tell you.
Go to the flock and fetch me two fine young goats. I will make them into the savoury dish your father loves,
and you will take it in to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies."
Jacob said to his mother Rebekah, "But my brother Esau is a hairy man, and my skin is smooth.
If my father touches me, he will see that I am deceiving him, and I will bring a curse on myself instead of a blessing."
His mother said to him, "Let any curse fall on me, my son. Just do as I say. Go and get them for me."
So he went, fetched them and brought them to his mother, and she made the savoury dish his father loved.
Rebekah took the best clothes of her elder son Esau, which she kept in the house, and put them on her younger son Jacob.
She covered his hands and the smooth part of his neck with the goatskins.
Then she put the savoury dish and the bread she had made into the hands of her son Jacob.
He went in to his father and said, "Father." "Yes, my son," he said. "Who are you?"
Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you told me. Please sit up and eat some of my game, so that you may give me your blessing."
Isaac said to his son, "How did you find it so quickly, my son?" He answered, "The LORD your God put it in my path."
Isaac said to Jacob, "Come closer, so that I can touch you, my son, and know whether you really are my son Esau."
Jacob went close to his father Isaac, who touched him and said, "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are Esau's hands."
He did not recognise him, because his hands were hairy like those of his brother Esau, so he blessed him.
"Are you really my son Esau?" he asked. "I am," he said.
Then he said, "Bring it to me, and let me eat some of my son's game, so that I may give you my blessing." Jacob brought it, and he ate; he brought him wine too, and he drank.
Then his father Isaac said to him, "Come close and kiss me, my son."
So he came close and kissed him, and Isaac caught the smell of his clothes, and blessed him, saying: "The smell of my son is the smell of a field the LORD has blessed.
May God give you dew from the sky and richness of the earth, abundant grain and new wine.
May peoples serve you and nations bow down to you. Be master over your brothers, and let your mother's sons bow down to you. Cursed be those who curse you, and blessed be those who bless you."
Isaac had just finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had barely left his father's presence, when his brother Esau came back from hunting.
He too made a savoury dish and brought it to his father. He said to him, "Father, sit up and eat some of your son's game, so that you may give me your blessing."
His father Isaac asked him, "Who are you?" "I am your son," he answered, "your firstborn, Esau."
Isaac began to tremble violently. "Then who was it," he said, "who hunted game and brought it to me? I ate it all before you came, and I blessed him, and he will remain blessed."
When Esau heard his father's words, he let out a loud and bitter cry and said to his father, "Bless me too, Father!"
But he said, "Your brother came and deceived me, and he has taken your blessing."
Esau said, "Is he not rightly named Jacob? He has cheated me twice now. He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing!" Then he asked, "Have you not kept a blessing for me?"
Isaac answered Esau, "I have made him master over you, and given him all his brothers as servants, and provided him with grain and new wine. What is left that I can do for you, my son?"
Esau said to his father, "Do you have only one blessing, Father? Bless me too, Father!" And Esau wept aloud.
His father Isaac answered him: "Far from the richness of the earth will your home be, far from the dew of the sky above.
You will live by your sword, and you will serve your brother. But when you break free, you will throw his yoke from your neck."
Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. Esau said to himself, "The days of mourning for my father are near. Then I will kill my brother Jacob."
When Rebekah was told what her elder son Esau had said, she sent for her younger son Jacob and said to him, "Your brother Esau is consoling himself with the thought of killing you.
Now, my son, listen to me. Get up and flee to my brother Laban in Haran.
Stay with him for a while, until your brother's fury cools.
When your brother's anger against you has turned away, and he has forgotten what you did to him, I will send word and bring you back from there. Why should I lose both of you in one day?"
Rebekah said to Isaac, "I am sick of my life because of these Hittite women. If Jacob marries a Hittite woman like these, a woman of this land, what is my life worth?"
So Isaac called Jacob, blessed him and gave him this command: "You must not marry a Canaanite woman.
Go at once to Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel, your mother's father, and take a wife from there, from the daughters of Laban, your mother's brother.
May God Almighty bless you, make you fruitful and increase your numbers, so that you become an assembly of peoples.
May he give you the blessing of Abraham, to you and to your descendants with you, so that you may possess the land where you now live as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham."
Then Isaac sent Jacob on his way, and he went to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, who was the mother of Jacob and Esau.
Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that when he blessed him he had commanded him, "You must not marry a Canaanite woman,"
and that Jacob had obeyed his father and mother and gone to Paddan-aram.
Esau then saw that the Canaanite women did not please his father Isaac,
so Esau went to Ishmael and married Mahalath, the daughter of Abraham's son Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth, in addition to the wives he already had.
Jacob left Beersheba and set out for Haran.
He reached a certain place and stayed there for the night, because the sun had set. He took one of the stones of that place, put it under his head, and lay down there to sleep.
He dreamed that he saw a stairway set on the ground, its top reaching to heaven, and the angels of God were going up and down on it.
And there beside him stood the LORD, who said, "I am the LORD, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. The land on which you are lying I will give to you and to your descendants.

Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth, and you will spread out to the west and the east, to the north and the south. Through you and your descendants all the families of the earth will find blessing.
Know that I am with you. I will guard you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you."
Jacob woke from his sleep and said, "The LORD is in this place, and I did not know it."
He was afraid, and said, "How awesome this place is! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven."
Early in the morning Jacob took the stone he had put under his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil over the top of it.
He named that place Bethel, though the city had earlier been called Luz.
Then Jacob made a vow: "If God will be with me, and guard me on this journey I am making, and give me bread to eat and clothes to wear,
and if I come back safely to my father's house, then the LORD will be my God,
and this stone that I have set up as a pillar will be God's house. And of everything you give me, I will give you a tenth."
Jacob went on his way and came to the land of the people of the east.
He looked, and saw a well in the open country, with three flocks of sheep lying beside it, because the flocks were watered from that well. A large stone lay over the mouth of the well.
When all the flocks had gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone off the mouth of the well, water the sheep, and then put the stone back in its place.
Jacob asked them, "My brothers, where are you from?" "We are from Haran," they said.
He asked them, "Do you know Laban, the grandson of Nahor?" "We know him," they said.
"Is he well?" he asked. "He is well," they said, "and here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep."
He said, "Look, it is still the middle of the day, and not time for the flocks to be gathered. Water the sheep and take them back to graze."
But they said, "We cannot until all the flocks have been gathered and the stone is rolled away from the mouth of the well. Then we water the sheep."
While he was still talking with them, Rachel came with her father's sheep, for she was a shepherdess.
When Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of his mother's brother Laban, with the sheep of his uncle Laban, he went up and rolled the stone off the mouth of the well and watered his uncle Laban's sheep.
Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud.
He told Rachel that he was a relative of her father, the son of Rebekah, and she ran and told her father.
As soon as Laban heard the news of his sister's son Jacob, he ran to meet him. He embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his house, and Jacob told Laban all that had happened.
Laban said to him, "You are my own flesh and blood." And Jacob stayed with him for a month.
Then Laban said to Jacob, "Just because you are a relative, should you work for me for nothing? Tell me what your wages should be."
Now Laban had two daughters. The elder was named Leah, and the younger was named Rachel.
Leah's eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and in looks.
Jacob loved Rachel, and he said, "I will work for you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel."
Laban said, "Better that I give her to you than to some other man. Stay with me."
So Jacob worked seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him like a few days because of his love for her.
Then Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife, for my time is completed, so that I may sleep with her."
Laban gathered all the people of the place and held a feast.
But that evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob slept with her.
(Laban gave his servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her maid.)
In the morning, there was Leah! Jacob said to Laban, "What is this you have done to me? Did I not work for you for Rachel? Why have you deceived me?"
Laban said, "It is not the custom in our place to give the younger before the firstborn.
Finish this one's bridal week, and we will give you the other also, in return for another seven years of work."
Jacob did so. He finished the week with Leah, and then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife.
(Laban gave his servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her maid.)
Jacob slept with Rachel also, and he loved Rachel more than Leah. He worked for Laban another seven years.
When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, he opened her womb, but Rachel was childless.
Leah conceived and bore a son, and she named him Reuben, for she said, "The LORD has seen my misery, and now my husband will love me."
She conceived again and bore a son, and said, "The LORD has heard that I am unloved, and so he has given me this son also." She named him Simeon.
Again she conceived and bore a son, and said, "Now at last my husband will become attached to me, because I have borne him three sons." So he was named Levi.
She conceived again and bore a son, and said, "This time I will praise the LORD." So she named him Judah. Then she stopped bearing children.
When Rachel saw that she was not bearing children for Jacob, she became jealous of her sister. She said to Jacob, "Give me children, or I will die!"
Jacob was angry with Rachel and said, "Am I in the place of God, who has kept you from having children?"
She said, "Here is my servant Bilhah. Sleep with her, so that she may give birth on my knees, and through her I too may have a family."
So she gave him her servant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob slept with her.
Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.
Rachel said, "God has judged in my favour. He has heard my plea and given me a son." So she named him Dan.
Rachel's servant Bilhah conceived again and bore Jacob a second son.
Rachel said, "I have struggled hard with my sister, and I have won." So she named him Naphtali.
When Leah saw that she had stopped bearing children, she took her servant Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
Leah's servant Zilpah bore Jacob a son.
Leah said, "What good fortune!" So she named him Gad.
Leah's servant Zilpah bore Jacob a second son.
Leah said, "How happy I am! Women will call me happy." So she named him Asher.
During the wheat harvest Reuben went out and found some mandrakes in the field and brought them to his mother Leah. Rachel said to Leah, "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes."
But Leah said to her, "Was it not enough that you took my husband? Now you would take my son's mandrakes too?" Rachel said, "Then he may sleep with you tonight, in exchange for your son's mandrakes."
When Jacob came in from the field that evening, Leah went out to meet him. "You must sleep with me," she said, "for I have hired you with my son's mandrakes." So he slept with her that night.
God heard Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.
Leah said, "God has given me my wages for giving my servant to my husband." So she named him Issachar.
Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son.
Then Leah said, "God has given me a fine gift. Now my husband will honour me, because I have borne him six sons." So she named him Zebulun.
Afterwards she gave birth to a daughter and named her Dinah.
Then God remembered Rachel. God heard her and opened her womb.
She conceived and bore a son and said, "God has taken away my disgrace."
She named him Joseph, saying, "May the LORD add another son to me."
After Rachel had given birth to Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, "Send me on my way, so that I can go back to my own home and country.
Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have worked for you, and let me go. You know how much work I have done for you."
Laban said to him, "If I have found favour with you, please stay. I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.
Name your wages, and I will pay them."
Jacob said to him, "You know how I have worked for you, and how your livestock has fared under my care.
The little you had before I came has grown to a great deal, and the LORD has blessed you wherever I have been. But now, when may I provide for my own household as well?"
"What shall I give you?" he asked. Jacob said, "You do not have to give me anything. If you will do this one thing for me, I will go on tending and keeping your flocks:
let me go through all your flocks today and remove from them every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-coloured lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat. These will be my wages.

My honesty will testify for me in the future, whenever you come to check on my wages. Any goat that is not speckled or spotted, and any lamb that is not dark, if it is found with me, will count as stolen."
"Agreed," said Laban. "Let it be as you say."

That same day Laban removed the male goats that were streaked or spotted, and all the female goats that were speckled or spotted, every one with white on it, and all the dark lambs, and put them in the care of his sons.
Then he put a three-day journey between himself and Jacob, while Jacob went on tending the rest of Laban's flocks.
Jacob took fresh branches of poplar, almond and plane trees, and peeled white strips in them, exposing the white inner wood.
He set the peeled branches in front of the flocks, in the troughs, the watering places where the flocks came to drink. When they came to drink, the flocks mated,
and they mated in front of the branches, and so they bore young that were streaked, speckled and spotted.
Jacob set the lambs apart, and made the flocks face the streaked and dark animals in Laban's flock. He kept his own animals separate, and did not put them with Laban's flock.
Whenever the stronger animals were mating, Jacob would place the branches in the troughs in full view of the flock, so that they would mate among the branches,
but when the animals were weak, he did not put them there. So the weak animals went to Laban, and the strong to Jacob.
In this way the man grew exceedingly rich, and had large flocks, and female and male servants, and camels and donkeys.
Jacob heard that Laban's sons were saying, "Jacob has taken everything that belonged to our father, and out of our father's property he has made all this wealth for himself."
Jacob also noticed that Laban's attitude towards him was not what it had been before.
Then the LORD said to Jacob, "Go back to the land of your fathers and to your relatives, and I will be with you."
So Jacob sent word and called Rachel and Leah out to the field where his flock was.
He said to them, "I can see that your father's attitude towards me is not what it was, but the God of my father has been with me.
You know that I have served your father with all my strength,
yet your father has cheated me and changed my wages ten times. But God did not let him harm me.
If he said, 'The speckled animals will be your wages,' then the whole flock bore speckled young; and if he said, 'The streaked ones will be your wages,' then the whole flock bore streaked young.
So God has taken your father's livestock and given it to me.
Once, at the time when the flocks were mating, I looked up in a dream and saw that the male goats mating with the flock were streaked, speckled and spotted.
The angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob.' I answered, 'Here I am.'
He said, 'Look up and see that all the male goats mating with the flock are streaked, speckled and spotted, for I have seen all that Laban has been doing to you.
I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar and made a vow to me. Now get up, leave this land, and go back to the land of your birth.'"
Rachel and Leah answered him, "Do we still have any share or inheritance in our father's house?
Does he not treat us as foreigners? He has sold us, and has used up the money paid for us.
All the wealth that God took from our father belongs to us and to our children. So do whatever God has told you."
Then Jacob put his children and his wives on camels,
and he drove all his livestock before him, with all the property he had gathered in Paddan-aram, to go to his father Isaac in the land of Canaan.
Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole her father's household gods.
And Jacob deceived Laban the Aramean by not telling him that he was running away.
He fled with all that he had. He crossed the river Euphrates and headed for the hill country of Gilead.
On the third day Laban was told that Jacob had fled.
He took his relatives with him and pursued Jacob for seven days, and caught up with him in the hill country of Gilead.
But God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream by night and said to him, "Take care that you say nothing to Jacob, good or bad."
Laban caught up with Jacob. Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban and his relatives pitched theirs in the hill country of Gilead.
Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done? You have deceived me, and carried off my daughters like prisoners of war.
Why did you run away in secret and deceive me? Why did you not tell me, so that I could send you off with joy and singing, with tambourine and lyre?
You did not even let me kiss my grandchildren and my daughters goodbye. What you have done is foolish.
I have the power to do you harm, but last night the God of your father said to me, 'Take care that you say nothing to Jacob, good or bad.'
Now you have left because you were so homesick for your father's house. But why did you steal my gods?"
Jacob answered Laban, "I was afraid, because I thought you would take your daughters from me by force.

But if you find your gods with anyone here, that person will not live. In the presence of our relatives, see for yourself whether anything of yours is here with me, and take it." Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen the gods.
So Laban went into Jacob's tent, then into Leah's tent, then into the tent of the two female servants, but he found nothing. Leaving Leah's tent, he entered Rachel's.
Rachel had taken the household gods and put them in the camel's saddle, and she was sitting on them. Laban searched through the whole tent but found nothing.
Rachel said to her father, "Do not be angry, my lord, that I cannot stand up before you. I am having my monthly period." So he searched, but he could not find the household gods.
Jacob was angry, and he challenged Laban. "What is my offence?" he demanded. "What wrong have I done, that you hunt me down like this?
You have searched through all my belongings. What have you found that belongs to your household? Set it here before my relatives and yours, and let them decide between us.
For twenty years I have been with you. Your ewes and your female goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your flocks.
I did not bring you any animal torn by wild beasts; I bore the loss myself. And you demanded payment from me for anything stolen, whether by day or by night.
This is how it was with me: the heat consumed me by day and the frost by night, and sleep fled from my eyes.
For twenty years I have lived in your house. I worked fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flock, and you changed my wages ten times.

If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with me, you would surely have sent me away empty-handed. But God saw my hardship and the labour of my hands, and last night he gave his verdict."

Laban answered Jacob, "The women are my daughters, the children are my children, and the flocks are my flocks. All that you see is mine. Yet what can I do today about these daughters of mine, or about the children they have borne?
Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it be a witness between us."
So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.
He said to his relatives, "Gather stones." They took stones and made a heap, and they ate there beside the heap.
Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, and Jacob called it Galeed.
Laban said, "This heap is a witness between you and me today." That is why it was named Galeed.
It was also called Mizpah, because he said, "May the LORD keep watch between you and me when we are out of each other's sight.
If you ill-treat my daughters, or take other wives besides my daughters, though no one is with us, remember that God is witness between you and me."
Laban also said to Jacob, "Here is this heap, and here is the pillar that I have set up between you and me.
This heap is a witness, and this pillar is a witness, that I will not cross this heap to harm you, and that you will not cross this heap and this pillar to harm me.
May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us." So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
He offered a sacrifice there in the hill country and invited his relatives to a meal. They ate, and spent the night in the hills.
Early the next morning Laban kissed his grandchildren and his daughters and blessed them. Then he left and returned home.
Jacob went on his way, and angels of God met him.
When Jacob saw them he said, "This is God's camp!" So he named that place Mahanaim.
Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, the country of Edom.
He gave them these instructions: "This is what you are to say to my lord Esau: 'Your servant Jacob says, I have been living with Laban and have stayed there until now.
I own cattle, donkeys, flocks, and male and female servants. I am sending word to my lord, hoping to find favour in your eyes.'"
The messengers came back to Jacob and said, "We went to your brother Esau, and now he is coming to meet you, with four hundred men."
Jacob was very afraid and distressed. He divided the people with him, and the flocks and herds and camels, into two camps,
thinking, "If Esau comes and attacks one camp, the other camp may escape."
Jacob prayed, "God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac, LORD, you said to me, 'Go back to your country and your relatives, and I will make you prosper.'
I am not worthy of all the faithful love and truth you have shown to your servant. I crossed this Jordan with only my staff, and now I have become two camps.
Rescue me, I pray, from my brother Esau, for I am afraid of him. He may come and strike me down, the mothers along with their children.
But you said, 'I will make you prosper, and I will make your descendants like the sand of the sea, too many to count.'"
He spent the night there, and from what he had with him he chose a gift for his brother Esau:
two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,
thirty milking camels with their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys.
He handed them over to his servants, each herd by itself, and said to his servants, "Go on ahead of me, and leave a space between one herd and the next."
He told the first one: "When my brother Esau meets you and asks, 'Who is your master, where are you going, and whose are these animals ahead of you?'
you are to say, 'They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift sent to my lord Esau, and he is coming behind us.'"
He gave the same instructions to the second, the third and all who followed the herds: "This is what you are to say to Esau when you meet him.
And you are to say, 'Your servant Jacob is right behind us.'" For he thought, "I will appease him with the gift that goes ahead of me. Then, when I see him face to face, perhaps he will welcome me."
So the gift went on ahead of him, while he himself spent that night in the camp.
That night he got up and took his two wives, his two female servants and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them and sent them across the stream, and sent over all that he had.
Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until daybreak.
When the man saw that he could not overcome him, he struck the socket of Jacob's hip, so that Jacob's hip was wrenched as he wrestled with him.
Then he said, "Let me go, for day is breaking." But Jacob said, "I will not let you go unless you bless me."
The man asked him, "What is your name?" "Jacob," he answered.
Then the man said, "Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with human beings, and have prevailed."
Jacob asked, "Please tell me your name." But he said, "Why do you ask my name?" And there he blessed him.
Jacob named the place Peniel, saying, "I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been spared."
The sun rose as he passed Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip.
That is why to this day the Israelites do not eat the sinew of the thigh that is on the hip socket, because the man struck Jacob's hip socket at the sinew.
Jacob looked up and saw Esau coming, with four hundred men. So he divided the children among Leah, Rachel and the two female servants.
He put the servants with their children first, then Leah with her children, and Rachel and Joseph last.
He himself went on ahead of them, and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother.
But Esau ran to meet him and embraced him. He threw his arms around his neck and kissed him, and they both wept.
Esau looked up and saw the women and children. "Who are these with you?" he asked. Jacob answered, "They are the children God has graciously given to your servant."
Then the servants came near with their children, and they bowed down.
Leah also came near with her children, and they bowed down. Last of all came Joseph and Rachel, and they too bowed down.
Esau asked, "What was the meaning of all those herds I met?" "To find favour in your eyes, my lord," he said.
But Esau said, "I have plenty, my brother. Keep what you have."
"No, please," said Jacob. "If I have found favour in your eyes, accept my gift. To see your face is like seeing the face of God, now that you have received me so kindly.
Please accept the gift I brought you, for God has been gracious to me, and I have all that I need." And because he insisted, Esau accepted.
Then Esau said, "Let us be on our way. I will go ahead of you."
But Jacob said to him, "My lord knows that the children are weak, and that I have to care for the nursing ewes and cows. If they are driven hard for even one day, all the animals will die.
Let my lord go on ahead of his servant, and I will move along slowly, at the pace of the livestock ahead of me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my lord in Seir."
Esau said, "Then let me leave some of my men with you." "Why do that?" Jacob asked. "Just let me find favour with my lord."
So that day Esau started back on his way to Seir.
But Jacob went on to Succoth, where he built a house for himself and made shelters for his livestock. That is why the place is called Succoth.
After Jacob came from Paddan-aram, he arrived safely at the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan, and he camped within sight of the city.
For a hundred pieces of silver he bought from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, the piece of land where he had pitched his tent.
There he set up an altar and called it El-elohe-israel.
Dinah, the daughter Leah had borne to Jacob, went out to visit the women of the land.
When Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of that region, saw her, he seized her and raped her.
His heart was drawn to Dinah daughter of Jacob. He loved the young woman, and spoke tenderly to her.
Shechem said to his father Hamor, "Get me this girl as my wife."
Jacob heard that he had defiled his daughter Dinah, but his sons were out in the fields with his livestock, so Jacob said nothing until they came home.
Then Shechem's father Hamor went out to Jacob to speak with him.

Meanwhile Jacob's sons had come in from the field when they heard the news. The men were deeply grieved and furious, because Shechem had committed an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter, a thing that must not be done.
But Hamor said to them, "My son Shechem's heart is set on your daughter. Please give her to him as his wife.
Intermarry with us. Give us your daughters, and take our daughters for yourselves.
You can live among us, and the land will be open to you. Settle in it, trade in it and acquire property in it."
Shechem said to Dinah's father and brothers, "Let me find favour with you, and I will give whatever you ask.
Set the bride-price and gift as high as you like, and I will pay what you ask. Only give me the young woman as my wife."
Jacob's sons replied deceitfully to Shechem and his father Hamor, because he had defiled their sister Dinah.
They said to them, "We cannot do this thing, to give our sister to a man who is uncircumcised, for that would be a disgrace to us.
We will agree to your request on one condition only: that you become like us by circumcising every male among you.
Then we will give you our daughters and take your daughters for ourselves, and we will live among you and become one people.
But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, we will take our sister and go."
Their proposal pleased Hamor and his son Shechem.
The young man lost no time in doing what they asked, because he was delighted with Jacob's daughter. He was the most respected man in his family.
So Hamor and his son Shechem went to the gate of their city and spoke to the men of the city:
"These men are friendly towards us. Let them live in the land and trade in it, for the land is wide enough for them. We can marry their daughters and give them ours.
But the men will agree to live with us as one people only on this condition: that every male among us be circumcised, as they are.
Will not their livestock, their property and all their animals become ours? Let us only agree to their terms, and they will settle among us."
All who went out of the city gate listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male was circumcised, all who went out of the city gate.
On the third day, while they were still in pain, two of Jacob's sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, took their swords and attacked the unsuspecting city, and killed every male.
They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword, took Dinah out of Shechem's house, and left.
Jacob's other sons came upon the dead and plundered the city, because their sister had been defiled.
They seized their flocks and herds and donkeys, and everything in the city and in the fields.
They carried off all their wealth, all their children and their wives, and everything in the houses.

Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, "You have brought trouble on me, making me a stench to the people of this land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. We are few in number, and if they join forces against me and attack, I and my household will be destroyed."
But they answered, "Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?"
God said to Jacob, "Get up, go up to Bethel and live there. Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from your brother Esau."
So Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, "Get rid of the foreign gods you have with you. Purify yourselves and change your clothes.
Then let us get up and go to Bethel, where I will make an altar to the God who answered me in the day of my distress and has been with me wherever I have gone."
So they handed over to Jacob all the foreign gods they had, and the rings in their ears, and Jacob buried them under the oak near Shechem.
As they set out, a terror from God fell on the towns around them, so that no one pursued the sons of Jacob.
Jacob and all the people with him came to Luz, that is Bethel, in the land of Canaan.
There he built an altar and called the place El-bethel, because it was there that God had revealed himself to him when he was fleeing from his brother.
Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and she was buried below Bethel under the oak. So it was named Allon-bacuth.
After Jacob came back from Paddan-aram, God appeared to him again and blessed him.
God said to him, "Your name is Jacob. You will no longer be called Jacob. Israel will be your name." So he named him Israel.
God said to him, "I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation, a community of nations, will come from you, and kings will be among your descendants.
The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I give to you, and to your descendants after you I will give the land."
Then God went up from him, from the place where he had spoken with him.
Jacob set up a pillar in the place where God had spoken with him, a pillar of stone. He poured a drink offering on it and poured oil over it.
Jacob named the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
They set out from Bethel. When they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel went into labour, and her labour was hard.
When her labour was at its worst, the midwife said to her, "Do not be afraid. You have another son."
As she breathed her last, for she was dying, she named him Ben-oni, but his father named him Benjamin.
So Rachel died, and she was buried on the road to Ephrath, that is Bethlehem.
Jacob set up a pillar over her grave. It is the pillar of Rachel's grave to this day.
Israel moved on and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder.
While Israel was living in that region, Reuben went and slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel heard of it. Jacob had twelve sons.
The sons of Leah: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, then Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
The sons of Rachel's servant Bilhah: Dan and Naphtali.
The sons of Leah's servant Zilpah: Gad and Asher. These were the sons of Jacob, born to him in Paddan-aram.
Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath-arba, that is Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac had lived as foreigners.
Isaac lived 180 years.
Isaac breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people, old and full of years. His sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
This is the record of the descendants of Esau, that is, Edom.
Esau took his wives from the Canaanite women: Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah daughter of Anah, the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite,
and Basemath daughter of Ishmael, sister of Nebaioth.
Adah bore Eliphaz to Esau; Basemath bore Reuel;
and Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam and Korah. These were Esau's sons, born to him in the land of Canaan.

Esau took his wives, his sons and daughters, and all the members of his household, his livestock and all his animals, and all the property he had acquired in Canaan, and moved to a land away from his brother Jacob.
Their possessions were too great for them to live together. The land where they were staying could not support them both because of their livestock.
So Esau, that is Edom, settled in the hill country of Seir.
This is the record of the descendants of Esau, the father of the Edomites, in the hill country of Seir.
These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz, son of Esau's wife Adah, and Reuel, son of Esau's wife Basemath.
The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz.
Timna was a concubine of Esau's son Eliphaz, and she bore Amalek to Eliphaz. These were the descendants of Esau's wife Adah.
The sons of Reuel were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. These were the descendants of Esau's wife Basemath.
The sons of Esau's wife Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon, were Jeush, Jalam and Korah, whom she bore to Esau.
These are the chiefs among the descendants of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn: the chiefs Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz,
Korah, Gatam and Amalek. These are the chiefs descended from Eliphaz in the land of Edom; they are the sons of Adah.
The sons of Esau's son Reuel: the chiefs Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. These are the chiefs descended from Reuel in the land of Edom; they are the sons of Esau's wife Basemath.
The sons of Esau's wife Oholibamah: the chiefs Jeush, Jalam and Korah. These are the chiefs descended from Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, Esau's wife.
These are the sons of Esau, that is Edom, and these are their chiefs.
These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who lived in that land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir, in the land of Edom.
The sons of Lotan were Hori and Heman, and Lotan's sister was Timna.
The sons of Shobal were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho and Onam.
The sons of Zibeon were Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness while he was pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon.
The children of Anah were Dishon and Oholibamah, daughter of Anah.
The sons of Dishon were Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran and Keran.
The sons of Ezer were Bilhan, Zaavan and Akan.
The sons of Dishan were Uz and Aran.
These are the chiefs of the Horites: the chiefs Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, clan by clan, in the land of Seir.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites:
Bela son of Beor was king in Edom, and the name of his city was Dinhabah.
When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah of Bozrah became king in his place.
When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites became king in his place.
When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, became king in his place. The name of his city was Avith.
When Hadad died, Samlah of Masrekah became king in his place.
When Samlah died, Shaul of Rehoboth on the river became king in his place.
When Shaul died, Baal-hanan son of Achbor became king in his place.
When Baal-hanan son of Achbor died, Hadar became king in his place. The name of his city was Pau, and his wife's name was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab.
These are the names of the chiefs of Esau, by their clans and regions, by name: the chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth,
Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon,
Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar,
Magdiel and Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, by their settlements in the land they held. This is Esau, the father of the Edomites.
Jacob settled in the land of Canaan, where his father had lived as a resident foreigner.

This is the account of Jacob's family. Joseph, a young man of seventeen, was shepherding the flock with his brothers. He was working with the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father's wives, and he brought their father a damaging report about them.
Israel loved Joseph more than all his other sons, for Joseph was the child of his old age, and he had a long-sleeved tunic made for him.
When his brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.
Joseph dreamed a dream, and when he told it to his brothers, they hated him all the more.
He said to them, "Please listen to this dream I dreamed.
We were out in the field tying up sheaves, and my sheaf stood up and remained upright, and your sheaves gathered round and bowed down to it."
His brothers said to him, "So you will be king over us? You will really rule us?" And they hated him still more for his dreams and for what he said.
He dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers: "Look, I have dreamed again. The sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me."

He told it to his father as well as his brothers, and his father rebuked him: "What is this dream you have dreamed? Will I and your mother and your brothers actually come and bow ourselves to the ground before you?"
His brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the saying in mind.
His brothers went to pasture their father's flock at Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, "Your brothers are pasturing the flock at Shechem. Come, I will send you to them." He said, "Here I am."
"Go," he said, "see how your brothers are and how the flock is, and bring me word." So he sent him from the valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.
A man found him wandering in the countryside and asked him, "What are you looking for?"
"I am looking for my brothers," he said. "Tell me, please, where they are pasturing the flock."
The man said, "They have gone from here. I heard them say, 'Let us go to Dothan.'" So Joseph went after his brothers and found them in Dothan.
They saw him from far off, and before he reached them they plotted to put him to death.
They said to each other, "Here comes that master dreamer.
Come on, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits, and we will say that a wild animal ate him. Then we will see what becomes of his dreams."
Reuben heard this and rescued him from their hands, saying, "Let us not strike him dead."
Reuben said to them, "Do not shed blood. Throw him into this pit in the wilderness, but lay no hand on him." He meant to save him from them and bring him back to his father.
When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his tunic, the long-sleeved tunic he was wearing,
and took him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty, with no water in it.
Then they sat down to eat. When they looked up, there was a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, their camels carrying gum, balm and resin, on their way down to Egypt.
Judah said to his brothers, "What profit is there in killing our brother and covering up his blood?
Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let our hands not be on him, for he is our brother, our own flesh." His brothers listened.
Midianite traders passed by. They drew Joseph up and lifted him out of the pit, and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty silver pieces, and they brought Joseph to Egypt.
Reuben came back to the pit, and there was no Joseph in it. He tore his clothes,
went back to his brothers and said, "The boy is not there! And I, where am I to go?"
They took Joseph's tunic, slaughtered a he-goat, and dipped the tunic in the blood.
They sent the long-sleeved tunic and had it brought to their father, and said, "We found this. Please examine it: is it your son's tunic or not?"
He examined it and said, "It is my son's tunic. A wild animal has eaten him. Joseph has certainly been torn apart."
Jacob tore his garments, put sackcloth round his waist, and mourned for his son many days.
All his sons and daughters rose to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. "No," he said, "I will go down to Sheol to my son, mourning." So his father wept for him.
The Midianites sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard.
About that time Judah went down from his brothers and pitched his tent near an Adullamite named Hirah.
There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite named Shua, and he married her and went in to her.
She conceived and bore a son, and he named him Er.
She conceived again and bore a son, and she named him Onan.
Once more she bore a son, and she named him Shelah. It was at Chezib that she bore him.
Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn. Her name was Tamar.
But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD took his life.
Judah said to Onan, "Go in to your brother's wife, perform your duty as her husband's brother, and raise up offspring for your brother."
But Onan knew that the offspring would not be his own. So whenever he went in to his brother's wife, he wasted his seed on the ground, so as not to give offspring to his brother.
What he did was evil in the sight of the LORD, and he took his life also.

Then Judah said to his daughter-in-law Tamar, "Remain a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah is grown." For he thought, "He too might die, like his brothers." So Tamar went and lived in her father's house.
A long time passed, and Judah's wife, Shua's daughter, died. When Judah's mourning was over, he went up to his sheepshearers at Timnah, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite.
Tamar was told, "Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep."

She took off her widow's clothes, covered herself with a veil, wrapped herself up, and sat at the entrance to Enaim, on the road to Timnah, for she saw that Shelah was grown up, yet she had not been given to him as a wife.
Judah saw her and took her for a prostitute, because she had covered her face.
He turned aside to her by the road and said, "Come, let me go in to you," for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She said, "What will you give me, if you come in to me?"
He said, "I will send you a kid from the flock." She said, "Only if you give me a pledge until you send it."
He said, "What pledge should I give you?" She said, "Your seal, your cord and the staff in your hand." He gave them to her and went in to her, and she conceived by him.
She got up and went away, took off her veil and put on her widow's clothes.
Judah sent the kid by his friend the Adullamite to recover the pledge from the woman, but he did not find her.
He asked the men of her place, "Where is the cult woman who was at Enaim, by the road?" They said, "There has been no cult woman here."
So he returned to Judah and said, "I did not find her. The men of the place also said, 'There has been no cult woman here.'"
Judah said, "Let her keep them, or we will be laughed at. I did send this kid, and you did not find her."
About three months later Judah was told, "Your daughter-in-law Tamar has behaved like a prostitute, and she is pregnant as a result." Judah said, "Bring her out, and let her be burned."
As she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law: "I am pregnant by the man to whom these belong." And she said, "Please identify whose seal and cord and staff these are."
Judah identified them and said, "She is more in the right than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah." And he did not lie with her again.
When the time came for her to give birth, there were twins in her womb.
While she was giving birth, one put out a hand, and the midwife took a scarlet thread and tied it on his hand, saying, "This one came out first."
But as he drew back his hand, his brother came out, and she said, "What a breach you have made for yourself!" So he was named Perez.
Afterwards his brother came out, with the scarlet thread on his hand, and he was named Zerah.
Joseph had been taken down to Egypt. Potiphar, an Egyptian officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had taken him there.
The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a man who prospered, and he lived in the house of his Egyptian master.
His master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD made everything he did prosper in his hands.
So Joseph found favour with him and became his personal servant. He made him overseer of his house and put everything he owned in his charge.

From the time he made him overseer in his house and over all that he owned, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake. The LORD's blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field.
He left all that he had in Joseph's hands and, with Joseph there, concerned himself with nothing but the food he ate. Joseph was handsome in form and handsome in appearance.
After these events, his master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, "Lie with me."
He refused. He said to his master's wife, "Look, with me here my master does not concern himself with anything in the house, and he has put all that he owns in my hands.
No one in this house is greater than I am, and he has kept nothing back from me except you, because you are his wife. How then could I do this great evil and sin against God?"
Though she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her, to lie beside her or to be with her.
One day he went into the house to do his work, and none of the household was there inside.
She grabbed his garment, saying, "Lie with me." But he left his garment in her hand, and fled and ran outside.
When she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and had fled outside,
she called to the people of her household and said to them, "Look, he has brought a Hebrew man in to us to mock us. He came in to me to lie with me, and I screamed loudly.
When he heard that I raised my voice and screamed, he left his garment beside me and fled outside."
She kept his garment beside her until his master came home.
Then she told him the same story: "The Hebrew servant whom you brought to us came in to me to mock me.
But when I raised my voice and screamed, he left his garment beside me and fled outside."
When his master heard the words his wife spoke to him, "This is what your servant did to me," his anger was kindled.
Joseph's master took him and put him in the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were confined, and he was there in the prison.
But the LORD was with Joseph and extended faithful love to him, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison.
The keeper of the prison put all the prisoners who were in the prison in Joseph's care, and whatever was done there, he was the one who did it.
The keeper of the prison did not look into anything that was in his care, because the LORD was with Joseph, and whatever he did, the LORD made it prosper.
Some time afterwards, the royal cupbearer and the royal baker of Egypt gave offence to their master, the king of Egypt.
Pharaoh was enraged at his two officers, the chief of the cupbearers and the chief of the bakers,
and had them placed under guard in the house of the captain of the guard, in the same prison where Joseph was held.
The captain of the guard put Joseph in charge of them, and he attended to their needs. They remained in custody for a time.
One night the two of them, the king of Egypt's cupbearer and baker, who were held in the prison, each dreamed a dream, and each dream had a meaning of its own.
Joseph came to them in the morning and saw that they were downcast.
He asked Pharaoh's officers, who were with him in custody in his master's house, "Why are your faces so gloomy today?"
"We have each had a dream," they said, "and there is no one to explain it." Joseph said to them, "Does explaining dreams not belong to God? Tell me, please."
The chief cupbearer told his dream to Joseph. "In my dream," he said, "a vine stood in front of me.
The vine had three tendrils. It budded, its blossoms opened, and its clusters ripened into grapes.
Pharaoh's cup was in my hand. I picked the grapes, pressed them into Pharaoh's cup, and placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand."
Joseph said to him, "Here is the meaning: the three tendrils are three days.
In three more days Pharaoh will raise your head and return you to your post, and you will put Pharaoh's cup in his hand as you did before, when you were his cupbearer.
But if you remember me when it goes well with you, I beg you, show me kindness and speak of me to Pharaoh, and so bring me out of this house.
I was stolen from the land of the Hebrews, and even here I have done nothing to deserve being put in the pit."
When the chief baker saw that the meaning was good, he said to Joseph, "I too had a dream: three baskets of white bread were on my head.
In the top basket was every kind of baked food for Pharaoh, and birds were eating it from the basket on my head."
Joseph answered, "Here is the meaning: the three baskets are three days.
In three more days Pharaoh will raise your head off you and hang you on a pole, and the birds will eat your flesh from you."
On the third day, Pharaoh's birthday, he held a feast for all his servants, and he raised the heads of the chief cupbearer and the chief baker among them.
He returned the chief cupbearer to his post, and he placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand,
but the chief baker he hanged, just as Joseph had explained to them.
The chief cupbearer, however, did not think of Joseph again. He forgot him.
Two years later Pharaoh dreamed that he was standing beside the Nile.
Seven cows came up out of the river, healthy-looking and fat, and began to feed in the reed-grass.
Behind them seven other cows came up out of the Nile, ugly and gaunt, and stood next to the first cows on the riverbank.
Then the ugly, gaunt cows devoured the seven healthy, fat cows. And Pharaoh woke.
He slept again and dreamed a second time: seven ears of grain, plump and good, were growing on one stalk.
Then seven ears, thin and scorched by the east wind, sprouted behind them.
The thin ears swallowed up the seven plump, full ears. Pharaoh woke, and realised it was a dream.
In the morning his mind was disturbed, and he summoned all the diviner-priests of Egypt and all its wise men. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but no one could explain them to him.
Then the chief cupbearer spoke up to Pharaoh: "I must today recall my own failing.
Pharaoh was once furious with his servants and put me under guard in the house of the captain of the guard, together with the chief baker.
On a single night he and I each had a dream, and each dream had its own meaning.
With us there was a young Hebrew, a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams, and he explained them to us, each according to his dream.
And it happened exactly as he had explained: I was returned to my post, and the other man was hanged."
Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and they brought him quickly out of the dungeon. He shaved, changed his clothes, and came before Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I have had a dream, and there is no one to explain it. But I have heard it said of you that you need only hear a dream to explain it."
Joseph answered Pharaoh, "That is not in my power. It is God who will give Pharaoh a reassuring answer."
Pharaoh told Joseph, "In my dream I was standing on the bank of the Nile.
Seven cows came up out of the river, fat and healthy, and fed in the reed-grass.
Then seven other cows came up behind them, wretched, very ugly and emaciated. I have never seen cows so bad-looking in all the land of Egypt.
The emaciated, ugly cows devoured the first seven fat cows.
They went into their bellies, but no one could have told it, for they looked as ugly as before. Then I woke.
In another dream I saw seven ears of grain growing on a single stalk, full and good.
Seven other ears sprouted behind them, withered, thin and scorched by the east wind.
The thin ears swallowed up the seven good ears. I told this to the diviner-priests, but none could explain it to me."
Joseph said to Pharaoh, "Pharaoh's two dreams are a single dream. God has told Pharaoh what he is about to do.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years. It is one dream.
The seven emaciated, ugly cows that came up after them are seven years, as are the seven empty ears scorched by the east wind. They are seven years of famine.
This is what I meant when I told Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.
Seven years are coming of great abundance across the whole land of Egypt.
After them will follow seven years of famine, and all the abundance will be forgotten in the land of Egypt. The famine will devour the land.
The abundance will be forgotten in the land because the famine that follows will be so heavy.
As for the dream being doubled for Pharaoh, it means that the matter is firmly fixed by God, and God is about to carry it out.
So now, let Pharaoh find a man who is discerning and wise, and put him in charge of the land of Egypt.
Let Pharaoh act, and appoint officials over the land, to take one fifth of Egypt's produce during the seven years of abundance.
Let them collect all the food of these good years that are coming and store the grain in the cities under Pharaoh's authority, to be guarded as food.
That food will be a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine that will come on Egypt, so that the land is not destroyed by the famine."
This advice pleased Pharaoh and all his officials.
Pharaoh said to his officials, "Could we find anyone like this man, who has the spirit of God in him?"
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has made all this known to you, there is no one as discerning and wise as you.
You will be in charge of my household, and all my people will do as you command. Only the throne will make me greater than you."
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Look, I am placing you in charge of the whole land of Egypt."
Pharaoh took off his signet ring and put it on Joseph's finger. He had him dressed in fine linen and hung a gold chain round his neck.
He had him ride in the chariot of his deputy, and men cried before him, "Bow down!" Thus he placed him over the whole land of Egypt.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh; yet without your leave no one in all Egypt will raise a hand or a foot."
Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah, and gave him Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, as his wife. And Joseph set out to tour the land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt. He left Pharaoh's presence and travelled the length of Egypt.
During the seven years of abundance the land yielded in handfuls.
He gathered all the food of those seven years in the land of Egypt, and stored it in the cities, placing in each city the food from the fields around it.
Joseph heaped up grain like the sand of the sea, so much that he stopped counting, for it could not be counted.
Before the years of famine arrived, two sons were born to Joseph, by Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh, "because," he said, "God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father's house."
The second he named Ephraim, "because God has made me fruitful in the land of my suffering."
The seven years of abundance in Egypt came to an end,
and the seven years of famine began, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in every country, but in the whole land of Egypt there was bread.
When the whole land of Egypt began to go hungry, the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread. Pharaoh told all the Egyptians, "Go to Joseph, and do whatever he tells you."
The famine spread across the whole land, and Joseph opened the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians, for the famine was heavy in Egypt.
People from every country came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, because the famine was heavy over the whole earth.
Jacob learned that there was grain to be had in Egypt, and he said to his sons, "Why do you keep staring at one another?
I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down and buy some there for us, so that we may live and not die."
So ten of Joseph's brothers went down to buy grain in Egypt.
But Jacob did not send Joseph's brother Benjamin with the others, for he said, "Some harm may come to him."
So the sons of Israel were among those who came to buy grain, because the famine had reached the land of Canaan.
Joseph was the one in authority over the land, the one who sold grain to all its people. When Joseph's brothers came, they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground.
Joseph saw his brothers and knew them, but he made himself a stranger to them and spoke roughly. "Where have you come from?" he asked. "From the land of Canaan," they said, "to buy food."
Joseph knew his brothers, but they did not know him.
Joseph remembered the dreams he had dreamed about them. He said to them, "You are spies. You have come to find out where our land is weak."
"No, my lord," they said. "Your servants have come to buy food.
We are all sons of one man. We are honest men. Your servants are not spies."
"No," he said. "You have come to find out where our land is weak."
They said, "There were twelve of us, your servants, brothers, sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is with our father at present, and one is gone."
Joseph said to them, "It is as I said to you: you are spies.
This is how you will be tested. As Pharaoh lives, you will not leave this place unless your youngest brother comes here.
Send one of you to fetch your brother. The rest of you will stay in prison, so that your words can be tested to see whether there is truth in you. If not, then as Pharaoh lives, you are spies."
And he put them all in custody together for three days.
On the third day Joseph said to them, "Do this and you will live, for I fear God.
If you are honest men, let one of your brothers be held in your prison, while the rest of you go and carry grain home for your hungry households.
Then bring your youngest brother to me, so that your words may be proved true and you will not die." And they agreed.
They said to one another, "We are paying for what we did to our brother. We saw his anguish when he begged us, and we would not listen. That is why this trouble has come to us."
Reuben answered them, "Did I not tell you, 'Do not wrong the boy'? But you would not listen. Now we are called to account for his blood."
They did not know that Joseph understood them, because there was an interpreter between them.
He turned away from them and wept. Then he came back and spoke to them. He took Simeon from among them and had him bound before their eyes.
Joseph gave orders to fill their containers with grain, to return each man's silver to his sack, and to give them supplies for the journey. This was done for them.
They loaded their grain on their donkeys and set out.
At the lodging place, one of them opened his sack to give fodder to his donkey, and he saw his silver there at the mouth of his sack.
He said to his brothers, "My silver has been put back! Here it is, in my sack." Their hearts failed them, and they turned to one another, trembling. "What is this that God has done to us?"
When they came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan, they told him everything that had happened to them:
"The man who is lord of the land spoke roughly to us and took us for spies on the land.
We told him, 'We are honest men. We are not spies.
There were twelve of us, brothers, sons of our father. One is gone, and the youngest is with our father now in the land of Canaan.'
Then the man who is lord of the land said to us, 'This is how I will know whether you are honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, take grain for your hungry households, and go.
Bring your youngest brother to me, and I will know that you are not spies but honest men. Then I will give your brother back to you, and you may trade in the land.'"
As they emptied their sacks, there in each man's sack was his bundle of silver. When they and their father saw the bundles of silver, they were afraid.
Their father Jacob said to them, "You are making me childless. Joseph is gone, and Simeon is gone, and now you would take Benjamin. All this is against me."
Reuben said to his father, "You may kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you. Put him in my care, and I will bring him back."
But he said, "My son will not go down with you. His brother is dead, and he alone is left. If harm comes to him on the journey you are making, you will bring my grey head down to Sheol in sorrow."
The famine was heavy in the land.
When they had eaten all the grain they had brought from Egypt, their father said to them, "Go back and buy us a little more food."
But Judah said to him, "The man solemnly warned us, 'You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.'
If you will send our brother with us, we will go down and buy food for you.
But if you will not send him, we will not go down, because the man said to us, 'You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.'"
Israel said, "Why did you bring this trouble on me by telling the man that you had another brother?"

They replied, "The man questioned us closely about ourselves and our family. 'Is your father still alive?' he asked. 'Do you have another brother?' We answered his questions. How could we know that he would say, 'Bring your brother down'?"
Judah said to Israel his father, "Send the boy with me, and we will go at once, so that we may live and not die, we and you and our little ones.
I myself will be surety for him. You may hold me responsible. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, let me bear the blame all my life.
If we had not delayed, we could have gone and come back twice by now."

Their father Israel said to them, "If it must be so, then do this: put some of the best products of the land in your bags, and take them down to the man as a gift: a little balm and a little honey, gum and resin, pistachio nuts and almonds.
Take double the amount of silver with you, and carry back the silver that was returned in the mouths of your sacks. Perhaps it was a mistake.
Take your brother also, and go back to the man.
May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, so that he will release your other brother and Benjamin. As for me, if I am to be bereaved, I am bereaved."
So the men took the gift, and they took double the silver with them, and Benjamin. They set out and went down to Egypt and stood before Joseph.
When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the steward of his house, "Bring the men into the house, slaughter an animal and prepare a meal, for the men will eat with me at noon."
The man did as Joseph said and brought the men to Joseph's house.

The men were frightened when they were brought to Joseph's house. They said, "It is because of the silver that was put back in our sacks the first time that we are being brought in, so that he can fall upon us, overpower us and take us as slaves, with our donkeys."
So they went up to Joseph's steward and spoke to him at the entrance of the house.
"Please, my lord," they said, "we came down once before to buy food.
But at the lodging place, when we opened our sacks, there was each man's silver, the full weight, in the mouth of his sack. We have brought it back with us.
We have also brought more silver with us to buy food. We do not know who put our silver in our sacks."
"Be at peace," he said. "Do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your father has put treasure in your sacks for you. I received your silver." Then he brought Simeon out to them.
The steward brought the men into Joseph's house, gave them water to wash their feet, and gave fodder to their donkeys.
They prepared the gift for Joseph's coming at noon, because they had heard that they would eat a meal there.
When Joseph came home, they brought him the gift that they had brought into the house, and bowed down to the ground before him.
He asked how they were, and said, "Is your father well, the old man you told me about? Is he still alive?"
They said, "Your servant our father is well. He is still alive." And they bowed down and paid him honour.
He looked up and saw his brother Benjamin, his mother's son, and said, "Is this your youngest brother, of whom you spoke to me? God be gracious to you, my son."
Joseph hurried out, for he was overcome with feeling for his brother, and he looked for a place to weep. He went into his room and wept there.
Then he washed his face and came out. He controlled himself and said, "Serve the meal."
They served him by himself, and them by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves, because Egyptians could not eat with Hebrews, for that is detestable to Egyptians.
They were seated before him in order of age, from the firstborn to the youngest, and they looked at one another in amazement.
Portions were taken to them from Joseph's table, but Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs. So they drank and were merry with him.
Joseph gave his steward these orders: "Fill the men's sacks with as much food as they can carry, and put each man's silver at the mouth of his sack.
Put my cup, the silver cup, at the mouth of the youngest one's sack, along with the silver for his grain." And he did as Joseph told him.
At first light the men were sent on their way, with their donkeys.
They had left the city but had not gone far when Joseph said to his steward, "Up, go after the men, and when you overtake them, say to them, 'Why have you repaid good with evil?
Is this not the cup my master drinks from and uses to read omens? You have done wrong in this.'"
He overtook them and said these words to them.
They said to him, "Why does my lord say such things? Heaven forbid that your servants should do any such thing.
We brought back to you from the land of Canaan the silver we found at the mouths of our sacks. How then could we steal silver or gold from your master's house?
If any of your servants is found to have it, he will die, and the rest of us will become my lord's slaves."
He said, "Very well, let it be as you say. The one who is found with it will become my slave, and the rest of you will be blameless."
Each man quickly lowered his sack to the ground and opened it.
The steward searched, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest, and the cup was found in Benjamin's sack.
They tore their clothes. Then each man loaded his donkey, and they returned to the city.
Judah and his brothers came to Joseph's house, where he was still present, and they threw themselves on the ground before him.
Joseph said to them, "What is this that you have done? Did you not know that a man like me can read such signs?"

Judah said, "What can we say to my lord? What can we speak? How can we prove ourselves innocent? God has found out the guilt of your servants. Here we are, my lord's slaves, we and the one in whose possession the cup was found."
But he said, "Heaven forbid that I should do this. The man in whose possession the cup was found will be my slave. As for you, go back in peace to your father."
Then Judah stepped up to him and said, "Please, my lord, let your servant speak a word in my lord's ears, and do not be angry with your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself.
My lord asked his servants, 'Have you a father or a brother?'
We said to my lord, 'We have an old father, and a young brother born to him in his old age. His brother is dead, so he alone is left of his mother's sons, and his father loves him.'
Then you said to your servants, 'Bring him down to me, so that I may set my eyes on him.'
We said to my lord, 'The boy cannot leave his father, for if he leaves, his father will die.'
But you said to your servants, 'Unless your youngest brother comes down with you, you will not see my face again.'
When we went back to your servant my father, we told him what my lord had said.
Then our father said, 'Go back and buy us a little food.'
We said, 'We cannot go down. If our youngest brother is with us, we will go down, for we cannot see the man's face unless our youngest brother is with us.'
Your servant my father said to us, 'You know that my wife bore me two sons.
One went away from me, and I said, "Surely he has been torn to pieces," and I have not seen him since.
If you take this one from me too, and harm comes to him, you will bring my grey head down to Sheol in misery.'
Now if I come to your servant my father and the boy is not with us, since his life is bound up with the boy's life,
when he sees that the boy is not with us, he will die, and your servants will have brought the grey head of your servant our father down to Sheol in sorrow.
For your servant became surety for the boy to my father, saying, 'If I do not bring him back to you, I will bear the blame before my father all my life.'
So now, please let your servant stay as my lord's slave in place of the boy, and let the boy go back with his brothers.
For how can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me? I could not bear to see the misery that would come upon my father."
Joseph could no longer hold himself back before all those who stood beside him, and he cried out, "Make everyone leave me!" So no one stood with him when Joseph made himself known to his brothers.
He wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard it, and the household of Pharaoh heard of it.
Joseph said to his brothers, "I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?" But his brothers could not answer him, for they were terrified before him.
Then Joseph said to his brothers, "Come closer to me, please." They came closer. And he said, "I am your brother Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.
Now do not be distressed, and do not be angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me ahead of you to preserve life.
For two years now there has been famine in the land, and for five more years there will be neither ploughing nor harvest.
God sent me ahead of you to make sure that you have a remnant on the earth, and to keep you alive by a great escape.
So it was not you who sent me here, but God. He has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord of all his household and ruler over all the land of Egypt.
Hurry back to my father and tell him, 'This is what your son Joseph says: God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me; do not delay.
You will live in the land of Goshen and be near me, you and your children and your grandchildren, your flocks and herds, and everything you have.
I will provide for you there, for there are five more years of famine to come, so that you and your household and all that is yours do not come to poverty.'
Now your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see, that it is my own mouth that speaks to you.
Tell my father of all my honour in Egypt, and of all that you have seen. And bring my father down here quickly."
Then he fell on the neck of his brother Benjamin and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck.
He kissed all his brothers and wept over them. After that his brothers talked with him.
When the report was heard in Pharaoh's house, "Joseph's brothers have come," it pleased Pharaoh and his servants.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Say to your brothers, 'Do this: load your animals and go back to the land of Canaan.
Take your father and your households and come to me. I will give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you will eat the fat of the land.'
You are also commanded to say, 'Do this: take wagons from the land of Egypt for your little ones and for your wives, and bring your father and come.
Do not worry about your possessions, for the best of all the land of Egypt is yours.'"
The sons of Israel did so. Joseph gave them wagons, as Pharaoh had commanded, and gave them provisions for the journey.
