To all of them he gave a change of clothing, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of clothing.
To his father he sent as follows: ten donkeys loaded with the best things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain, bread and provisions for his father on the journey.
Then he sent his brothers on their way, and as they left he said to them, "Do not quarrel on the road."
So they went up out of Egypt and came to the land of Canaan, to their father Jacob.
They told him, "Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt." His heart went numb, for he did not believe them.
But when they told him all the words that Joseph had spoken to them, and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of their father Jacob revived.
Israel said, "It is enough! My son Joseph is still alive. I will go and see him before I die."
Israel set out with everything he had, and came to Beersheba, where he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
God spoke to Israel in visions of the night: "Jacob, Jacob!" "Here I am," he answered.
God said, "I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation.
I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I myself will bring you up again. Joseph's own hand will close your eyes."
Jacob left Beersheba. The sons of Israel carried their father Jacob, their little ones and their wives in the wagons Pharaoh had sent to carry him.
They took their livestock and the possessions they had gained in the land of Canaan, and came to Egypt, Jacob and all his descendants with him,
his sons and grandsons, his daughters and granddaughters. All his descendants he brought with him to Egypt.
These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt, Jacob and his sons: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn.
The sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron and Carmi.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman.
The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath and Merari.
The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez and Zerah. Er and Onan had died in the land of Canaan. The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.
The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Yob and Shimron.
The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon and Jahleel.
These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan-aram, together with his daughter Dinah. His sons and daughters numbered thirty-three in all.
The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi and Areli.
The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah. The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malkiel.
These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah. She bore these to Jacob: sixteen persons.
The sons of Jacob's wife Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
In the land of Egypt, Manasseh and Ephraim were born to Joseph, borne to him by Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim and Ard.
These are the sons of Rachel who were born to Jacob: fourteen persons in all.
The son of Dan: Hushim.
The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer and Shillem.
These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel. She bore these to Jacob: seven persons in all.
All the persons belonging to Jacob who came to Egypt, his own descendants, not counting the wives of Jacob's sons, were sixty-six in all.
The sons of Joseph who were born to him in Egypt were two. All the persons of the house of Jacob who came to Egypt were seventy.
Jacob sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to point out the way to Goshen. When they arrived in the region of Goshen,
Joseph had his chariot made ready and went up to meet his father Israel in Goshen. As soon as he appeared before him, he threw his arms around his neck and wept on his neck for a long time.
Israel said to Joseph, "Now I am ready to die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive."
Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's household, "I will go up and tell Pharaoh, 'My brothers and my father's household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.
The men are shepherds, for they have always kept livestock, and they have brought their flocks and herds and all that they own.'
When Pharaoh summons you and asks, 'What is your occupation?'

you are to say, 'Your servants have kept livestock from our youth until now, both we and our fathers.' Then you will be allowed to settle in the land of Goshen, because all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians."
So Joseph went in and told Pharaoh, "My father and my brothers, with their flocks and herds and all that they own, have come from the land of Canaan. They are now in the land of Goshen."
From among his brothers he took five men and presented them to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked the brothers, "What is your occupation?" They answered Pharaoh, "Your servants are shepherds, as our fathers were."

They said to Pharaoh, "We have come to live as foreigners in the land, because there is no pasture for your servants' flocks, for the famine is severe in the land of Canaan. So now, please let your servants settle in the land of Goshen."
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Your father and your brothers have come to you.

The land of Egypt is open before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best of the land. Let them live in the land of Goshen. And if you know of any capable men among them, put them in charge of my own livestock."
Then Joseph brought in his father Jacob and presented him to Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked Jacob, "How many years have you lived?"
Jacob answered Pharaoh, "The years of my wandering are 130. They have been few and hard, and they have not reached the years of my fathers in the days of their wandering."
Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and left his presence.
So Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a holding in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the district of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.
Joseph provided his father, his brothers and all his father's household with food, according to the number of their dependants.
There was no food in all the land, for the famine was very severe, and the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan wasted away because of the famine.
Joseph collected all the silver that was to be found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, in payment for the grain they were buying, and Joseph brought the silver into Pharaoh's palace.
When the silver was spent in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, "Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? Our silver is gone."
Joseph said, "Give me your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for your livestock, since your silver is gone."

So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them food in exchange for their horses, their flocks of sheep and goats, their herds of cattle, and their donkeys. He supplied them with food that year in exchange for all their livestock.

When that year was over, they came to him the following year and said to him, "We cannot hide it from my lord: our silver is spent, and the herds of livestock are my lord's. There is nothing left before my lord but our bodies and our land.

Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land in exchange for food, and we and our land will be servants to Pharaoh. Give us seed, so that we may live and not die, and so that the land may not become desolate."
So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh. Every Egyptian sold his field, because the famine was too hard on them. The land became Pharaoh's,
and as for the people, he made slaves of them from one end of Egypt to the other.
Only the land of the priests he did not buy, for the priests had a fixed allowance from Pharaoh and lived on the allowance Pharaoh gave them. That is why they did not sell their land.
Then Joseph said to the people, "Now I have bought you and your land today for Pharaoh. Here is seed for you, and you can sow the land.
At harvest you are to give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four parts will be yours, as seed for the field and as food for yourselves, for your households and for your little ones."
They said, "You have saved our lives. May we find favour with my lord, and we will be Pharaoh's servants."
So Joseph made it a law for the land of Egypt, which is still in force today, that a fifth belongs to Pharaoh. Only the land of the priests did not become Pharaoh's.
Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in the region of Goshen. They gained possessions in it, and were fruitful and multiplied greatly.
Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years, so the length of Jacob's life was 147 years.

When the time drew near for Israel to die, he called for his son Joseph and said to him, "If I have found favour with you, put your hand under my thigh and deal with me in faithful love and truth. Do not bury me in Egypt,
but let me lie with my fathers. Carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burial place." He said, "I will do as you say."
He said, "Swear to me." And he swore to him. Then Israel bowed in worship at the head of the bed.
Some time later Joseph was told, "Your father is ill." So he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.
When Jacob was told, "Your son Joseph has come to you," Israel gathered his strength and sat up in bed.
Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and blessed me,
and said to me, 'I will make you fruitful and numerous, and I will make you a company of peoples. I will give this land to your descendants after you as an everlasting possession.'
Now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine. Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are.
But the children born to you after them will be yours. In the inheritance they receive, they will be called by the names of their brothers.

As for me, when I came from Paddan, Rachel died beside me in the land of Canaan on the way, when we were still some distance from Ephrath, and I buried her there on the road to Ephrath, that is Bethlehem."
When Israel saw Joseph's sons, he asked, "Who are these?"
Joseph said to his father, "They are my sons, whom God has given me here." He said, "Bring them to me, please, so that I may bless them."
Israel's eyes were dim with age, and he could not see. So Joseph brought them close to him, and he kissed them and embraced them.
Israel said to Joseph, "I never expected to see your face again, and now God has let me see your children too."
Then Joseph took them from between his knees, and he bowed with his face to the ground.
Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand towards Israel's left, and Manasseh in his left hand towards Israel's right, and brought them close to him.
But Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, who was the younger, and his left hand on the head of Manasseh, crossing his hands, for Manasseh was the firstborn.
He blessed Joseph and said: "The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day,

the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless these boys. Let my name be carried on in them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth."
When Joseph saw that his father had laid his right hand on Ephraim's head, he was displeased, and he took his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's.
Joseph said to his father, "Not so, my father. This one is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head."

But his father refused and said, "I know, my son, I know. He too will become a people, and he too will be great. Yet his younger brother will be greater than he, and his descendants will become a multitude of nations."
So he blessed them that day, saying, "By you Israel will bless, saying, 'God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh.'" Thus he put Ephraim before Manasseh.
Then Israel said to Joseph, "I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers.
And I give to you one portion more than to your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorites with my sword and with my bow."
Jacob called his sons and said, "Gather round, and I will tell you what will befall you in days to come.
Assemble and listen, sons of Jacob; listen to Israel your father.
Reuben, you are my firstborn, my strength and the first sign of my vigour, first in rank and first in power.
Unstable as water, you will not be first, because you climbed onto your father's bed and defiled it. He climbed onto my couch.
Simeon and Levi are brothers, their swords are weapons of violence.
Let me not enter their council, let me not join their assembly, for in their anger they killed men, and on a whim they crippled oxen.
Cursed be their anger, so fierce, and their wrath, so cruel. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.
Judah, your brothers will praise you. Your hand will be on the neck of your enemies, and your father's sons will bow before you.
Judah is a young lion. You return from the kill, my son. He crouches, he lies down like a lion, like a lioness. Who will dare rouse him?
The sceptre will not leave Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him, and the peoples obey him.
He ties his donkey to the vine, his colt to the choice vine. He washes his garments in wine, his robe in the blood of grapes.
His eyes are darker than wine, his teeth whiter than milk.
Zebulun will live by the shore of the sea. He will be a harbour for ships, and his border will reach to Sidon.
Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the saddlebags.
He saw that a resting place was good, and that the land was pleasant, so he bent his shoulder to carry and became a labourer under forced work.
Dan will judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel.
Dan will be a snake beside the road, a viper along the path, biting the horse's heels so that its rider falls backwards.
I wait for your rescue, LORD.
Gad will be raided by raiders, but he will raid at their heels.
Asher's food will be rich, and he will give royal delicacies.
Naphtali is a doe let loose, who bears lovely fawns.
Joseph is a fruitful bough, a fruitful bough by a spring, whose branches climb over the wall.
Archers attacked him fiercely, they shot at him and harassed him.
But his bow stayed firm, and his arms were made supple by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, by the name of the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel,
by the God of your father, who helps you, and by the Almighty, who blesses you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that lies below, blessings of the breast and of the womb.

The blessings of your father surpass the blessings of the ancient mountains, the desire of the everlasting hills. May they rest on the head of Joseph, on the brow of the one set apart from his brothers.
Benjamin is a ravenous wolf. In the morning he devours the prey, and in the evening he divides the spoil."
All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father said to them when he blessed them, each with the blessing that was his.
Then he gave them these instructions: "I am about to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
the cave in the field at Machpelah, east of Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place.
There they buried Abraham and his wife Sarah. There they buried Isaac and his wife Rebekah, and there I buried Leah.
The field and the cave in it were bought from the Hittites."
When Jacob had finished giving these instructions to his sons, he drew his feet up into the bed, breathed his last, and was gathered to his people.
Joseph threw himself on his father's face and wept over him and kissed him.
Then Joseph ordered the physicians in his service to embalm his father. So the physicians embalmed Israel.
Forty days were needed for it, for that is the time needed for embalming. The Egyptians wept for him seventy days.
When the days of weeping were over, Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh: "If I have found favour with you, please speak to Pharaoh on my behalf. Say to him,
'My father made me swear an oath. He said, "I am about to die. Bury me in the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan." Now let me go up and bury my father, and then I will return.'"
Pharaoh answered, "Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear."
So Joseph went up to bury his father. With him went all Pharaoh's servants, the elders of his household and all the elders of the land of Egypt,
and all the household of Joseph, his brothers and his father's household. Only their little ones and their flocks and herds were left in the land of Goshen.
Chariots and horsemen also went up with him. It was a very large company.
When they came to the threshing floor of Atad, beyond the Jordan, they mourned there with a very great and bitter lament, and Joseph observed seven days of mourning for his father.

When the Canaanites who lived in the land saw the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, they said, "This is a heavy mourning on the part of the Egyptians." That is why it was named Abel-mizraim. It is beyond the Jordan.
So Jacob's sons did for him as he had commanded them.
His sons carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field at Machpelah, east of Mamre, which Abraham had bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place.
After he had buried his father, Joseph returned to Egypt, he and his brothers and all who had gone up with him to bury his father.
When Joseph's brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, "What if Joseph bears a grudge against us and pays us back in full for all the wrong we did to him?"
So they sent a message to Joseph, saying, "Before he died your father gave this command:

'Say to Joseph, Please forgive the offence of your brothers and their sin, because they did you wrong.' Now, please forgive the offence of the servants of the God of your father." Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
His brothers also came and bowed down before him. "Here we are," they said, "your slaves."
But Joseph said to them, "Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?
You meant to harm me, but God meant it for good, to bring about what is happening now, the saving of many lives.
So do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones." So he comforted them and spoke kindly to them.
Joseph lived in Egypt, he and his father's household. Joseph lived 110 years.
He saw Ephraim's children to the third generation. The children of Machir the son of Manasseh were also born on Joseph's knees.
Joseph said to his brothers, "I am about to die, but God will surely visit you and bring you up out of this land to the land he promised on oath to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob."
Then Joseph made the sons of Israel swear an oath: "God will surely visit you, and you must carry my bones up from here."
So Joseph died at the age of 110. They embalmed him, and he was placed in a coffin in Egypt.
These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household:
Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah,
Issachar, Zebulun and Benjamin,
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
All the descendants of Jacob numbered seventy persons. Joseph was already in Egypt.
In time Joseph died, and all his brothers, and all that generation.
But the Israelites were fruitful and teemed. They multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, until the land was filled with them.
Then a new king arose over Egypt, one who did not know Joseph.
He said to his people, "Look, the Israelite people are more numerous and stronger than we are.
Come, let us deal shrewdly with them. Otherwise they will multiply further, and if war breaks out they may join our enemies and fight against us and leave the country."
So they set slave-masters over them to oppress them with heavy labour, and they built supply cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Rameses.
But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread, until the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites.
The Egyptians made the Israelites work without mercy
and made their lives bitter with hard labour at mortar and brick and with every kind of work in the fields. In all the work they forced on them, they were merciless.
The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, one named Shiphrah and the other Puah:
"When you help the Hebrew women give birth, look at the birthstool. If it is a boy, kill him. If it is a girl, let her live."
But the midwives feared God, and did not do what the king of Egypt had told them. They let the boys live.
The king of Egypt summoned the midwives and said to them, "Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?"
The midwives answered Pharaoh, "Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women. They are strong and give birth before the midwife arrives."
God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied and became very strong.
And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families of their own.
Then Pharaoh gave this order to all his people: "Every boy that is born to the Hebrews you are to throw into the Nile, but let every girl live."
A man from the house of Levi went and married a Levite woman.
The woman conceived and bore a son. When she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him for three months.
When she could hide him no longer, she took a basket of papyrus, coated it with bitumen and pitch, put the child in it, and set it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile.
His sister stood some distance away to see what would happen to him.
Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe at the Nile, while her maids walked along the bank. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her slave woman to fetch it.
She opened it and saw the child. He was crying, and she took pity on him. "This is one of the Hebrews' children," she said.
Then his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, "Shall I go and call a Hebrew woman to nurse the child for you?"
"Yes, go," Pharaoh's daughter said. So the girl went and called the child's mother.
Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay your wages." So the woman took the child and nursed him.
When the child had grown, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, saying, "Because I drew him out of the water."
One day, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his own people and saw how hard they were made to work. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people.
He looked around, and seeing no one, he struck the Egyptian down and hid his body in the sand.
The next day he went out and saw two Hebrews fighting. He said to the one in the wrong, "Why are you striking your own countryman?"
The man answered, "Who made you a ruler and judge over us? Are you going to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" Then Moses was afraid and thought, "The thing is known."
When Pharaoh heard of it, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian, and he sat down beside a well.
The priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came to draw water and fill the troughs for their father's flock,
but some shepherds came and drove them away. Moses got up and came to their defence and watered their flock.
When they went back to their father Reuel, he asked, "Why have you come back so soon today?"
"An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds," they said. "He even drew water for us and watered the flock."
"Where is he?" he asked his daughters. "Why did you leave the man? Invite him to eat with us."
Moses agreed to stay with the man, and he gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses as his wife.
She bore a son, and Moses named him Gershom, saying, "I have become a foreigner in a foreign land."
During those many days, the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned under their slavery, and cried out, and their cry for help rose up to God.
God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac and with Jacob.
God looked on the Israelites, and God took notice of them.
Moses was shepherding the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian. He led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire from the heart of a bush. He looked, and saw that the bush was burning, yet it was not burned up.
Moses said, "I will go over and look at this great sight, and see why the bush is not burning up."
When the LORD saw that he had turned aside to look, God called to him from the middle of the bush: "Moses! Moses!" "Here I am," he said.
God said, "Come no closer. Take your sandals off your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground."
He said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob." Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.
The LORD said, "I have seen the suffering of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry under their slave-drivers. I know their pain.

I have come down to rescue them from the grip of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land into a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey, the country of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites.
Now the cry of the Israelites has come to me, and I have seen how the Egyptians crush them.
So go. I am sending you to Pharaoh, to bring my people, the Israelites, out of Egypt."
But Moses said to God, "Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?"
God said, "I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain."
Moses said to God, "If I go to the Israelites and tell them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' what am I to tell them?"
God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." And he said, "This is what you are to say to the Israelites: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"

God also said to Moses, "Tell the Israelites this: 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' This is my name for ever, and this is how I am to be remembered from one generation to the next.

Go and gather the elders of Israel, and say to them: 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, has appeared to me and said: I have taken note of you and of what has been done to you in Egypt.

I have said that I will bring you up out of the misery of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey.'

They will listen to you. Then you and the elders of Israel are to go to the king of Egypt and say to him: 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Now let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness, to offer sacrifice to the LORD our God.'
I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless a mighty hand forces him.
So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all the wonders I will do among them. After that he will let you go.
I will make the Egyptians look kindly on this people, so that when you leave, you will not leave empty-handed.

Every woman is to ask her neighbour, and any woman staying in her house, for articles of silver and gold and for clothing, and you will put them on your sons and daughters. In this way you will strip the Egyptians."
Moses answered, "What if they will not believe me or listen to what I say? They may say, 'The LORD did not appear to you.'"
The LORD said to him, "What is that in your hand?" "A staff," he said.
The LORD said, "Throw it on the ground." He threw it on the ground and it became a snake, and Moses ran from it.
The LORD said to Moses, "Reach out your hand and grab it by the tail." He reached out and took hold of it, and it became a staff in his hand.
"This is so that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you."
Then the LORD said to him, "Put your hand inside your cloak." He put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, his hand was diseased, white as snow.
He said, "Put your hand back inside your cloak." He put his hand back inside his cloak, and when he took it out, it was healthy again, like the rest of his skin.
"If they will not believe you or take notice of the first sign, they may believe the second.
And if they will not believe even these two signs or listen to you, take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground. The water you take from the Nile will turn to blood on the ground."
Moses said to the LORD, "Please, Lord, I am not a man of words, neither in the past nor since you began speaking to your servant. I am slow of speech and slow of tongue."
The LORD said to him, "Who gave human beings their mouths? Who makes them mute or deaf, sighted or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?
Now go. I will be with your mouth and teach you what to say."
But he said, "Please, Lord, send someone else."

Then the LORD's anger burned against Moses, and he said, "Is there not your brother Aaron the Levite? I know that he can speak well. He is even now coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad.
You will speak to him and put the words in his mouth. I will be with your mouth and with his mouth, and I will teach you both what you are to do.
He will speak for you to the people. He will be your mouth, and you will be as God to him.
Take this staff in your hand, for with it you will perform the signs."
Moses went back to Jethro his father-in-law and said to him, "Let me go back to my relatives in Egypt to see whether they are still alive." Jethro said to Moses, "Go in peace."
The LORD had said to Moses in Midian, "Go back to Egypt, for all the men who wanted to kill you are dead."
So Moses took his wife and his sons, set them on a donkey, and went back to the land of Egypt, with the staff of God in his hand.
The LORD said to Moses, "When you go back to Egypt, make sure that you do before Pharaoh all the wonders I have put in your power. But I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go.
Then you will say to Pharaoh, 'This is what the LORD says: Israel is my firstborn son,
and I told you, "Let my son go, so that he may serve me." You refused to let him go, so I will kill your firstborn son.'"
On the way, at a lodging place, the LORD met him and tried to kill him.
Then Zipporah took a flint, cut off her son's foreskin, and touched his feet with it. "You are a bridegroom of blood to me," she said.
So he let him alone. (She said "bridegroom of blood" because of the circumcision.)
The LORD said to Aaron, "Go to meet Moses in the wilderness." He went and met him at the mountain of God and kissed him.
Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which he had sent him, and all the signs he had commanded him to do.
Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the elders of the Israelites.
Aaron told them all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses, and performed the signs in the sight of the people.
The people believed, and when they heard that the LORD had visited the Israelites and had seen their misery, they bowed down and worshipped.
Afterwards Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'Let my people go, so that they may hold a festival to me in the wilderness.'"
Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should listen to his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go."

They said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness to offer sacrifice to the LORD our God, or he may strike us with plague or with the sword."
But the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why are you pulling the people away from their work? Get back to your labour."
Pharaoh said, "Look, the people of the land are many now, and you would have them stop their work."
That same day Pharaoh gave orders to the slave-drivers and the foremen of the people:
"You are no longer to give the people straw for making bricks, as you have done until now. Let them go and gather straw for themselves.
But you are to require the same number of bricks as before. Do not reduce it. They are idle, and that is why they cry out, 'Let us go and sacrifice to our God.'
Make the work heavier for the men, so that they are kept busy and pay no attention to lies."
So the slave-drivers and the foremen of the people went out and said to the people, "This is what Pharaoh says: 'I will not give you straw.
Go and get straw for yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced in the slightest.'"
So the people scattered throughout the land of Egypt to gather stubble to use for straw.
The slave-drivers kept pressing them: "Finish your work, your daily quota, just as when there was straw."
And the Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh's slave-drivers had set over them, were beaten and asked, "Why have you not completed your quota of bricks, yesterday and today, as you did before?"
Then the Israelite foremen came and appealed to Pharaoh: "Why do you treat your servants like this?
No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, 'Make bricks!' Your servants are beaten, but the fault is with your own people."
He said, "You are idle, idle! That is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.'
Now go and work. No straw will be given you, but you must deliver the same quota of bricks."
The Israelite foremen saw that they were in trouble when they were told, "You must not reduce your daily quota of bricks."
As they left Pharaoh, they met Moses and Aaron, who were standing there to meet them.
They said to them, "May the LORD look on you and judge you, for you have made us a stench in the nostrils of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us."
Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me?
Since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not rescued your people at all."
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. Compelled by a mighty hand he will let them go; compelled by a mighty hand he will drive them out of his land."
God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the LORD.
I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob as God Almighty, but I did not make myself known to them by my name, the LORD.
I also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land in which they lived as foreigners.
I have also heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians hold as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.

Therefore say to the Israelites: 'I am the LORD. I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgement.
I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God. You will know that I am the LORD your God, who brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
I will bring you into the land that I swore with raised hand to give to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob. I will give it to you as a possession. I am the LORD.'"
Moses told this to the Israelites, but they would not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and their hard slavery.
Then the LORD spoke to Moses:
"Go in and tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the Israelites go out of his land."
But Moses said to the LORD, "If the Israelites will not listen to me, how will Pharaoh listen to me, a man with uncircumcised lips?"
But the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, and gave them a charge for the Israelites and for Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.
These are the heads of their ancestral houses. The sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron and Carmi. These are the clans of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These are the clans of Simeon.
These are the names of the sons of Levi, in the order of their records: Gershon, Kohath and Merari. Levi lived 137 years.
The sons of Gershon, by their clans: Libni and Shimei.
The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel. Kohath lived 133 years.
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites, in the order of their records.
Amram took his father's sister Jochebed as his wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses. Amram lived 137 years.
The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg and Zichri.
The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan and Sithri.
Aaron took as his wife Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah and Abiasaph. These are the clans of the Korahites.
Aaron's son Eleazar took as his wife one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the ancestral houses of the Levites by their clans.
It was this Aaron and this Moses to whom the LORD said, "Bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt, company by company."
It was they who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt about bringing the Israelites out of Egypt, this same Moses and Aaron.
On the day when the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,
the LORD said to Moses, "I am the LORD. Tell Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say to you."
But Moses said before the LORD, "Look, I am a man with uncircumcised lips. How will Pharaoh listen to me?"
The LORD said to Moses, "Understand this: I have set you in God's place before Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your spokesman.
You will say everything I command you, and your brother Aaron will tell Pharaoh to release the Israelites from his land.
But I will make Pharaoh's heart stubborn, and however many signs and wonders I perform in Egypt,
Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will bring my hand down on Egypt, and I will lead out my companies, my people the Israelites, from Egypt with mighty acts of judgement.
The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand over Egypt and lead the Israelites out from among them."
Moses and Aaron did exactly what the LORD had commanded them.
Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three, when they spoke to Pharaoh.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron,
"When Pharaoh says to you, 'Prove yourselves by a wonder,' tell Aaron, 'Take your staff and throw it down in front of Pharaoh.' It will turn into a great serpent."
Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did exactly as the LORD had commanded. Aaron threw his staff down in front of Pharaoh and his courtiers, and it turned into a serpent.
Pharaoh called for his wise men and sorcerers, and the magicians of Egypt did the same with their secret arts.
Each threw down his staff, and each became a serpent, but Aaron's staff swallowed theirs.
Even so, Pharaoh's heart stayed hard, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
The LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is stubborn. He refuses to release the people.
Go to Pharaoh in the morning, when he goes out to the river. Wait for him on the bank of the Nile, and carry in your hand the staff that turned into a snake.
Tell him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to you with this message: Release my people, so that they may worship me in the wilderness. Until now you have not listened.
This is what the LORD says: Here is how you will know that I am the LORD. I am about to strike the water of the Nile with the staff in my hand, and it will turn to blood.
The fish in the river will die, the river will stink, and the Egyptians will find the Nile water undrinkable.'"

The LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron: 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over its rivers, canals, ponds and every reservoir, and they will turn to blood.' Throughout Egypt there will be blood, even in wooden buckets and stone jars."
Moses and Aaron did exactly as the LORD commanded. Raising the staff in full view of Pharaoh and his courtiers, he struck the water of the Nile, and all the water in the river turned to blood.
The fish in the Nile died, and the river stank so badly that the Egyptians could not drink from it. There was blood throughout Egypt.
The Egyptian magicians did the same with their secret arts. So Pharaoh's heart stayed hard, and he would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said.
Pharaoh turned and went back to his palace, and he did not take even this to heart.
All the Egyptians dug around the Nile for drinking water, because they could not drink the river water.
Seven days went by after the LORD had struck the Nile.
The LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him, 'This is what the LORD says: Release my people, so that they may worship me.
If you refuse to release them, I will strike your whole country with frogs.
The Nile will teem with frogs. They will come up and enter your palace, your bedroom and your bed, the houses of your courtiers and your people, your ovens and your kneading bowls.
The frogs will climb over you, over your people and over all your courtiers.'"
The LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron: 'Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, canals and ponds, and bring frogs up over the land of Egypt.'"
Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land.
The magicians did the same with their secret arts, and they too brought frogs up over the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "Pray to the LORD to remove the frogs from me and from my people, and I will release the people to offer sacrifices to the LORD."

Moses said to Pharaoh, "I give you the honour. Tell me when I am to pray for you, your courtiers and your people, so that the frogs will be removed from you and your houses and be left only in the Nile."
"Tomorrow," he said. Moses said, "It will be as you say, so that you will know there is no one like the LORD our God.
The frogs will leave you, your houses, your courtiers and your people. They will be left only in the Nile."
Moses and Aaron left Pharaoh, and Moses cried out to the LORD concerning the frogs he had inflicted on Pharaoh.
The LORD did as Moses asked. The frogs died in the houses, in the courtyards and in the fields.
They were piled up in heaps, and the land stank.
But when Pharaoh saw that relief had come, he made his heart heavy and would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
The LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron: 'Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the ground,' and it will turn into gnats throughout the land of Egypt."

They did so. Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the ground, and gnats came on people and animals. All the dust of the ground turned into gnats throughout the land of Egypt.
The magicians tried to produce gnats with their secret arts, but they could not. The gnats stayed on people and animals.
The magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God!" But Pharaoh's heart stayed hard, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
The LORD said to Moses, "Rise early in the morning and stand in Pharaoh's path as he goes out to the water. Tell him, 'This is what the LORD says: Release my people, so that they may worship me.

If you do not release my people, I will send swarms of flies on you, your courtiers, your people and your houses. The houses of the Egyptians will be full of flies, and so will the very ground they stand on.
But on that day I will treat the land of Goshen, where my people live, differently. No swarms of flies will be there, so that you will know that I, the LORD, am present in this land.
I will set a separation between my people and yours. Tomorrow this sign will happen.'"
The LORD did so. Thick swarms of flies poured into Pharaoh's palace and the houses of his courtiers, and throughout Egypt the land was ruined by the flies.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "Go and sacrifice to your God here in this country."
Moses said, "That would not be right. The sacrifices we offer to the LORD our God are detestable to the Egyptians. If we offer sacrifices that are detestable in their eyes, will they not stone us?
We must go a three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God, as he instructs us."
Pharaoh said, "I will release you to sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness, but you must not go very far. Pray for me."

Moses said, "As soon as I leave you, I will pray to the LORD, and tomorrow the swarms of flies will leave Pharaoh, his courtiers and his people. Only let Pharaoh stop dealing deceitfully and refusing to release the people to sacrifice to the LORD."
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD.
The LORD did as Moses asked, and removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, his courtiers and his people. Not one was left.
But Pharaoh made his heart heavy this time too, and did not release the people.
The LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him, 'This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Release my people, so that they may worship me.
If you refuse to release them and keep holding on to them,
the hand of the LORD will strike your livestock in the fields: your horses, donkeys and camels, your herds and flocks, with a severe plague.
But the LORD will draw a line between the livestock of Israel and that of Egypt, so that nothing that belongs to the Israelites will die.'"
The LORD set a time: "Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land."
The next day the LORD did it. All the Egyptians' livestock died, but not one animal of the Israelites died.
Pharaoh sent men to check, and not one of the Israelites' animals had died. Yet Pharaoh's heart stayed stubborn, and he would not release the people.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from a brick kiln, and Moses is to scatter it towards the sky in Pharaoh's sight.
It will become fine dust over the whole land of Egypt, and wherever it settles on people and animals it will cause festering sores."
They took soot from a kiln and stood before Pharaoh, and Moses scattered it towards the sky, and it caused festering sores on people and animals.
The magicians could not stand in front of Moses because of the sores, for the sores were on the magicians as on all the Egyptians.
But the LORD strengthened Pharaoh's resolve, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had told Moses.
The LORD said to Moses, "Get up early in the morning, present yourself to Pharaoh and tell him, 'This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Release my people, so that they may worship me.
This time I will send all my plagues straight at you, at your courtiers and at your people, so that you will know there is no one like me in all the earth.
By now I could have stretched out my hand and struck you and your people with a pestilence that would have wiped you from the earth.
But I have let you stand for this reason: to show you my power, and so that my name will be told throughout the earth.
You are still setting yourself up against my people and will not release them.
So tomorrow at this time I will send down a hailstorm so heavy that nothing like it has fallen in Egypt from the day it was founded until now.
Order now that your livestock and everything you have in the open be brought under shelter. Any person or animal left in the open and not brought indoors will be struck by the hail and will die.'"
Those of Pharaoh's courtiers who feared the LORD's word hurried their slaves and livestock indoors.
But those who paid no heed to the LORD's word left their slaves and livestock in the open.
The LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand towards the sky, and hail will fall over the whole land of Egypt, on people and animals and every plant in the fields."
Moses stretched out his staff towards the sky, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and fire flashed down to the ground. The LORD rained hail on the land of Egypt.
There was hail, with lightning flashing back and forth within it, a storm so severe that nothing like it had ever been seen in Egypt since it became a nation.
Throughout Egypt the hail struck down everything in the open, people and animals alike. It beat down every plant in the fields and broke every tree.
Only in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, was there no hail.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them, "This time I have done wrong. The LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong.
Pray to the LORD, for we have had enough of this thunder and hail. I will release you. You need not stay any longer."
Moses said to him, "As soon as I leave the city, I will spread out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will stop and there will be no more hail, so that you may know the earth belongs to the LORD.
But as for you and your courtiers, I know you still have no fear of the LORD God."
(The flax and the barley were ruined, for the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom.
The wheat and the spelt were not ruined, because they come up later.)
Moses left Pharaoh and went out of the city, and spread out his hands to the LORD. The thunder and hail stopped, and the rain no longer poured down on the land.
When Pharaoh saw that the rain, hail and thunder had stopped, he did wrong again and made his heart heavy, he and his courtiers.
Pharaoh's heart stayed hard, and he did not release the Israelites, just as the LORD had said through Moses.
The LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh, for I have made his heart and the hearts of his courtiers stubborn, so that I may set these signs of mine among them,
and so that you can tell your children and grandchildren how I made a mockery of the Egyptians and what signs I did among them, and you will know that I am the LORD."

Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said to him, "This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Release my people, so that they may worship me.
If you refuse to release my people, then tomorrow I will bring locusts into your territory.
They will cover the surface of the land so that no one can see the ground. They will eat what survived the hail, and every tree that grows in your fields.

They will fill your houses, and the houses of all your courtiers and all the Egyptians, as neither your parents nor your grandparents have seen since they first lived on this soil.'" Then he turned and left Pharaoh.
Pharaoh's courtiers said to him, "How long will this man be a snare to us? Release the people to worship the LORD their God. Do you not yet see that Egypt is ruined?"
Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh, who said to them, "Go and worship the LORD your God. But who exactly is going?"
Moses said, "We will go with our young and our old, with our sons and daughters, with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a festival to the LORD."
He said to them, "The LORD be with you, if I ever release you with your little ones! Look, you have evil in mind.
No. Only the men may go and worship the LORD, since that is what you have been asking for." And they were driven from Pharaoh's presence.
The LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt, so that locusts will come up over it and eat every plant in the land, everything the hail left."
Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD sent an east wind over the land all that day and all that night. By morning the east wind had brought the locusts.
The locusts came up over the whole land of Egypt and settled throughout its territory in huge swarms. There had never been so many locusts before, and there never will be again.

They covered the surface of the whole land until it was dark with them, and they ate every plant in the land and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left. Nothing green was left on any tree or any plant in the whole land of Egypt.
Pharaoh hurriedly summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "I have done wrong against the LORD your God and against you.
Now forgive my offence just this once, and pray to the LORD your God to take this deadly thing away from me."
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD.
The LORD turned the wind into a very strong west wind, which lifted the locusts and swept them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust was left in the whole territory of Egypt.
But the LORD strengthened Pharaoh's resolve, and he would not release the Israelites.
The LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand towards the sky, and darkness will spread over the land of Egypt, a darkness you can touch."
Moses stretched out his hand towards the sky, and deep darkness lay over all the land of Egypt for three days.
No one could see anyone else, and no one moved from where he was for three days. But all the Israelites had light in their homes.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and said, "Go and worship the LORD. Even your little ones may go with you. Only your flocks and herds must stay behind."
Moses said, "You must also let us have sacrifices and burnt offerings to give to the LORD our God.
Our livestock must go with us. Not a hoof will be left behind. We will need some of them to worship the LORD our God, and we cannot know what we need to worship the LORD until we get there."
But the LORD strengthened Pharaoh's resolve, and he was unwilling to let them go.
Pharaoh said to him, "Get out of my sight! Make sure you never see my face again. On the day you see my face you will die."
Moses said, "You have spoken well. I will never see your face again."
The LORD said to Moses, "I will bring one more plague on Pharaoh and on Egypt. After that he will release you from this place. When he does release you, he will drive you out completely.
Speak to the people and tell them that each man and each woman is to ask a neighbour for objects of silver and gold."
The LORD made the Egyptians look kindly on the people. Moses himself was also held in very high regard in the land of Egypt, by Pharaoh's courtiers and by the people.
Moses said, "This is what the LORD says: 'About midnight I will go out through the middle of Egypt.
Every firstborn in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the slave girl behind the hand-mill, and every firstborn of the animals.
There will be a great cry throughout the land of Egypt, such as there has never been and never will be again.
But not a dog will growl at any of the Israelites, whether person or animal, so that you will know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.'

All these courtiers of yours will come down to me and bow before me, saying, 'Leave, you and all the people who follow you.' After that I will leave." And Moses went out from Pharaoh in burning anger.
The LORD had said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt."
Moses and Aaron performed all these wonders in front of Pharaoh, but the LORD made Pharaoh's heart stubborn, and he did not release the Israelites from his land.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt,
"This month will be the beginning of months for you. It will be the first month of the year for you.
Speak to the whole community of Israel and say: On the tenth day of this month, each man is to take a lamb for his family, a lamb for each household.
If the household is too small for a whole lamb, it is to share one with its nearest neighbour, according to the number of persons. Calculate how much lamb each person will eat.
Your lamb must be without blemish, a year-old male. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats.
Keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, when the whole assembled community of Israel will slaughter it at twilight.
They are to take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.
They are to eat the meat that night, roasted over the fire, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted over the fire, its head with its legs and its inner parts.
You must not leave any of it until morning. Whatever is left until morning, you are to burn.
This is how you are to eat it: with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. You are to eat it in haste. It is the LORD's Passover.

For on this night I will pass through the land of Egypt, and I will strike down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both people and animals, and I will carry out judgements against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD.
The blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you live. When I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.
This day will be a day of remembrance for you. You are to celebrate it as a festival to the LORD. Throughout your generations you are to celebrate it as a lasting ordinance.

For seven days you are to eat unleavened bread. On the first day you are to remove yeast from your houses, for anyone who eats leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day will be cut off from Israel.
On the first day you are to hold a sacred assembly, and on the seventh day another sacred assembly. No work is to be done on those days, except what each person must eat. That alone you may prepare.

You are to observe the Festival of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your companies out of the land of Egypt. You are to observe this day throughout your generations as a lasting ordinance.
In the first month, from the evening of the fourteenth day until the evening of the twenty-first day, you are to eat unleavened bread.
For seven days no yeast is to be found in your houses. Anyone who eats what is leavened, whether a foreigner or a native of the land, will be cut off from the community of Israel.
You are to eat nothing leavened. In all your settlements you are to eat unleavened bread."
Moses summoned all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Go at once, select lambs for your families, and slaughter the Passover lamb.
Take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood in the basin, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood in the basin. None of you is to go out through the door of his house until morning.

The LORD will pass through to strike down the Egyptians. When he sees the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, the LORD will pass over the door and will not let the destroyer enter your houses to strike you down.
You are to observe this as a lasting ordinance for you and for your children.
When you enter the land that the LORD will give you, as he has promised, you are to keep this observance.
When your children ask you, 'What does this observance mean?'

you are to say, 'It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD, who passed over the houses of the Israelites in Egypt when he struck down the Egyptians and spared our houses.'" Then the people bowed down and worshipped.
The Israelites went and did exactly as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.

At midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, and every firstborn of the animals.
Pharaoh got up in the night, he and all his courtiers and all the Egyptians, and there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house without someone dead.
In the night he summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "Up, get out from among my people, both you and the Israelites. Go, worship the LORD, as you have said.
Take your flocks and your herds too, as you have said, and be gone. And bless me also."
The Egyptians pressed the people to hurry and leave the country, for they said, "We are all about to die."
So the people picked up their dough before it was leavened, with their kneading bowls wrapped in their cloaks on their shoulders.
The Israelites did as Moses had told them and asked the Egyptians for objects of silver and gold, and for clothing.
The LORD had made the Egyptians look kindly on the people, and they let them have what they asked. In this way they stripped the Egyptians.
The Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children.
A mixed crowd also went up with them, along with very large flocks and herds of livestock.

They baked the dough they had brought out of Egypt into cakes of unleavened bread, for it had not risen. They had been driven out of Egypt and could not delay, and they had not prepared any provisions for themselves.
The time the Israelites lived in Egypt was 430 years.
At the end of the 430 years, on that very day, all the LORD's companies left the land of Egypt.
It was a night of watching by the LORD, to bring them out of the land of Egypt. This same night is a night of watching to be kept for the LORD by all the Israelites throughout their generations.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "This is the law of the Passover. No foreigner may eat of it,
but any slave bought with money may eat of it once you have circumcised him.
A resident foreigner and a hired worker may not eat of it.
It is to be eaten in one house. You are not to take any of the meat outside the house, and you are not to break any of its bones.
The whole community of Israel is to keep it.

If a foreigner living among you wishes to keep the LORD's Passover, all his males must be circumcised. Then he may come near and keep it, and he will be as a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person may eat of it.
The same law will apply to the native and to the foreigner who lives among you."
All the Israelites did exactly as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.
On that very day the LORD brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt, company by company.
The LORD said to Moses,
"Set apart to me every firstborn. Whatever first opens the womb among the Israelites, of people and of animals, is mine."
Moses said to the people, "Remember this day on which you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for the LORD brought you out from here with a strong hand. Nothing leavened is to be eaten.
Today, in the month of Abib, you are leaving.

When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, which he swore to your ancestors to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you are to keep this observance in this month.
For seven days you are to eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there is to be a festival to the LORD.
Unleavened bread is to be eaten for the seven days. Nothing leavened is to be seen with you, and no yeast is to be seen anywhere in your territory.
On that day you are to tell your child, 'It is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.'
It will be for you as a sign on your hand and as a reminder between your eyes, so that the teaching of the LORD may be in your mouth, for with a strong hand the LORD brought you out of Egypt.
You are to keep this rule at its appointed time, year after year.
When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and to your ancestors, and gives it to you,
you are to give to the LORD everything that first opens the womb. Every firstborn male of your livestock belongs to the LORD.
Every firstborn donkey you are to redeem with a lamb. If you do not redeem it, you must break its neck. Every firstborn among your sons you are to redeem.
When in time to come your child asks you, 'What does this mean?' you are to say to him, 'With a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

When Pharaoh refused stubbornly to let us go, the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both human and animal. That is why I sacrifice to the LORD every male that first opens the womb, and why I redeem every firstborn of my sons.'
It will be as a sign on your hand and as a symbol between your eyes, for with a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt."

When Pharaoh released the people, God did not lead them by the road through the land of the Philistines, though it was near, for God said, "If the people face war, they may change their minds and go back to Egypt."
So God led the people by the roundabout way of the wilderness towards the Red Sea. The Israelites went up out of the land of Egypt equipped for battle.
Moses took with him the bones of Joseph, for Joseph had made the Israelites swear a solemn oath, saying, "God will surely visit you, and you must carry my bones with you from here."
They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness.
The LORD went in front of them by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on the way, and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light, so that they could travel by day and by night.
The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night never left its place in front of the people.
The LORD said to Moses,
"Tell the Israelites to turn back and camp in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea. You are to camp opposite Baal-zephon, beside the sea.
Pharaoh will say of the Israelites, 'They are wandering aimlessly in the land. The wilderness has shut them in.'
I will make Pharaoh's heart stubborn, and he will chase after them. I will win glory for myself over Pharaoh and all his army, and the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD." And they did so.
When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, Pharaoh and his courtiers had a change of heart about them. "What have we done?" they said. "We have let Israel go from serving us."
So he had his chariot harnessed and took his army with him.
He took six hundred picked chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers over every one.
The LORD made the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt stubborn, and he pursued the Israelites as they went out boldly.
The Egyptians, with all Pharaoh's horses and chariots, his horsemen and his army, pursued them and caught up with them camping beside the sea, near Pi-hahiroth, opposite Baal-zephon.
As Pharaoh drew near, the Israelites looked up and saw the Egyptians marching after them. They were terrified, and the Israelites cried out to the LORD.
They said to Moses, "Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you took us away to die in the wilderness? What have you done to us, bringing us out of Egypt?
Is this not what we told you in Egypt: 'Leave us alone, so that we may serve the Egyptians'? It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness."
Moses said to the people, "Do not be afraid. Stand firm, and you will see the rescue the LORD will work for you today. The Egyptians you see today you will never see again.
The LORD will fight for you. You need only keep still."
The LORD said to Moses, "Why are you crying out to me? Tell the Israelites to go forward.
Lift up your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea and split it, so that the Israelites may go into the sea on dry ground.
I will make the hearts of the Egyptians stubborn, so that they follow them in, and I will win glory over Pharaoh and all his army, his chariots and his horsemen.
The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD when I have won glory over Pharaoh, his chariots and his horsemen."
The angel of God, who had been going in front of the camp of Israel, moved and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from in front of them and stood behind them,
coming between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel. It was cloud and darkness for one side, and it lit up the night for the other, so that one did not come near the other all night.
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. The LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night, and turned the sea into dry ground. The waters were split,
and the Israelites went into the sea on dry ground, with the waters like a wall to their right and to their left.
The Egyptians pursued and went into the sea after them, all Pharaoh's horses, his chariots and his horsemen.
At the morning watch the LORD looked down on the Egyptian army from the pillar of fire and cloud, and threw the Egyptian army into panic.
He clogged their chariot wheels so that they drove with difficulty. The Egyptians said, "Let us flee from Israel, for the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt."
The LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the water may flow back over the Egyptians, over their chariots and their horsemen."
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea returned to its normal place. The Egyptians were fleeing into it, and the LORD tossed the Egyptians into the middle of the sea.
The water returned and covered the chariots and the horsemen, the whole army of Pharaoh that had followed them into the sea. Not one of them was left.
But the Israelites had walked through the sea on dry ground, with the waters like a wall to their right and to their left.
That day the LORD saved Israel from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore of the sea.
Israel saw the great power that the LORD had used against the Egyptians, and the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses.
Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the LORD: "I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously. Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.
The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation. This is my God, and I will praise him, my father's God, and I will lift him high.
The LORD is a warrior. The LORD is his name.
Pharaoh's chariots and his army he has cast into the sea. The pick of his officers are sunk in the Red Sea.
The deeps have covered them. They went down into the depths like a stone.
Your right hand, LORD, is glorious in power. Your right hand, LORD, shatters the enemy.
In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow those who rise against you. You send out your fury, and it consumes them like straw.
At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up. The floods stood up like a heap. The deeps congealed in the heart of the sea.
The enemy said, 'I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the plunder. My appetite will be filled with them. I will draw my sword, my hand will destroy them.'
You blew with your wind, and the sea covered them. They sank like lead in the mighty waters.
Who is like you among the gods, LORD? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in praises, doing wonders?
You stretched out your right hand, and the earth swallowed them.
In your faithful love you led the people you redeemed. In your strength you guided them to your holy dwelling.
The peoples heard and trembled. Anguish seized the inhabitants of Philistia.
Then the chiefs of Edom were dismayed. Trembling seized the leaders of Moab. All the inhabitants of Canaan melted away.
Terror and dread fell on them. By the greatness of your arm they were still as a stone, until your people passed by, LORD, until the people you acquired passed by.
You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your own possession, the place, LORD, that you made for your dwelling, the sanctuary, Lord, that your hands established.
The LORD will reign for ever and ever."
When Pharaoh's horses, with his chariots and his horsemen, went into the sea, the LORD brought the waters of the sea back over them. But the Israelites walked on dry ground through the sea.
Then the prophet Miriam, Aaron's sister, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dancing.
Miriam answered them: "Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously. Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea."
Then Moses led Israel on from the Red Sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur. They travelled for three days in the wilderness and found no water.
When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter. That is why it was named Marah.
The people grumbled against Moses and said, "What shall we drink?"

He cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a piece of wood. He threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There the LORD set down a rule and a ruling for them, and there he tested them.

He said, "If you will listen closely to the voice of the LORD your God, and do what is right in his eyes, and give ear to his commands and keep all his rules, I will not put on you any of the diseases that I put on the Egyptians, for I am the LORD, your healer."
Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there beside the water.
The whole assembly of Israel journeyed from Elim and reached the wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after their departure from Egypt.
There in the wilderness the whole assembly murmured against Moses and Aaron.

"If only the LORD had put us to death in Egypt!" the Israelites said to them. "There we sat by the meat-pots and ate bread to our fill. But you have led us out into this wilderness to starve the entire gathering to death."

The LORD said to Moses, "Watch: I am going to make bread rain down from the sky for you. The people are to go out and gather their portion for each day, so that I can test whether they will walk by my teaching or not.
On the sixth day, when they prepare what they have brought in, it will be double what they gather on the other days."
Moses and Aaron said to all the Israelites, "By evening you will know that it was the LORD who brought you out of Egypt,
and by morning you will see the LORD's glory, for he has heard your murmuring against him. And who are we, that you murmur against us?"

Moses went on, "It will be when the LORD gives you meat to eat in the evening and bread to fill you in the morning, because the LORD has heard the murmuring you direct at him. Who are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against the LORD."
Moses said to Aaron, "Tell the whole assembly of Israel: 'Come forward before the LORD, for he has heard your murmuring.'"
While Aaron was speaking to the whole assembly of Israel, they turned towards the wilderness, and there the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud.
The LORD spoke to Moses:
"I have heard the murmuring of the Israelites. Tell them: 'As evening falls you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God.'"
That evening a flock of quail flew in and covered the camp, and in the morning a layer of dew lay around the camp.
When the layer of dew had evaporated, there on the desert floor lay something fine and flaky, thin as hoarfrost on the earth.
The Israelites saw it and asked one another, "What is it?" For they did not know what it was. Moses told them, "This is the bread the LORD has given you for food.
This is what the LORD has commanded: each of you is to gather according to what he can eat, an omer a head, by the number of persons in your tent."
The Israelites did this. Some gathered a lot and some a little,
and when they measured it by the omer, the one who had gathered a lot had no surplus, and the one who had gathered a little had no shortfall. Each had gathered what he could eat.
Moses said to them, "No one is to leave any of it until morning."
But some paid no attention to Moses and left some until morning, and it crawled with maggots and stank, and Moses was furious with them.
They gathered it morning after morning, each according to what he could eat, and when the sun grew hot, it melted away.
On the sixth day they gathered a double portion of food, two omers each, and all the community's leaders came and reported it to Moses.

He told them, "This is what the LORD said: Tomorrow is a day of rest, a holy Sabbath for the LORD. Bake what you will bake and boil what you will boil, and put aside all that is left over, to keep until morning."
They put it aside until morning, as Moses had commanded, and it did not stink, nor did maggots appear in it.
"Eat it today," Moses said, "for today is a Sabbath for the LORD. Today you will find none in the field.
For six days you may gather it, but the seventh day is the Sabbath. On it there will be none."
Even so, some of the people went out on the seventh day to gather, and found nothing.
The LORD said to Moses, "How long will you people refuse to keep my commands and my teachings?
Remember that the LORD has given you the Sabbath. That is why on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. On the seventh day everyone is to stay in place. No one is to leave his spot."
So the people rested on the seventh day.
The house of Israel named it manna. It was white like coriander seed, and tasted like honey wafers.
Moses said, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Fill an omer with it, to be kept for your descendants, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of Egypt.'"
Moses told Aaron, "Take a jar and put an omer of manna in it, and set it down before the LORD, to be kept for your descendants."
As the LORD had commanded Moses, Aaron set it down before the Testimony for safekeeping.
The Israelites ate manna for forty years, until they reached inhabited land. They ate manna until they came to the edge of Canaan.
(An omer is a tenth of an ephah.)
The whole assembly of Israel travelled on from the wilderness of Sin, stage by stage, at the LORD's command, and camped at Rephidim. But there was no water there for the people to drink.
The people took Moses to task: "Give us water to drink!" Moses answered, "Why take me to task? Why put the LORD to the test?"
But the people were parched with thirst there, and they murmured against Moses: "Why did you bring us up from Egypt? To kill us, our children and our livestock with thirst?"
Moses cried out to the LORD, "What can I do with these people? Any moment now they will stone me!"
The LORD said to Moses, "Pass on ahead of the people, and take some of the elders of Israel with you. Take along the staff you struck the Nile with, and go.
I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will come out of it for the people to drink." Moses did so in front of the elders of Israel.
He named the place Massah and Meribah, because of the Israelites' quarrelling and because they put the LORD to the test, asking, "Is the LORD among us or not?"
Amalek came and attacked Israel at Rephidim.
Moses said to Joshua, "Pick men for us and go out to fight Amalek. Tomorrow I will take my stand on the hilltop, with God's staff in my hand."
Joshua did as Moses had told him and fought Amalek, while Moses, Aaron and Hur climbed to the top of the hill.
Whenever Moses raised his hand, Israel was winning. Whenever he lowered it, Amalek was winning.
Moses' hands grew heavy, so they took a stone and set it beneath him, and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on each side, and so his hands stayed steady until sunset.
Joshua cut Amalek and his people down with the sword.
The LORD said to Moses, "Write this down in a scroll as a reminder, and recite it to Joshua: I will utterly wipe out the memory of Amalek from under the sky."
Moses built an altar and named it "The LORD is my Banner."
He said, "A hand is raised against the throne of the LORD! The LORD will be at war with Amalek from generation to generation."
