From the tribes of Judah and Simeon they gave the following towns, named here,
for the descendants of Aaron who were of the Kohathite clans of the Levites, because the first lot fell to them:
they gave them Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), with its pasture lands round it, in the hill country of Judah. (Arba was the father of Anak.)
But the fields and villages of the town they had given to Caleb son of Jephunneh as his possession.
To the descendants of Aaron the priest they gave Hebron (a city of refuge for the one who killed), Libnah,
Jattir, Eshtemoa,
Holon, Debir,
Ain, Juttah and Beth-shemesh, with their pasture lands: nine towns from these two tribes.
From the tribe of Benjamin they gave Gibeon, Geba,
Anathoth and Almon, with their pasture lands: four towns.
The towns of the priests, the descendants of Aaron, came to thirteen in all, with their pasture lands.
The rest of the Kohathite clans of the Levites received towns by lot from the tribe of Ephraim.
In the hill country of Ephraim they were given Shechem (a city of refuge for the one who killed), Gezer,
Kibzaim and Beth-horon, with their pasture lands: four towns.
From the tribe of Dan they received Eltekeh, Gibbethon,
Aijalon and Gath-rimmon, with their pasture lands: four towns.
From half the tribe of Manasseh they received Taanach and Gath-rimmon, with their pasture lands: two towns.
All these ten towns with their pasture lands were for the rest of the Kohathite clans.
The Gershonite clans of the Levites received from the half-tribe of Manasseh Golan in Bashan (a city of refuge for the one who killed) and Be-eshterah, with their pasture lands: two towns;
from the tribe of Issachar, Kishion, Daberath,
Jarmuth and En-gannim, with their pasture lands: four towns;
from the tribe of Asher, Mishal, Abdon,
Helkath and Rehob, with their pasture lands: four towns;
from the tribe of Naphtali, Kedesh in Galilee (a city of refuge for the one who killed), Hammoth-dor and Kartan, with their pasture lands: three towns.
The towns of the Gershonite clans came to thirteen in all, with their pasture lands.
The Merarite clans (the rest of the Levites) received from the tribe of Zebulun Jokneam, Kartah,
Dimnah and Nahalal, with their pasture lands: four towns;
from the tribe of Reuben, Bezer, Jahaz,
Kedemoth and Mephaath, with their pasture lands: four towns;
from the tribe of Gad, Ramoth in Gilead (a city of refuge for the one who killed), Mahanaim,
Heshbon and Jazer, with their pasture lands: four towns in all.
All the towns for the Merarite clans, the rest of the Levite clans, came to twelve by their lot.
The towns of the Levites within the possession of the Israelites were forty-eight in all, with their pasture lands.
Each of these towns had its own pasture lands round it. That was so for all these towns.
So the LORD gave Israel all the land that he had sworn to give to their ancestors, and they took possession of it and settled there.
The LORD gave them rest on every side, as he had sworn to their ancestors. Not one of all their enemies stood against them. The LORD handed all their enemies over to them.
Not one of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel failed. All came to pass.
Then Joshua called the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh
and said to them, "You have kept all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, and you have listened to my voice in everything I commanded you.
You have not abandoned your kinsmen all these many days, to this day, but have kept the charge of the command of the LORD your God.

Now the LORD your God has given rest to your kinsmen, as he promised them. So now turn and go to your tents, to the land of your possession that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you across the Jordan.

Only take great care to do the command and the teaching that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you: to love the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commands, to hold fast to him and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul."
So Joshua blessed them and sent them away, and they went to their tents.

(To one half of the tribe of Manasseh Moses had given a possession in Bashan, but to the other half Joshua had given a possession among their kinsmen west of the Jordan.) When Joshua sent them away to their tents and blessed them,

he said to them, "Go back to your tents with great wealth, with very many livestock, with silver, gold, bronze and iron, and a very large amount of clothing. Share the plunder from your enemies with your kinsmen."

So the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh went back, leaving the Israelites at Shiloh in the land of Canaan, to go to the land of Gilead, the land of their own possession, which they had taken in keeping with the command of the LORD through Moses.
When they came to the region of the Jordan in the land of Canaan, the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh built an altar there beside the Jordan, an altar of impressive size.

The Israelites heard it said, "Look, the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh have built an altar at the edge of the land of Canaan, in the region of the Jordan, on the side that belongs to the Israelites."
When the Israelites heard this, the whole community of the Israelites gathered at Shiloh to go up against them in war.
Then the Israelites sent Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh in the land of Gilead,
and with him ten chiefs, one chief for each ancestral house of the tribes of Israel, each of them the head of an ancestral house among the clans of Israel.
They came to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh in the land of Gilead and said to them:

"This is what the whole community of the LORD says: What is this breach of faith that you have committed against the God of Israel, turning away today from following the LORD by building yourselves an altar, in rebellion against the LORD today?
Was the sin at Peor too little for us? We have not cleansed ourselves from it to this day, though a plague came on the community of the LORD,
and now you are turning away today from following the LORD! If you rebel against the LORD today, tomorrow he will be angry with the whole community of Israel.

But if the land of your possession is unclean, cross over into the land that belongs to the LORD, where the LORD's tabernacle stands, and take a possession among us. Only do not rebel against the LORD, and do not rebel against us by building yourselves an altar other than the altar of the LORD our God.
Did not Achan son of Zerah break faith over what was devoted, and wrath fell on the whole community of Israel? He was not the only one to die for his sin."
Then the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh answered the heads of the clans of Israel:
"The Mighty One, God, the LORD! The Mighty One, God, the LORD! He knows, and may Israel know too. If it was in rebellion or in breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today

for building an altar to turn away from following the LORD. If we built it to offer burnt offerings or grain offerings on it, or to make peace offerings on it, may the LORD himself call us to account.
No, we did it out of fear of what might be said. In time to come your children might say to our children, 'What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel?
The LORD has made the Jordan a border between us and you, you Reubenites and Gadites. You have no share in the LORD.' So your children might make our children stop fearing the LORD.
So we said, 'Let us act and build an altar, not for burnt offering and not for sacrifice,

but as a witness between us and you, and between the generations after us, that we do serve the LORD in his presence with our burnt offerings, our sacrifices and our peace offerings. Then in time to come your children will not say to our children, "You have no share in the LORD."'

And we said, 'If they should ever say this to us or to our descendants, we will say: Look at the copy of the altar of the LORD that our ancestors made, not for burnt offerings and not for sacrifice, but as a witness between us and you.'

Far be it from us to rebel against the LORD and turn away today from following the LORD by building an altar for burnt offering, grain offering or sacrifice, other than the altar of the LORD our God that stands before his tabernacle."

When Phinehas the priest and the chiefs of the community, the heads of the clans of Israel who were with him, heard the words that the Reubenites, the Gadites and the Manassites spoke, they were satisfied.

Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest said to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the Manassites, "Today we know that the LORD is among us, because you have not committed this breach of faith against the LORD. Now you have saved the Israelites from the hand of the LORD."
Then Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest and the chiefs returned from the Reubenites and the Gadites in the land of Gilead to the land of Canaan, to the Israelites, and brought back a report to them.
The report was good in the eyes of the Israelites. They blessed God, and spoke no more of going up against them in war to destroy the land where the Reubenites and the Gadites lived.
The Reubenites and the Gadites called the altar Witness, "For it is a witness between us that the LORD is God."
A long time after the LORD had given Israel rest from all their enemies around them, when Joshua was old and well advanced in years,
Joshua called all Israel, their elders, their heads, their judges and their officers, and said to them: "I am old and well advanced in years.
You have seen everything the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, for it is the LORD your God who has fought for you.
See, I have allotted to you as an inheritance for your tribes the nations that remain, as well as all the nations I have cut off, from the Jordan to the Great Sea in the west.
The LORD your God himself will push them back before you and drive them out ahead of you, and you will take possession of their land, as the LORD your God promised you.
So be very strong, to keep and to do all that is written in the book of the teaching of Moses, without turning aside from it to the right or to the left,
so that you do not mix with these nations that remain among you, or mention the names of their gods, or swear by them, or serve them or bow down to them,
but hold fast to the LORD your God, as you have done to this day.
For the LORD has driven out great and strong nations before you, and to this day no one has been able to stand against you.
One of you chases a thousand, because it is the LORD your God who fights for you, as he promised you.
So take great care, for your own lives, to love the LORD your God.
For if you turn back and attach yourselves to the survivors of these nations that remain among you, and intermarry with them, and mix with them and they with you,

know for certain that the LORD your God will not go on driving out these nations before you. They will become a snare and a trap for you, a whip on your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from this good land that the LORD your God has given you.

Now I am about to go the way of all the earth. You know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good words that the LORD your God spoke about you. All have come to pass for you. Not one of them has failed.

But just as all the good words that the LORD your God spoke to you have come to pass, so the LORD will bring on you every evil word, until he has destroyed you from this good land that the LORD your God has given you,

if you break the covenant of the LORD your God, which he commanded you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them. Then the anger of the LORD will blaze against you, and you will quickly perish from the good land that he has given you."
Then Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel at Shechem. He called the elders, the heads, the judges and the officers of Israel, and they presented themselves before God.
Joshua said to all the people, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'Long ago your ancestors lived beyond the River, Terah, the father of Abraham and of Nahor, and they served other gods.
Then I took your father Abraham from beyond the River and led him through all the land of Canaan, and I made his descendants many. I gave him Isaac.
To Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. To Esau I gave the hill country of Seir as a possession, but Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt.
I sent Moses and Aaron, and I struck Egypt with what I did in the middle of it, and afterwards I brought you out.
I brought your ancestors out of Egypt, and you came to the sea. The Egyptians chased your ancestors with chariots and horsemen as far as the Red Sea.

When they cried out to the LORD, he put darkness between you and the Egyptians, and made the sea come over them and cover them. Your own eyes saw what I did in Egypt. Then you lived in the wilderness for a long time.
I brought you to the land of the Amorites who lived across the Jordan. They fought against you, and I handed them over to you, and you took possession of their land. I destroyed them before you.
Then Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, got up and fought against Israel. He sent and called Balaam son of Beor to curse you,
but I would not listen to Balaam, so he blessed you instead. So I saved you from his hand.

You crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho, and the citizens of Jericho fought against you, and also the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Hivites and the Jebusites. I handed them over to you.
I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove them out before you, the two kings of the Amorites. It was not by your sword or your bow.
I gave you a land on which you had not worked, and towns that you had not built, and you live in them. You eat from vineyards and olive groves that you did not plant.'
"So now fear the LORD and serve him completely and faithfully. Put away the gods that your ancestors served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD.

If it seems wrong to you to serve the LORD, choose today whom you will serve, whether the gods your ancestors served beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living. But as for me and my household, we will serve the LORD."
The people answered, "Far be it from us to abandon the LORD and serve other gods.

For it is the LORD our God who brought us and our ancestors up out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, and who did those great signs before our eyes, and protected us all along the way we went and among all the peoples we passed through.
The LORD drove out before us all the peoples, the Amorites who lived in the land. We too will serve the LORD, for he is our God."
But Joshua said to the people, "You cannot serve the LORD, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God. He will not forgive your rebellion or your sins.
If you abandon the LORD and serve foreign gods, he will turn and bring harm on you, and finish you off, after having done you good."
The people said to Joshua, "No, we will serve the LORD."
Joshua said to the people, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the LORD for yourselves, to serve him." They said, "We are witnesses."
"Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and turn your hearts to the LORD, the God of Israel."
The people said to Joshua, "We will serve the LORD our God, and we will listen to his voice."
So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and set down a statute and a ruling for them at Shechem.
Joshua wrote these words in the book of the teaching of God. He took a large stone and set it up there under the oak that was by the sanctuary of the LORD.

Joshua said to all the people, "See, this stone will be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words of the LORD that he spoke to us. It will be a witness against you, so that you do not deny your God."
Then Joshua sent the people away, each to his own inheritance.
After these things Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of a hundred and ten.
They buried him in the land of his own inheritance at Timnath-serah, which is in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.
Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua and who knew all that the LORD had done for Israel.

The bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up from Egypt, they buried at Shechem, in the plot of ground that Jacob had bought from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred pieces of silver. It became the inheritance of the descendants of Joseph.
And Eleazar son of Aaron died, and they buried him at Gibeah, which belonged to his son Phinehas, which had been given to him in the hill country of Ephraim.
After the death of Joshua, the Israelites asked the LORD, "Who is to go up first for us against the Canaanites, to fight against them?"
The LORD said, "Judah is to go up. See, I have given the land into his hand."

Judah said to his brother Simeon, "Come up with me into the territory allotted to me, so that we may fight against the Canaanites. Then I will go with you into the territory allotted to you." So Simeon went with him.
Judah went up, and the LORD gave the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hands, and they struck down ten thousand of them at Bezek.
They found Adoni-bezek at Bezek and fought against him, and they struck down the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
Adoni-bezek ran away, but they chased him and caught him and cut off his thumbs and his big toes.
Adoni-bezek said, "Seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off used to pick up scraps under my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me." They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.
The people of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it. They struck it down with the edge of the sword and set the city on fire.
Afterwards the people of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, in the Negev and in the lowland.
Judah marched against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron (formerly called Kiriath-arba) and struck down Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai.
From there they marched against the people of Debir (formerly called Kiriath-sepher).
Caleb said, "I will give my daughter Achsah as a wife to the man who attacks and captures Kiriath-sepher."
Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, captured it, and Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as a wife.
When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. She got down from her donkey, and Caleb asked her, "What do you want?"
She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me also springs of water." So Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
The descendants of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, went up with the people of Judah from the City of Palms into the wilderness of Judah, in the Negev near Arad, and went and lived among the people.
Judah went with his brother Simeon, and they struck down the Canaanites who lived in Zephath and devoted it to destruction. So the town was called Hormah.
Judah also took Gaza with its territory, Ashkelon with its territory and Ekron with its territory.
The LORD was with Judah. They took possession of the hill country, but they could not drive out the people of the plain, because they had iron chariots.
As Moses had promised, Hebron was given to Caleb, who drove out from it the three sons of Anak.
The Benjaminites did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem. To this day the Jebusites live with the Benjaminites in Jerusalem.
The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and the LORD was with them.
The house of Joseph sent men to spy out Bethel (the town was formerly called Luz).
The spies saw a man coming out of the town and said to him, "Show us the way into the town, and we will deal kindly with you."
He showed them the way into the town, and they struck the town down with the edge of the sword, but they let the man and all his family go.
The man went to the land of the Hittites and built a town and named it Luz, which is its name to this day.

Manasseh did not drive out the people of Beth-shean and its villages, or Taanach and its villages, or the people of Dor and its villages, or the people of Ibleam and its villages, or the people of Megiddo and its villages, for the Canaanites were determined to stay in that land.
When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labour, but did not drive them out completely.
Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites lived among them in Gezer.
Zebulun did not drive out the people of Kitron or the people of Nahalol, so the Canaanites lived among them, but they became forced labourers.
Asher did not drive out the people of Acco, or the people of Sidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphek or Rehob.
So the Asherites lived among the Canaanites who lived in the land, for they did not drive them out.

Naphtali did not drive out the people of Beth-shemesh or the people of Beth-anath, but lived among the Canaanites who lived in the land. The people of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath became forced labourers for them.
The Amorites pressed the Danites back into the hill country, for they did not let them come down into the plain.
The Amorites were determined to stay in Mount Heres, in Aijalon and in Shaalbim, but when the house of Joseph grew strong, they too were put to forced labour.
The border of the Amorites ran from the ascent of Akrabbim, from Sela and upwards.

The angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim and said, "I brought you up out of Egypt and led you into the land that I swore to give to your ancestors. I said, 'I will never break my covenant with you.
You are not to make a covenant with the people of this land. You are to tear down their altars.' But you have not listened to my voice. What is this that you have done?
So now I say: I will not drive them out before you. They will be thorns in your sides, and their gods will be a snare to you."
When the angel of the LORD spoke these words to all the Israelites, the people raised their voices and wept.
So they called that place Bochim, and there they sacrificed to the LORD.
When Joshua had sent the people away, the Israelites went each to his own inheritance to take possession of the land.
The people served the LORD all the days of Joshua and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work that the LORD had done for Israel.
Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of a hundred and ten.
They buried him in the land of his own inheritance, at Timnath-heres in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.
That whole generation was also gathered to their ancestors. Another generation grew up after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel.
The Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD and served the Baals.

They abandoned the LORD, the God of their ancestors, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They followed other gods, from among the gods of the peoples around them, and bowed down to them. They made the LORD angry.
They abandoned the LORD and served Baal and the Ashtoreths.
The anger of the LORD blazed against Israel, and he handed them over to raiders who plundered them. He sold them into the hands of their enemies all round, whom they could no longer stand against.
Whenever they went out, the hand of the LORD was against them for harm, as the LORD had warned and had sworn to them. They were in great distress.
Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them from the hands of those who plundered them.

Yet they did not listen to their judges, for they prostituted themselves to other gods and bowed down to them. They quickly turned from the way that their ancestors had walked, in obedience to the commands of the LORD. They did not do as their ancestors had done.

Whenever the LORD raised up judges for them, the LORD was with the judge and saved them from the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge, for the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who oppressed and crushed them.

But when the judge died, they would turn back and act even more corruptly than their ancestors, following other gods, serving them and bowing down to them. They would not give up their evil practices or their stubborn ways.
So the anger of the LORD blazed against Israel, and he said, "Because this people has broken my covenant that I commanded their ancestors, and has not listened to my voice,
I too will no longer drive out before them any of the nations that Joshua left when he died,
so that by them I may test Israel, to see whether they will keep the way of the LORD and walk in it, as their ancestors did."
So the LORD left those nations. He did not drive them out at once, and he did not hand them over to Joshua.
These are the nations that the LORD left, to test all those in Israel who had not experienced any of the wars of Canaan.
(This was only so that the generations of the Israelites might know war, at least those who had not known it before.)
These were the five rulers of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites living in the hill country of Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon to Lebo-hamath.
They were left to test Israel, to find out whether they would listen to the commands of the LORD that he gave to their ancestors through Moses.
So the Israelites lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites.
They took their daughters as wives for themselves, and gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods.
The Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD. They forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs.
The anger of the LORD blazed against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram-naharaim, and the Israelites served Cushan-rishathaim for eight years.
When the Israelites cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer for the Israelites, who saved them: Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.
The spirit of the LORD came on him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and the LORD gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram into his hand, and he overpowered Cushan-rishathaim.
The land had rest for forty years. Then Othniel son of Kenaz died.
The Israelites again did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD made Eglon king of Moab strong against Israel, because they had done what was evil in the eyes of the LORD.
Eglon gathered the Ammonites and the Amalekites to himself, and went and struck Israel down, and they took possession of the City of Palms.
The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years.
When the Israelites cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer for them, Ehud son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a left-handed man. The Israelites sent tribute by him to Eglon king of Moab.
Ehud made himself a double-edged sword, a cubit long, and strapped it on his right thigh under his clothes.
He presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.
When Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who had carried it.
But he himself turned back at the carved stones near Gilgal and said, "I have a secret word for you, O king." The king said, "Silence." All those standing by him left him.
Ehud came to him as he was sitting alone in his cool upper room. Ehud said, "I have a word from God for you." And the king rose from his seat.
Ehud reached out with his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh and thrust it into his belly.
Even the hilt went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, for he did not pull the sword out of his belly. And the filth came out.
Then Ehud went out through the porch and shut the doors of the upper room on him and locked them.
When he had gone, the servants came and looked, and the doors of the upper room were locked. They said, "He must be relieving himself in the cool chamber."
They waited until they were embarrassed. But when he still did not open the doors of the upper room, they took the key and opened them, and there was their lord lying dead on the floor.
Ehud got away while they delayed. He passed the carved stones and escaped to Seirah.
When he arrived, he blew the trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites went down with him from the hill country, with him at their head.
He said to them, "Follow me, for the LORD has given your enemies the Moabites into your hands." They went down after him and seized the fords of the Jordan against Moab, and let no one cross over.
At that time they struck down about ten thousand Moabites, all strong and able-bodied men. Not one escaped.
So Moab was brought under the hand of Israel that day. And the land had rest for eighty years.
After him came Shamgar son of Anath, who struck down six hundred Philistines with an ox-goad. He too saved Israel.
The Israelites again did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD, after Ehud died.
So the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who ruled in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-haggoyim.
The Israelites cried out to the LORD, for Jabin had nine hundred iron chariots and had oppressed the Israelites harshly for twenty years.
Now Deborah, a prophet, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time.
She used to sit under the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites came up to her for judgement.

She sent and called Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and said to him, "The LORD, the God of Israel, commands you: 'Go, take up your position on Mount Tabor, with ten thousand men from Naphtali and Zebulun.
I will draw out Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army, to you at the Wadi Kishon, with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand.'"
Barak said to her, "If you will go with me, I will go. But if you will not go with me, I will not go."

She said, "I will certainly go with you. But the road you are taking will not bring you glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." So Deborah got up and went with Barak to Kedesh.
Barak called Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh, and ten thousand men went up behind him, and Deborah went up with him.
Now Heber the Kenite had separated from the other Kenites, the descendants of Hobab, Moses' father-in-law, and had pitched his tent as far away as the oak of Zaanannim, which is near Kedesh.
When Sisera was told that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor,
Sisera called out all his chariots, nine hundred iron chariots, and all the men with him, from Harosheth-haggoyim to the Wadi Kishon.

Deborah said to Barak, "Up. This is the day on which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Has the LORD not gone out ahead of you?" So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men behind him.
The LORD threw Sisera and all his chariots and all his army into confusion before Barak, at the edge of the sword. Sisera got down from his chariot and ran away on foot.
Barak chased the chariots and the army as far as Harosheth-haggoyim, and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword. Not one was left.
But Sisera ran away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the household of Heber the Kenite.
Jael went out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Turn aside, my lord, turn aside to me. Do not be afraid." So he turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with a rug.
He said to her, "Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty." She opened a skin of milk and gave him a drink, and covered him.
He said to her, "Stand at the entrance of the tent, and if anyone comes and asks you, 'Is there a man here?' say, 'No.'"
But Jael wife of Heber took a tent peg and picked up a hammer. She went quietly to him and drove the peg through his temple and into the ground, as he lay fast asleep, exhausted. So he died.

Just then Barak came, chasing Sisera, and Jael went out to meet him and said to him, "Come, and I will show you the man you are looking for." He went in to her, and there lay Sisera dead, with the tent peg through his temple.
So on that day God brought Jabin king of Canaan down before the Israelites.
The hand of the Israelites pressed harder and harder against Jabin king of Canaan, until they had destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang:
When the leaders took the lead in Israel, when the people gave themselves willingly, bless the LORD.
Hear, you kings. Listen, you rulers. I will sing to the LORD, I, I will make music to the LORD, the God of Israel.
LORD, when you came out from Seir, when you marched from the fields of Edom, the earth shook, and the heavens poured down, the clouds poured down water.
The mountains flowed before the LORD, the One of Sinai, before the LORD, the God of Israel.
In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways stood empty, and travellers went by roundabout paths.
Village life stopped in Israel. It stopped, until you arose, Deborah, until you arose, a mother in Israel.
They chose new gods, then war was at the gates. Was a shield or spear to be seen among forty thousand in Israel?
My heart is with the commanders of Israel, with those who gave themselves willingly among the people. Bless the LORD.
You who ride on tawny donkeys, you who sit on saddle rugs, and you who walk on the road, tell of it.

Far from the sound of the archers, at the watering places, there they recite the righteous acts of the LORD, his righteous acts for the villages of Israel. Then the people of the LORD went down to the gates.
Wake up, wake up, Deborah. Wake up, wake up, sing a song. Get up, Barak, and lead away your captives, son of Abinoam.
Then a remnant came down to the nobles, the people of the LORD came down for me against the mighty.
From Ephraim they came down into the valley, behind you, Benjamin, with your clans. From Machir the commanders came down, and from Zebulun those who carry the marshal's staff.
The princes of Issachar were with Deborah, and Issachar was with Barak. Into the valley they were sent at his heels. Among the clans of Reuben there was great searching of heart.
Why did you stay among the sheepfolds, listening to the pipes calling the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there was great searching of heart.
Gilead stayed across the Jordan. And Dan, why did he linger by the ships? Asher sat still at the shore of the sea and stayed by his harbours.
Zebulun was a people who risked their lives to the death, and Naphtali, on the heights of the field.
Kings came and fought. Then the kings of Canaan fought, at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo. They took no plunder of silver.
From heaven the stars fought. From their courses they fought against Sisera.
The Wadi Kishon swept them away, the ancient wadi, the Wadi Kishon. March on, my soul, with strength.
Then the horses' hooves pounded, the galloping, galloping of his stallions.
"Curse Meroz," said the angel of the LORD. "Curse its people with a curse, because they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty."
Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, most blessed of tent-dwelling women.
He asked for water, and she gave him milk. In a noble's bowl she brought him curds.
Her hand reached for the tent peg, her right hand for the workman's hammer. She struck Sisera, she crushed his head, she shattered and pierced his temple.
Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay. Between her feet he sank, he fell. Where he sank, there he fell, destroyed.
Through the window she looked out, Sisera's mother cried through the lattice: "Why is his chariot so slow to come? Why are the hoofbeats of his chariots delayed?"
The wisest of her princesses answer, and she gives herself the same answer:

"Are they not finding and dividing the spoil? A girl or two for every man, spoil of dyed cloth for Sisera, spoil of dyed cloth, embroidered, a dyed and embroidered cloth for the neck of the plunderer."
So may all your enemies perish, LORD. But may those who love him be like the sun going out in its strength.
And the land had rest for forty years.
The Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD handed them over to Midian for seven years.
The hand of Midian was strong against Israel. Because of Midian the Israelites made for themselves the hideouts in the mountains, the caves and the strongholds.
Whenever the Israelites sowed seed, the Midianites, the Amalekites and the people of the east would come up against them.
They camped against them and destroyed the produce of the land as far as Gaza, and left nothing for Israel to live on, no sheep, ox or donkey.
They came up with their livestock and their tents, as thick as locusts. They and their camels could not be counted, and they came into the land to destroy it.
Israel was brought very low because of Midian, and the Israelites cried out to the LORD.
When the Israelites cried out to the LORD because of Midian,
the LORD sent a prophet to the Israelites. He said to them, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I brought you up out of Egypt, and I brought you out of the house of slavery.
I rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all who oppressed you. I drove them out before you and gave you their land.
I said to you, 'I am the LORD your God. You are not to fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you live.' But you have not listened to my voice."
The angel of the LORD came and sat under the oak at Ophrah that belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, while his son Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress, to hide it from the Midianites.
The angel of the LORD appeared to him and said, "The LORD is with you, mighty warrior."

Gideon said to him, "Please, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us? Where are all his wonders that our ancestors told us about, saying, 'Did the LORD not bring us up out of Egypt?' But now the LORD has abandoned us and handed us over to Midian."
The LORD turned to him and said, "Go in this strength of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Am I not sending you?"
He said to him, "Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father's house."
The LORD said to him, "But I will be with you, and you will strike down Midian as if it were one man."
He said to him, "If I have found favour in your eyes, give me a sign that it is you who are speaking with me.
Please do not leave here until I come back to you and bring out my gift and set it before you." And he said, "I will stay until you return."
Gideon went in and prepared a young goat and unleavened bread from an ephah of flour. He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot, and brought them out to him under the oak and presented them.
The angel of God said to him, "Take the meat and the unleavened bread and put them on this rock, and pour the broth over them." And he did so.

The angel of the LORD put out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened bread. Fire came up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread, and the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight.
Then Gideon saw that he was the angel of the LORD. Gideon said, "Alas, Lord GOD, for I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face."
But the LORD said to him, "Peace to you. Do not be afraid. You will not die."
Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and called it The LORD Is Peace. It is still at Ophrah of the Abiezrites to this day.
That night the LORD said to him, "Take your father's bull, the second bull, seven years old, and pull down the altar of Baal that belongs to your father, and cut down the Asherah beside it.
Then build an altar to the LORD your God on top of this stronghold, in the proper way. Take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah that you cut down."
So Gideon took ten of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his household and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night.
When the men of the town got up early in the morning, there was the altar of Baal torn down, and the Asherah beside it cut down, and the second bull offered on the altar that had been built.
They said to one another, "Who did this?" After they had searched and asked, they were told, "Gideon son of Joash did it."
Then the men of the town said to Joash, "Bring out your son, so that he may die, for he has pulled down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah beside it."

But Joash said to all who stood against him, "Will you defend Baal? Will you save him? Whoever defends him will be put to death by morning. If he is a god, let him defend himself, because his altar has been torn down."
So on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, meaning "Let Baal defend himself against him," because he had torn down his altar.
All the Midianites, the Amalekites and the people of the east gathered together, crossed the Jordan and camped in the Valley of Jezreel.
But the spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, and he blew the trumpet, and the Abiezrites were called to follow him.
He sent messengers throughout Manasseh, and they too were called to follow him. He also sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali, and they came up to meet them.
Then Gideon said to God, "If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said,

look, I am putting a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I will know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said."
And it was so. When he got up early the next morning and squeezed the fleece, he wrung out the dew from the fleece, a bowlful of water.

Then Gideon said to God, "Do not let your anger blaze against me. Let me speak just once more. Let me test just once more with the fleece. Let it be dry on the fleece alone, and let there be dew on all the ground."
And God did so that night. It was dry on the fleece alone, and there was dew on all the ground.
Jerubbaal, that is Gideon, and all the people with him got up early and camped beside the spring of Harod. The camp of Midian was north of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley.
The LORD said to Gideon, "There are too many people with you for me to hand the Midianites over to them, or Israel will boast against me and say, 'My own hand has saved me.'
So now announce to the people, 'Whoever is afraid and trembling may turn back and leave Mount Gilead.'" Twenty-two thousand of the people turned back, and ten thousand were left.

The LORD said to Gideon, "There are still too many people. Take them down to the water, and I will sift them for you there. Whoever I say to you, 'This one will go with you,' he is to go with you. And whoever I say to you, 'This one will not go with you,' he is not to go."

So he took the people down to the water. The LORD said to Gideon, "Everyone who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you are to set apart by himself. Do the same with everyone who kneels down to drink."
The number of those who lapped, bringing their hands to their mouths, was three hundred men. All the rest of the people knelt down to drink water.
The LORD said to Gideon, "With the three hundred men who lapped I will save you and hand the Midianites over to you. Let all the others go home."

So the people took the food and the trumpets in their hands, and Gideon sent all the other Israelites home, each to his tent, but kept the three hundred. The camp of Midian was below him in the valley.
That night the LORD said to him, "Get up and go down against the camp, for I have handed it over to you.
But if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with your servant Purah,
and listen to what they say. After that you will be strengthened, and you will go down against the camp." So he went down with his servant Purah to the edge of the armed men in the camp.
The Midianites, the Amalekites and all the people of the east lay in the valley as thick as locusts, and their camels could not be counted, as many as the sand on the seashore.

When Gideon came, there was a man telling a dream to his friend. He said, "I had a dream. A loaf of barley bread was rolling into the camp of Midian. It came to the tent and struck it so that it fell, and turned it upside down, and the tent collapsed."
His friend answered, "This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, a man of Israel. God has handed Midian and all the camp over to him."
When Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its meaning, he bowed down in worship. He went back to the camp of Israel and said, "Get up, for the LORD has handed the camp of Midian over to you."
He divided the three hundred men into three companies, and put trumpets in the hands of all of them, and empty jars with torches inside the jars.
He said to them, "Watch me and do as I do. When I come to the edge of the camp, do as I do.
When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, you also blow the trumpets all round the whole camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"

Gideon and the hundred men with him came to the edge of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, just after the guard had been changed. They blew the trumpets and smashed the jars that were in their hands.
The three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars. They held the torches in their left hands and the trumpets in their right hands to blow, and shouted, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon."
Each man stood in his place round the camp, and the whole army ran. They shouted and fled.

When the three hundred trumpets sounded, the LORD set every man's sword against his friend and against the whole army. The army fled as far as Beth-shittah towards Zererah, as far as the border of Abel-meholah, by Tabbath.
The men of Israel were called out from Naphtali, Asher and all Manasseh, and they chased after Midian.

Gideon sent messengers throughout the hill country of Ephraim: "Come down against the Midianites and seize the waters ahead of them, as far as Beth-barah, and the Jordan also." So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they seized the waters as far as Beth-barah, and the Jordan also.

They captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb, as they chased Midian. They brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan.
The Ephraimites said to him, "What is this that you have done to us, not calling us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they quarrelled with him fiercely.
He said to them, "What have I done now compared with you? Is not the gleaning of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer?
God has handed the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, over to you. What have I been able to do compared with you?" When he said this, their anger against him cooled.
Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the three hundred men with him, worn out but still chasing.
He said to the men of Succoth, "Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me, for they are worn out, and I am chasing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian."
But the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?"
Gideon said, "Very well. When the LORD has handed Zebah and Zalmunna over to me, I will thresh your bodies with desert thorns and briers."
From there he went up to Penuel and spoke to them in the same way, and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered.
So he said to the men of Penuel, "When I come back safely, I will pull down this tower."

Now Zebah and Zalmunna were at Karkor with their army, about fifteen thousand men, all that were left of the whole army of the people of the east, for a hundred and twenty thousand men who drew the sword had fallen.
Gideon went up by the caravan route east of Nobah and Jogbehah and struck the camp, for the camp felt secure.
Zebah and Zalmunna ran away, and he chased them. He captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and threw the whole army into panic.
Gideon son of Joash came back from the battle by the ascent of Heres.
He caught a young man of Succoth and questioned him, and the young man wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth, seventy-seven men.

Then he came to the men of Succoth and said, "Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, 'Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your exhausted men?'"
He took the elders of the town and took desert thorns and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth a lesson.
He also pulled down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the town.
Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, "What were the men like whom you killed at Tabor?" They answered, "Like you. Each one looked like a king's son."
He said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had let them live, I would not kill you."
He said to Jether his firstborn, "Get up and kill them." But the boy did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a boy.

Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, "You get up and strike us, for a man is judged by his strength." So Gideon got up and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and took the crescent ornaments that were on the necks of their camels.
The men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian."
Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you. The LORD will rule over you."
Gideon said to them, "I have one request for you: each of you give me the earrings from his plunder." (The enemy had gold earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.)
They answered, "We will gladly give them." They spread out a cloak, and each man threw into it the earrings from his plunder.

The weight of the gold earrings that he asked for was seventeen hundred shekels of gold, not counting the crescents and the pendants and the purple garments worn by the kings of Midian, and not counting the chains that were round the necks of their camels.
Gideon made an ephod from it and put it in his town, in Ophrah. All Israel prostituted themselves to it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his household.
So Midian was brought low before the Israelites, and they raised their heads no more. And the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon.
Jerubbaal son of Joash went and lived in his own house.
Gideon had seventy sons, his own descendants, for he had many wives.
His concubine, who was in Shechem, also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech.
Gideon son of Joash died at a good old age and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
As soon as Gideon died, the Israelites turned again and prostituted themselves to the Baals, and made Baal-berith their god.
The Israelites did not remember the LORD their God, who had rescued them from the hand of all their enemies on every side,
and they did not show faithful love to the household of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) in return for all the good he had done for Israel.
Abimelech son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem, to his mother's brothers, and spoke to them and to the whole clan of his mother's family:

"Say in the hearing of all the lords of Shechem: Which is better for you, that seventy men, all the sons of Jerubbaal, rule over you, or that one man rules over you? Remember also that I am your own flesh and blood."
His mother's brothers spoke all these words about him in the hearing of all the lords of Shechem, and their hearts were drawn to follow Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother."
They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baal-berith, and Abimelech used it to hire worthless and reckless men, who followed him.
He went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers, the seventy sons of Jerubbaal, on one stone. But Jotham, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, survived, because he hid.
All the lords of Shechem and all Beth-millo gathered and made Abimelech king, by the oak of the pillar at Shechem.
When it was told to Jotham, he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim and shouted to them: "Listen to me, lords of Shechem, so that God may listen to you.
The trees once went out to anoint a king over them. They said to the olive tree, 'Be our king.'
But the olive tree said to them, 'Should I give up my oil, by which gods and people are honoured, and go to sway over the trees?'
So the trees said to the fig tree, 'Come and be our king.'
But the fig tree said to them, 'Should I give up my sweetness and my good fruit, and go to sway over the trees?'
So the trees said to the vine, 'Come and be our king.'
But the vine said to them, 'Should I give up my wine, which cheers gods and people, and go to sway over the trees?'
Finally all the trees said to the thornbush, 'Come and be our king.'
The thornbush said to the trees, 'If you really are anointing me king over you, come and take shelter in my shade. But if not, let fire come out from the thornbush and burn up the cedars of Lebanon.'
Now, if you acted honestly and with integrity when you made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his household and treated him as his deeds deserved
(for my father fought for you and risked his life and rescued you from the hand of Midian,

but today you have risen against my father's household and killed his sons, seventy men on one stone, and made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the lords of Shechem, because he is your kinsman),
if you have acted honestly and with integrity towards Jerubbaal and his household today, then rejoice in Abimelech, and may he rejoice in you.
But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and burn up the lords of Shechem and Beth-millo, and let fire come out from the lords of Shechem and Beth-millo and burn up Abimelech."
Then Jotham ran away and fled and went to Beer, and lived there, out of fear of his brother Abimelech.
Abimelech ruled over Israel for three years.
God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the lords of Shechem, and the lords of Shechem acted treacherously against Abimelech,

so that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come back, and their blood be laid on their brother Abimelech, who killed them, and on the lords of Shechem, who had strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.
The lords of Shechem set an ambush for him on the tops of the mountains, and they robbed everyone who passed by them on the road. It was reported to Abimelech.
Gaal son of Ebed came with his kinsmen and moved into Shechem, and the lords of Shechem put their trust in him.
They went out into the fields and gathered the grapes from their vineyards and trod them and held a festival. They went into the house of their god and ate and drank and cursed Abimelech.

Gaal son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Did not the son of Jerubbaal and his officer Zebul serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem? Why should we serve him?
If only this people were under my hand. Then I would remove Abimelech. I would say to Abimelech, 'Increase your army and come out.'"
When Zebul, the ruler of the city, heard the words of Gaal son of Ebed, he was furious.
He sent messengers to Abimelech secretly, saying, "Gaal son of Ebed and his kinsmen have come to Shechem, and they are stirring up the city against you.
So now, go by night, you and the people with you, and lie in ambush in the fields.
In the morning, as soon as the sun is up, get up early and attack the city. When he and the people with him come out against you, do to them whatever you can."
So Abimelech and all the people with him got up by night and lay in ambush against Shechem in four companies.
Gaal son of Ebed went out and stood at the entrance of the city gate, and Abimelech and the people with him rose from their ambush.
When Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the tops of the mountains." Zebul said to him, "You are seeing the shadows of the mountains as if they were men."
Gaal spoke again and said, "Look, people are coming down from the centre of the land, and one company is coming from the direction of the Diviners' Oak."
Then Zebul said to him, "Where is your mouth now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Are these not the people you despised? Go out now and fight them."
So Gaal went out at the head of the lords of Shechem and fought against Abimelech.
Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him. Many fell wounded, as far as the entrance of the gate.
Abimelech stayed at Arumah, and Zebul drove Gaal and his kinsmen out, so that they could not live in Shechem.
The next day the people went out into the field, and Abimelech was told.
He took his people and divided them into three companies and lay in ambush in the fields. When he saw the people coming out of the city, he rose against them and struck them down.
Abimelech and the company with him rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the city gate, while the other two companies rushed on all who were in the field and struck them down.
Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people in it. He pulled the city down and sowed it with salt.
When all the lords of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they went into the stronghold of the temple of El-berith.
Abimelech was told that all the lords of the Tower of Shechem had gathered together.

So Abimelech went up Mount Zalmon, he and all the people with him. Abimelech took an axe in his hand and cut down a branch from the trees and lifted it and put it on his shoulder. He said to the people with him, "What you have seen me do, hurry and do the same."

So each of the people cut down a branch and followed Abimelech, and put them against the stronghold, and set the stronghold on fire over them. So all the people of the Tower of Shechem died too, about a thousand men and women.
Then Abimelech went to Thebez and camped against Thebez and captured it.
There was a strong tower inside the city, and all the people of the city, men and women, fled to it and shut themselves in, and went up to the roof of the tower.
Abimelech came up to the tower and attacked it, and went close to the door of the tower to set it on fire.
But a woman threw an upper millstone down on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.

He quickly called his young man, his armour-bearer, and said to him, "Draw your sword and kill me, so that they will not say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" So his young man ran him through, and he died.
When the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, they went home, each to his own place.
So God repaid Abimelech for the evil that he did to his father by killing his seventy brothers.
God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem fall back on their own heads, and the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came on them.
After Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, rose to save Israel. He lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.
He judged Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried at Shamir.
After him came Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel for twenty-two years.
He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty towns, called Havvoth-jair to this day, which are in the land of Gilead.
Jair died and was buried at Kamon.

The Israelites again did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD. They served the Baals and the Ashtoreths, the gods of Aram, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites and the gods of the Philistines. They abandoned the LORD and did not serve him.
The anger of the LORD blazed against Israel, and he sold them into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites,
who shattered and crushed the Israelites that year. For eighteen years they oppressed all the Israelites who were across the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead.
The Ammonites also crossed the Jordan to fight against Judah, Benjamin and the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was in great distress.
The Israelites cried out to the LORD: "We have sinned against you, because we have abandoned our God and served the Baals."
The LORD said to the Israelites, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians, from the Amorites, from the Ammonites and from the Philistines?
When the Sidonians, the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you, and you cried out to me, did I not save you from their hand?
Yet you have abandoned me and served other gods. So I will not save you again.
Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen. Let them save you in your time of distress."
The Israelites said to the LORD, "We have sinned. Do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please rescue us today."
So they got rid of the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and he could bear Israel's misery no longer.
The Ammonites were called out and camped in Gilead, and the Israelites gathered and camped at Mizpah.
The people, the leaders of Gilead, said to one another, "Who is the man who will begin the fight against the Ammonites? He will be head over all who live in Gilead."
Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. Gilead was Jephthah's father.

Gilead's wife also bore him sons, and when his wife's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, "You will not inherit anything in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman."
So Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob, and worthless men gathered round Jephthah and went out raiding with him.
Some time later the Ammonites made war against Israel.
When the Ammonites made war against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah back from the land of Tob.
They said to Jephthah, "Come and be our commander, so that we may fight against the Ammonites."
But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now, when you are in trouble?"
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have come back to you now. Go with us and fight against the Ammonites, and you will be our head, over all who live in Gilead."
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you take me back to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD hands them over to me, I will be your head."
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "The LORD will be witness between us. We will certainly do as you say."
So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and commander over them. And Jephthah repeated all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.
Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites with the question: "What quarrel do you have with me, that you have come to fight against my land?"
The king of the Ammonites answered Jephthah's messengers, "When Israel came up from Egypt, they took my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan. Now give it back peacefully."
Jephthah sent messengers again to the king of the Ammonites
and said to him, "This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites.
When they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh.

Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom: 'Please let us pass through your land.' But the king of Edom would not listen. They also sent to the king of Moab, but he refused. So Israel stayed at Kadesh.

Then they went through the wilderness and round the land of Edom and the land of Moab, and came to the east side of the land of Moab and camped across the Arnon. They did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was the border of Moab.
Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, the king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to our own place.'
But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory. Sihon gathered all his people, camped at Jahaz and fought against Israel.
The LORD, the God of Israel, handed Sihon and all his people over to Israel, and they struck them down. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites who lived in that country.
They took possession of all the territory of the Amorites from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
Now the LORD, the God of Israel, drove out the Amorites before his people Israel. And should you take possession of it?
Do you not take possession of what Chemosh your god gives you? And all that the LORD our God has driven out before us, we will possess.
Now, are you any better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever quarrel with Israel, or fight against them?
Israel has lived in Heshbon and its villages, in Aroer and its villages, and in all the towns along the Arnon for three hundred years. Why did you not take them back during that time?
I have not sinned against you, but you are doing me wrong by making war on me. May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites."
But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the message that Jephthah sent him.
Then the spirit of the LORD came on Jephthah. He crossed Gilead and Manasseh, and passed on to Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he crossed to the Ammonites.
Jephthah made a vow to the LORD: "If you will hand the Ammonites over to me,
then whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return safely from the Ammonites will belong to the LORD, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering."
So Jephthah crossed over to fight the Ammonites, and the LORD handed them over to him.
He struck them down from Aroer to near Minnith, twenty towns, and as far as Abel-keramim, with a very great slaughter. So the Ammonites were brought low before the Israelites.
When Jephthah came home to Mizpah, there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing. She was his only child. He had no other son or daughter.

When he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, "Oh, my daughter. You have brought me very low, and you are the one who brings me trouble. For I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take it back."
She said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD. Do to me what you have said, now that the LORD has given you vengeance on your enemies, the Ammonites."
She said to her father, "Let me have this one thing: leave me alone for two months, so that I may go and wander on the mountains and weep for my youth, I and my companions."
He said, "Go." He sent her away for two months, and she went with her companions and wept for her youth on the mountains.
At the end of the two months she came back to her father, and he did to her what he had vowed. She had never lain with a man. So it became a custom in Israel
that each year the daughters of Israel went to mourn for the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite, four days in the year.

The men of Ephraim were called out, and they crossed over to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you go to fight against the Ammonites and not call us to go with you? We will burn your house down over you."
Jephthah said to them, "I and my people were in a great dispute with the Ammonites, and when I called you, you did not save me from their hand.
When I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hands and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the LORD handed them over to me. Why have you come up to me today to fight against me?"

Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. The men of Gilead struck down Ephraim, because they said, "You Gileadites are fugitives from Ephraim, in the middle of Ephraim and Manasseh."

The Gileadites seized the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. When any Ephraimite fugitive said, "Let me cross over," the men of Gilead said to him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" If he said, "No,"

they said to him, "Then say 'Shibboleth.'" If he said "Sibboleth," because he could not say it properly, they seized him and killed him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time forty-two thousand of the Ephraimites fell.
Jephthah judged Israel for six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his town in Gilead.
After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.
He had thirty sons, and thirty daughters whom he gave in marriage outside his clan, and he brought in thirty young women from outside for his sons. He judged Israel for seven years.
Then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.
After him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel, and he judged Israel for ten years.
Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.
After him Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. He judged Israel for eight years.
Then Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
The Israelites again did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD handed them over to the Philistines for forty years.
There was a certain man from Zorah, from the clan of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. His wife was barren and had borne no children.
The angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, "You are barren and have borne no children, but you will conceive and bear a son.
Now be careful not to drink wine or strong drink, and not to eat anything unclean,
for you will conceive and bear a son. No razor is to touch his head, for the boy will be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he will begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines."

Then the woman went and told her husband, "A man of God came to me. His appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask him where he came from, and he did not tell me his name,
but he said to me, 'You will conceive and bear a son. So now drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for the boy will be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.'"
Then Manoah prayed to the LORD: "Please, Lord, let the man of God whom you sent come to us again and teach us what we are to do for the boy who is to be born."
God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman while she was sitting in the field. But her husband Manoah was not with her.
The woman ran quickly and told her husband, "The man who came to me the other day has appeared to me."
Manoah got up and followed his wife. He came to the man and said to him, "Are you the man who spoke to this woman?" He said, "I am."
Manoah said, "Now, when your words come true, what is to be the boy's way of life, and what is he to do?"
The angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "The woman is to be careful about everything I told her.
She is not to eat anything that comes from the vine, or drink wine or strong drink, or eat anything unclean. She is to keep everything I commanded her."
Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "Please let us keep you here and prepare a young goat for you."

The angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "If you keep me here, I will not eat your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD." (Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the LORD.)
Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "What is your name, so that we may honour you when your words come true?"
The angel of the LORD said to him, "Why do you ask my name? It is wonderful."
So Manoah took the young goat with the grain offering and offered it on the rock to the LORD, to the one who works wonders, while Manoah and his wife looked on.
As the flame went up from the altar towards heaven, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame of the altar. When Manoah and his wife saw it, they fell on their faces to the ground.
The angel of the LORD did not appear again to Manoah and his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the LORD.
Manoah said to his wife, "We will surely die, for we have seen God."

But his wife said to him, "If the LORD had wanted to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering from our hands, or shown us all this, or told us such things as these now."
The woman bore a son and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the LORD blessed him.
And the spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson went down to Timnah, and in Timnah he saw one of the Philistine women.
He came back and told his father and mother, "I saw one of the Philistine women in Timnah. Now get her for me as my wife."

His father and mother said to him, "Is there no woman among your kinsmen's daughters, or among all our people, that you must go and take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes."
His father and mother did not know that this was from the LORD, who was looking for an opportunity against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.
Samson went down with his father and mother to Timnah. When he came to the vineyards of Timnah, a young lion came roaring towards him.
The spirit of the LORD rushed on him, and with nothing in his hand he tore the lion apart, as one tears a young goat. But he did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
Then he went down and talked to the woman, and she was right in Samson's eyes.
Some time later, when he came back to marry her, he turned aside to look at the body of the lion, and there was a swarm of bees in the lion's body, and honey.

He scooped it out into his hands and went on, eating as he went. He came to his father and mother and gave some to them, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the body of the lion.
His father went down to the woman, and Samson held a feast there, as young men used to do.
When the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.
Samson said to them, "Let me tell you a riddle. If you can tell me the answer within the seven days of the feast and find it out, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes.
But if you cannot tell me, you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes." They said to him, "Tell us your riddle, so that we can hear it."
He said to them,
"Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet."
For three days they could not tell the riddle.
On the fourth day they said to Samson's wife, "Coax your husband to tell us the riddle, or we will burn you and your father's house with fire. Did you invite us here to rob us?"

Samson's wife wept on him and said, "You only hate me. You do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me the answer." He said to her, "Look, I have not told it to my father or my mother. Should I tell you?"
She wept on him for the seven days of the feast, and on the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him so hard. Then she told the riddle to her people.
On the seventh day, before the sun went down, the men of the town said to him,
"What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?"
He said to them,
"If you had not ploughed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle."

Then the spirit of the LORD rushed on him, and he went down to Ashkelon and killed thirty men of the town. He took their clothes and gave the changes of clothes to those who had told the riddle. In burning anger he went back to his father's house.
And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.
After some time, at the time of the wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife, taking a young goat. He said, "I am going in to my wife in her room." But her father would not let him go in.
Her father said, "I was certain that you hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is her younger sister not more beautiful than she? Please take her instead."
Samson said to them, "This time I will be blameless in regard to the Philistines when I do them harm."
Samson went and caught three hundred foxes, and took torches, and turned them tail to tail, and put one torch between each pair of tails.
He lit the torches and let the foxes go into the standing grain of the Philistines. He burned up the heaps of grain and the standing grain, and the vineyards and olive groves as well.

The Philistines said, "Who did this?" They were told, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he took his wife and gave her to his companion." So the Philistines came up and burned her and her father with fire.
Samson said to them, "If this is how you act, I swear I will take revenge on you, and after that I will stop."
He struck them down, leg and thigh, in a great slaughter. Then he went down and stayed in a cleft of the rock of Etam.
The Philistines went up and camped in Judah and spread out at Lehi.
The men of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" They said, "We have come up to tie up Samson, to do to him what he did to us."

Then three thousand men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? What is this that you have done to us?" He said to them, "As they did to me, so I did to them."
They said to him, "We have come down to tie you up and hand you over to the Philistines." Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves."
They said to him, "No, we will only tie you up and hand you over to them. We will certainly not kill you." So they tied him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.

When he came to Lehi, the Philistines came shouting to meet him. Then the spirit of the LORD rushed on him, and the ropes on his arms became like flax burned with fire, and his bonds melted off his hands.
He found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, reached out his hand and took it, and with it he struck down a thousand men.
Samson said,
"With the jawbone of a donkey, a heap, two heaps. With the jawbone of a donkey I have struck down a thousand men."
When he had finished speaking, he threw the jawbone from his hand. That place was called Ramath-lehi.
He was very thirsty, and he called on the LORD: "You have given this great deliverance by the hand of your servant. Now am I to die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"
God split open the hollow place at Lehi, and water came out of it. When he drank, his spirit returned and he revived. So it was named En-hakkore, which is at Lehi to this day.
He judged Israel in the days of the Philistines for twenty years.
Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute and went in to her.

The people of Gaza were told, "Samson has come here." They surrounded the place and lay in wait for him all night at the city gate. They were quiet all night, saying, "At first light in the morning we will kill him."

But Samson lay there until midnight. At midnight he got up and took hold of the doors of the city gate and the two gateposts, and pulled them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders and carried them to the top of the hill that faces Hebron.
After this he fell in love with a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.
