The rulers of the Philistines came up to her and said, "Coax him and find out where his great strength lies, and how we can overpower him, so that we can tie him up and subdue him. Each of us will give you eleven hundred pieces of silver."
So Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me where your great strength lies, and how you could be tied up and subdued."
Samson said to her, "If they tie me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I will become weak and be like any other man."
The rulers of the Philistines brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she tied him with them.

She had men waiting in ambush in the inner room. She said to him, "The Philistines are on you, Samson." But he snapped the bowstrings as a string of flax snaps when it touches fire. So the secret of his strength was not known.
Delilah said to Samson, "You have made a fool of me. You have told me lies. Now please tell me how you could be tied up."
He said to her, "If they tie me tightly with new ropes that have never been used, I will become weak and be like any other man."

So Delilah took new ropes and tied him with them and said to him, "The Philistines are on you, Samson." The men were waiting in ambush in the inner room. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like thread.

Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have made a fool of me and told me lies. Tell me how you could be tied up." He said to her, "If you weave the seven locks of my head into the fabric on the loom and fasten it with the pin, I will become weak and be like any other man."

So while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the fabric, and fastened it with the pin, and said to him, "The Philistines are on you, Samson." He woke from his sleep and pulled out the pin of the loom and the fabric.
She said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? Three times now you have made a fool of me, and you have not told me where your great strength lies."
When she pressed him day after day with her words and urged him, he became sick to death of it.

So he told her everything that was in his heart. He said to her, "A razor has never touched my head, for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I will become weak and be like any other man."

When Delilah saw that he had told her everything that was in his heart, she sent and called the rulers of the Philistines: "Come up this once, for he has told me everything." The rulers of the Philistines came up to her and brought the silver in their hands.
She put him to sleep on her knees. She called a man and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to bring him low, and his strength left him.
She said, "The Philistines are on you, Samson." He woke from his sleep and thought, "I will go out as I did before and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had left him.
The Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes. They brought him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles, and he ground grain in the prison.
But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
The rulers of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to their god Dagon and to celebrate. They said, "Our god has handed Samson our enemy over to us."
When the people saw him, they praised their god, for they said, "Our god has handed our enemy over to us, the one who laid waste our land and killed so many of us."
When their hearts were merry, they said, "Call Samson, so that he can entertain us." So they called Samson out of the prison, and he performed for them. They made him stand between the pillars.
Samson said to the young man who held his hand, "Let me feel the pillars that support the house, so that I can lean on them."
Now the house was full of men and women. All the rulers of the Philistines were there, and on the roof there were about three thousand men and women watching Samson perform.
Samson called to the LORD: "Lord GOD, please remember me. Please strengthen me just this once, God, so that I can take revenge on the Philistines for my two eyes."
Samson took hold of the two middle pillars that supported the house, and braced himself against them, his right hand on one and his left hand on the other.

Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines." He pushed with all his strength, and the house fell on the rulers and on all the people in it. So those he killed at his death were more than those he had killed in his life.

Then his brothers and all his father's household came down and took him, and brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah. He had judged Israel for twenty years.
There was a man from the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Micah.

He said to his mother, "The eleven hundred pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse, and also spoke it in my hearing, look, the silver is with me. I took it." His mother said, "May my son be blessed by the LORD."

He gave back the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother. His mother said, "I solemnly dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a cast image. So now I will give it back to you."

So when he gave the silver back to his mother, his mother took two hundred pieces of silver and gave them to a silversmith, who made them into a carved image and a cast image. They were in the house of Micah.
This man Micah had a shrine. He made an ephod and household gods, and installed one of his sons, who became his priest.
In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
There was a young man from Bethlehem in Judah, from the clan of Judah. He was a Levite, and he was living there as a resident.
The man left the town of Bethlehem in Judah to live wherever he could find a place. On his journey he came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah.
Micah said to him, "Where do you come from?" He said to him, "I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am travelling to find a place to live."
Micah said to him, "Stay with me and be a father and a priest to me, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year, a set of clothes and your food." So the Levite went in.
The Levite agreed to live with the man, and the young man was to him like one of his sons.
Micah installed the Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in the house of Micah.
Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will do me good, because I have a Levite as my priest."

In those days there was no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of the Danites was looking for a territory to live in, for until then no territory had been allotted to them among the tribes of Israel.

So the Danites sent five men from their whole clan, brave men from Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out the land and explore it. They said to them, "Go and explore the land." They came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and spent the night there.

When they were near the house of Micah, they recognised the voice of the young Levite. They turned aside there and said to him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What do you have here?"
He said to them, "This is what Micah did for me: he hired me, and I have become his priest."
They said to him, "Please ask God whether the journey we are taking will succeed."
The priest said to them, "Go in peace. The journey you are taking is under the eye of the LORD."

So the five men went on and came to Laish. They saw that the people there lived in safety, in the way of the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting, lacking nothing on earth, and wealthy. They were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone.
When they came back to their kinsmen at Zorah and Eshtaol, their kinsmen said to them, "What is your report?"
They said, "Get up, and let us go up against them. We have seen the land, and it is very good. Will you do nothing? Do not be slow to go and take possession of the land.
When you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people. The land is wide, and God has given it into your hands, a place where nothing on earth is lacking."
So six hundred men of the clan of the Danites, armed for war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol,
and went up and camped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. That is why the place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day. It is west of Kiriath-jearim.
From there they passed on to the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah.

Then the five men who had gone to spy out the land of Laish said to their kinsmen, "Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household gods, a carved image and a cast image? Now think about what you should do."
They turned aside there and went to the house of the young Levite, at the home of Micah, and asked how he was.
The six hundred Danites, armed for war, stood at the entrance of the gate.

The five men who had gone to spy out the land went in and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods and the cast image, while the priest stood at the entrance of the gate with the six hundred men armed for war.
When these men went into Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods and the cast image, the priest said to them, "What are you doing?"

They said to him, "Be quiet. Put your hand over your mouth and come with us, and be a father and a priest to us. Is it better for you to be a priest for the household of one man, or to be a priest for a tribe and a clan in Israel?"
The priest was glad. He took the ephod, the household gods and the carved image, and went along with the people.
So they turned and left, putting the little ones, the livestock and the goods in front of them.
When they had gone some distance from the house of Micah, the men who lived in the houses near Micah's house were called out, and they caught up with the Danites.
They shouted to the Danites, who turned and said to Micah, "What is the matter, that you have come with such a crowd?"
He said, "You have taken my gods that I made, and the priest, and have gone away. What do I have left? How can you ask me, 'What is the matter?'"
The Danites said to him, "Do not let us hear your voice again, or some bad-tempered men will attack you, and you will lose your life and the lives of your household."
Then the Danites went on their way. When Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his house.

But the Danites took what Micah had made and the priest who had belonged to him, and came to Laish, to a quiet and unsuspecting people, and struck them down with the edge of the sword and burned the town with fire.
There was no one to rescue them, because it was far from Sidon and they had no dealings with anyone. It was in the valley near Beth-rehob. They rebuilt the town and lived in it.
They named the town Dan, after the name of their ancestor Dan, who was born to Israel. But the name of the town had been Laish at first.
The Danites set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day the land went into exile.
So they set up for themselves Micah's carved image, which he had made, and it stayed there all the time the house of God was at Shiloh.
In those days, when there was no king in Israel, there was a Levite living in the far part of the hill country of Ephraim, who took a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.
But his concubine was unfaithful to him and left him to go to her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah, and she was there for four months.

Then her husband got up and went after her, to speak kindly to her and bring her back. He had his servant with him, and a pair of donkeys. She brought him into her father's house, and when the young woman's father saw him, he came out gladly to meet him.
His father-in-law, the young woman's father, kept him there, and he stayed with him three days. They ate and drank and spent the night there.
On the fourth day they got up early in the morning, and he prepared to go. But the young woman's father said to his son-in-law, "Strengthen yourself with a piece of bread, and after that you may go."
So the two of them sat down and ate and drank together. Then the young woman's father said to the man, "Please stay another night and enjoy yourself."
When the man got up to go, his father-in-law urged him, and he stayed there again that night.
On the fifth day he got up early in the morning to leave. The young woman's father said, "Strengthen yourself. Wait until the day is almost over." So the two of them ate.

When the man got up to leave, with his concubine and his servant, his father-in-law, the young woman's father, said to him, "Look, the day is nearly over, and it is almost evening. Please stay the night. Look, the day is ending. Stay here and enjoy yourself, and tomorrow you can get up early for your journey and go home."
But the man would not stay the night. He got up and left, and came opposite Jebus (that is, Jerusalem). He had with him a pair of saddled donkeys, and his concubine was with him.
When they were near Jebus, the day was almost gone, and the servant said to his master, "Come, let us turn aside to this town of the Jebusites and spend the night in it."
His master said to him, "We will not turn aside into a foreign town, whose people are not Israelites. We will go on to Gibeah."
He said to his servant, "Come, let us go on to one of those places and spend the night in Gibeah or Ramah."
So they went on, and the sun went down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin.
They turned aside there to spend the night in Gibeah. He went in and sat down in the town square, for no one took them into his house for the night.
Then an old man came in from his work in the field at evening. He was from the hill country of Ephraim and was living in Gibeah as a resident. (The men of the place were Benjaminites.)
He looked up and saw the traveller in the town square. The old man said, "Where are you going, and where do you come from?"

He said to him, "We are travelling from Bethlehem in Judah to the far part of the hill country of Ephraim, where I am from. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going to the house of the LORD, and no one has taken me into his house.
We have straw and fodder for our donkeys, and bread and wine for me, your servant woman and the young man with your servants. We lack nothing."
The old man said, "Peace to you. Let me take care of all you need. Only do not spend the night in the square."
So he brought him into his house and fed the donkeys. They washed their feet, and ate and drank.

While they were enjoying themselves, the men of the town, worthless men, surrounded the house and beat on the door. They said to the old man, the owner of the house, "Bring out the man who came into your house, so that we can have sex with him."
The man, the owner of the house, went out to them and said, "No, my brothers, please do not act so wickedly. Since this man has come into my house, do not do this disgraceful thing.
Look, here are my virgin daughter and his concubine. Let me bring them out now. Rape them and do to them whatever you want, but do not do this disgraceful thing to this man."
But the men would not listen to him. So the man took his concubine and pushed her out to them. They raped her and abused her all night until the morning, and let her go at the first light of dawn.
As morning came, the woman came and fell down at the door of the man's house where her master was, and lay there until it was light.
Her master got up in the morning and opened the doors of the house and went out to go on his way. And there was his concubine, lying at the door of the house, with her hands on the threshold.
He said to her, "Get up. Let us go." But there was no answer. Then he put her on the donkey, and the man set out for his home.
When he came to his house, he took a knife, and took hold of his concubine and cut her into twelve pieces, limb by limb, and sent her throughout all the territory of Israel.
Everyone who saw it said, "Nothing like this has ever happened or been seen from the day the Israelites came up out of the land of Egypt until this day. Think about it, take counsel and speak."
Then all the Israelites came out, from Dan to Beersheba and including the land of Gilead, and the community assembled as one before the LORD at Mizpah.
The chiefs of all the people, of all the tribes of Israel, took their places in the assembly of the people of God, four hundred thousand foot soldiers who drew the sword.
(The Benjaminites heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah.) The Israelites said, "Tell us, how did this evil happen?"
The Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, answered, "I came to Gibeah in Benjamin, I and my concubine, to spend the night.
The lords of Gibeah rose up against me and surrounded the house at night, meaning to kill me. They raped my concubine, and she died.
So I took my concubine and cut her into pieces and sent her throughout all the land of Israel's inheritance, because they committed a lewd and disgraceful act in Israel.
Now, all you Israelites, give your word and your counsel here."
All the people rose as one man and said, "None of us will go to his tent, and none of us will return to his house.
Now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot.

We will take ten men out of every hundred from all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred out of every thousand, and a thousand out of every ten thousand, to fetch food for the army, so that when they come to Gibeah of Benjamin, they may repay it for all the disgrace that it has done in Israel."
So all the men of Israel gathered against the town, united as one man.
The tribes of Israel sent men through the whole tribe of Benjamin, saying, "What is this evil that has happened among you?
Now hand over the worthless men in Gibeah, so that we may put them to death and clear the evil out of Israel." But the Benjaminites would not listen to the voice of their kinsmen, the Israelites.
The Benjaminites gathered from their towns to Gibeah, to go out to battle against the Israelites.
On that day the Benjaminites mustered from their towns twenty-six thousand men who drew the sword, besides the people of Gibeah, who mustered seven hundred chosen men.
Among all these troops there were seven hundred chosen men who were left-handed. Each one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss.
The men of Israel, apart from Benjamin, mustered four hundred thousand men who drew the sword. All these were men of war.
The Israelites got up and went up to Bethel and asked God, "Which of us is to go up first to fight against the Benjaminites?" The LORD said, "Judah is to go first."
In the morning the Israelites got up and camped against Gibeah.
The men of Israel went out to fight against Benjamin, and drew up their battle line against them at Gibeah.
The Benjaminites came out of Gibeah and struck down twenty-two thousand of the Israelites on that day.
But the Israelites took courage, and again drew up their battle line in the same place where they had drawn it up on the first day.
The Israelites went up and wept before the LORD until evening. They asked the LORD, "Shall we again go into battle against our kinsmen the Benjaminites?" The LORD said, "Go up against them."
So the Israelites advanced against the Benjaminites on the second day.
Benjamin came out against them from Gibeah on the second day and struck down eighteen thousand more of the Israelites. All of these drew the sword.

Then all the Israelites, the whole army, went up and came to Bethel and wept. They sat there before the LORD and fasted that day until evening, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.
The Israelites asked the LORD (the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days,

and Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, was serving before it in those days), "Shall we go out again to fight against our kinsmen the Benjaminites, or shall we stop?" The LORD said, "Go up, for tomorrow I will hand them over to you."
So Israel set an ambush all round Gibeah.
The Israelites went up against the Benjaminites on the third day and took their positions against Gibeah, as before.

The Benjaminites came out against the army and were drawn away from the town. As before, they began to strike down some of the people on the roads, one of which goes up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah, and in the open country, about thirty men of Israel.
The Benjaminites said, "They are being beaten before us, as at the first." But the Israelites said, "Let us run away and draw them away from the town to the roads."
All the men of Israel got up from their places and took their positions at Baal-tamar, and the men of Israel who were in ambush rushed out from their place west of Geba.
Ten thousand chosen men from all Israel came against Gibeah, and the battle was fierce. But the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was close on them.
The LORD struck down Benjamin before Israel, and on that day the Israelites killed twenty-five thousand one hundred men of Benjamin, all of them men who drew the sword.
Then the Benjaminites saw that they were beaten. The men of Israel had given ground to Benjamin, because they trusted the ambush that they had set against Gibeah.
The men in ambush rushed quickly against Gibeah, spread out and struck down the whole town with the edge of the sword.
Now the agreed sign between the men of Israel and the men in ambush was that they would send up a great cloud of smoke from the town,
and then the men of Israel would turn in the battle. Benjamin had begun to strike down about thirty of the Israelites. They said, "Surely they are beaten before us, as in the first battle."
But when the cloud began to rise from the town in a column of smoke, the Benjaminites looked behind them, and the whole town was going up in smoke to the sky.
Then the men of Israel turned, and the men of Benjamin were terrified, for they saw that disaster was close on them.
So they turned their backs before the men of Israel and ran towards the wilderness, but the battle overtook them. And those who came out of the towns struck them down in the middle.
They surrounded the Benjaminites, chased them and trampled them down from Nohah as far as opposite Gibeah on the east.
Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all of them mighty warriors.
The rest turned and fled towards the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon. Five thousand of them were cut down on the roads. They were chased as far as Gidom, and two thousand of them were struck down.
So all the Benjaminites who fell that day were twenty-five thousand men who drew the sword, all of them mighty warriors.
But six hundred men turned and fled towards the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, and stayed at the rock of Rimmon for four months.

The men of Israel turned back against the Benjaminites and struck them down with the edge of the sword, the whole town, people and animals and everything they found. All the towns that they came to they set on fire.
The men of Israel had sworn an oath at Mizpah: "None of us will give his daughter in marriage to a Benjaminite."
The people came to Bethel and sat there before God until evening, and they raised their voices and wept bitterly.
They said, "LORD, God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that today one tribe should be missing from Israel?"
The next day the people got up early and built an altar there and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.

The Israelites said, "Who among all the tribes of Israel did not come up with the assembly to the LORD?" For they had taken a solemn oath about anyone who did not come up to the LORD at Mizpah: "He will surely be put to death."
The Israelites felt sorry for their kinsman Benjamin and said, "Today one tribe has been cut off from Israel.
What can we do to provide wives for those who are left, since we have sworn by the LORD not to give them any of our daughters as wives?"
They said, "Which one of the tribes of Israel did not come up to the LORD at Mizpah?" And it turned out that no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp, to the assembly.
For when the people were counted, there was not one of the people of Jabesh-gilead there.
So the community sent twelve thousand of their bravest men there and commanded them: "Go and strike down the people of Jabesh-gilead with the edge of the sword, with the women and the little ones.
This is what you are to do: devote to destruction every male, and every woman who has lain with a male."
They found among the people of Jabesh-gilead four hundred young women who were virgins, who had not lain with a man, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.
Then the whole community sent word to the Benjaminites who were at the rock of Rimmon and offered them peace.
The Benjaminites came back at that time, and they gave them the women of Jabesh-gilead whom they had kept alive. But there were not enough for them.
The people felt sorry for Benjamin, because the LORD had made a gap in the tribes of Israel.
The elders of the community said, "What can we do to provide wives for those who are left, since the women of Benjamin have been wiped out?"
They said, "There must be an inheritance for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe is not wiped out from Israel.
But we cannot give them wives from our daughters." For the Israelites had sworn, "Cursed is anyone who gives a wife to Benjamin."
So they said, "Look, there is a yearly festival of the LORD at Shiloh, which is north of Bethel, east of the road that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah."
They commanded the Benjaminites: "Go and lie in wait in the vineyards,

and watch. When the young women of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, come out of the vineyards, and each of you seize a wife for himself from the young women of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.

When their fathers or their brothers come to us to complain, we will say to them, 'Be kind and give them to us, because we did not take a wife for each man in the war, and you did not give them yourselves, or you would now be guilty.'"

The Benjaminites did so. They took wives for themselves, according to their number, from the dancers whom they carried off. Then they went back to their inheritance and rebuilt the towns and lived in them.
The Israelites left there at that time, each to his tribe and clan, each to his own inheritance.
In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land, and a man from Bethlehem in Judah went to live in the country of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons.

The man's name was Elimelech, his wife's name was Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They came to the country of Moab and stayed there.
Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died, and she was left with her two sons.
They took Moabite women as wives, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth. They lived there for about ten years,
and then both Mahlon and Chilion died, so the woman was left without her two sons and without her husband.
Then she got up with her daughters-in-law to come back from the country of Moab, for in the country of Moab she had heard that the LORD had turned his attention to his people and given them food.
So she left the place where she had been living, and her two daughters-in-law with her, and they set out on the road to go back to the land of Judah.
Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go back, each of you, to your mother's house. May the LORD show faithful love to you, as you have shown to the dead and to me.
May the LORD grant that each of you finds a home of security in the house of a husband." Then she kissed them, and they raised their voices and wept.
They said to her, "No, we will go back with you to your people."
But Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters. Why would you go with me? Do I still have sons in my womb, who could become your husbands?
Turn back, my daughters, go, for I am too old to have a husband. Even if I thought there was hope for me, even if I had a husband tonight and bore sons,

would you wait for them until they were grown? Would you shut yourselves away, and not marry? No, my daughters. My bitterness is greater than yours, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me."
They raised their voices and wept again. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth held on to her.
Naomi said, "Look, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her gods. Go back after your sister-in-law."
But Ruth said:
"Do not urge me to leave you, or to turn back from following you. Wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.
Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD do this to me, and more as well, if anything but death separates you and me."
When Naomi saw that she was determined to go with her, she said no more.
So the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem. When they came to Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them, and the women said, "Is this Naomi?"
She said to them, "Do not call me Naomi. Call me Mara, for the Almighty has made my life very bitter.
I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi, when the LORD has testified against me, and the Almighty has brought trouble on me?"
So Naomi came back, and with her Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, who returned from the country of Moab. They came to Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
Now Naomi had a relative on her husband's side, a man of standing, from the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz.
Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go to the fields and glean among the ears of grain behind someone in whose eyes I may find favour." She said to her, "Go, my daughter."
So she went and came and gleaned in the field behind the reapers. As it happened, she came to the part of the field that belonged to Boaz, who was of the clan of Elimelech.
Just then Boaz came from Bethlehem and said to the reapers, "The LORD be with you." They answered, "The LORD bless you."
Boaz said to his servant who was in charge of the reapers, "Whose young woman is this?"
The servant in charge of the reapers answered, "She is the young Moabite woman who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab.
She said, 'Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves behind the reapers.' She came, and she has been on her feet from morning until now, except for a short rest in the shelter."
Then Boaz said to Ruth, "Listen, my daughter. Do not go to glean in another field, and do not leave this one, but stay here close to my young women.

Keep your eyes on the field they are reaping, and follow behind them. I have ordered the young men not to touch you. When you are thirsty, go to the water jars and drink from what the young men have drawn."
Then she fell on her face, bowing to the ground, and said to him, "Why have I found favour in your eyes, that you should notice me, when I am a foreigner?"

Boaz answered her, "I have been told all that you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband, how you left your father and mother and the land of your birth and came to a people you did not know before.
May the LORD repay you for what you have done, and may you have a full reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge."
She said, "May I continue to find favour in your eyes, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not even one of your servants."

At mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come over here and eat some of the bread, and dip your piece in the vinegar." So she sat beside the reapers, and he passed her roasted grain. She ate until she was satisfied, and had some left over.
When she got up to glean, Boaz ordered his young men, "Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not shame her.
Pull out some from the bundles for her, and leave it for her to glean, and do not rebuke her."
So she gleaned in the field until evening. Then she beat out what she had gleaned, and it came to about an ephah of barley.
She picked it up and went into the town. Her mother-in-law saw what she had gleaned. She also took out what she had left over after she was satisfied, and gave it to her.

Her mother-in-law said to her, "Where did you glean today? Where did you work? Blessed be the one who took notice of you." So she told her mother-in-law whom she had worked with, and said, "The name of the man I worked with today is Boaz."

Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "May he be blessed by the LORD, whose faithful love has not abandoned the living or the dead." Naomi also said to her, "The man is a close relative of ours. He is one of our redeemers."
Ruth the Moabite said, "He also said to me, 'Stay close to my young people until they have finished all my harvest.'"
Naomi said to Ruth her daughter-in-law, "It is good, my daughter, that you go out with his young women, so that no one will harm you in another field."
So she stayed close to the young women of Boaz, gleaning until the end of the barley and wheat harvests. And she lived with her mother-in-law.
Naomi her mother-in-law said to her, "My daughter, should I not look for a home for you, so that it may go well with you?
Now, is not Boaz our relative, with whose young women you were? Look, he is winnowing barley tonight at the threshing floor.
So wash and anoint yourself, and put on your best clothes and go down to the threshing floor. But do not make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking.
When he lies down, notice the place where he lies. Then go and uncover his feet and lie down, and he will tell you what to do."
She said to her, "I will do everything you say."
So she went down to the threshing floor and did just as her mother-in-law had told her.
When Boaz had eaten and drunk and his heart was glad, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain. Then she came quietly and uncovered his feet and lay down.
In the middle of the night the man was startled and turned over, and there was a woman lying at his feet.
He said, "Who are you?" She answered, "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wing over your servant, for you are a redeemer."
He said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter. This last act of faithful love of yours is better than the first, because you have not gone after young men, whether poor or rich.
Now, my daughter, do not be afraid. I will do for you all that you ask, for everyone in the gate of my people knows that you are a woman of worth.
It is true that I am a redeemer, but there is a redeemer closer than I.
Stay here tonight, and in the morning, if he will redeem you, good, let him redeem you. But if he does not want to redeem you, then, as the LORD lives, I will redeem you. Lie down until morning."
So she lay at his feet until morning, but got up before one person could recognise another. He said, "Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor."
He said, "Bring the cloak you are wearing and hold it out." She held it, and he measured out six measures of barley and put it on her. Then she went into the town.
When she came to her mother-in-law, she said, "How did it go, my daughter?" Then she told her everything the man had done for her,
and said, "He gave me these six measures of barley, for he said, 'You must not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed.'"
She said, "Wait, my daughter, until you know how the matter turns out, for the man will not rest until he has settled it today."
Boaz went up to the gate and sat down there. Just then the redeemer of whom Boaz had spoken came by. Boaz said, "Come over here, friend, and sit down." So he came over and sat down.
Boaz took ten of the elders of the town and said, "Sit down here." So they sat down.
He said to the redeemer, "Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is selling the piece of land that belonged to our relative Elimelech.

I thought I should tell you, and say: Buy it in the presence of those sitting here and in the presence of the elders of my people. If you will redeem it, redeem it. But if you will not, tell me, so that I may know, for there is no one but you to redeem it, and I come after you." He said, "I will redeem it."
Then Boaz said, "On the day you buy the field from Naomi, you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the widow of the dead man, to keep the name of the dead man alive on his inheritance."
The redeemer said, "I cannot redeem it for myself, or I would damage my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption yourself, for I cannot redeem it."

Now this was the custom in Israel in earlier times concerning redeeming and exchanging, to make any matter binding: one man took off his sandal and gave it to the other. This was the way of confirming a matter in Israel.
So when the redeemer said to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself," he took off his sandal.
Then Boaz said to the elders and all the people, "You are witnesses today that I have bought from Naomi everything that belonged to Elimelech and everything that belonged to Chilion and Mahlon.

I have also acquired Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon, to be my wife, to keep the name of the dead man alive on his inheritance, so that the name of the dead man is not cut off from among his kinsmen and from the gate of his town. You are witnesses today."

All the people at the gate and the elders said, "We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman who is coming into your house like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you prosper in Ephrathah and have a name in Bethlehem,
and may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, through the children that the LORD will give you by this young woman."
So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. He went in to her, and the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she bore a son.
The women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you today without a redeemer. May his name be renowned in Israel.
He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you, who is better to you than seven sons, has given birth to him."
Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap, and she became his nurse.
The women of the neighbourhood gave him a name, saying, "A son has been born to Naomi." They named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David.
These are the generations of Perez: Perez was the father of Hezron,
Hezron was the father of Ram, and Ram was the father of Amminadab,
Amminadab was the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon was the father of Salmon,
Salmon was the father of Boaz, and Boaz was the father of Obed,
Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David.
There was a certain man from Ramathaim, a Zuphite from the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Elkanah son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He had two wives. The name of one was Hannah, and the name of the other was Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.
Every year this man went up from his town to worship and to sacrifice to the LORD of hosts at Shiloh, where the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the LORD.
On the day that Elkanah sacrificed, he would give portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters.
But to Hannah he would give a double portion, because he loved her, though the LORD had closed her womb.
Her rival would provoke her bitterly to make her miserable, because the LORD had closed her womb.
This went on year after year. Whenever she went up to the house of the LORD, her rival would provoke her, and she would weep and not eat.
Her husband Elkanah said to her, "Hannah, why are you weeping? Why do you not eat? Why is your heart sad? Am I not better to you than ten sons?"
After they had eaten and drunk at Shiloh, Hannah got up. Now Eli the priest was sitting on his seat by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD.
She was deeply bitter, and she prayed to the LORD and wept without ceasing.

She made a vow and said, "LORD of hosts, if you will look on the misery of your servant and remember me, and not forget your servant, but give your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor will touch his head."
As she kept on praying before the LORD, Eli watched her mouth.
Hannah was speaking in her heart. Only her lips moved, and her voice could not be heard. So Eli thought she was drunk.
Eli said to her, "How long will you go on being drunk? Put away your wine."
But Hannah answered, "No, my lord, I am a woman with a heavy spirit. I have drunk no wine or strong drink, but I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD.
Do not take your servant for a worthless woman, for I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and grief until now."
Then Eli answered, "Go in peace, and may the God of Israel grant what you have asked of him."
She said, "May your servant find favour in your eyes." Then the woman went on her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.
They got up early in the morning and bowed down before the LORD, and then went back to their house at Ramah. Elkanah knew his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her.
In due time Hannah conceived and bore a son. She named him Samuel, "for," she said, "I asked the LORD for him."
The man Elkanah went up with all his household to offer the yearly sacrifice to the LORD and to keep his vow.
But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, "After the child is weaned, I will bring him, so that he may appear before the LORD and stay there for ever."
Her husband Elkanah said to her, "Do what seems best to you. Stay until you have weaned him. Only may the LORD make his word come true." So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she weaned him.
When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour and a skin of wine, and brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. The boy was young.
Then they slaughtered the bull and brought the boy to Eli.
She said, "Please, my lord, as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you, praying to the LORD.
I prayed for this boy, and the LORD has granted me what I asked of him.
So I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD." And he worshipped the LORD there.
Hannah prayed and said:
"My heart exults in the LORD. My horn is lifted high in the LORD. My mouth opens wide against my enemies, because I rejoice in your saving help.
There is no one holy like the LORD, for there is no one but you. There is no rock like our God.
Do not go on talking so proudly. Do not let arrogance come out of your mouth, for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him deeds are weighed.
The bows of the mighty are broken, but the stumbling gird on strength.
Those who were full hire themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry are hungry no more. The barren woman has borne seven, but she who has many sons languishes.
The LORD kills and brings to life. He brings down to Sheol and raises up.
The LORD makes poor and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up.

He raises the poor from the dust. He lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes and to give them a seat of honour. For the pillars of the earth are the LORD's, and on them he has set the world.
He guards the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked are silenced in darkness, for not by strength does a person prevail.

Those who oppose the LORD will be shattered. The Most High will thunder against them from heaven. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth. He will give strength to his king and raise the horn of his anointed."
Then Elkanah went home to Ramah. But the boy served the LORD in the presence of Eli the priest.
Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD.
This was the custom of the priests with the people: when anyone offered a sacrifice, the priest's servant would come while the meat was boiling, with a three-pronged fork in his hand,

and would thrust it into the pan, or kettle, or cauldron, or pot. Whatever the fork brought up, the priest would take for himself. This is what they did at Shiloh to all the Israelites who came there.
Even before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, "Give the priest some meat to roast, for he will not accept boiled meat from you, only raw."
If the man said to him, "Let them burn the fat first, and then take as much as you want," he would say, "No, give it now, or I will take it by force."
So the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the LORD, for they were treating the offering of the LORD with contempt.
Samuel was serving in the presence of the LORD, a boy wearing a linen ephod.
His mother used to make him a little robe and take it to him each year when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
Then Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, saying, "May the LORD give you children by this woman, in place of the one she lent to the LORD." Then they would go to their home.
The LORD visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the LORD.
Now Eli was very old. He heard all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they lay with the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
He said to them, "Why do you do such things? I hear of your evil dealings from all the people.
No, my sons. The report I hear the LORD's people spreading is not good.

If one person sins against another, God will mediate for him. But if someone sins against the LORD, who will intercede for him?" But they would not listen to the voice of their father, for it was the LORD's will to put them to death.
The boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favour, both with the LORD and with people.
A man of God came to Eli and said to him, "This is what the LORD says: Did I not plainly reveal myself to your father's house when they were in Egypt, in slavery to Pharaoh's house?

Did I not choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, to wear an ephod before me? Did I not give to your father's house all the offerings by fire of the Israelites?
Why do you look with greed at my sacrifice and my offering that I commanded for my dwelling, and honour your sons above me by fattening yourselves on the best of every offering of my people Israel?

Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: I did say that your house and your father's house would walk before me for ever. But now the LORD declares: Far be it from me. For those who honour me I will honour, and those who despise me will be treated as nothing.
The days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father's house, so that there will not be an old man in your house.
You will see distress in my dwelling, in all the good that I do for Israel, and there will never again be an old man in your house.
The man of yours whom I do not cut off from my altar will be left to weep out his eyes and grieve his heart. All the descendants of your house will die by the sword.
This will be the sign for you: what happens to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, will happen to both of them on the same day.
And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do what is in my heart and in my mind. I will build him a lasting house, and he will walk before my anointed for ever.

Everyone who is left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread, and say, 'Please put me in one of the priestly offices, so that I may eat a morsel of bread.'"
The boy Samuel was serving the LORD in the presence of Eli. In those days the word of the LORD was rare. There was no widespread vision.
At that time Eli, whose eyesight had begun to grow dim so that he could not see, was lying down in his room.
The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was.
Then the LORD called, "Samuel." He answered, "Here I am."
He ran to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call. Go back and lie down." So he went and lay down.
The LORD called again, "Samuel." Samuel got up and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call, my son. Go back and lie down."
Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.
The LORD called Samuel again, a third time. He got up and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." Then Eli understood that the LORD was calling the boy.
So Eli said to Samuel, "Go and lie down. If he calls you, say, 'Speak, LORD, for your servant is listening.'" So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
The LORD came and stood and called as before, "Samuel, Samuel." Samuel said, "Speak, for your servant is listening."
Then the LORD said to Samuel, "See, I am about to do something in Israel that will make both ears of everyone who hears of it tingle.
On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken about his house, from beginning to end.
For I told him that I am going to judge his house for ever, for the guilt that he knew, because his sons were bringing a curse on themselves, and he did not restrain them.
So I have sworn to the house of Eli that the guilt of Eli's house will never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering."
Samuel lay down until morning. Then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. But Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli.
But Eli called Samuel and said, "Samuel, my son." He said, "Here I am."
Eli said, "What was it that he told you? Do not hide it from me. May God do this to you, and more also, if you hide anything from me of all that he told you."
So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. Eli said, "It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him."
Samuel grew up, and the LORD was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground.
All Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD.
The LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, for the LORD revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of the LORD.
And Samuel's word came to all Israel. Israel went out to meet the Philistines in battle and camped at Ebenezer, while the Philistines camped at Aphek.
The Philistines drew up their lines against Israel, and when the battle spread, Israel was beaten by the Philistines, who struck down about four thousand men on the battlefield.

When the people came back to the camp, the elders of Israel said, "Why has the LORD beaten us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, so that it may come among us and save us from the hand of our enemies."

So the people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the LORD of hosts, who sits enthroned on the cherubim. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.
When the ark of the covenant of the LORD came into the camp, all Israel gave a great shout, so that the ground shook.
When the Philistines heard the sound of the shouting, they said, "What is this great shouting in the camp of the Hebrews?" Then they learned that the ark of the LORD had come into the camp.
The Philistines were afraid, for they said, "A god has come into the camp." They said, "Woe to us. Nothing like this has happened before.
Woe to us. Who will save us from the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every kind of plague in the wilderness.
Be strong and be men, Philistines, or you will be slaves to the Hebrews, as they have been to you. Be men and fight."
So the Philistines fought, and Israel was beaten, and each man fled to his tent. The slaughter was very great, for thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell.
The ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
A man of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh that same day, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head.
When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat by the road, watching, because his heart trembled for the ark of God. When the man came into the town and told the news, the whole town cried out.
When Eli heard the sound of the outcry, he said, "What is this noise of uproar?" The man hurried and came and told Eli.
Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his eyes were fixed so that he could not see.
The man said to Eli, "I am the one who has come from the battle line. I ran away from the battle line today." He said, "How did it go, my son?"

The messenger answered, "Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has also been a great slaughter among the people. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been captured."
When he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backwards from his seat by the side of the gate. His neck was broken and he died, for he was old and heavy. He had judged Israel for forty years.

His daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and near to giving birth. When she heard the news that the ark of God had been captured, and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she knelt and gave birth, for her pains came on her.
As she was dying, the women standing by her said, "Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son." But she did not answer or take notice.
She named the boy Ichabod, saying, "The glory has gone from Israel," because the ark of God had been captured and because of her father-in-law and her husband.
She said, "The glory has gone from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured."
When the Philistines captured the ark of God, they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
The Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the temple of Dagon and placed it beside Dagon.
When the people of Ashdod got up early the next day, there was Dagon, fallen face down on the ground before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and set him back in his place.

But when they got up early the next morning, there was Dagon, fallen face down on the ground before the ark of the LORD, and the head of Dagon and both his hands were lying cut off on the threshold. Only the trunk of Dagon was left.
This is why the priests of Dagon and all who enter the temple of Dagon in Ashdod do not step on the threshold to this day.
The hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod, and he terrified them and struck them with tumours, Ashdod and its territory.
When the people of Ashdod saw how it was, they said, "The ark of the god of Israel must not stay with us, for his hand is hard on us and on our god Dagon."

So they sent and gathered all the rulers of the Philistines to them and said, "What should we do with the ark of the god of Israel?" They answered, "Let the ark of the god of Israel be moved to Gath." So they moved the ark of the god of Israel there.
But after they had moved it, the hand of the LORD was against the town, causing a very great panic. He struck the people of the town, small and great, so that tumours broke out on them.
So they sent the ark of God to Ekron. But as the ark of God was coming into Ekron, the people of Ekron cried out, "They have moved the ark of the god of Israel to us, to kill us and our people."

They sent and gathered all the rulers of the Philistines and said, "Send away the ark of the god of Israel, and let it go back to its own place, so that it does not kill us and our people." For there was a deadly panic throughout the whole town. The hand of God was very heavy there.
The people who did not die were struck with tumours, and the cry of the town went up to heaven.
The ark of the LORD was in the land of the Philistines seven months.
The Philistines called for the priests and the diviners and said, "What should we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us how we should send it back to its place."

They said, "If you send away the ark of the god of Israel, do not send it empty. You must send a guilt offering with it. Then you will be healed, and it will be known to you why his hand has not turned away from you."

They said, "What is the guilt offering that we should send back to him?" They answered, "Five gold tumours and five gold mice, according to the number of the rulers of the Philistines, for the same plague was on all of you and on your rulers.
Make images of your tumours and images of your mice that are ravaging the land, and give glory to the god of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand on you and on your gods and on your land.
Why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? When he had dealt harshly with them, did they not let the people go, so that they left?
Now then, get a new cart ready, and two milking cows that have never been under a yoke. Yoke the cows to the cart, but take their calves home, away from them.
Take the ark of the LORD and put it on the cart, and put the gold objects that you are sending to him as a guilt offering in a box at its side. Then send it off, and let it go.

And watch. If it goes up on the road to its own land, to Beth-shemesh, then it is he who has done us this great harm. But if not, then we will know that it was not his hand that struck us. It happened to us by chance."
The men did so. They took two milking cows and yoked them to the cart and shut their calves up at home.
They put the ark of the LORD on the cart, and the box with the gold mice and the images of their tumours.

The cows went straight ahead on the road towards Beth-shemesh, keeping to one road, lowing as they went. They did not turn to the right or to the left, and the rulers of the Philistines followed them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh.
Now the people of Beth-shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley. When they looked up and saw the ark, they were glad to see it.
The cart came to the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there, where there was a large stone. They split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.

The Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the box beside it that held the gold objects, and put them on the large stone. The people of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and made sacrifices that day to the LORD.
When the five rulers of the Philistines saw it, they went back to Ekron that day.
These are the gold tumours that the Philistines sent back as a guilt offering to the LORD: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath and one for Ekron,

and the gold mice, according to the number of all the towns of the Philistines belonging to the five rulers, both fortified towns and unwalled villages. The large stone on which they set down the ark of the LORD is a witness to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.

He struck down some of the people of Beth-shemesh, because they looked into the ark of the LORD. He struck down seventy of them, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck the people with a great blow.
The people of Beth-shemesh said, "Who can stand before the LORD, this holy God? And to whom will he go up from us?"
So they sent messengers to the people of Kiriath-jearim, saying, "The Philistines have brought back the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up to you."
The people of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the LORD and brought it to the house of Abinadab on the hill. They set apart his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the LORD.
From the day that the ark stayed at Kiriath-jearim a long time passed, some twenty years, and the whole house of Israel longed for the LORD.

Samuel said to the whole house of Israel, "If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtoreths from among you, and set your hearts on the LORD and serve him alone, and he will rescue you from the hand of the Philistines."
So the Israelites put away the Baals and the Ashtoreths, and served the LORD alone.
Then Samuel said, "Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you."
So they gathered at Mizpah and drew water and poured it out before the LORD. They fasted that day and said there, "We have sinned against the LORD." And Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah.
When the Philistines heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, the rulers of the Philistines went up against Israel. When the Israelites heard of it, they were afraid of the Philistines.
The Israelites said to Samuel, "Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us, so that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines."
So Samuel took a suckling lamb and offered it whole as a burnt offering to the LORD. Samuel cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him.

While Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines came near to attack Israel. But the LORD thundered with a loud voice that day against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and they were beaten before Israel.
The men of Israel went out from Mizpah and chased the Philistines and struck them down, as far as below Beth-car.
Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen. He called it Ebenezer, saying, "The LORD has helped us up to here."
So the Philistines were subdued and did not come again into the territory of Israel. The hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.

The towns that the Philistines had taken from Israel were returned to Israel, from Ekron to Gath, and Israel took their territory back from the hand of the Philistines. There was peace also between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life.
Each year he went on a circuit to Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah, and judged Israel in all those places.
Then he would come back to Ramah, for his home was there, and there too he judged Israel. And he built an altar there to the LORD.
When Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.
The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of his second son was Abijah. They were judges at Beersheba.
But his sons did not follow his ways. They turned aside after dishonest gain, took bribes and twisted justice.
So all the elders of Israel gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah
and said to him, "Look, you are old, and your sons do not follow your ways. Now appoint a king for us to judge us, like all the nations."
But what they said, "Give us a king to judge us," was evil in Samuel's eyes. So Samuel prayed to the LORD.
The LORD said to Samuel, "Listen to the voice of the people in everything they say to you, for it is not you they have rejected, but me, from being king over them.
As they have done from the day I brought them up out of Egypt to this day, abandoning me and serving other gods, so they are doing to you also.
Now then, listen to their voice. But you must solemnly warn them and tell them how the king who will rule over them will behave."
So Samuel told all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking him for a king.
He said, "This is how the king who will rule over you will behave: he will take your sons and put them to work on his chariots and with his horsemen, and some will run in front of his chariots.
He will appoint for himself commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties, and some to plough his ground and reap his harvest, and to make his weapons of war and the equipment for his chariots.
He will take your daughters as perfumers, cooks and bakers.
He will take the best of your fields, vineyards and olive groves and give them to his servants.
He will take a tenth of your grain and of your vineyards and give it to his officials and his servants.
He will take your male and female servants and your best young men and your donkeys, and put them to work for him.
He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves.
On that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you on that day."
But the people refused to listen to the voice of Samuel. They said, "No. There will be a king over us,
so that we too may be like all the nations, and our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles."
When Samuel had heard all the words of the people, he repeated them in the hearing of the LORD.
The LORD said to Samuel, "Listen to their voice and make a king for them." Samuel said to the men of Israel, "Each of you, go back to your town."
There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjaminite, a man of standing.
He had a son whose name was Saul, a fine young man. There was no one among the Israelites finer than he. He stood a head taller than anyone else.
The donkeys of Saul's father Kish had strayed. So Kish said to his son Saul, "Take one of the servants with you and go and look for the donkeys."

They passed through the hill country of Ephraim and through the land of Shalisha, but they did not find them. They passed through the land of Shaalim, but they were not there. They passed through the land of Benjamin, but they did not find them.
When they came to the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant who was with him, "Come, let us go back, or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us."
But he said to him, "Look, there is a man of God in this town, and he is a man held in honour. Everything he says comes true. Let us go there now. Perhaps he can tell us which way we should go."
Saul said to his servant, "But if we go, what can we take the man? The bread in our sacks is gone, and we have no gift to take to the man of God. What do we have?"
The servant answered Saul again, "Look, I have a quarter of a shekel of silver in my hand. I will give it to the man of God, and he will tell us our way."
(In former times in Israel, when someone went to ask God, he would say, "Come, let us go to the seer," for the prophet of today used to be called a seer.)
Saul said to his servant, "Well said. Come, let us go." So they went to the town where the man of God was.
As they were going up the slope to the town, they met some young women coming out to draw water and said to them, "Is the seer here?"
They answered, "He is. He is just ahead of you. Hurry, for he has come to the town today, because the people have a sacrifice at the high place today.

As soon as you enter the town, you will find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people will not eat until he comes, because he has to bless the sacrifice. After that, those who are invited will eat. Go up now, for you will find him at once."
So they went up to the town. As they were entering the town, there was Samuel coming out towards them on his way up to the high place.
Now the day before Saul came, the LORD had told Samuel:

"At this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you are to anoint him as ruler over my people Israel. He will save my people from the hand of the Philistines. For I have seen my people, because their cry has come to me."
When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, "There is the man I spoke to you about. He will govern my people."
Then Saul approached Samuel in the gateway and said, "Please tell me where the house of the seer is."
Samuel answered Saul, "I am the seer. Go up ahead of me to the high place, for you will eat with me today. In the morning I will let you go, and I will tell you everything that is on your mind.

As for your donkeys that were lost three days ago, do not worry about them, for they have been found. And who is all that is desirable in Israel for? Is it not for you and for all your father's house?"
Saul answered, "Am I not a Benjaminite, from the smallest of the tribes of Israel? And is my clan not the least of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin? Why do you speak to me like this?"
Then Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the hall and gave them a place at the head of those who were invited, about thirty people.
Samuel said to the cook, "Bring the portion I gave you, the one I told you to put aside."

The cook took up the leg and what was on it and set it in front of Saul. Samuel said, "See, what was kept is set before you. Eat, because it was kept for you for the appointed time, when I said I had invited the people." So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
When they came down from the high place into the town, a bed was made up for Saul on the roof, and he lay down to sleep.
At daybreak Samuel called to Saul on the roof, "Get up, and I will send you on your way." Saul got up, and he and Samuel went out into the street.

As they were going down to the edge of the town, Samuel said to Saul, "Tell the servant to go on ahead of us, and when he has gone on, you stay here for a while, so that I may tell you the word of God."
Then Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it on his head, and kissed him and said, "Has the LORD not anointed you ruler over his inheritance?

When you leave me today, you will meet two men near Rachel's tomb, at Zelzah on the border of Benjamin, and they will say to you, 'The donkeys you went to look for have been found, and now your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and is worrying about you, saying, "What shall I do about my son?"'

Then you will go on from there and come to the oak of Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there, one carrying three young goats, one carrying three loaves of bread, and one carrying a skin of wine.
They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you are to accept from their hands.

After that you will come to Gibeath-elohim, where there is a Philistine garrison. As you come to the town there, you will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with harp, tambourine, flute and lyre before them, and they will be prophesying.
Then the spirit of the LORD will rush on you, and you will prophesy with them and be changed into a different man.
When these signs come to you, do whatever your hand finds to do, for God is with you.
Then go down ahead of me to Gilgal. I will come down to you to offer burnt offerings and sacrifice peace offerings. You are to wait seven days, until I come to you and tell you what you are to do."
When he turned his back to leave Samuel, God gave him another heart, and all those signs came about that day.
When they came to Gibeah, there was a company of prophets coming to meet him, and the spirit of God rushed on him, and he prophesied among them.
When all who had known him before saw him prophesying with the prophets, the people said to one another, "What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?"
A man from there answered, "And who is their father?" So it became a saying: "Is Saul also among the prophets?"
When he had finished prophesying, he went to the high place.
Saul's uncle said to him and to his servant, "Where did you go?" He said, "To look for the donkeys. When we saw that they were nowhere to be found, we went to Samuel."
Saul's uncle said, "Please tell me what Samuel said to you."
Saul said to his uncle, "He told us plainly that the donkeys had been found." But about the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel had spoken, he told him nothing.
Samuel called the people together to the LORD at Mizpah.

He said to the Israelites, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.

But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your troubles and distresses, and you have said to him, 'Set a king over us.' Now present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and by your clans."
Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was chosen by lot.
He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its families, and the family of the Matrites was chosen, and then Saul son of Kish was chosen. But when they looked for him, he could not be found.
So they asked the LORD again, "Has the man come here yet?" The LORD said, "He has hidden himself among the baggage."
They ran and brought him from there. When he stood among the people, he was a head taller than any of them.
Samuel said to all the people, "Do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people." And all the people shouted, "Long live the king."
Then Samuel told the people the rules of the kingship, and wrote them in a book and placed it before the LORD. Then Samuel sent all the people away, each to his home.
Saul also went to his home at Gibeah, and with him went the warriors whose hearts God had touched.
But some worthless men said, "How can this man save us?" They despised him and brought him no gift. But he kept silent.
Nahash the Ammonite went up and besieged Jabesh-gilead, and all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, "Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you."
But Nahash the Ammonite said to them, "I will make a treaty with you on this condition: that I gouge out the right eye of every one of you, and so bring shame on all Israel."
The elders of Jabesh said to him, "Give us seven days, so that we can send messengers throughout the whole territory of Israel. If no one comes to save us, we will come out to you."
When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and told these words in the hearing of the people, all the people raised their voices and wept.
Just then Saul was coming in from the field behind the oxen. Saul said, "What is the matter with the people, that they are weeping?" So they told him the words of the men of Jabesh.
The spirit of God rushed on Saul when he heard these words, and his anger blazed.

He took a pair of oxen and cut them in pieces and sent them throughout the whole territory of Israel by messengers, saying, "Whoever does not come out after Saul and after Samuel, this is what will be done to his oxen." Then the dread of the LORD fell on the people, and they came out as one man.
When he counted them at Bezek, the Israelites were three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand.

They said to the messengers who had come, "This is what you are to say to the men of Jabesh-gilead: 'Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you will be rescued.'" When the messengers came and told the men of Jabesh, they were glad.
The men of Jabesh said, "Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you can do to us whatever seems good to you."

The next day Saul put the people in three companies. They came into the middle of the camp at the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. Those who were left were scattered, so that no two of them were left together.
The people said to Samuel, "Who was it who said, 'Shall Saul rule over us?' Bring those men, so that we can put them to death."
But Saul said, "No one will be put to death today, for today the LORD has brought rescue to Israel."
Samuel said to the people, "Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there."
So all the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the LORD at Gilgal. There they offered peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.
Samuel said to all Israel, "Look, I have listened to your voice in everything you said to me, and I have set a king over you.
Now the king walks before you, and I am old and grey, and my sons are with you. I have walked before you from my youth to this day.

Here I am. Testify against me before the LORD and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated? Whom have I oppressed? From whose hand have I taken a bribe to blind my eyes with it? Testify, and I will return it to you."
They said, "You have not cheated us or oppressed us or taken anything from anyone's hand."
He said to them, "The LORD is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have found nothing in my hand." They said, "He is witness."
Samuel said to the people, "The LORD is the witness, who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your ancestors up out of the land of Egypt.
Now stand here, and I will put my case against you before the LORD concerning all the righteous acts of the LORD that he did for you and for your ancestors.

When Jacob went into Egypt, and the Egyptians oppressed them, your ancestors cried out to the LORD, and the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your ancestors out of Egypt and made them live in this place.

But they forgot the LORD their God, and he sold them into the hand of Sisera, the commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab. They fought against them.

They cried out to the LORD and said, 'We have sinned, because we have abandoned the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtoreths. But now rescue us from the hand of our enemies, and we will serve you.'
The LORD sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah and Samuel, and rescued you from the hand of your enemies on every side, so that you lived in safety.
But when you saw that Nahash king of the Ammonites was coming against you, you said to me, 'No, a king will rule over us,' though the LORD your God was your king.
Now here is the king you have chosen, the one you asked for. See, the LORD has set a king over you.

If you fear the LORD and serve him and listen to his voice and do not rebel against the command of the LORD, and if both you and the king who rules over you follow the LORD your God, then all will be well.
But if you do not listen to the voice of the LORD, and rebel against the command of the LORD, then the hand of the LORD will be against you and your king.
Now stand still and see this great thing that the LORD will do before your eyes.

Is it not the wheat harvest today? I will call on the LORD, and he will send thunder and rain. Then you will know and see that the evil you did in the eyes of the LORD in asking for a king for yourselves was great."
So Samuel called on the LORD, and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day, and all the people were very afraid of the LORD and of Samuel.
All the people said to Samuel, "Pray to the LORD your God for your servants, so that we do not die, for we have added to all our sins the evil of asking for a king for ourselves."
Samuel said to the people, "Do not be afraid. You have done all this evil. Yet do not turn away from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart.
Do not turn aside after empty things that cannot profit or save, for they are empty.
For the LORD will not abandon his people, for the sake of his great name, because it pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself.
As for me, far be it from me to sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you. I will teach you the good and right way.
Only fear the LORD and serve him faithfully with all your heart. Consider what great things he has done for you.
But if you still do evil, you will be swept away, both you and your king."
Saul was \[number missing\] years old when he became king, and he ruled \[number missing\] and two years over Israel.

Saul chose three thousand men of Israel. Two thousand were with Saul at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the people he sent home, each to his tent.
