Jonathan struck down the Philistine garrison at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. Saul blew the trumpet throughout the land, saying, "Let the Hebrews hear."
All Israel heard the news: "Saul has struck down the Philistine garrison, and Israel has become a stench to the Philistines." And the people were called out to join Saul at Gilgal.
The Philistines gathered to fight Israel, with thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and troops as many as the sand on the seashore. They went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven.
When the men of Israel saw that they were in trouble, because the people were hard pressed, they hid in caves, in holes, among rocks, in tombs and in cisterns.
Some Hebrews crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead. But Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people with him were trembling.
He waited seven days, the time that Samuel had set. But Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people began to scatter from him.
So Saul said, "Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings." And he offered the burnt offering.
Just as he finished offering the burnt offering, Samuel arrived. Saul went out to meet him and greet him.
Samuel said, "What have you done?" Saul said, "I saw that the people were scattering from me, and that you did not come within the days set, and that the Philistines were gathering at Michmash.
I thought, 'Now the Philistines will come down on me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favour of the LORD.' So I forced myself and offered the burnt offering."
Samuel said to Saul, "You have acted foolishly. You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you. For now the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel for ever.
But now your kingdom will not last. The LORD has looked for a man after his own heart, and the LORD has appointed him ruler over his people, because you have not kept what the LORD commanded you."
Then Samuel got up and went from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul counted the people who were with him, about six hundred men.
Saul and his son Jonathan and the people with them stayed in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Michmash.
Raiders went out from the Philistine camp in three companies. One company turned towards Ophrah, to the land of Shual,
another turned towards Beth-horon, and another turned towards the border that looks down on the Valley of Zeboim towards the wilderness.
No blacksmith could be found in the whole land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, "The Hebrews must not make swords or spears."
So all the Israelites had to go down to the Philistines to sharpen their ploughshares, mattocks, axes and sickles,
and the charge was two-thirds of a shekel for ploughshares and mattocks, and a third of a shekel for sharpening axes and setting ox-goads.
So on the day of battle there was neither sword nor spear in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had them.
Now a Philistine outpost went out to the pass of Michmash.
One day Jonathan son of Saul said to the young man who carried his armour, "Come, let us go over to the Philistine outpost on the other side." But he did not tell his father.
Saul was staying on the edge of Gibeah, under the pomegranate tree at Migron. The people with him were about six hundred men,
including Ahijah son of Ahitub, the brother of Ichabod son of Phinehas, son of Eli, the priest of the LORD at Shiloh, who was wearing an ephod. The people did not know that Jonathan had gone.
Between the passes by which Jonathan tried to cross to the Philistine outpost there was a rocky crag on one side and a rocky crag on the other. One was called Bozez, and the other Seneh.
One crag stood on the north, facing Michmash, and the other on the south, facing Geba.

Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armour, "Come, let us go over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will act for us, for nothing can stop the LORD from saving by many or by few."
His armour-bearer said to him, "Do whatever is in your heart. Go ahead. I am with you, heart and soul."
Jonathan said, "Look, we will cross over to the men and let them see us.
If they say to us, 'Wait until we come to you,' then we will stay where we are and not go up to them.
But if they say, 'Come up to us,' then we will go up, because the LORD has handed them over to us. That will be our sign."
So the two of them showed themselves to the Philistine outpost. The Philistines said, "Look, Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they hid."

The men of the outpost called out to Jonathan and his armour-bearer, "Come up to us, and we will teach you a lesson." Jonathan said to his armour-bearer, "Come up after me, for the LORD has handed them over to Israel."
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, with his armour-bearer behind him. The Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armour-bearer killed them behind him.
In that first attack, Jonathan and his armour-bearer killed about twenty men, within about half a furrow's length of a field.
Then panic spread in the camp, in the field and among all the people. The outpost and the raiders also trembled. The earth shook, and it became a panic from God.
Saul's lookouts at Gibeah of Benjamin saw the crowd melting away in all directions.
Saul said to the people with him, "Count and see who has gone from us." When they counted, Jonathan and his armour-bearer were not there.
Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here." (For at that time the ark of God was with the Israelites.)
While Saul was speaking to the priest, the uproar in the Philistine camp kept growing. So Saul said to the priest, "Withdraw your hand."
Then Saul and all the people with him were called out and went into the battle. There every Philistine's sword was against his fellow, and there was great confusion.
The Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before that, and had gone up with them into the camp, now turned and joined the Israelites with Saul and Jonathan.
When all the men of Israel who had hidden in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were running away, they too followed closely behind them in the battle.
So the LORD saved Israel that day, and the battle passed beyond Beth-aven.

The men of Israel were worn out that day, because Saul had put the people under an oath: "Cursed is anyone who eats food before evening, before I have taken revenge on my enemies." So none of the people tasted food.
Now all the people came into the forest, and there was honey on the ground.
When the people came into the forest, there was the honey dripping, but no one put his hand to his mouth, because they feared the oath.

But Jonathan had not heard his father put the people under the oath. He stretched out the tip of the staff in his hand and dipped it in the honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes brightened.
Then one of the people said to him, "Your father strictly put the people under an oath, saying, 'Cursed is anyone who eats food today.'" And the people were faint.
Jonathan said, "My father has brought trouble on the land. See how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey.
How much better if the people had eaten freely today of the plunder they took from their enemies. The slaughter of the Philistines would then have been much greater."
They struck down the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon, and the people were very faint.
The people rushed on the plunder and took sheep, cattle and calves and slaughtered them on the ground, and the people ate them with the blood.
They told Saul, "Look, the people are sinning against the LORD by eating meat with the blood." He said, "You have broken faith. Roll a large stone over to me now."

Saul said, "Go among the people and tell them, 'Each of you bring me his ox or his sheep, and slaughter it here and eat, and do not sin against the LORD by eating with the blood.'" So each of the people brought his ox with him that night and slaughtered it there.
Saul built an altar to the LORD. It was the first altar he built to the LORD.

Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until the morning light. Let us not leave one of them alive." They said, "Do whatever seems good to you." But the priest said, "Let us approach God here."
Saul asked God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you hand them over to Israel?" But he did not answer him that day.
Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the people, and find out how this sin happened today.
For as the LORD lives, who saves Israel, even if it is my son Jonathan, he must die." But none of all the people answered him.
He said to all Israel, "You stand on one side, and I and my son Jonathan will stand on the other side." The people said to Saul, "Do whatever seems good to you."
Saul said to the LORD, the God of Israel, "Give a true lot." Jonathan and Saul were taken, and the people were cleared.
Saul said, "Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan." And Jonathan was taken.
Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." Jonathan told him, "I tasted a little honey with the tip of the staff in my hand. Here I am. I will die."
Saul said, "May God do this to me, and more also, if you do not surely die, Jonathan."

But the people said to Saul, "Is Jonathan to die, who has brought about this great victory in Israel? Far from it. As the LORD lives, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground, for he acted with God today." So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.
Then Saul stopped chasing the Philistines, and the Philistines went back to their own place.
When Saul had taken the kingship over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side: Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he defeated them.
He fought bravely and struck down the Amalekites, and saved Israel from the hands of those who plundered them.
Saul's sons were Jonathan, Ishvi and Malchi-shua. The names of his two daughters were Merab, the firstborn, and Michal, the younger.
The name of Saul's wife was Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The name of the commander of his army was Abner son of Ner, Saul's uncle.
Kish was the father of Saul, and Ner the father of Abner was a son of Abiel.
There was fierce fighting against the Philistines all the days of Saul. Whenever Saul saw any strong or brave man, he took him into his service.
Samuel said to Saul, "The LORD sent me to anoint you king over his people Israel. So now listen to the words of the LORD.
This is what the LORD of hosts says: I will call Amalek to account for what he did to Israel, how he stood against them on the road when they came up out of Egypt.
Now go and strike down Amalek, and devote to destruction everything that belongs to them. Do not spare them. Kill man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey."
So Saul summoned the people and counted them at Telaim, two hundred thousand foot soldiers and ten thousand men of Judah.
Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the wadi.

Saul said to the Kenites, "Go, leave, go down from among the Amalekites, so that I do not destroy you with them, for you showed faithful love to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt." So the Kenites left the Amalekites.
Saul struck down the Amalekites from Havilah as far as Shur, which is east of Egypt.
He captured Agag king of the Amalekites alive, and devoted all the people to destruction with the edge of the sword.

But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and the lambs, and everything that was good. They were not willing to devote them to destruction. Everything that was worthless and weak they devoted to destruction.
The word of the LORD came to Samuel:
"I regret that I made Saul king, for he has turned away from following me and has not carried out my commands." Samuel was angry, and he cried out to the LORD all night.
Samuel got up early in the morning to meet Saul. It was told to Samuel, "Saul went to Carmel, and there he has set up a monument for himself. Then he turned and went on down to Gilgal."
Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, "May the LORD bless you. I have carried out the command of the LORD."
Samuel said, "Then what is this bleating of sheep in my ears, and the lowing of cattle that I hear?"
Saul said, "They were brought from the Amalekites, because the people spared the best of the sheep and cattle to sacrifice to the LORD your God. The rest we devoted to destruction."
Then Samuel said to Saul, "Stop. Let me tell you what the LORD said to me last night." He said to him, "Speak."
Samuel said, "Though you were small in your own eyes, were you not made the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel.
The LORD sent you on a mission and said, 'Go and devote the sinners, the Amalekites, to destruction, and fight against them until they are finished.'
Why did you not obey the voice of the LORD? Why did you rush on the plunder and do what was evil in the eyes of the LORD?"
Saul said to Samuel, "But I did obey the voice of the LORD. I went on the mission on which the LORD sent me. I brought back Agag king of Amalek, and I devoted the Amalekites to destruction.
But the people took from the plunder sheep and cattle, the best of what was devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to the LORD your God at Gilgal."
Samuel said:
"Does the LORD delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obeying the voice of the LORD? See, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen better than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is the sin of divination, and arrogance is iniquity and idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has rejected you as king."
Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned, for I have broken the command of the LORD and your words, because I was afraid of the people and listened to their voice.
Now please forgive my sin and come back with me, so that I may bow down to the LORD."
Samuel said to Saul, "I will not go back with you. For you have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you as king over Israel."
As Samuel turned to go, Saul seized the edge of his robe, and it tore.
Samuel said to him, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to a neighbour of yours who is better than you.
The Glory of Israel does not lie or change his mind, for he is not a human being, that he should change his mind."
Saul said, "I have sinned. Now please honour me before the elders of my people and before Israel, and come back with me, so that I may bow down to the LORD your God."
So Samuel went back after Saul, and Saul bowed down to the LORD.
Then Samuel said, "Bring Agag king of the Amalekites to me." Agag came to him in chains. Agag said, "Surely the bitterness of death is past."
Samuel said, "As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women." And Samuel cut Agag to pieces before the LORD at Gilgal.
Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah of Saul.
Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, but Samuel grieved over Saul. And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.

The LORD said to Samuel, "How long will you grieve over Saul, when I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have chosen a king for myself from among his sons."
Samuel said, "How can I go? If Saul hears of it, he will kill me." The LORD said, "Take a heifer with you and say, 'I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.'
Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you are to do. You are to anoint for me the one I name to you."
Samuel did what the LORD said and came to Bethlehem. The elders of the town came trembling to meet him and said, "Do you come in peace?"
He said, "In peace. I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Make yourselves holy and come with me to the sacrifice." And he made Jesse and his sons holy and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they came, he looked at Eliab and thought, "Surely the LORD's anointed stands here before him."

But the LORD said to Samuel, "Do not look at his appearance or at his height, for I have rejected him. The LORD does not see as people see. People look at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart."
Then Jesse called Abinadab and had him pass before Samuel. He said, "The LORD has not chosen this one either."
Then Jesse had Shammah pass by. He said, "The LORD has not chosen this one either."
Jesse had seven of his sons pass before Samuel, but Samuel said to Jesse, "The LORD has not chosen any of these."

Samuel said to Jesse, "Are these all the young men?" He said, "There is still the youngest, but he is out keeping the sheep." Samuel said to Jesse, "Send for him, for we will not sit down until he comes here."
So he sent and brought him in. He was ruddy, with fine eyes and a handsome appearance. The LORD said, "Get up and anoint him, for this is the one."
Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the middle of his brothers. And the spirit of the LORD rushed on David from that day on. Samuel got up and went to Ramah.
Now the spirit of the LORD left Saul, and a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented him.
Saul's servants said to him, "Look, a harmful spirit from God is tormenting you.
Let our lord command your servants here in front of you to look for someone who can play the lyre. When the harmful spirit from God comes on you, he will play, and you will feel better."
So Saul said to his servants, "Find me someone who plays well and bring him to me."
One of the young men answered, "I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play. He is a brave man and a fighter, wise in speech and handsome, and the LORD is with him."
So Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, "Send me your son David, who is with the sheep."
Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine and a young goat, and sent them with his son David to Saul.
David came to Saul and entered his service, and Saul loved him greatly, and he became his armour-bearer.
Saul sent word to Jesse: "Let David stay in my service, for he has found favour in my eyes."
Whenever the harmful spirit from God came on Saul, David would take the lyre and play it. Saul would be relieved and feel better, and the harmful spirit would leave him.
The Philistines gathered their armies for war. They gathered at Socoh in Judah and camped between Socoh and Azekah, at Ephes-dammim.
Saul and the men of Israel gathered and camped in the Valley of Elah and drew up their battle line to meet the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on one hill, and the Israelites stood on the other hill, with the valley between them.
A champion came out from the Philistine camp, named Goliath, from Gath. His height was six cubits and a span.
He had a bronze helmet on his head, and he wore a coat of scale armour, and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of bronze.
He had bronze armour on his legs, and a bronze javelin slung between his shoulders.
The shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and the iron head of his spear weighed six hundred shekels. His shield-bearer walked in front of him.

He stood and shouted to the ranks of Israel, "Why do you come out and line up for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me.
If he is able to fight me and kill me, we will be your servants. But if I defeat him and kill him, you will be our servants and serve us."
The Philistine said, "I defy the ranks of Israel today. Give me a man, so that we can fight each other."
When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were shaken and very afraid.
Now David was the son of an Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah, whose name was Jesse. He had eight sons, and in the days of Saul he was already old, well on in years.
The three oldest sons of Jesse had followed Saul to the war. The names of the three sons who went to the war were Eliab the firstborn, then Abinadab, and the third, Shammah.
David was the youngest. The three oldest followed Saul,
but David went back and forth from Saul to tend his father's sheep at Bethlehem.
For forty days the Philistine came forward morning and evening and took his stand.
Jesse said to his son David, "Take for your brothers an ephah of this roasted grain and these ten loaves, and hurry to the camp to your brothers.
Also take these ten cuts of cheese to the commander of their unit. See how your brothers are, and bring back some token from them."
Saul and the brothers and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah, fighting the Philistines.

David got up early in the morning and left the sheep with a keeper, and took the food and went, as Jesse had commanded him. He came to the camp as the army was going out to the battle line, shouting the war cry.
Israel and the Philistines drew up their lines, army against army.
David left his things with the keeper of the baggage and ran to the battle line and went and greeted his brothers.
While he was talking with them, the champion, the Philistine from Gath named Goliath, came up out of the Philistine ranks and spoke the same words as before. And David heard him.
All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, ran away from him and were very afraid.

The men of Israel said, "Have you seen this man who keeps coming up? He comes up to defy Israel. The king will make the man who kills him very rich, and will give him his daughter and make his father's house free in Israel."

David said to the men standing near him, "What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and removes the disgrace from Israel? Who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?"
The people told him the same thing: "This is what will be done for the man who kills him."

His eldest brother Eliab heard him speaking to the men, and Eliab's anger blazed against David. He said, "Why have you come down here? And who have you left those few sheep with in the wilderness? I know your arrogance and the evil of your heart. You have come down to watch the battle."
David said, "What have I done now? It was only a question."
He turned away from him to someone else and said the same thing, and the people answered him as before.
When the words that David spoke were heard, they told them to Saul, and he sent for him.
David said to Saul, "Let no one lose heart because of him. Your servant will go and fight this Philistine."
Saul said to David, "You cannot go against this Philistine and fight him, for you are only a boy, and he has been a fighter from his youth."
But David said to Saul, "Your servant has been keeping his father's sheep. When a lion or a bear came and took a lamb from the flock,
I went after it and struck it and rescued the lamb from its mouth. If it turned on me, I seized it by its beard and struck it and killed it.
Your servant has killed both lions and bears, and this uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, for he has defied the armies of the living God."
David said, "The LORD who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine." Saul said to David, "Go, and the LORD be with you."
Saul dressed David in his own armour. He put a bronze helmet on his head and dressed him in a coat of armour.
David strapped his sword over the armour and tried to walk, but he was not used to them. David said to Saul, "I cannot go with these, for I am not used to them." So David took them off.
He took his staff in his hand and chose five smooth stones from the stream and put them in his shepherd's bag, his pouch. With his sling in his hand he went towards the Philistine.
The Philistine came closer and closer to David, with his shield-bearer in front of him.
When the Philistine looked and saw David, he looked down on him, for he was only a boy, ruddy and handsome.
The Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?" And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said to David, "Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and the wild animals of the field."
David said to the Philistine, "You come against me with sword and spear and javelin. But I come against you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.

Today the LORD will hand you over to me, and I will strike you down and cut off your head. Today I will give the corpses of the Philistine army to the birds of the sky and the wild animals of the earth, so that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel,
and that all this assembly may know that the LORD does not save by sword or spear. For the battle is the LORD's, and he will hand you over to us."
When the Philistine started forward to meet David, David ran quickly towards the battle line to meet the Philistine.
David put his hand in his bag and took out a stone and slung it, and struck the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the ground.
So David defeated the Philistine with a sling and a stone. He struck the Philistine and killed him. There was no sword in David's hand.

David ran and stood over the Philistine and took his sword and drew it from its sheath and killed him, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they ran away.

The men of Israel and Judah got up with a shout and chased the Philistines as far as Gath and the gates of Ekron, and the wounded Philistines fell along the road from Shaaraim as far as Gath and Ekron.
The Israelites came back from chasing the Philistines, and plundered their camp.
David took the Philistine's head and brought it to Jerusalem, but he put the Philistine's weapons in his own tent.
When Saul saw David going out to meet the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is this boy?" Abner said, "As you live, O king, I do not know."
The king said, "Find out whose son the young man is."
When David came back from killing the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him to Saul, with the Philistine's head in his hand.
Saul said to him, "Whose son are you, young man?" David said, "I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem."
When David had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was bound to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
Saul took him that day and would not let him go back to his father's house.
Then Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul.
Jonathan took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, with his armour, and even his sword, his bow and his belt.
David went out and was successful wherever Saul sent him, so that Saul put him over the men of war. This pleased all the people and also Saul's servants.

As they were coming home, when David returned from killing the Philistine, the women came out from all the towns of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet King Saul, with tambourines, with joyful songs and with three-stringed instruments.
The women sang as they danced:
"Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands."
Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, "They have given David tens of thousands, and they have given me only thousands. What more can he have but the kingdom?"
And from that day on Saul kept a jealous eye on David.
The next day a harmful spirit from God rushed on Saul, and he raved in the house, while David was playing the lyre as he did every day. Saul had a spear in his hand.
Saul threw the spear, for he thought, "I will pin David to the wall." But David got out of his way twice.
Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with David but had left Saul.
So Saul removed him from his presence and made him a commander of a thousand, and he went out and came in at the head of the troops.
David was successful in all he did, for the LORD was with him.
When Saul saw that he was very successful, he stood in dread of him.
But all Israel and Judah loved David, for he went out and came in at their head.

Then Saul said to David, "Here is my elder daughter Merab. I will give her to you as a wife. Only be a brave man for me and fight the LORD's battles." For Saul thought, "My hand must not be against him. Let the hand of the Philistines be against him."
David said to Saul, "Who am I, and what is my family, my father's clan in Israel, that I should be the king's son-in-law?"
But when the time came to give Merab, Saul's daughter, to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite as a wife.
Saul's daughter Michal loved David. They told Saul, and it pleased him.
Saul thought, "I will give her to him, so that she may be a trap for him and the hand of the Philistines may be against him." So Saul said to David a second time, "You can now become my son-in-law."
Saul commanded his servants: "Speak to David privately and say, 'Look, the king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you. Now become the king's son-in-law.'"
Saul's servants spoke these words in David's hearing. David said, "Do you think it a small thing to become the king's son-in-law, when I am a poor man and of no account?"
The servants of Saul told him what David had said.

Saul said, "This is what you are to say to David: 'The king wants no bride-price except a hundred Philistine foreskins, to take revenge on the king's enemies.'" Saul planned to have David fall by the hand of the Philistines.
When his servants told David these words, it pleased David to become the king's son-in-law. Before the time had passed,

David got up and went out with his men and killed two hundred Philistines. David brought their foreskins, and they counted out the full number for the king, so that he might become the king's son-in-law. And Saul gave him his daughter Michal as a wife.
When Saul saw and knew that the LORD was with David, and that all Israel loved him,
Saul was even more afraid of David, and Saul was David's enemy from then on.
The Philistine commanders went out to battle, and every time they went out, David had more success than all the other servants of Saul, so that his name was held in high honour.
Saul told his son Jonathan and all his servants to kill David. But Jonathan, Saul's son, was very fond of David.
Jonathan told David, "My father Saul is trying to kill you. So be on your guard in the morning. Stay in a secret place and hide.
I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will speak to my father about you. If I find out anything, I will tell you."

Jonathan spoke well of David to his father Saul and said to him, "The king must not sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and because what he has done has been very good for you.

He took his life in his hands and struck down the Philistine, and the LORD brought about a great victory for all Israel. You saw it and were glad. Why then would you sin against innocent blood by killing David for no reason?"
Saul listened to Jonathan and swore, "As the LORD lives, he will not be put to death."
So Jonathan called David and told him all these things. Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he served him as before.
There was war again, and David went out and fought the Philistines and defeated them with a great slaughter, so that they ran away from him.
Then a harmful spirit from the LORD came on Saul as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand, while David was playing the lyre.
Saul tried to pin David to the wall with the spear, but he slipped away from Saul, and the spear struck the wall. David ran away and escaped that night.
Saul sent messengers to David's house to watch it, so that he could kill him in the morning. But David's wife Michal told him, "If you do not save your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed."
So Michal let David down through a window, and he ran away and escaped.
Michal took the household god and laid it on the bed, and put a net of goats' hair at its head and covered it with a cloth.
When Saul sent messengers to take David, she said, "He is ill."
Then Saul sent the messengers to see David and said, "Bring him up to me on his bed, so that I can kill him."
When the messengers came in, there was the household god in the bed, with the net of goats' hair at its head.
Saul said to Michal, "Why have you deceived me like this and let my enemy go, so that he has escaped?" Michal answered Saul, "He said to me, 'Let me go. Why should I kill you?'"
David ran away and escaped, and he came to Samuel at Ramah and told him everything that Saul had done to him. Then he and Samuel went and stayed at Naioth.
Saul was told, "David is at Naioth in Ramah."
Saul sent messengers to take David. When they saw the company of prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing as their leader, the spirit of God came on Saul's messengers, and they too prophesied.
When this was told to Saul, he sent other messengers, and they also prophesied. Saul sent messengers again a third time, and they also prophesied.
Then he himself went to Ramah. He came to the great cistern at Secu and asked, "Where are Samuel and David?" Someone said, "They are at Naioth in Ramah."
He went there to Naioth in Ramah, and the spirit of God came on him too. As he went along he prophesied until he came to Naioth in Ramah.
He too took off his clothes, and he too prophesied before Samuel. He lay naked all that day and all that night. This is why they say, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"
David ran away from Naioth in Ramah. He came to Jonathan and said, "What have I done? What is my guilt? What is my sin against your father, that he is trying to take my life?"
Jonathan said to him, "Far from it. You will not die. Look, my father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. Why would my father hide this from me? It is not so."

But David swore again and said, "Your father knows well that I have found favour in your eyes, and he thinks, 'Jonathan must not know this, or he will be grieved.' But as the LORD lives and as you live, there is only a step between me and death."
Jonathan said to David, "Whatever you say, I will do for you."
David said to Jonathan, "Look, tomorrow is the new moon, and I am supposed to sit with the king at the meal. Let me go, and I will hide in the field until the evening of the third day.
If your father misses me at all, say, 'David asked me earnestly for leave to run to Bethlehem, his town, for there is a yearly sacrifice there for the whole clan.'
If he says, 'Good,' then your servant is safe. But if he is angry, you will know that he has decided on harm.
So show faithful love to your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant of the LORD with you. But if there is guilt in me, kill me yourself. Why bring me to your father?"
Jonathan said, "Far be it from you. If I knew for certain that my father had decided to bring harm on you, would I not tell you?"
David said to Jonathan, "Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?"
Jonathan said to David, "Come, let us go out into the field." So the two of them went out into the field.

Jonathan said to David, "The LORD, the God of Israel, is witness. When I have sounded out my father about this time tomorrow, or the third day, if there is good for David, will I not send and tell you?

But if my father means to do you harm, may the LORD do this to Jonathan, and more also, if I do not tell you and send you away, so that you can go in safety. May the LORD be with you, as he has been with my father.
If I am still alive, show me the faithful love of the LORD, so that I do not die.
And do not ever cut off your faithful love from my household, not even when the LORD has cut off every one of David's enemies from the face of the earth."
So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David: "May the LORD call David's enemies to account."
Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, because he loved him as he loved his own life.
Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
On the third day you will be missed even more. Go to the place where you hid on the day of the trouble, and stay beside the stone heap.
I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as if I were aiming at a target.

Then I will send the boy, saying, 'Go and find the arrows.' If I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are on this side of you, get them,' then come, for as the LORD lives, you are safe and there is no danger.
But if I say to the young man, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then go, for the LORD has sent you away.
As for the matter that you and I have spoken about, the LORD is between you and me for ever."
So David hid in the field. When the new moon came, the king sat down to eat the meal.
The king sat on his seat, as usual, the seat by the wall. Jonathan sat opposite, and Abner sat at Saul's side, but David's place was empty.
Saul said nothing that day, for he thought, "Something has happened to him. He is unclean. Surely he is unclean."

But on the second day of the month, the day after the new moon, David's place was empty again. Saul said to his son Jonathan, "Why has the son of Jesse not come to the meal, either yesterday or today?"
Jonathan answered Saul, "David earnestly asked me for leave to go to Bethlehem.

He said, 'Please let me go, for our clan has a sacrifice in the town, and my brother has commanded me to be there. Now, if I have found favour in your eyes, let me get away and see my brothers.' That is why he has not come to the king's table."

Then Saul's anger blazed against Jonathan, and he said to him, "You son of a twisted and rebellious woman. Do I not know that you have sided with the son of Jesse, to your own shame and to the shame of your mother's nakedness?
For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom will be established. Now send and bring him to me, for he must die."
Jonathan answered his father Saul, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?"
But Saul hurled his spear at him to strike him down. So Jonathan knew that his father had decided to put David to death.
Jonathan got up from the table in fierce anger and ate no food on the second day of the month, for he was grieved for David, because his father had humiliated him.
In the morning Jonathan went out into the field for the meeting with David, with a small boy.
He said to his boy, "Run and find the arrows I shoot." As the boy ran, he shot an arrow beyond him.
When the boy came to the place of the arrow that Jonathan had shot, Jonathan called after the boy, "Is the arrow not beyond you?"
Jonathan called after the boy, "Hurry. Be quick. Do not stop." So Jonathan's boy gathered up the arrow and came to his master.
But the boy knew nothing. Only Jonathan and David knew the matter.
Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy and said to him, "Go and take them to the town."
As soon as the boy had gone, David got up from beside the stone heap and fell on his face to the ground and bowed down three times. They kissed each other and wept together, David most of all.

Then Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace, since we have sworn to each other in the name of the LORD, saying, 'The LORD will be between you and me, and between my descendants and your descendants, for ever.'" Then David got up and left, and Jonathan went back into the town.
David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came trembling to meet David and said to him, "Why are you alone, with no one with you?"

David said to Ahimelech the priest, "The king gave me a task and said to me, 'No one must know anything about the matter on which I am sending you and what I have commanded you.' I have told the young men to meet at a certain place.
Now, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever can be found."
The priest answered David, "I have no ordinary bread on hand, but there is holy bread, if the young men have kept themselves from women."

David answered the priest, "Women have been kept from us, as always when I go out on a campaign. The young men's bodies are holy, even on an ordinary journey. How much more today will their bodies be holy?"

So the priest gave him the holy bread, for there was no bread there except the bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the LORD, to be replaced by warm bread on the day it was taken away.
One of Saul's servants was there that day, kept back before the LORD. His name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's shepherds.
David said to Ahimelech, "Do you not have a spear or sword here at hand? I did not bring my sword or my weapons with me, because the king's business was urgent."

The priest said, "The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the Valley of Elah, is here, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you want to take it, take it, for there is no other here." David said, "There is none like it. Give it to me."
David got up and ran away that day from Saul and went to Achish king of Gath.
The servants of Achish said to him, "Is this not David, the king of the land? Did they not sing of him as they danced:
'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands'?"
David took these words to heart and was very afraid of Achish king of Gath.
So he changed his behaviour in front of them, and pretended to be mad in their hands. He scratched marks on the doors of the gate and let spittle run down his beard.
Achish said to his servants, "Look, you can see the man is mad. Why have you brought him to me?
Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this man to act mad in front of me? Is this man to come into my house?"
David left there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and all his father's household heard of it, they went down there to him.
Everyone who was in trouble, everyone who was in debt and everyone who was bitter in spirit gathered round him, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were with him.
From there David went to Mizpah in Moab. He said to the king of Moab, "Please let my father and mother stay with you until I know what God will do for me."
He left them with the king of Moab, and they stayed with him all the time that David was in the stronghold.
The prophet Gad said to David, "Do not stay in the stronghold. Go into the land of Judah." So David left and went to the forest of Hereth.
Saul heard that David and the men with him had been discovered. Saul was sitting in Gibeah, under the tamarisk tree on the hill, with his spear in his hand, and all his servants stood round him.

Saul said to his servants who stood round him, "Listen, you Benjaminites. Will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and vineyards? Will he make you all commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds,

that all of you have plotted against me? No one tells me when my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you is sorry for me or tells me that my son has stirred up my servant against me, to lie in ambush, as he is doing today."
Then Doeg the Edomite, who stood among Saul's servants, answered, "I saw the son of Jesse come to Nob, to Ahimelech son of Ahitub.
He asked the LORD for him, and gave him food, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine."
The king sent for the priest Ahimelech son of Ahitub and all his father's household, the priests who were at Nob, and all of them came to the king.
Saul said, "Listen now, son of Ahitub." He answered, "Here I am, my lord."

Saul said to him, "Why have you plotted against me, you and the son of Jesse, by giving him bread and a sword and asking God for him, so that he has risen against me to lie in ambush, as he is doing today?"
Ahimelech answered the king, "And who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king's son-in-law, captain of your bodyguard and honoured in your house?
Was today the first time I asked God for him? Far from it. Do not let the king accuse your servant or any of my father's household, for your servant knew nothing at all about this."
The king said, "You will surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father's household."

The king said to the guards who stood round him, "Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because they too are with David. They knew he was running away and did not tell me." But the king's servants would not raise a hand to strike the priests of the LORD.
Then the king said to Doeg, "You turn and strike the priests." Doeg the Edomite turned and struck down the priests, and that day he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod.
Nob, the town of the priests, he put to the sword, men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys and sheep. He put them all to the sword.
But one of the sons of Ahimelech son of Ahitub, whose name was Abiathar, escaped and ran away to join David.
Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD.
David said to Abiathar, "I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I am responsible for the death of everyone in your father's household.
Stay with me. Do not be afraid. The one who seeks my life seeks yours too. You will be safe with me."
They told David, "Look, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and are robbing the threshing floors."
David asked the LORD, "Shall I go and strike these Philistines?" The LORD said to David, "Go and strike the Philistines and save Keilah."
But David's men said to him, "Look, we are afraid here in Judah. How much more if we go to Keilah against the Philistine forces?"
David asked the LORD again, and the LORD answered him, "Get up and go down to Keilah, for I will hand the Philistines over to you."
David and his men went to Keilah and fought the Philistines, and took away their livestock and struck them with a great slaughter. So David saved the people of Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelech ran away to David at Keilah, he came down with an ephod in his hand.
Saul was told that David had come to Keilah. Saul said, "God has handed him over to me, for he has shut himself in by entering a town with gates and bars."
Saul called out all the people for war, to go down to Keilah and besiege David and his men.
David knew that Saul was plotting harm against him. He said to Abiathar the priest, "Bring the ephod here."
David said, "LORD, God of Israel, your servant has heard for certain that Saul intends to come to Keilah and destroy the town because of me.
Will the people of Keilah hand me over to him? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? LORD, God of Israel, please tell your servant." The LORD said, "He will come down."
David said, "Will the people of Keilah hand me and my men over to Saul?" The LORD said, "They will hand you over."
So David and his men, about six hundred, got up and left Keilah, and went wherever they could. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he gave up the expedition.
David stayed in the wilderness, in the strongholds, in the hill country of the wilderness of Ziph. Saul searched for him every day, but God did not hand him over to him.
David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph at Horesh.
Saul's son Jonathan got up and went to David at Horesh and strengthened his hand in God.
He said to him, "Do not be afraid, for my father Saul's hand will not find you. You will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you. My father Saul knows this too."
The two of them made a covenant before the LORD. David stayed at Horesh, and Jonathan went home.
Then the Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah and said, "Is David not hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah, south of Jeshimon?
Now come down, O king, whenever you wish, and it will be our part to hand him over to the king."
Saul said, "May the LORD bless you, for you have taken pity on me.
Go and make sure. Find out where he goes, and who has seen him there, for I am told he is very cunning.
Look and find out all the hiding places where he hides, and come back to me with sure information. Then I will go with you. If he is in the land, I will search him out among all the clans of Judah."
So they got up and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah south of Jeshimon.
Saul and his men went to look for him. David was told, and he went down to the rock and stayed in the wilderness of Maon. When Saul heard it, he chased David into the wilderness of Maon.

Saul went along one side of the mountain, and David and his men along the other side of the mountain. David was hurrying to get away from Saul. As Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to seize them,
a messenger came to Saul, saying, "Come quickly, for the Philistines have raided the land."
So Saul gave up the chase after David and went to meet the Philistines. That is why that place was called the Rock of Parting.
David went up from there and stayed in the strongholds of En-gedi.
When Saul came back from following the Philistines, he was told, "David is in the wilderness of En-gedi."
Saul took three thousand chosen men from all Israel and went to look for David and his men in front of the Rocks of the Wild Goats.
He came to the sheepfolds by the road, where there was a cave, and Saul went in to relieve himself. Now David and his men were sitting in the far recesses of the cave.

David's men said to him, "This is the day of which the LORD said to you, 'I will hand your enemy over to you, and you can do to him whatever seems good to you.'" Then David got up and quietly cut off a corner of Saul's robe.
Afterwards David's conscience troubled him because he had cut off a corner of Saul's robe.
He said to his men, "The LORD forbid that I should do such a thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed, to raise my hand against him, for he is the LORD's anointed."
So David held back his men with these words and did not let them attack Saul. Then Saul got up and left the cave and went on his way.
After that David also got up and went out of the cave and called after Saul, "My lord the king." When Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the ground and did homage.
David said to Saul, "Why do you listen to the words of people who say, 'David is seeking your harm'?

Today your own eyes have seen how the LORD handed you over to me in the cave. Some told me to kill you, but I spared you. I said, 'I will not raise my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD's anointed.'

See, my father, see the corner of your robe in my hand. I cut off a corner of your robe but did not kill you. So you can know and see that there is no wrong or rebellion in my hands. I have not sinned against you, though you are hunting me to take my life.
May the LORD judge between me and you, and may the LORD take revenge on you for me. But my hand will not be against you.
As the old saying goes, 'Wickedness comes from the wicked.' But my hand will not be against you.
Who has the king of Israel come out after? Who are you chasing? A dead dog. A single flea.
May the LORD be judge and decide between me and you. May he see and plead my cause and rescue me from your hand."
When David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said, "Is this your voice, my son David?" And Saul raised his voice and wept.
He said to David, "You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me with good, though I have repaid you with evil.
Today you have shown how you have dealt well with me, since you did not kill me when the LORD handed me over to you.
When someone finds his enemy, does he send him away unharmed? May the LORD reward you with good for what you have done for me today.
Now I know that you will surely be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hand.
So swear to me now by the LORD that you will not cut off my descendants after me, and that you will not wipe out my name from my father's house."
David swore this to Saul. Then Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.
Samuel died. All Israel gathered to mourn for him, and they buried him at his home in Ramah. Then David set out and went down to the wilderness of Paran.
There was a man in Maon whose business was in Carmel. He was very rich: he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, and he was shearing his sheep at Carmel.
The man's name was Nabal, and his wife's name was Abigail. She was sensible and beautiful. He was harsh and badly behaved. He was a Calebite.
David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his flock,
and he sent ten young men. He told them, "Go up to Carmel and visit Nabal, and greet him in my name.
Say to my brother: 'Peace to you, peace to your household, and peace to everything you own.
I hear that you have the shearers. Your shepherds have been with us, and we did them no harm. Nothing of theirs went missing all the time they were at Carmel.
Ask your own young men, and they will tell you. So let my young men find favour with you, for we have come on a feast day. Please give whatever you can spare to your servants and to your son David.'"
David's young men went and gave Nabal all this message in David's name, and then waited.
Nabal answered David's servants, "Who is David? Who is this son of Jesse? These days there are many servants who break away from their masters.
Am I to take my bread and my water and the meat I have slaughtered for my shearers, and give it to men who come from I do not know where?"
David's young men turned round and went back and told him all this.
David said to his men, "Every man, put on your sword." Every man put on his sword, and David put on his. About four hundred men went up behind David, and two hundred stayed with the baggage.
One of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, "David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet our master, and he shouted abuse at them.
Yet the men were very good to us. We were not harmed, and nothing went missing all the time we were out in the fields with them.
They were a wall round us day and night, all the time we were with them looking after the sheep.
So now think what you can do, for disaster has been decided against our master and his whole household. He is such a worthless man that no one can speak to him."

Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves, two skins of wine, five sheep ready dressed, five measures of roasted grain, a hundred bunches of raisins and two hundred cakes of figs, and loaded them on donkeys.
She told her young men, "Go on ahead. I am coming behind you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
She was riding her donkey and coming down under cover of the mountain, and there were David and his men coming down towards her, and she met them.
David had just been saying, "It was all for nothing, protecting everything this man had in the wilderness, so that nothing of his went missing. He has paid me back evil for good.
May God do this to David, and more also, if by morning I leave alive a single male of all who belong to him."
When Abigail saw David, she quickly got down from her donkey and fell on her face before David and bowed to the ground.
She fell at his feet and said, "On me, my lord, on me let the blame fall. Please let your servant speak in your hearing, and listen to what your servant says.

Do not take any notice, my lord, of this worthless man Nabal, for he is just what his name says. His name is Fool, and folly goes with him. But I, your servant, did not see the young men whom my lord sent.

Now, my lord, as the LORD lives and as you live, since the LORD has kept you from bloodguilt and from saving yourself with your own hand, may your enemies and all who seek to harm my lord be like Nabal.
Now let this gift that your servant has brought to my lord be given to the young men who follow my lord.

Please forgive the offence of your servant, for the LORD will certainly make a lasting house for my lord, because my lord fights the battles of the LORD, and no evil will be found in you as long as you live.

If anyone rises to chase you and seek your life, the life of my lord will be bound up in the bundle of the living with the LORD your God. But the lives of your enemies he will sling away as from the cup of a sling.
When the LORD has done for my lord all the good that he has promised you, and has made you ruler over Israel,

this will not be a cause of grief to you, or a weight on the conscience of my lord, that you shed blood for no reason, or that my lord saved himself. And when the LORD has done good to my lord, remember your servant."
David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today.
Blessed be your good sense, and blessed be you, who have kept me today from bloodguilt and from saving myself with my own hand.
For as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who has kept me from harming you, if you had not hurried to meet me, there would not have been one male left to Nabal by morning light."
Then David took from her hand what she had brought him and said to her, "Go home in peace. See, I have listened to you and granted your request."
Abigail came to Nabal, and he was holding a feast in his house, a feast fit for a king. Nabal was in high spirits and very drunk, so she told him nothing at all until the morning light.
In the morning, when the wine had left Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became like a stone.
About ten days later the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.

When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has taken up my case against Nabal's insult and kept his servant from doing wrong. The LORD has brought Nabal's wrongdoing down on his own head." Then David sent word to Abigail, to take her as his wife.
When David's servants came to Abigail at Carmel, they said to her, "David has sent us to you, to take you as his wife."
She got up and bowed with her face to the ground and said, "Here is your servant, ready to serve, to wash the feet of the servants of my lord."
Abigail got up quickly and rode on a donkey, with her five young women attending her. She followed David's messengers and became his wife.
David had also taken Ahinoam of Jezreel, and both of them became his wives.
But Saul had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.
The Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah and said, "David is hiding on the hill of Hachilah, facing Jeshimon."
So Saul got up and went down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel, to look for David there.
Saul camped beside the road on the hill of Hachilah, facing Jeshimon. David was living in the wilderness, and he saw that Saul had followed him there.
David sent out scouts, and learned that Saul had indeed come.

David set out and went to the place where Saul had camped. He saw where Saul was lying, with Abner son of Ner, the commander of his army. Saul was lying inside the ring of the camp, with the army camped round him.
David said to Ahimelech the Hittite and to Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, "Who will go down with me into the camp to Saul?" Abishai said, "I will go down with you."

So David and Abishai went into the camp by night, and there was Saul, lying asleep inside the ring of the camp, with his spear stuck in the ground at his head, and Abner and the troops lying round him.
Abishai said to David, "Today God has handed your enemy over to you. Now let me pin him to the ground with one thrust of the spear. I will not need a second."
But David said to Abishai, "Do not destroy him. Who can raise a hand against the LORD's anointed and be without guilt?"
David said, "As the LORD lives, the LORD himself will strike him down, either when his day comes and he dies, or when he goes into battle and is lost.
The LORD forbid that I should raise a hand against the LORD's anointed. Now take the spear at his head and the water jug, and let us go."
So David took the spear and the water jug from beside Saul's head, and they went away. No one saw it or knew it or woke up. They were all asleep, for a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them.
David crossed over to the other side and stood on the top of the mountain, some distance away, with a wide space between them.
David called to the army and to Abner son of Ner: "Will you not answer, Abner?" Abner answered, "Who are you, to call out to the king?"
David said to Abner, "Are you not a man? Who is like you in Israel? Why did you not guard your lord the king? Someone came in to destroy the king your lord.

What you have done is not good. As the LORD lives, you deserve to die, because you did not guard your lord, the LORD's anointed. Now look. Where are the king's spear and the water jug that were at his head?"
Saul recognised David's voice and said, "Is that your voice, my son David?" David said, "It is my voice, my lord the king."
He said, "Why is my lord chasing his servant? What have I done? What wrong have I committed?

Now let my lord the king listen to the words of his servant. If the LORD has stirred you up against me, may he accept an offering. But if it is people, may they be cursed before the LORD, for they have driven me out today from my share in the LORD's inheritance, saying, 'Go and serve other gods.'
Now do not let my blood fall to the ground far from the presence of the LORD, for the king of Israel has come out to look for a single flea, as one hunts a partridge in the mountains."
Saul said, "I have sinned. Come back, my son David. I will not harm you again, because my life was precious in your eyes today. I have acted foolishly and made a great mistake."
David answered, "Here is the king's spear. Let one of the young men come over and take it.
The LORD repays each person for his righteousness and faithfulness. The LORD handed you over to me today, but I would not raise a hand against the LORD's anointed.
As your life was precious in my eyes today, so may my life be precious in the eyes of the LORD, and may he rescue me from all trouble."
Saul said to David, "May you be blessed, my son David. You will do great things, and you will surely succeed." So David went on his way, and Saul returned to his place.

David thought to himself, "One day I will be swept away by Saul's hand. There is nothing better for me than to escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will give up searching for me anywhere in Israel, and I will escape from his hand."
So David got up and crossed over, he and the six hundred men with him, to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.
David stayed with Achish at Gath, he and his men, each man with his household, David with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail of Carmel, Nabal's widow.
When Saul was told that David had fled to Gath, he no longer searched for him.
David said to Achish, "If I have found favour in your eyes, let me be given a place in one of the country towns, so that I can live there. Why should your servant live in the royal city with you?"
So that day Achish gave him Ziklag. That is why Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.
The time David lived in Philistine country was a year and four months.
David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites and the Amalekites, for they were the people who had lived in the land from long ago, as you go towards Shur and as far as Egypt.
David struck the land and left neither man nor woman alive, but took sheep and cattle, donkeys and camels, and clothes, and came back to Achish.
When Achish asked, "Where did you raid today?" David would say, "The Negev of Judah," or "The Negev of the Jerahmeelites," or "The Negev of the Kenites."

David left neither man nor woman alive to bring back to Gath, for he thought, "They might tell about us and say, 'This is what David did.'" This was his practice all the time he lived in Philistine country.
Achish trusted David, thinking, "He has made himself a stench among his own people Israel, so he will be my servant for ever."
In those days the Philistines gathered their forces for war, to fight against Israel. Achish said to David, "You must understand that you and your men will march out with me in the army."
David said to Achish, "Then you will see for yourself what your servant can do." Achish said to David, "Then I will make you my bodyguard for life."
Samuel was dead. All Israel had mourned for him and buried him at Ramah, in his own town. And Saul had driven the mediums and the consulters of spirits out of the land.
The Philistines gathered and came and camped at Shunem. Saul gathered all Israel, and they camped at Gilboa.
When Saul saw the Philistine camp, he was afraid, and his heart shook.
Saul asked the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him, by dreams, by the Urim or by prophets.
Then Saul said to his servants, "Find me a woman who is a medium, and I will go and ask her." His servants said to him, "There is a woman at En-dor who is a medium."
So Saul disguised himself, putting on other clothes, and went with two men. They came to the woman by night. He said, "Please consult a spirit for me and bring up for me the one I name."
The woman said to him, "You know what Saul has done, how he has cut off the mediums and the consulters of spirits from the land. Why are you setting a trap for my life, to have me killed?"
Saul swore to her by the LORD, "As the LORD lives, no punishment will come to you for this."
The woman said, "Whom shall I bring up for you?" He said, "Bring up Samuel for me."
When the woman saw Samuel, she screamed at the top of her voice. She said to Saul, "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul."
The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What do you see?" The woman said to Saul, "I see a divine being coming up out of the earth."
He said to her, "What does he look like?" She said, "An old man is coming up, wrapped in a robe." Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground and did homage.

Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?" Saul said, "I am in great distress. The Philistines are making war on me, and God has turned away from me and no longer answers me, by prophets or by dreams. So I have called you, to tell me what to do."
Samuel said, "Why do you ask me, when the LORD has turned away from you and become your enemy?
The LORD has done to you what he said through me. The LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbour, to David.
Because you did not obey the voice of the LORD and did not carry out his burning anger against Amalek, the LORD has done this to you today.
The LORD will hand Israel over with you to the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. The LORD will also hand the army of Israel over to the Philistines."
At once Saul fell full length on the ground, terrified by the words of Samuel. There was no strength left in him, for he had eaten nothing all day and all night.
The woman came to Saul and saw that he was badly shaken. She said to him, "Look, your servant has listened to you. I took my life in my hands and did what you asked of me.
Now please listen to your servant. Let me set a little food before you, and eat, so that you have strength for your journey."
He refused and said, "I will not eat." But his servants, together with the woman, urged him, and he listened to them. He got up from the ground and sat on the couch.
The woman had a fattened calf in the house. She hurried and killed it, took flour and kneaded it, and baked flat bread from it,
and set it before Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they got up and went away that night.
The Philistines gathered all their forces at Aphek, while Israel camped by the spring at Jezreel.
The Philistine rulers were marching past by hundreds and by thousands, and David and his men were marching past at the rear with Achish.

The Philistine commanders said, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Achish said to the Philistine commanders, "Is this not David, the servant of Saul king of Israel, who has been with me for days and years? I have found no fault in him from the day he came over to me until now."

But the Philistine commanders were angry with him and said to him, "Send the man back, so that he returns to the place you gave him. He must not go down with us into the battle, or he will turn against us in the fighting. How could this man win back his master's favour? Would it not be with the heads of our men?
Is this not David, of whom they sang as they danced:
'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands'?"

Achish called David and said to him, "As the LORD lives, you have been honest, and it seems right to me to have you march out and in with me in the army. I have found no fault in you from the day you came to me until now. But the rulers do not approve of you.
So now go back in peace, and do nothing to displease the Philistine rulers."
David said to Achish, "But what have I done? What have you found in your servant from the day I came to you until now, that I cannot go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?"
Achish answered David, "I know that you are as good in my eyes as an angel of God. But the Philistine commanders have said, 'He must not go up with us into the battle.'

So get up early in the morning, you and your lord's servants who came with you, and go to the place I gave you. Do not take any bad thought to heart, for you are good in my eyes. Get up early in the morning, and when it is light, go."
So David and his men got up early in the morning to go back to the land of the Philistines, and the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
When David and his men reached Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had raided the Negev and Ziklag. They had attacked Ziklag and burned it down.
They had taken captive the women and everyone in it, young and old. They had not killed anyone, but had carried them off and gone on their way.
When David and his men came to the town, there it was, burned down, and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive.
David and the people with him raised their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep.
David's two wives had been taken captive, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel.
David was in great distress, for the people spoke of stoning him, because all of them were bitter in spirit, each for his sons and daughters. But David found strength in the LORD his God.
David said to the priest Abiathar son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." Abiathar brought the ephod to David.
David asked the LORD, "Shall I chase this raiding band? Will I overtake them?" He said to him, "Chase them, for you will certainly overtake them, and you will certainly rescue the captives."
So David set out, he and the six hundred men with him, and they came to the Wadi Besor, where some stayed behind.
David went on with four hundred men, for two hundred stayed behind, too exhausted to cross the Wadi Besor.
They found an Egyptian in the open country and brought him to David. They gave him bread and he ate, and they gave him water to drink,
and gave him a piece of a fig cake and two bunches of raisins. When he had eaten, his strength returned, for he had not eaten bread or drunk water for three days and three nights.
David said to him, "Whose man are you? Where are you from?" He said, "I am a young Egyptian, the servant of an Amalekite. My master left me behind because I fell ill three days ago.
We raided the Negev of the Cherethites and the territory of Judah and the Negev of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag down."
David said to him, "Will you take me down to this raiding band?" He said, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or hand me over to my master, and I will take you down to this band."

He took him down, and there they were, spread out over the whole ground, eating and drinking and dancing because of all the great plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah.
David struck them down from twilight until the evening of the next day. Not one of them escaped, except four hundred young men who rode off on camels.
David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, and David rescued his two wives.
Nothing was missing, small or great, sons or daughters, plunder or anything they had taken. David brought everything back.
David also took all the flocks and herds, and the people drove them ahead of the other livestock and said, "This is David's plunder."

David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow him, who had been left at the Wadi Besor. They came out to meet David and the people with him. When David came near the people, he greeted them.

Then all the wicked and worthless men among those who had gone with David said, "Because they did not go with us, we will not give them any of the plunder we recovered, except that each man may take his wife and children and go."
But David said, "You must not do that, my brothers, with what the LORD has given us. He has kept us safe and handed over to us the raiding band that came against us.
Who will listen to you in this matter? The share of the one who goes down into battle and the share of the one who stays by the baggage will be the same. They will share alike."
From that day on it has been a statute and a rule for Israel, to this day.
When David came to Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to the elders of Judah, his friends, saying, "Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD's enemies."
It was for those in Bethel, in Ramoth of the Negev, in Jattir,
in Aroer, in Siphmoth, in Eshtemoa,
in Racal, in the towns of the Jerahmeelites, in the towns of the Kenites,
in Hormah, in Bor-ashan, in Athach,
in Hebron, and in all the places where David and his men had roamed.
The Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell dead on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines caught up with Saul and his sons, and the Philistines killed Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul.
The battle pressed hard on Saul, and the archers found him, and he was badly wounded by the archers.

Saul said to his armour-bearer, "Draw your sword and run me through, so that these uncircumcised men do not come and run me through and make sport of me." But his armour-bearer would not, for he was terrified. So Saul took his own sword and fell on it.
When his armour-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell on his sword and died with him.
So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armour-bearer, and all his men, on the same day together.

When the men of Israel on the other side of the valley and those beyond the Jordan saw that the army of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their towns and fled, and the Philistines came and lived in them.
The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found Saul and his three sons lying on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off his head and stripped off his armour, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to carry the news to their idols and to the people.
They put his armour in the temple of the Ashtoreths, and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan.
When the people of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul,
all the brave men set out and travelled through the night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, and they came to Jabesh and burned them there.
Then they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree at Jabesh, and fasted for seven days.
After the death of Saul, when David had come back from defeating the Amalekites, David stayed in Ziklag two days.
On the third day a man came from Saul's camp, with his clothes torn and earth on his head. When he came to David, he fell to the ground and bowed down.
David said to him, "Where have you come from?" He said to him, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel."
David said to him, "What happened? Tell me." He said, "The people fled from the battle, and many of them fell and died. Saul and his son Jonathan are dead too."
David said to the young man who told him, "How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?"
The young man who told him said, "I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul leaning on his spear, with the chariots and the horsemen closing in on him.
He looked behind him and saw me, and called to me. I said, 'Here I am.'
He said to me, 'Who are you?' I answered him, 'I am an Amalekite.'
He said to me, 'Stand over me and kill me, for I am in agony, and my life still holds on.'
So I stood over him and killed him, for I knew that he could not live after he had fallen. I took the crown from his head and the band from his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord."
Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men with him.
They mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and his son Jonathan, and for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.
David said to the young man who had told him, "Where are you from?" He answered, "I am the son of a foreigner living among you, an Amalekite."
David said to him, "How were you not afraid to raise your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?"
Then David called one of the young men and said, "Go and strike him down." So he struck him down, and he died.
David said to him, "Your blood is on your own head, for your own mouth testified against you when you said, 'I have killed the LORD's anointed.'"
David sang this lament over Saul and over his son Jonathan,
and he ordered that the people of Judah be taught the Song of the Bow. It is written in the Book of Jashar.
Your glory, Israel, lies slain on your heights. How the mighty have fallen.
Do not tell it in Gath. Do not announce it in the streets of Ashkelon, or the daughters of the Philistines will rejoice, the daughters of the uncircumcised will celebrate.
Mountains of Gilboa, let no dew or rain fall on you, no fields that give offerings. For there the shield of the mighty was thrown down in shame, the shield of Saul, no longer rubbed with oil.
From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan never turned back, the sword of Saul never came home empty.
Saul and Jonathan, loved and lovely, in life and in death they were not parted. They were swifter than eagles, stronger than lions.
Daughters of Israel, weep for Saul, who dressed you in scarlet and fine things, who put gold ornaments on your clothes.
How the mighty have fallen in the middle of the battle. Jonathan lies slain on your heights.
I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan. You were very dear to me. Your love for me was wonderful, more than the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war are lost.
After this David asked the LORD, "Shall I go up to one of the towns of Judah?" The LORD said to him, "Go up." David said, "Where shall I go?" He said, "To Hebron."
So David went up there, with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel.
David also brought up the men who were with him, each with his household, and they settled in the towns round Hebron.
The men of Judah came and anointed David there as king over the house of Judah. When David was told, "It was the people of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul,"
he sent messengers to the people of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him.
Now may the LORD show you faithful love and truth. And I too will do good to you, because you have done this.
