Now be strong and be brave, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."
But Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul's army, had taken Ish-bosheth son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim.
He made him king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin and all Israel.
Ish-bosheth son of Saul was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he ruled for two years. But the house of Judah followed David.
The time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.
Joab son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. They sat down, one group on one side of the pool and the other on the other side.
Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men get up and compete in front of us." Joab said, "Let them get up."
So they got up and were counted off, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve of David's servants.
Each one grabbed his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his opponent's side, and they fell down together. So that place at Gibeon was called Helkath-hazzurim.
The battle that day was very fierce, and Abner and the men of Israel were beaten by David's servants.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab, Abishai and Asahel. Asahel was as fast on his feet as a wild gazelle.
Asahel chased Abner, and he did not turn to the right or to the left as he followed him.
Abner looked behind him and said, "Is that you, Asahel?" He answered, "It is."
Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right or to your left, and seize one of the young men and take his gear." But Asahel would not turn aside from following him.
Abner said again to Asahel, "Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How could I look your brother Joab in the face?"

But he refused to turn aside. So Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, and the spear came out through his back. He fell there and died on the spot. Everyone who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died stopped still.
But Joab and Abishai chased Abner. As the sun was going down, they came to the hill of Ammah, which faces Giah on the road to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjaminites gathered behind Abner and formed one group, and took their stand on top of a hill.
Abner called to Joab, "Must the sword eat for ever? Do you not know that this will end in bitterness? How long before you tell your people to stop chasing their brothers?"
Joab said, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, the people would not have given up the chase of their brothers until morning."
So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the people stopped. They did not chase Israel any more or fight any more.
Abner and his men went all that night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan and marched the whole morning and came to Mahanaim.
Joab came back from chasing Abner. When he had gathered all the people, nineteen of David's servants were missing, besides Asahel.
But David's servants had struck down three hundred and sixty of the Benjaminites who were with Abner.
They took Asahel and buried him in his father's tomb at Bethlehem. Joab and his men marched all night, and the light broke on them at Hebron.
The war between the house of Saul and the house of David went on for a long time. David grew steadily stronger, and the house of Saul grew steadily weaker.
Sons were born to David at Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel.
His second was Chileab, by Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel. The third was Absalom, son of Maacah daughter of Talmai king of Geshur.
The fourth was Adonijah, son of Haggith. The fifth was Shephatiah, son of Abital.
The sixth was Ithream, by David's wife Eglah. These were born to David at Hebron.
During the war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was making himself more and more powerful in the house of Saul.
Now Saul had had a concubine whose name was Rizpah daughter of Aiah. Ish-bosheth said to Abner, "Why have you slept with my father's concubine?"

Abner was furious at Ish-bosheth's words and said, "Am I a dog's head for Judah? All this time I have shown faithful love to the house of your father Saul, to his brothers and his friends, and have not handed you over to David. And now you charge me today with a fault over this woman.
May God do this to Abner, and more also, if I do not do for David what the LORD has sworn to him:
to take the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba."
Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he was afraid of him.
Abner sent messengers to David at once, saying, "Whose is the land? Make a covenant with me, and I will help you bring all Israel over to you."
David said, "Good. I will make a covenant with you. But I ask one thing of you: you will not see my face unless you bring Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come to see me."
Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, saying, "Give me my wife Michal, whom I won for a hundred Philistine foreskins."
Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband Paltiel son of Laish.
Her husband went with her, weeping behind her all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go back." And he went back.
Abner had talked with the elders of Israel and said, "For some time now you have wanted David as your king.
Now do it, for the LORD has said of David, 'By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from the hand of all their enemies.'"
Abner also spoke to the Benjaminites. Then Abner went to tell David at Hebron all that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin were willing to do.
When Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men, David gave a feast for Abner and the men with him.

Abner said to David, "Let me go and gather all Israel to my lord the king, so that they may make a covenant with you, and you may rule over all that your heart desires." So David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.

Just then David's servants and Joab came back from a raid, bringing a great deal of plunder with them. But Abner was no longer with David at Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he had gone in peace.
When Joab and all the army with him arrived, Joab was told, "Abner son of Ner came to the king, and he sent him away, and he has gone in peace."
Then Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Look, Abner came to you. Why did you send him away? Now he is gone.
You know Abner son of Ner. He came to deceive you, to learn your movements and everything you are doing."
When Joab left David, he sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the cistern of Sirah. But David did not know it.

When Abner came back to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the middle of the gateway to speak to him privately, and there he stabbed him in the stomach, and he died, to pay for the blood of his brother Asahel.
Afterwards, when David heard of it, he said, "I and my kingdom are for ever innocent before the LORD of the blood of Abner son of Ner.

May it fall on the head of Joab and on all his father's house. May the house of Joab never be without someone with a discharge, or a skin disease, or one who holds a spindle, or one who falls by the sword, or one who lacks bread."
So Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner, because he had killed their brother Asahel in the battle at Gibeon.
David said to Joab and to all the people with him, "Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth and mourn in front of Abner." And King David himself walked behind the bier.
They buried Abner at Hebron, and the king raised his voice and wept at Abner's grave, and all the people wept.
The king sang a lament for Abner:
"Should Abner have died as a fool dies?
Your hands were not bound, your feet were not put in chains. As one falls before wicked men, you fell."
And all the people wept over him again.
Then all the people came to urge David to eat something while it was still day. But David swore, "May God do this to me, and more also, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun goes down."
All the people took note of it, and it pleased them, as everything the king did pleased them.
So on that day all the people and all Israel understood that it had not been the king's will to kill Abner son of Ner.
The king said to his servants, "Do you not know that a commander, a great man, has fallen today in Israel?
And today I am weak, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too hard for me. May the LORD repay the one who does evil according to his evil."
When Saul's son heard that Abner had died at Hebron, his courage failed, and all Israel was dismayed.
Saul's son had two men who were leaders of raiding bands. One was named Baanah and the other Rechab, sons of Rimmon of Beeroth, a Benjaminite. (Beeroth is also counted as part of Benjamin,
and the people of Beeroth had fled to Gittaim, where they have lived as foreigners to this day.)

Jonathan son of Saul had a son who was crippled in both feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and ran away, and as she hurried to flee, he fell and was left lame. His name was Mephibosheth.
The sons of Rimmon of Beeroth, Rechab and Baanah, set out and came to the house of Ish-bosheth at the hottest part of the day, while he was taking his midday rest.
They went into the middle of the house, as if to fetch wheat, and stabbed him in the stomach. Then Rechab and his brother Baanah slipped away.

They had come into the house while he was lying on his bed in his bedroom, and they struck him down and killed him and cut off his head. They took his head and travelled all night by the way of the Arabah,

and brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron. They said to the king, "Here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy, who tried to take your life. Today the LORD has avenged my lord the king on Saul and his descendants."
But David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon of Beeroth, "As the LORD lives, who has rescued me from every trouble,
when someone told me, 'Saul is dead,' and thought he was bringing good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag. That was the reward I gave him for his news.
How much more, when wicked men have killed an innocent man in his own house, on his own bed, will I not demand his blood from your hands and wipe you from the earth?"

David gave the order to his young men, and they killed them and cut off their hands and feet and hung them beside the pool at Hebron. But they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in the tomb of Abner at Hebron.
All the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, "Look, we are your own flesh and bone.
In the past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led Israel out and brought it back. And the LORD said to you, 'You will shepherd my people Israel, and you will be ruler over Israel.'"
So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD, and they anointed David king over Israel.
David was thirty years old when he became king, and he ruled for forty years.
In Hebron he ruled over Judah for seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he ruled over all Israel and Judah for thirty-three years.

The king and his men marched to Jerusalem against the Jebusites who lived there. They said to David, "You will not get in here. Even the blind and the lame can turn you back," thinking, "David cannot get in here."
But David captured the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David.

On that day David said, "Whoever strikes down the Jebusites, let him go up the water shaft and strike those lame and blind enemies of David." That is why people say, "The blind and the lame may not enter the house."
David lived in the stronghold and called it the city of David. He built all round it, from the Millo inwards.
David grew greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him.
Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, with cedar trees and carpenters and stonemasons, and they built a house for David.
David knew that the LORD had established him as king over Israel, and that he had raised his kingdom high for the sake of his people Israel.
After he came from Hebron, David took more concubines and wives in Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him.
These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,
Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia,
Elishama, Eliada and Eliphelet.
When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, they all went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went down to the stronghold.
The Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
David asked the LORD, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you hand them over to me?" The LORD said to David, "Go up, for I will certainly hand the Philistines over to you."
So David came to Baal-perazim, and David defeated them there. He said, "The LORD has broken through my enemies before me like a bursting flood." So that place is called Baal-perazim.
The Philistines left their idols there, and David and his men carried them off.
The Philistines came up again and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
When David asked the LORD, he said, "Do not go straight up. Circle round behind them and come at them opposite the balsam trees.
When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then move quickly, for the LORD has gone out ahead of you to strike down the Philistine army."
David did as the LORD commanded him, and struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer.
David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand.
David and all the people with him set out from Baale-judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD of hosts, who sits enthroned on the cherubim.
They put the ark of God on a new cart and brought it out of Abinadab's house on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, sons of Abinadab, were guiding the new cart,
with the ark of God on it, and Ahio walked in front of the ark.
David and the whole house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD with all their strength, with songs and with lyres, harps, tambourines, rattles and cymbals.
When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, because the oxen had stumbled.
The anger of the LORD blazed against Uzzah, and God struck him down there for his error, and he died there beside the ark of God.
David was angry because the LORD had burst out against Uzzah. That place is called Perez-uzzah to this day.
David was afraid of the LORD that day, and he said, "How can the ark of the LORD come to me?"
So David was not willing to take the ark of the LORD into the city of David. David took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.
The ark of the LORD stayed in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household.

It was told to King David, "The LORD has blessed the household of Obed-edom and everything he has, because of the ark of God." So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David with rejoicing.
When those who carried the ark of the LORD had gone six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal.
David danced before the LORD with all his strength. David was wearing a linen ephod.
So David and the whole house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and the sound of the ram's horn.
As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart.
They brought in the ark of the LORD and set it in its place, inside the tent that David had pitched for it. David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.
When David had finished offering the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of hosts,
and gave to all the people, the whole crowd of Israel, men and women alike, a loaf of bread, a portion of meat and a cake of raisins to each. Then all the people went home, each to his house.

David went home to bless his household. But Michal daughter of Saul came out to meet David and said, "How the king of Israel honoured himself today, uncovering himself in front of his servants' maidservants, as one of the vulgar men shamelessly uncovers himself."
David said to Michal, "It was before the LORD, who chose me over your father and over all his house, to appoint me ruler over Israel, the LORD's people. I will celebrate before the LORD.
I will make myself even more lowly than this, and I will be humble in my own eyes. But with the maidservants of whom you have spoken, with them I will be held in honour."
And Michal daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.
When the king was settled in his house, and the LORD had given him rest from all his enemies around him,
the king said to Nathan the prophet, "Look, I am living in a house of cedar, while the ark of God stays in a tent."
Nathan said to the king, "Go and do whatever is in your heart, for the LORD is with you."
But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan:
"Go and tell my servant David, 'This is what the LORD says: Are you the one to build me a house to live in?
I have not lived in a house from the day I brought the Israelites up out of Egypt to this day. I have been moving about in a tent as my dwelling.

In all the places where I moved about among all the Israelites, did I ever say a word to any of the leaders of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel: "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'
Now say this to my servant David: 'This is what the LORD of hosts says: I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people Israel.
I have been with you wherever you went, and I have cut off all your enemies from in front of you. I will make you a great name, like the names of the greatest in the earth.
I will set a place for my people Israel and plant them, so that they can live in their own place and not be disturbed again. Violent people will not oppress them any more, as they did at first,
from the day I appointed judges over my people Israel. I will give you rest from all your enemies. And the LORD tells you that the LORD will make a house for you.
When your days are over and you lie down with your ancestors, I will raise up your offspring after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom.
He will build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever.
I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me. When he does wrong, I will correct him with a human rod and with human blows.
But my faithful love will not leave him, as I took it from Saul, whom I removed from before you.
Your house and your kingdom will be secure for ever before me. Your throne will be established for ever.'"
Nathan spoke to David in keeping with all these words and with all this vision.
Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far?
And yet this was a small thing in your eyes, Lord GOD, for you have also spoken about your servant's house for a long time to come. And this is the way of a human being, Lord GOD.
What more can David say to you? You know your servant, Lord GOD.
For the sake of your word, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness and made it known to your servant.
So you are great, LORD God. There is no one like you, and there is no God but you, in everything we have heard with our own ears.

And who is like your people Israel, one nation on earth whom God went out to redeem as his people, to make a name for himself and to do great and awesome things for them, driving out nations and their gods before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt?
You made your people Israel your own people for ever, and you, LORD, became their God.
And now, LORD God, keep for ever the word that you have spoken about your servant and his house, and do as you have said.
Then your name will be great for ever, and people will say, 'The LORD of hosts is God over Israel.' And the house of your servant David will be established before you.
For you, LORD of hosts, God of Israel, have uncovered the ear of your servant, saying, 'I will build you a house.' That is why your servant has found the courage to pray this prayer to you.
Now, Lord GOD, you are God, and your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.

So now, be pleased to bless the house of your servant, so that it may continue for ever before you. For you, Lord GOD, have spoken, and by your blessing the house of your servant will be blessed for ever."
After this David defeated the Philistines and brought them under his rule, and David took Metheg-ammah from the Philistines.

He also defeated Moab. He made them lie on the ground and measured them with a line. He measured two lengths to be put to death, and one full length to be kept alive. So the Moabites became David's servants and brought tribute.
David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to restore his power at the River Euphrates.
David captured from him seventeen hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers. David hamstrung all the chariot horses but kept enough for a hundred chariots.
When the Arameans of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand of the Arameans.
Then David set garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became David's servants and brought tribute. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
David took the gold shields that belonged to Hadadezer's servants and brought them to Jerusalem.
From Betah and Berothai, towns of Hadadezer, King David took a great deal of bronze.
When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer,

Toi sent his son Joram to King David to greet him and bless him, because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him, for Hadadezer had often been at war with Toi. Joram brought with him objects of silver, gold and bronze.
King David also dedicated these to the LORD, along with the silver and gold that he had dedicated from all the nations he had conquered:
from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines and Amalek, and from the plunder of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt.
He set garrisons in Edom, throughout Edom, and all the Edomites became David's servants. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
David ruled over all Israel, and David did what was just and right for all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army, Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder,
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests, Seraiah was the secretary,
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and David's sons were priests.
David asked, "Is there anyone left of the house of Saul, so that I can show him faithful love for Jonathan's sake?"
There was a servant of the house of Saul whose name was Ziba. They called him to David, and the king said to him, "Are you Ziba?" He said, "Your servant."
The king said, "Is there no one left of the house of Saul, so that I can show him the kindness of God?" Ziba said to the king, "There is still a son of Jonathan, crippled in both feet."
The king said to him, "Where is he?" Ziba said to the king, "He is in the house of Machir son of Ammiel at Lo-debar."
Then King David sent and brought him from the house of Machir son of Ammiel at Lo-debar.
Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face and did homage. David said, "Mephibosheth." He answered, "Here is your servant."

David said to him, "Do not be afraid, for I will show you faithful love for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will give back to you all the land of your grandfather Saul, and you will eat at my table always."
He bowed down and said, "What is your servant, that you should take notice of a dead dog like me?"
Then the king called Saul's servant Ziba and said to him, "All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master's grandson.

You and your sons and your servants are to farm the land for him and bring in the harvest, so that your master's grandson has food to eat. But Mephibosheth your master's grandson will always eat at my table." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba said to the king, "Your servant will do all that my lord the king commands." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table like one of the king's sons.
Mephibosheth had a young son whose name was Mica. All who lived in Ziba's house became Mephibosheth's servants.
So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he always ate at the king's table. He was lame in both feet.
After this the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun became king in his place.

David said, "I will show faithful love to Hanun son of Nahash, as his father showed faithful love to me." So David sent messengers to comfort him about his father. When David's servants came to the land of the Ammonites,

the Ammonite commanders said to their lord Hanun, "Do you think David is honouring your father because he has sent comforters to you? Has David not sent his servants to you to search the city and spy it out and overthrow it?"
So Hanun took David's servants and shaved off half of each man's beard and cut off their clothes in the middle, at the hips, and sent them away.
When David was told, he sent to meet them, for the men were deeply ashamed. The king said, "Stay at Jericho until your beards have grown, and then come back."

When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, they sent and hired the Arameans of Beth-rehob and the Arameans of Zobah, twenty thousand foot soldiers, and the king of Maacah with a thousand men, and the men of Tob, twelve thousand men.
When David heard of it, he sent Joab and the whole army of warriors.
The Ammonites came out and drew up their battle line at the entrance of the gate, while the Arameans of Zobah and Rehob and the men of Tob and Maacah were by themselves in the open country.
When Joab saw that the battle line was facing him in front and behind, he chose some of the best men of Israel and drew them up against the Arameans.
The rest of the army he put under the command of his brother Abishai, and he drew them up against the Ammonites.
He said, "If the Arameans are too strong for me, you will help me. But if the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will come and help you.
Be strong, and let us show strength for the sake of our people and for the towns of our God. And may the LORD do what seems good to him."
So Joab and the troops with him advanced to fight the Arameans, and they ran away from him.
When the Ammonites saw that the Arameans had run away, they too ran away from Abishai and went into the town. Then Joab came back from fighting the Ammonites and returned to Jerusalem.
When the Arameans saw that they had been beaten by Israel, they gathered together.
Hadadezer sent and brought out the Arameans who were beyond the River, and they came to Helam, with Shobach the commander of Hadadezer's army at their head.
When David was told, he gathered all Israel and crossed the Jordan and came to Helam. The Arameans drew up against David and fought with him.

The Arameans ran away from Israel, and David killed the men of seven hundred chariots of the Arameans, and forty thousand horsemen, and struck down Shobach the commander of their army, so that he died there.
When all the kings who were servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been beaten by Israel, they made peace with Israel and served them. So the Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites any more.
In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to war, David sent Joab with his servants and all Israel. They destroyed the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David stayed in Jerusalem.
One evening David got up from his bed and was walking on the roof of the king's house. From the roof he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful.
David sent and asked about the woman. Someone said, "Is this not Bathsheba daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?"
David sent messengers and took her. She came to him, and he lay with her. (She had just purified herself from her uncleanness.) Then she went back to her house.
The woman conceived, and she sent word to David: "I am pregnant."
So David sent word to Joab: "Send me Uriah the Hittite." And Joab sent Uriah to David.
When Uriah came to him, David asked how Joab was, and how the army was, and how the war was going.
Then David said to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." Uriah left the king's house, and a gift from the king followed him.
But Uriah slept at the entrance to the king's house with all his lord's servants, and did not go down to his house.
When they told David, "Uriah did not go down to his house," David said to Uriah, "Have you not just come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?"

Uriah said to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah are staying in tents, and my lord Joab and my lord's servants are camped in the open field. Should I go to my house to eat and drink and lie with my wife? As you live, and as your life lives, I will not do this."
Then David said to Uriah, "Stay here today also, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him, and he ate and drank in his presence, and David made him drunk. In the evening he went out to lie on his bed with his lord's servants, but he did not go down to his house.
In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.
In the letter he wrote, "Put Uriah at the front, where the fighting is fiercest, and then pull back from him, so that he is struck down and dies."
So when Joab was besieging the city, he put Uriah at the place where he knew there were strong fighters.
The men of the city came out and fought against Joab, and some of the people, some of David's servants, fell. Uriah the Hittite also died.
Then Joab sent and told David all the news of the battle.
He told the messenger, "When you have finished telling the king all the news of the battle,
if the king's anger rises and he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the town to fight? Did you not know that they would shoot from the wall?

Who killed Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth? Did a woman not throw an upper millstone down on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?' then say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too.'"
The messenger went and came and told David everything that Joab had sent him to say.
The messenger said to David, "The men had the better of us and came out against us in the open field, but we pushed them back to the entrance of the gate.
Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too."
David said to the messenger, "Say this to Joab: 'Do not let this trouble you, for the sword eats one as well as another. Press the attack on the city harder and overthrow it.' And encourage him."
When Uriah's wife heard that her husband Uriah was dead, she mourned for him.
When the time of mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But what David had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD.
The LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said, "There were two men in one town, one rich and one poor.
The rich man had very many sheep and cattle,

but the poor man had nothing except one small ewe lamb that he had bought. He raised it, and it grew up with him and with his children. It shared his food and drank from his cup and slept in his arms, and it was like a daughter to him.

A traveller came to the rich man, and he could not bring himself to take one from his own flock or herd to prepare a meal for the guest who had come to him. So he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come."
David's anger blazed against the man, and he said to Nathan, "As the LORD lives, the man who did this deserves to die.
He must pay for the lamb four times over, because he did this and had no pity."
Nathan said to David, "You are the man. This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I anointed you king over Israel, and I rescued you from the hand of Saul.
I gave you your master's house, and your master's wives into your arms, and I gave you the house of Israel and Judah. And if that was too little, I would have given you as much again.

Why have you despised the word of the LORD by doing what is evil in his eyes? You struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife to be your wife. You killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.
Now the sword will never leave your house, because you despised me and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.

This is what the LORD says: I will raise up trouble against you from your own house. I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbour, and he will lie with your wives in broad daylight.
You did it in secret, but I will do this before all Israel and in the light of the sun."
David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." Nathan said to David, "The LORD has also taken away your sin. You will not die.
But because by this deed you have shown utter contempt for the LORD, the son born to you will die."
Then Nathan went home. The LORD struck the child that Uriah's wife had borne to David, and he became very ill.
David pleaded with God for the child. David fasted and went in and spent the night lying on the ground.
The elders of his household stood beside him to raise him from the ground, but he would not, and he would not eat with them.

On the seventh day the child died. David's servants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, "While the child was still alive, we spoke to him, and he would not listen to us. How can we tell him the child is dead? He may do himself harm."
David saw that his servants were whispering to each other, and David understood that the child was dead. David said to his servants, "Is the child dead?" They said, "He is dead."

Then David got up from the ground and washed and anointed himself and changed his clothes. He went into the house of the LORD and worshipped. Then he went to his own house, and when he asked, they set food before him, and he ate.
His servants said to him, "What is this that you have done? While the child was alive you fasted and wept, but when the child died, you got up and ate."
He said, "While the child was alive, I fasted and wept, for I thought, 'Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me, and the child may live.'
But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back? I will go to him, but he will not come back to me."
Then David comforted his wife Bathsheba, and went in to her and lay with her. She bore a son and named him Solomon. The LORD loved him
and sent word by Nathan the prophet, and he named him Jedidiah, because of the LORD.
Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah and have captured the water supply of the city.
Now gather the rest of the people, camp against the city and capture it, or I will capture it myself, and it will be called by my name."
So David gathered all the people and went to Rabbah and fought against it and captured it.
He took the crown of their king from his head. It weighed a talent of gold, and it had a precious stone in it, and it was put on David's head. He also took a great amount of plunder from the city.

He brought out the people who were in it and put them to work with saws, iron picks and iron axes, and made them work at the brick kilns. He did the same to all the towns of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people went back to Jerusalem.
Some time later, Absalom son of David had a beautiful sister whose name was Tamar, and Amnon son of David loved her.
Amnon was so tormented that he made himself ill over his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her.
But Amnon had a friend whose name was Jonadab son of Shimeah, David's brother. Jonadab was a very clever man.
He said to him, "Why are you, the king's son, so low, morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I love Tamar, the sister of my brother Absalom."

Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. When your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Please let my sister Tamar come and give me something to eat. Let her prepare the food in front of me, so that I can watch and eat it from her hand.'"

So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. When the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in front of me, so that I can eat from her hand."
David sent a message home to Tamar: "Go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him."
So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house, where he was lying down. She took dough and kneaded it, and made cakes in front of him, and baked them.
Then she took the pan and set the cakes out in front of him, but Amnon refused to eat. Amnon said, "Send everyone away from me." So everyone went out from him.
Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the bedroom, so that I can eat from your hand." So Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them to her brother Amnon in the bedroom.
But as she brought them to him to eat, he grabbed her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister."
She answered him, "No, my brother, do not force me, for this is not done in Israel. Do not do this shameful thing.
Where could I carry my shame? And you would be one of the fools in Israel. Now, please speak to the king, for he will not keep me from you."
But he would not listen to her. He was stronger than she was, and he overpowered her and raped her.
Then Amnon hated her with a very great hatred. The hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. Amnon said to her, "Get up. Go."
But she said to him, "No, sending me away is a greater wrong than the other thing you did to me." But he would not listen to her.
He called the young man who served him and said, "Put this woman out, away from me, and bolt the door after her."
(She was wearing a long robe with sleeves, for this is how the king's virgin daughters dressed in those days.) His servant put her out and bolted the door after her.
Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe she was wearing. She put her hand on her head and went away, crying out loud as she went.

Her brother Absalom said to her, "Has your brother Amnon been with you? Now, my sister, keep quiet. He is your brother. Do not take this to heart." So Tamar lived, desolate, in her brother Absalom's house.
When King David heard about all this, he was very angry.
But Absalom said nothing to Amnon, neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon because he had raped his sister Tamar.
Two years later, Absalom was having his sheep sheared at Baal-hazor, near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king's sons.
Absalom came to the king and said, "Your servant is having the sheep sheared. Please let the king and his servants come with your servant."
But the king said to Absalom, "No, my son, we should not all go, or we will be a burden to you." He pressed him, but he would not go, though he gave him his blessing.
Then Absalom said, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." The king said to him, "Why should he go with you?"
But Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him.
Absalom commanded his servants, "Watch, and when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not be afraid. Have I not commanded you? Be strong and brave."
So Absalom's servants did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons got up, and each mounted his mule and fled.
While they were on the way, the report came to David: "Absalom has struck down all the king's sons, and not one of them is left."
The king got up and tore his clothes and lay on the ground, and all his servants standing by tore their clothes.

But Jonadab son of Shimeah, David's brother, said, "My lord must not think that they have killed all the young men, the king's sons. Only Amnon is dead. This has been Absalom's plan from the day Amnon raped his sister Tamar.
So my lord the king must not take it to heart, thinking that all the king's sons are dead. Only Amnon is dead."
But Absalom ran away. The young man on watch looked up and saw many people coming on the road behind him, by the side of the hill.
Jonadab said to the king, "Look, the king's sons have come. It is as your servant said."
As soon as he had finished speaking, the king's sons came in and raised their voices and wept. The king and all his servants also wept very bitterly.
But Absalom had run away and gone to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day.
So Absalom ran away and went to Geshur, and was there three years.
And the king's spirit longed to go out to Absalom, for he had been comforted over the death of Amnon.
Joab son of Zeruiah saw that the king's heart was turned towards Absalom.

So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman. He said to her, "Pretend to be in mourning. Put on mourning clothes and do not anoint yourself with oil. Act like a woman who has been mourning for the dead for a long time.
Go to the king and speak to him in this way." And Joab put the words in her mouth.
When the woman of Tekoa came to the king, she fell with her face to the ground and bowed down and said, "Help me, O king."
The king said to her, "What is the matter?" She answered, "I am a widow. My husband is dead.
Your servant had two sons, and they fought each other in the field, and there was no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him.

Now the whole family has risen against your servant, and they say, 'Hand over the one who struck his brother, so that we can put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed.' If they do that, they will destroy the heir as well. They will put out the last ember I have left, and leave my husband neither name nor descendant on the face of the earth."
The king said to the woman, "Go home, and I will give orders about you."
The woman of Tekoa said to the king, "My lord the king, let the guilt be on me and on my father's house, and let the king and his throne be innocent."
The king said, "If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he will not touch you again."

She said, "Please let the king call on the LORD your God, so that the avenger of blood may not destroy any more, and my son may not be wiped out." He said, "As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son will fall to the ground."
The woman said, "Please let your servant speak one word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak."

The woman said, "Why then have you planned something like this against the people of God? In giving this decision the king condemns himself, because the king does not bring back the one he has banished.

We all must die. We are like water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered up again. But God does not take away life. He devises ways so that the one who is banished does not stay banished from him.
Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people have frightened me. Your servant thought, 'I will speak to the king. Perhaps the king will do what his servant asks.
For the king will listen and rescue his servant from the hand of the man who would cut off both me and my son from the inheritance of God.'
Your servant thought, 'The word of my lord the king will bring me rest,' for my lord the king is like the angel of God in knowing good and evil. May the LORD your God be with you."
The king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I ask you." The woman said, "Let my lord the king speak."

The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered, "As you live, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right or to the left from anything my lord the king says. Yes, it was your servant Joab who commanded me, and he put all these words in the mouth of your servant.
Your servant Joab did this to change how things look. But my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God, to know everything that happens on earth."
The king said to Joab, "Very well. I will do this. Go and bring back the young man Absalom."

Joab fell with his face to the ground and bowed down and blessed the king. Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favour in your eyes, my lord the king, because the king has done what his servant asked."
So Joab got up and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
But the king said, "He must live in his own house. He must not see my face." So Absalom lived in his own house and did not see the king's face.
In all Israel there was no one so much praised for his beauty as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the top of his head there was no flaw in him.
When he cut the hair of his head (he used to cut it at the end of every year, because it was heavy on him), he weighed the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king's weight.
Three sons were born to Absalom, and one daughter whose name was Tamar. She was a beautiful woman.
Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem without coming into the king's presence.
Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. He sent a second time, but Joab still would not come.
So he said to his servants, "Look, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire.
Then Joab got up and went to Absalom at his house and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?"

Absalom answered Joab, "Look, I sent for you and said, 'Come here, so that I can send you to the king to ask: Why did I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still.' Now let me see the king's face, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death."
Joab went to the king and told him, and he summoned Absalom. He came to the king and bowed with his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.
After this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses and fifty men to run in front of him.

Absalom used to get up early and stand beside the road to the gate. Whenever anyone had a dispute to bring to the king for judgement, Absalom would call to him and say, "Which town are you from?" He would answer, "Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel."
Absalom would say to him, "Look, your claims are good and right, but there is no one assigned by the king to hear you."
Absalom would add, "If only I were appointed judge in the land. Then everyone with a dispute or a case could come to me, and I would see that he got justice."
And whenever someone came near to bow down to him, he would reach out his hand and take hold of him and kiss him.
Absalom did this to all the Israelites who came to the king for judgement. So Absalom stole the hearts of the people of Israel.
At the end of four years Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go to Hebron and keep the vow that I made to the LORD.
For your servant made a vow while I was living at Geshur in Aram: 'If the LORD will bring me back to Jerusalem, I will serve the LORD.'"
The king said to him, "Go in peace." So he got up and went to Hebron.
But Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel with the message: "As soon as you hear the sound of the ram's horn, say, 'Absalom is king at Hebron.'"
Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom. They had been invited and went in innocence, knowing nothing.
While Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counsellor, from his town Giloh. The conspiracy grew strong, and the people with Absalom kept increasing.
A messenger came to David and said, "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom."

David said to all his servants who were with him in Jerusalem, "Get up, let us flee, or none of us will escape from Absalom. Go quickly, or he will move fast and catch us and bring disaster down on us and put the town to the sword."
The king's servants said to the king, "Whatever our lord the king decides, your servants are ready."
So the king left, with all his household following him. But the king left ten concubines to look after the house.
The king left, with all the people following him, and they stopped at the last house.
All his servants passed by him, and all the Cherethites and all the Pelethites, and all the six hundred Gittites who had come with him from Gath marched past the king.
The king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why are you also coming with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner and an exile from your own place.

You came only yesterday. Should I make you wander about with us today, when I do not know where I am going? Go back, and take your brothers with you, and may the LORD show you faithful love and truth."
But Ittai answered the king, "As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king is, whether for death or for life, your servant will be there too."
David said to Ittai, "Then go on." So Ittai the Gittite went on with all his men and all the little ones who were with him.
All the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the Wadi Kidron, and all the people crossed over on the road to the wilderness.

Zadok was there too, and all the Levites with him, carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set down the ark of God, and Abiathar went up, until all the people had finished passing out of the city.
The king said to Zadok, "Take the ark of God back into the city. If I find favour in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back and let me see it and his dwelling place again.
But if he says, 'I take no pleasure in you,' here I am. Let him do to me whatever seems good to him."
The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Are you not a seer? Go back to the town in peace, with your son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan, your two sons with you.
Look, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to tell me."
So Zadok and Abiathar took the ark of God back to Jerusalem and stayed there.
But David went up the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, with his head covered and his feet bare. All the people with him covered their heads and went up, weeping as they went.
It was told to David, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." David said, "LORD, please turn the advice of Ahithophel into foolishness."
When David came to the top, where God was worshipped, Hushai the Archite met him with his coat torn and earth on his head.
David said to him, "If you go on with me, you will be a burden to me.
But if you go back to the town and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king. I was your father's servant in the past, and now I will be yours,' then you can defeat Ahithophel's advice for me.
The priests Zadok and Abiathar will be with you there. Whatever you hear from the king's house, tell it to the priests Zadok and Abiathar.
Their two sons are there with them, Zadok's son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan, and you can send them to me with everything you hear."
So Hushai, David's friend, came into the town just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem.

When David had gone a little beyond the top of the hill, there was Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, coming to meet him with a pair of saddled donkeys, loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred summer fruits and a skin of wine.

The king said to Ziba, "Why have you brought these?" Ziba said, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride, the bread and the summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for those who grow faint in the wilderness to drink."
The king said, "And where is your master's grandson?" Ziba said to the king, "He is staying in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will give me back my grandfather's kingdom.'"
The king said to Ziba, "Everything that belonged to Mephibosheth is yours." Ziba said, "I bow down to you. May I find favour in your eyes, my lord the king."
When King David came to Bahurim, a man from the family of the house of Saul came out, whose name was Shimei son of Gera. He kept cursing as he came.
He threw stones at David and at all King David's servants, though all the people and all the warriors were on his right and on his left.
Shimei said as he cursed, "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man.

The LORD has brought back on you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have ruled, and the LORD has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. Now you are caught in your own evil, for you are a man of blood."
Then Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and cut off his head."
But the king said, "What do you and I have in common, sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because the LORD has told him, 'Curse David,' who can ask, 'Why have you done this?'"

David said to Abishai and to all his servants, "Look, my own son, who came from my body, is trying to take my life. How much more this Benjaminite. Leave him alone and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to.
Perhaps the LORD will see my distress, and the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today."
So David and his men went on along the road, while Shimei went along the hillside opposite him, cursing as he went and throwing stones and flinging dust at him.
The king and all the people with him arrived exhausted, and there he rested.
Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.
When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "Long live the king. Long live the king."
Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?"
Hushai said to Absalom, "No. The one whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, I will belong to him, and I will stay with him.
Besides, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I served your father, so I will serve you."
Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give us your advice. What shall we do?"

Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he left to look after the house. Then all Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father, and the hands of everyone with you will be strengthened."
So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.
In those days the advice that Ahithophel gave was like the word of God, when someone asked for it. That was how all Ahithophel's advice was regarded, both by David and by Absalom.
Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will set out and chase David tonight.
I will come on him while he is tired and discouraged, and throw him into a panic, and all the people with him will run away. I will strike down only the king,
and I will bring all the people back to you as a bride comes back to her husband. You are seeking the life of only one man, and all the people will be at peace."
The advice pleased Absalom and all the elders of Israel.
But Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear what he has to say."
When Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, "This is what Ahithophel has said. Shall we do what he says? If not, you speak."
Hushai said to Absalom, "This time the advice that Ahithophel has given is not good.

You know that your father and his men are warriors, and they are fierce, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the open country. Your father is a man of war, and he will not spend the night with the people.

Even now he is hiding in one of the pits or in some other place. If some of your men fall in the first attack, whoever hears of it will say, 'There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.'
Then even the brave man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, will lose all courage, for all Israel knows that your father is a warrior and that those with him are brave.
But this is my advice: let all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as many as the sand by the sea, and you yourself go into the battle.
Then we will come upon him wherever he can be found, and we will settle on him as the dew settles on the ground, and not one will be left of him or of all the men with him.
If he withdraws into a town, all Israel will bring ropes to that town, and we will drag it into the valley, until not even a pebble can be found there."

Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The advice of Hushai the Archite is better than the advice of Ahithophel." For the LORD had ordained that the good advice of Ahithophel be defeated, so that the LORD might bring disaster on Absalom.
Then Hushai said to the priests Zadok and Abiathar, "This is what Ahithophel advised Absalom and the elders of Israel, and this is what I advised.
Now send quickly and tell David, 'Do not spend the night at the fords of the wilderness, but cross over at once, or the king and all the people with him will be swallowed up.'"
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying at En-rogel. A female servant would go and tell them, and they would go and tell King David, for they could not be seen entering the town.
But a young man saw them and told Absalom. So the two of them left quickly and came to the house of a man at Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard, and they went down into it.
The man's wife took a covering and spread it over the mouth of the well and scattered grain on it, and nothing was known of it.

When Absalom's servants came to the woman at the house, they said, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" The woman said to them, "They have gone over the stream." When they had searched and could not find them, they went back to Jerusalem.
After they had gone, the two came up out of the well and went and told King David. They said to David, "Get up and cross the water quickly, for this is what Ahithophel has advised against you."
So David and all the people with him got up and crossed the Jordan. By daybreak not one of them was left who had not crossed the Jordan.

When Ahithophel saw that his advice had not been followed, he saddled his donkey and set out for his home in his own town. He put his house in order and hanged himself, and he died and was buried in his father's tomb.
David came to Mahanaim. And Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel.
Absalom had put Amasa over the army in place of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Israelite, who had married Abigal daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.
Israel and Absalom camped in the land of Gilead.
When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, and Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim
brought beds, bowls and clay pots, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans and lentils,
honey, curds, sheep and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat, for they said, "The people are hungry and tired and thirsty in the wilderness."
David counted the people who were with him and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.

David sent out the army in three parts, a third under Joab, a third under Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and a third under Ittai the Gittite. The king said to the people, "I myself will also go out with you."

But the people said, "You must not go out. If we have to run away, they will not care about us. Even if half of us die, they will not care. But you are worth ten thousand of us. So it is better if you support us from the town."
The king said to them, "I will do whatever seems best to you." So the king stood beside the gate while all the army marched out by hundreds and by thousands.
The king gave this order to Joab, Abishai and Ittai: "Be gentle with the young man Absalom, for my sake." All the people heard when the king gave the order to all the commanders about Absalom.
So the army went out into the field against Israel, and the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim.
There the army of Israel was beaten by David's servants, and the slaughter that day was great, twenty thousand men.
The battle spread over the whole countryside, and the forest swallowed up more people that day than the sword.

Absalom happened to meet David's servants. Absalom was riding his mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of a great oak, and his head was caught in the oak, and he was left hanging between heaven and earth, while the mule under him went on.
A man saw it and told Joab, "I saw Absalom hanging in an oak."
Joab said to the man who told him, "You saw him. Why did you not strike him to the ground there? I would have given you ten pieces of silver and a belt."

But the man said to Joab, "Even if I were to feel the weight of a thousand pieces of silver in my hand, I would not raise my hand against the king's son. In our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, 'Protect the young man Absalom for me.'
Or if I had acted treacherously against his life (and nothing is hidden from the king), you yourself would have kept away from me."
Joab said, "I will not waste time like this with you." He took three spears in his hand and thrust them into Absalom's heart while he was still alive in the oak.
Ten young men, Joab's armour-bearers, surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him.
Then Joab blew the trumpet, and the army turned back from chasing Israel, for Joab held the people back.
They took Absalom and threw him into a large pit in the forest and piled a very great heap of stones over him. All Israel fled, each to his own home.

In his lifetime Absalom had taken and set up for himself the pillar that is in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name alive." He named the pillar after himself, and it is called Absalom's Monument to this day.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, "Let me run and take the news to the king, that the LORD has rescued him from the hand of his enemies."
Joab said to him, "You will not be the bearer of news today. You may take news another day, but not today, because the king's son is dead."
Then Joab said to the Cushite, "Go and tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed to Joab and ran.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok said again to Joab, "Whatever happens, let me run after the Cushite too." Joab said, "Why do you want to run, my son? You will get no reward for this news."
"Whatever happens," he said, "I will run." So he said to him, "Run." Ahimaaz ran by way of the plain and passed the Cushite.
David was sitting between the two gates, and the watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, and looked up and saw a man running alone.
The watchman called out and told the king. The king said, "If he is alone, he has news." And he came nearer and nearer.
The watchman saw another man running, and the watchman called down to the gatekeeper, "Look, another man running alone." The king said, "He also brings news."
The watchman said, "I think the first one runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok." The king said, "He is a good man, and he comes with good news."

Ahimaaz called out to the king, "Peace." He bowed down to the king with his face to the ground and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has handed over the men who raised their hands against my lord the king."
The king said, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" Ahimaaz answered, "When Joab sent the king's servant, your servant, I saw a great commotion, but I do not know what it was."
The king said, "Step aside and stand here." So he stepped aside and stood there.
Then the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, "Good news for my lord the king. Today the LORD has rescued you from the hand of all who rose up against you."
The king said to the Cushite, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" The Cushite answered, "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you to harm you be like that young man."
The king was shaken, and he went up to the room over the gate and wept. As he went he said, "My son Absalom. My son, my son Absalom. If only I had died instead of you, Absalom, my son, my son."
Joab was told, "The king is weeping and mourning for Absalom."
So the victory that day became mourning for all the people, for the people heard it said that day, "The king is grieving for his son."
The people crept into the town that day as people creep in who are ashamed after running away from a battle.
The king covered his face, and the king cried out in a loud voice, "My son Absalom. Absalom, my son, my son."

Then Joab came into the house to the king and said, "Today you have shamed all your servants, who today saved your life and the lives of your sons and daughters, and the lives of your wives and concubines,

by loving those who hate you and hating those who love you. For you have made it plain today that commanders and servants mean nothing to you. I know today that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead, you would be pleased.

Now get up, go out and speak kindly to your servants. I swear by the LORD, if you do not go out, not one man will stay with you tonight, and that will be worse for you than all the trouble that has come on you from your youth until now."

So the king got up and took his seat in the gateway. The people were told, "The king is sitting in the gateway." And all the people came before the king. Meanwhile Israel had fled, each to his own home.

All the people throughout all the tribes of Israel were arguing among themselves, saying, "The king rescued us from the hand of our enemies and saved us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has had to flee from the land because of Absalom.
But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, has died in battle. So why do you say nothing about bringing the king back?"
King David sent to the priests Zadok and Abiathar: "Say to the elders of Judah, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, when the talk of all Israel has come to the king?
You are my brothers, my own flesh and bone. Why should you be the last to bring back the king?'
And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my own flesh and bone? May God do this to me, and more also, if you do not become commander of my army from now on in place of Joab.'"
He won over the hearts of all the men of Judah as one man, and they sent word to the king: "Come back, you and all your servants."
So the king came back to the Jordan, and Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and bring him across the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
With him were a thousand men of Benjamin. And Ziba, the servant of the house of Saul, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, rushed down to the Jordan ahead of the king,
and they crossed the ford to bring over the king's household and to do whatever he thought good. When he was about to cross the Jordan, Shimei son of Gera fell down before the king
and said to the king, "Do not let my lord hold me guilty or remember the wrong your servant did on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Do not let the king take it to heart.
For your servant knows that I have sinned. That is why I have come today, the first of all the house of Joseph to come down to meet my lord the king."
Abishai son of Zeruiah answered, "Should Shimei not be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?"

But David said, "What do you and I have in common, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should be my opponents today? Should anyone be put to death in Israel today? Do I not know that today I am king over Israel?"
The king said to Shimei, "You will not die." And the king gave him his oath.

Mephibosheth son of Saul also came down to meet the king. He had not looked after his feet, or trimmed his moustache, or washed his clothes, from the day the king left until the day he came back safely.
When he came from Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"
He answered, "My lord the king, my servant deceived me. Your servant said, 'I will have a donkey saddled for me, and I will ride on it and go with the king,' for your servant is lame.
He has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like the angel of God. Do what seems good to you.
All my father's house were nothing but dead men before my lord the king, yet you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What right do I have to cry out to the king any more?"
The king said to him, "Why say more about your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba will divide the land."
Mephibosheth said to the king, "Let him take it all, since my lord the king has come home safely."
Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he went on with the king to the Jordan, to see him off at the Jordan.
Barzillai was very old, eighty years old. He had provided the king with food while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very rich man.
The king said to Barzillai, "Come across with me, and I will provide for you at my side in Jerusalem."
But Barzillai said to the king, "How many years do I have left, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?

I am eighty years old today. Can I tell what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks? Can I still hear the voices of singing men and singing women? Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?
Your servant will go a little way across the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?

Please let your servant go back, so that I may die in my own town, near the grave of my father and mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you."
The king answered, "Chimham will cross over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and whatever you ask of me I will do for you."
Then all the people crossed the Jordan, and the king crossed over. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he went back to his own home.
The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went on with him. All the people of Judah, and also half the people of Israel, brought the king on his way.
Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to him, "Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought the king and his household across the Jordan, with all David's men?"
All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is closely related to us. Why are you angry about this? Have we eaten anything at the king's expense? Have we been given any gift?"

The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and in David also we have more than you. Why then did you treat us with contempt? Were we not the first to speak of bringing our king back?" But the words of the men of Judah were harsher than the words of the men of Israel.

There happened to be a worthless man there, whose name was Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. He blew the trumpet and said, "We have no share in David, no inheritance in the son of Jesse. Every man to his tents, Israel."
So all the men of Israel left David and followed Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah stayed with their king, from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

David came to his house in Jerusalem. The king took the ten concubines whom he had left to look after the house and put them in a house under guard. He provided for them but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as widows.
Then the king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together to me within three days, and be here yourself."
So Amasa went to call Judah together, but he took longer than the time he had been given.
David said to Abishai, "Now Sheba son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and chase him, or he will find fortified towns and slip away from us."
So Joab's men and the Cherethites and the Pelethites and all the warriors went out after him. They marched out of Jerusalem to chase Sheba son of Bichri.

When they were at the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Joab was wearing his soldier's tunic, and over it was a belt with a sword in its sheath fastened at his hip, and as he went forward it fell out.
Joab said to Amasa, "Is it well with you, my brother?" And Joab took hold of Amasa's beard with his right hand to kiss him.

But Amasa was not on guard against the sword in Joab's other hand, and Joab struck him in the stomach with it and spilled his bowels on the ground. He did not strike him again, and he died. Then Joab and his brother Abishai went on chasing Sheba son of Bichri.
One of Joab's young men stood by Amasa and said, "Whoever favours Joab, and whoever is for David, follow Joab."

Amasa lay writhing in his blood in the middle of the road. When the man saw that all the people stopped, he moved Amasa from the road into the field and threw a garment over him, for he saw that everyone who came by him stopped.
When he had been moved from the road, all the people went on after Joab to chase Sheba son of Bichri.
Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah, and all the Bichrites gathered and followed him in.

Joab's men came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah. They built a siege ramp against the town, and it stood against the outer wall. All the people with Joab were battering the wall to bring it down.
Then a wise woman called from the town, "Listen, listen. Tell Joab, 'Come here, so that I can speak to you.'"
He came near her, and the woman said, "Are you Joab?" He said, "I am." She said to him, "Listen to the words of your servant." He said, "I am listening."
Then she said, "In the old days they used to say, 'Ask at Abel,' and so they settled a matter.
I am one of the peaceful and faithful in Israel. You are trying to destroy a town that is a mother in Israel. Why would you swallow up the inheritance of the LORD?"
Joab answered, "Far be it, far be it from me, that I should swallow up or destroy.

That is not the case. A man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Sheba son of Bichri, has raised his hand against King David. Hand him over, him alone, and I will withdraw from the town." The woman said to Joab, "His head will be thrown to you over the wall."

Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet, and they left the town, each to his home. And Joab went back to the king in Jerusalem.
Joab was over all the army of Israel, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites,
Adoram was in charge of forced labour, Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder,
Sheva was secretary, Zadok and Abiathar were priests,
and Ira the Jairite was also a priest to David.

There was a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year. David sought the face of the LORD, and the LORD said, "There is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death."

So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. (The Gibeonites were not Israelites but a remnant of the Amorites. The Israelites had sworn an oath to them, but Saul had tried to wipe them out in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah.)
David said to the Gibeonites, "What shall I do for you? How can I make amends, so that you may bless the inheritance of the LORD?"

The Gibeonites said to him, "It is not a matter of silver or gold between us and Saul or his house, and it is not for us to put anyone in Israel to death." He said, "Then what do you say I should do for you?"
They said to the king, "The man who finished us off and planned to destroy us, so that we have no place anywhere within the borders of Israel,
let seven of his sons be handed over to us, and we will hang them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen one of the LORD." The king said, "I will hand them over."
But the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, because of the oath of the LORD between them, between David and Jonathan son of Saul.

The king took the two sons of Rizpah daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and the five sons of Merab daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.

He handed them over to the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the mountain before the LORD. The seven of them died together. They were put to death in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of the harvest until the rain fell on them from the sky. She did not let the birds of the air touch them by day, or the wild animals by night.
When David was told what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul's concubine, had done,

David went and took the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan from the people of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square at Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them on the day the Philistines struck Saul down at Gilboa.
He brought up from there the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan, and they gathered the bones of those who had been hanged.

They buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in the land of Benjamin at Zela, in the tomb of his father Kish. They did all that the king commanded. After that God answered the prayers for the land.
The Philistines were at war again with Israel, and David went down with his servants and fought the Philistines, and David grew weary.
Ishbi-benob, one of the descendants of the giants, whose spear weighed three hundred shekels of bronze, and who was armed with a new sword, said he would kill David.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid and struck the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men swore to him, "You will never again go out with us to battle, so that you do not put out the lamp of Israel."
After this there was again war with the Philistines at Gob. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, one of the descendants of the giants.
There was again war with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, killed Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver's beam.
There was war again at Gath, where there was a man of great size, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all, and he also was descended from the giants.
When he taunted Israel, Jonathan son of Shimei, David's brother, struck him down.
These four were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
David spoke the words of this song to the LORD on the day the LORD rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.
He said:
