Then the king spoke to the wise men who understood the times (for this was how the king handled matters with all who knew law and legal judgement,

and those closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena and Memucan, the seven officials of Persia and Media who had access to the king and held the first places in the kingdom):
"By law, what is to be done with Queen Vashti, because she did not obey the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"
Memucan said in front of the king and the officials, "Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king, but also all the officials and all the peoples in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus.
For the queen's conduct will become known to all women, and they will look down on their husbands, saying, 'King Ahasuerus ordered Queen Vashti to be brought before him, and she did not come.'
This very day the noble women of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen's conduct will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be plenty of contempt and anger.

If it pleases the king, let a royal order go out from him, and let it be written in the laws of Persia and Media so that it cannot be changed, that Vashti is never again to come before King Ahasuerus. And let the king give her royal position to another who is better than she.
When the king's decree is announced throughout his kingdom, large as it is, all women will give honour to their husbands, from the greatest to the least."
The advice pleased the king and the officials, and the king did as Memucan said.

He sent letters to all the royal provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, that every man should be master in his own house and speak in the language of his own people.
After these things, when the king's anger had cooled, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her.
Then the king's attendants said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king.

Let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather every beautiful young virgin to the women's quarters in Susa the citadel, under the care of Hegai the king's eunuch, who is in charge of the women. Let their beauty treatments be given them.
Then let the young woman who pleases the king be queen in place of Vashti." The advice pleased the king, and he did so.
In Susa the citadel there was a Jew whose name was Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite,
who had been taken from Jerusalem among the captives who were taken with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken captive.

He was bringing up Hadassah, that is Esther, his uncle's daughter, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman had a beautiful figure and was beautiful to look at, and when her father and mother died, Mordecai adopted her as his own daughter.

When the king's order and decree were announced and many young women were gathered in Susa the citadel under the care of Hegai, Esther was also taken to the king's palace and put under the care of Hegai, who was in charge of the women.

The young woman pleased him and won his favour. He quickly provided her with her beauty treatments and her food, and seven chosen young women from the king's palace, and moved her and her young women to the best place in the women's quarters.
Esther had not told anyone about her people or her family, for Mordecai had told her not to.
Every day Mordecai walked back and forth in front of the court of the women's quarters to find out how Esther was and what was happening to her.

When the turn came for each young woman to go in to King Ahasuerus, after twelve months of the treatment for women, since that was the length of their time of beautifying, six months with oil of myrrh and six months with perfumes and women's treatments,
when the young woman went in to the king, she was given whatever she asked for to take with her from the women's quarters to the king's palace.

In the evening she went in, and in the morning she came back to a second women's quarters, under the care of Shaashgaz the king's eunuch, who was in charge of the concubines. She did not go in to the king again unless he delighted in her and she was called by name.

When the turn came for Esther daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai, who had adopted her as his own daughter, to go in to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai the king's eunuch, in charge of the women, advised. And Esther won the favour of everyone who saw her.
Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus in his royal palace in the tenth month, the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign.

The king loved Esther more than all the other women, and she won more favour and kindness from him than all the other virgins, so that he put the royal crown on her head and made her queen in place of Vashti.
Then the king gave a great banquet for all his officials and servants, Esther's banquet. He also announced a holiday for the provinces and gave gifts with royal generosity.
When virgins were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.
Esther had not told anyone about her family or her people, as Mordecai had told her, for Esther still did what Mordecai said, as she had when he brought her up.
In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the doorway, became angry and plotted to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
The matter became known to Mordecai, and he told Queen Esther, and Esther told the king in Mordecai's name.
When the matter was looked into and found to be true, both men were hanged on a gallows. It was written in the book of the records in the king's presence.
After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite and raised him up and set his seat above all the officials who were with him.
All the king's servants who were at the king's gate knelt and bowed down to Haman, for the king had commanded this for him. But Mordecai did not kneel or bow down.
Then the king's servants at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why do you disobey the king's command?"
When they spoke to him day after day and he would not listen to them, they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai's words would hold, for he had told them that he was a Jew.
When Haman saw that Mordecai did not kneel or bow down to him, Haman was filled with rage.

But it seemed a small thing to him to lay hands on Mordecai alone, for they had told him who Mordecai's people were. So Haman sought to destroy all the Jews, Mordecai's people, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus.

In the first month, the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, Pur, that is the lot, was cast in front of Haman, day by day and month by month, until the twelfth month, the month of Adar.

Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people, scattered and separate among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king's laws, so it is not in the king's interest to leave them alone.

If it pleases the king, let it be written that they are to be destroyed, and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of those who do the king's business, to put into the king's treasuries."
So the king took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.
The king said to Haman, "The silver is given to you, and the people too, to do with them as you see fit."

Then the king's scribes were called on the thirteenth day of the first month, and an order was written, exactly as Haman commanded, to the king's satraps and to the governors of each province and to the officials of each people, to each province in its own script and each people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's ring.

Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces, to destroy, kill and wipe out all the Jews, young and old, women and children, in one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, and to plunder their possessions.
A copy of the document was to be issued as a law in every province and made known to all the peoples, so that they would be ready for that day.
The couriers went out in haste at the king's command, and the law was issued in Susa the citadel. The king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.
When Mordecai learned all that had been done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the middle of the city, crying with a loud and bitter cry.
He came as far as the front of the king's gate, for no one could enter the king's gate wearing sackcloth.
In every province, wherever the king's command and law reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting, weeping and wailing, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
When Esther's young women and her eunuchs came and told her, the queen was in great distress. She sent clothes for Mordecai to wear, to take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them.
Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs whom he had appointed to attend her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to find out what this was and why.
Hathach went out to Mordecai in the town square in front of the king's gate,
and Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of silver that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries for the destruction of the Jews.

He also gave him a copy of the written law that had been issued in Susa for their destruction, to show Esther and tell her, and to order her to go to the king to ask for his favour and plead with him for her people.
Hathach went and told Esther what Mordecai had said.
Then Esther spoke to Hathach and told him to say to Mordecai:

"All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that any man or woman who goes in to the king in the inner court without being called has one law: to be put to death, unless the king holds out the golden sceptre to him so that he may live. And I have not been called to come in to the king for these thirty days."
They told Mordecai what Esther had said.
Then Mordecai told them to reply to Esther: "Do not think that you will escape in the king's house any more than all the other Jews.

For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will come to the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for a time like this?"
Then Esther told them to reply to Mordecai:

"Go, gather all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my young women will fast in the same way. Then I will go in to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish."
So Mordecai went away and did all that Esther had told him.

On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king's palace, opposite the king's quarters. The king was sitting on his royal throne in the throne room, opposite the entrance of the palace.
When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won his favour, and the king held out to Esther the golden sceptre in his hand. Esther came near and touched the tip of the sceptre.
The king said to her, "What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? It will be given to you, even up to half the kingdom."
Esther said, "If it pleases the king, let the king and Haman come today to the banquet that I have prepared for him."
The king said, "Bring Haman at once, so that we may do as Esther asks." So the king and Haman came to the banquet that Esther had prepared.
While they were drinking wine, the king said to Esther, "What is your wish? It will be granted to you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be done."
Esther answered, "My wish and my request is this:

if I have found favour with the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my wish and do what I ask, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king says."
Haman went out that day glad and happy. But when Haman saw Mordecai at the king's gate, who did not stand up or tremble before him, Haman was filled with rage against Mordecai.
But Haman held himself back and went home, and he sent for his friends and his wife Zeresh.
Haman told them about the splendour of his riches, and the number of his sons, and all the ways the king had honoured him, and how he had raised him above the officials and the king's servants.
Haman said, "Even Queen Esther let no one but me come with the king to the banquet she had prepared. And tomorrow too I am invited by her, with the king.
But all this is worth nothing to me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."

His wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, "Have a gallows made, fifty cubits high, and in the morning ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go with the king to the banquet and enjoy yourself." The advice pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made.
That night the king could not sleep. He ordered the book of records, the chronicles, to be brought, and they were read to the king.
It was found written there that Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the doorway, who had plotted to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
The king said, "What honour or reward has been given to Mordecai for this?" The king's attendants said, "Nothing has been done for him."
The king said, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had just come into the outer court of the king's palace to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the gallows that he had prepared for him.
The king's attendants said to him, "Haman is standing in the court." The king said, "Let him come in."
So Haman came in, and the king said to him, "What should be done for the man whom the king wants to honour?" Haman said to himself, "Whom would the king want to honour more than me?"
So Haman said to the king, "For the man whom the king wants to honour,
let royal robes be brought, which the king has worn, and a horse that the king has ridden, with a royal crown on its head.

Let the robes and the horse be handed over to one of the king's most noble officials, and let them dress the man whom the king wants to honour, and lead him on the horse through the town square, calling out in front of him, 'This is what is done for the man whom the king wants to honour.'"

Then the king said to Haman, "Quickly, take the robes and the horse as you have said, and do this for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Do not leave out anything of all that you have said."

So Haman took the robes and the horse, and dressed Mordecai and led him on horseback through the town square, calling out in front of him, "This is what is done for the man whom the king wants to honour."
Then Mordecai went back to the king's gate. But Haman hurried home, mourning, with his head covered.

Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. His advisers and his wife Zeresh said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the Jewish people, you will not win against him, but will surely fall before him."
While they were still talking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried to bring Haman to the banquet that Esther had prepared.
So the king and Haman went to the banquet with Queen Esther.

On the second day, while they were drinking wine, the king said again to Esther, "What is your wish, Queen Esther? It will be granted to you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be done."
Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favour with you, king, and if it pleases the king, let my life be given to me as my wish, and my people as my request.

For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed and to be wiped out. If we had only been sold as male and female slaves, I would have kept silent, for the trouble would not be worth the king's loss."
King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?"
Esther said, "An enemy and adversary, this wicked Haman." Then Haman was terrified before the king and queen.
The king got up in anger from the wine and went out into the palace garden, but Haman stayed to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he saw that the king had decided on harm for him.

When the king came back from the palace garden to the place where they were drinking wine, Haman had thrown himself on the couch where Esther was. The king said, "Will he even assault the queen in front of me, in my own house?" As the word left the king's mouth, they covered Haman's face.

Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs who served the king, said, "There is also the gallows that Haman made for Mordecai, who spoke up for the king. It is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." The king said, "Hang him on it."
So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the king's anger cooled.
On that day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told what he was to her.
The king took off his signet ring, which he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther put Mordecai in charge of Haman's house.
Then Esther spoke to the king again and fell at his feet, weeping, and begged him to put an end to the evil of Haman the Agagite and his plan that he had made against the Jews.
The king held out the golden sceptre to Esther, and Esther got up and stood in front of the king.

She said, "If it pleases the king, and if I have found favour with him, and if the matter seems right to the king, and I am pleasing to him, let an order be written to cancel the letters that Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king's provinces.
For how can I bear to see the disaster that will come on my people? How can I bear to see the destruction of my family?"
King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and Mordecai the Jew, "Look, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and they have hanged him on the gallows because he lifted his hand against the Jews.
Now you write about the Jews as you see fit, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's ring, for what is written in the king's name and sealed with the king's ring cannot be reversed."

The king's scribes were called at that time, in the third month, the month of Sivan, on the twenty-third day. An order was written, exactly as Mordecai commanded, to the Jews and to the satraps, governors and officials of the provinces from India to Cush, a hundred and twenty-seven provinces, to each province in its own script and each people in its own language, and to the Jews in their own script and language.
He wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the king's ring, and sent the letters by mounted couriers riding fast horses from the royal stables.

The letters said that the king allowed the Jews in every town to gather and defend their lives, to destroy, kill and wipe out any armed force of any people or province that would attack them, with their women and children, and to plunder their possessions,
on one day in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar.
A copy of the document was to be issued as a law in every province and made known to all the peoples, so that the Jews would be ready on that day to take revenge on their enemies.
The couriers, riding their fast horses from the royal stables, went out in haste at the king's command. The law was issued in Susa the citadel.
Mordecai went out from the king's presence in royal robes of blue and white, with a large gold crown and a robe of fine linen and purple. The city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.
For the Jews there was light and gladness and joy and honour.

In every province and in every town, wherever the king's command and law reached, there was gladness and joy among the Jews, a banquet and a holiday. Many from the peoples of the land declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them.

In the twelfth month, the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day, when the king's command and law were due to be carried out, on the very day when the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them, it was turned round, so that the Jews overpowered those who hated them.
The Jews gathered in their towns in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to lay hands on those who sought their harm. No one could stand against them, for fear of them had fallen on all the peoples.
All the officials of the provinces, the satraps, the governors and the king's agents helped the Jews, because fear of Mordecai had fallen on them.
For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame spread through all the provinces, for the man Mordecai became greater and greater.
The Jews struck all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying, and did as they pleased to those who hated them.
In Susa the citadel the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men,
and they killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vaizatha,
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. But they did not lay a hand on the plunder.
That day the number of those killed in Susa the citadel was reported to the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, "In Susa the citadel the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman. What have they done in the rest of the king's provinces? Now what is your wish? It will be granted to you. What more do you ask? It will be done."
Esther said, "If it pleases the king, let the Jews in Susa be allowed to do tomorrow also as they did today, and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows."
So the king ordered that it be done. A law was issued in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.
The Jews in Susa gathered also on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and killed three hundred men in Susa, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.

The rest of the Jews in the king's provinces gathered and defended their lives and had rest from their enemies. They killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.
This was on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and on the fourteenth day they rested and made it a day of banqueting and gladness.
But the Jews in Susa gathered on the thirteenth and on the fourteenth, and on the fifteenth they rested and made it a day of banqueting and gladness.

For this reason the Jews of the villages, who live in unwalled towns, keep the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of gladness and banqueting, a holiday, a day for sending portions of food to one another.
Mordecai wrote down these things and sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, near and far,
requiring them to keep the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and the fifteenth day of the same month, every year,

as the days on which the Jews had rest from their enemies, and as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow to gladness and from mourning to a holiday. They were to make them days of banqueting and gladness, days for sending portions of food to one another and gifts to the poor.
So the Jews took on what they had begun to do, and what Mordecai had written to them.
For Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur, that is the lot, to crush and destroy them.

But when it came before the king, he ordered by letter that Haman's evil plan that he had made against the Jews should come back on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.
So they called these days Purim, after the word Pur. Because of all that was written in this letter, and what they had seen in this matter, and what had happened to them,
the Jews took on themselves and their descendants and all who joined them the duty, never to be dropped, of keeping these two days as written and at the time set, every year,

so that these days would be remembered and kept in every generation, in every family, province and town, and that these days of Purim would never cease among the Jews, and their memory would never fade among their descendants.
Queen Esther daughter of Abihail and Mordecai the Jew wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter about Purim.
Letters were sent to all the Jews in the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, in words of peace and truth,

to confirm these days of Purim at their set times, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had laid down for them, and as they had taken on themselves and their descendants, with the matters of the fasts and their crying out.
Esther's command confirmed these rules of Purim, and it was written in a book.
King Ahasuerus imposed forced labour on the land and on the coasts of the sea.
All his acts of power and strength, and the full account of the greatness of Mordecai, to which the king raised him, are they not written in the Book of the Records of the Kings of Media and Persia?
For Mordecai the Jew was second to King Ahasuerus, and great among the Jews and loved by the multitude of his relatives, for he sought the good of his people and spoke peace for all his descendants.
There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job. That man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil.
Seven sons and three daughters were born to him.
He owned seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred pairs of oxen and five hundred donkeys, and a very large household, so that this man was the greatest of all the people of the east.
His sons used to hold a feast in the house of each one in turn, on his day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.

When the days of the feast had gone round, Job would send for them and make them holy. He would get up early in the morning and offer a burnt offering for each of them, for Job said, "Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." This was Job's regular practice.
One day the sons of God came to stand before the LORD, and the adversary came among them.
The LORD said to the adversary, "Where have you come from?" The adversary answered the LORD, "From roaming the earth and walking about on it."
The LORD said to the adversary, "Have you considered my servant Job? There is no one like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil."
The adversary answered the LORD, "Does Job fear God for nothing?
Have you not put a fence round him and his house and everything he has? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his livestock has spread over the land.
But reach out your hand and strike everything he has, and he will curse you to your face."
The LORD said to the adversary, "Look, everything he has is in your hands. Only do not lay a hand on him." So the adversary went out from the presence of the LORD.
One day, when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother,
a messenger came to Job and said, "The oxen were ploughing and the donkeys were feeding beside them,
when the Sabeans attacked and took them, and killed the servants with the sword. I alone have escaped to tell you."
While he was still speaking, another came and said, "The fire of God fell from the sky and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them. I alone have escaped to tell you."
While he was still speaking, another came and said, "The Chaldeans formed three bands and raided the camels and took them, and killed the servants with the sword. I alone have escaped to tell you."
While he was still speaking, another came and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother,
when a great wind came from across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell on the young people and they are dead. I alone have escaped to tell you."
Then Job got up and tore his robe and shaved his head, and fell to the ground and worshipped.
He said:
"Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will go back there. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD."
In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong.
Again one day the sons of God came to stand before the LORD, and the adversary came among them to stand before the LORD.
The LORD said to the adversary, "Where have you come from?" The adversary answered the LORD, "From roaming the earth and walking about on it."

The LORD said to the adversary, "Have you considered my servant Job? There is no one like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil. He still holds on to his integrity, though you moved me against him to ruin him for no reason."
The adversary answered the LORD, "Skin for skin. A man will give all he has for his life.
But reach out your hand and strike his bone and his flesh, and he will curse you to your face."
The LORD said to the adversary, "Look, he is in your hands. Only spare his life."
So the adversary went out from the presence of the LORD and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to the top of his head.
Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself with, and sat among the ashes.
His wife said to him, "Do you still hold on to your integrity? Curse God and die."
But he said to her, "You speak like one of the foolish women. Shall we accept good from God and not accept bad?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.

When Job's three friends heard of all this trouble that had come on him, each came from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite. They agreed to meet together to go and show him sympathy and comfort him.
When they looked up from a distance, they did not recognise him. They raised their voices and wept, and each tore his robe and threw dust into the air over his head.
They sat down with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights, and no one said a word to him, for they saw that his pain was very great.
After this Job opened his mouth and cursed the day he was born.
He spoke up and said:
"May the day perish when I was born, and the night that said, 'A boy has been conceived.'
May that day be darkness. May God above not look for it, and no light shine on it.
May gloom and deep darkness claim it. May a cloud settle over it, and the blackness of the day terrify it.
As for that night, may darkness seize it. May it not be counted among the days of the year, nor come into the number of the months.
May that night be barren. May no cry of joy come into it.
May those who curse the day curse it, those who are ready to rouse Leviathan.
May its morning stars be dark. May it wait for light and have none, and never see the eyelids of the dawn,
because it did not shut the doors of the womb that bore me, or hide trouble from my eyes.
Why did I not die at birth, come out of the womb and breathe my last?
Why did knees receive me, and why the breasts, that I should suck?
For then I would be lying down and quiet. I would be asleep, and then I would be at rest,
with kings and counsellors of the earth who built ruins for themselves,
or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver.
Or why was I not hidden away like a stillborn child, like infants who never saw the light?
There the wicked stop their raging, and there the weary are at rest.
There the prisoners are at ease together. They do not hear the voice of the overseer.
Small and great are there, and the slave is free from his master.
Why is light given to one in misery, and life to those bitter in soul,
who long for death and it does not come, who dig for it more than for hidden treasure,
who are glad and full of joy when they find the grave?
Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has fenced in?
For my sighing comes in place of my food, and my groans pour out like water.
What I feared has come on me, and what I dreaded has happened to me.
I have no ease, no quiet, no rest, and trouble has come."
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
"If someone ventures a word with you, will you be weary? But who can hold back from speaking?
Look, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened weak hands.
Your words have lifted up the one who stumbled, and you have made firm the knees that gave way.
But now it has come to you, and you are worn out. It touches you, and you are dismayed.
Is your fear of God not your confidence, and the integrity of your ways your hope?
Think now: who that was innocent ever perished? Where were the upright ever wiped out?
As I have seen, those who plough trouble and sow harm reap the same.
By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are finished.
The roar of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, and the teeth of the young lions are broken.
The lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.
A word was brought to me in secret, and my ear caught a whisper of it.
In the unsettling thoughts of the visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on people,
dread came upon me, and trembling, and made all my bones shake.
A spirit glided past my face, and the hair of my flesh stood on end.
It stood still, but I could not make out its appearance. A form was before my eyes. There was silence, and then I heard a voice:
'Can a mortal be more righteous than God? Can a man be purer than his Maker?
If God puts no trust in his servants, and charges his angels with error,
how much more those who live in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed like a moth.
Between morning and evening they are broken in pieces. Without anyone noticing, they perish for ever.
Is their tent-cord not pulled up within them? They die, and without wisdom.'
"Call out now. Is there anyone who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
For resentment kills the foolish, and jealousy slays the simple.
I have seen the foolish take root, but suddenly I cursed his home.
His children are far from safety. They are crushed at the gate, and no one rescues them.
The hungry eat his harvest, and take it even from among thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.
For trouble does not come out of the dust, nor does hardship spring from the ground,
but people are born to trouble as sparks fly upward.
As for me, I would seek God, and I would lay my cause before God,
who does great things that cannot be searched out, wonders without number:
who gives rain on the earth and sends water on the fields,
setting the lowly on high, and lifting up the mourners to safety.
He frustrates the plans of the crafty, so that their hands cannot carry out their schemes.
He catches the wise in their own cunning, and the plans of the cunning are swept away.
They meet darkness in the daytime, and grope at noon as in the night.
But he saves the needy from the sword of their mouth, and from the hand of the strong.
So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth.
Happy is the one whom God corrects. So do not despise the discipline of the Almighty.
For he wounds, but he binds up. He strikes, but his hands heal.
From six troubles he will rescue you, and in seven no harm will touch you.
In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword.
You will be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and you will not fear destruction when it comes.
At destruction and famine you will laugh, and you will not fear the wild animals of the earth.
For you will be in league with the stones of the field, and the wild animals will be at peace with you.
You will know that your tent is secure, and you will visit your home and miss nothing.
You will know that your offspring will be many, and your descendants like the grass of the earth.
You will come to the grave in full vigour, like a shock of grain gathered in its season.
See, we have searched this out, and it is so. Hear it, and know it for yourself."
Then Job answered:
"If only my anguish could be weighed, and all my calamity laid in the scales together.
For then it would be heavier than the sand of the seas. That is why my words have been rash.
For the arrows of the Almighty are in me. My spirit drinks their poison. God's terrors are lined up against me.
Does the wild donkey bray when it has grass, or the ox low over its fodder?
Can tasteless food be eaten without salt, or is there flavour in the white of an egg?
My throat refuses to touch it. Such things are like food that makes me sick.
If only my request would be granted, and God would give me what I hope for:
that God would be willing to crush me, to let loose his hand and cut me off.
Then I would still have comfort, and I would leap for joy in unrelenting pain, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
What is my strength, that I should wait? What is my end, that I should be patient?
Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh bronze?
Is there any help in me, when success is driven from me?
A despairing person should have kindness from his friend, even one who forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
My brothers are treacherous like a wadi, like the channels of wadis that pass away,
dark with ice, and swollen with melting snow.
In the dry season they dwindle. In the heat they vanish from their place.
Caravans turn aside from their course. They go up into the wasteland and perish.
The caravans of Tema looked for water. The travelling companies of Sheba hoped for it.
They were ashamed, for they had trusted. They came there and were disappointed.
So you have now become like that. You see something terrible and are afraid.
Did I say, 'Give me something,' or 'Pay a ransom for me from your wealth,'
or 'Save me from the hand of the enemy,' or 'Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless'?
Teach me, and I will be silent. Make me understand where I have gone wrong.
How painful are honest words. But what does your reproof prove?
Do you think you can reprove words, when the speech of a desperate man is wind?
You would even cast lots over an orphan, and barter over your friend.
But now be good enough to look at me, for I will not lie to your face.
Think again; let there be no injustice. Think again; my case is still just.
Is there injustice on my tongue? Can my palate not discern trouble?"
"Is not human life on earth a time of service, and are not his days like the days of a hired hand?
Like a slave who longs for the shade, like a hired worker who waits for his wages,
so I have been given months of emptiness, and nights of misery have been counted out to me.
When I lie down I say, 'When will I get up?' But the night drags on, and I am full of tossing until dawn.
My flesh is clothed with worms and scabs of dust. My skin hardens and then breaks out again.
My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and they come to an end without hope.
Remember that my life is a breath. My eye will never again see good.
The eye that sees me will not see me again. Your eyes will be on me, and I will be gone.
As a cloud fades and vanishes, so the one who goes down to Sheol does not come up.
He will not return to his house, and his place will not know him any more.
So I will not restrain my mouth. I will speak in the anguish of my spirit. I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
Am I the Sea, or the sea monster, that you set a guard over me?
When I say, 'My bed will comfort me, my couch will ease my complaint,'
then you frighten me with dreams and terrify me with visions,
so that I would choose strangling, and death rather than my bones.
I loathe my life. I would not live for ever. Leave me alone, for my days are a breath.
What are human beings, that you make so much of them, that you set your mind on them,
that you inspect them every morning, and test them every moment?
How long before you look away from me, and let me alone until I swallow my spit?
If I have sinned, what have I done to you, you watcher of mankind? Why have you made me your target? Why have I become a burden to you?
Why do you not pardon my transgression and take away my guilt? For now I will lie down in the dust. You will seek me, but I will be gone."
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
"How long will you go on saying such things? Your words are a mighty wind.
Does God twist justice? Does the Almighty twist what is right?
If your children sinned against him, he handed them over to the power of their wrongdoing.
If you look for God and plead with the Almighty for mercy,
if you are pure and upright, then surely he will rouse himself for you and restore your rightful home.
Your beginning will seem small, but your end will grow very great.
Ask the former generation, and take note of what their ancestors learned,
for we were born only yesterday and know nothing, and our days on earth are a shadow.
Will they not teach you and tell you, and bring words out of their understanding?
Can papyrus grow tall where there is no marsh? Can reeds flourish without water?
While still in flower and not cut, they wither before any other plant.
Such is the path of all who forget God, and the hope of the godless perishes.
Their confidence is cut off, and what they trust in is a spider's web.
They lean on their house, but it does not stand. They cling to it, but it does not last.
They are green in the sun, and their shoots spread over the garden.
Their roots twine round a heap of stones. They look for a home among the rocks.
If he swallows them up from their place, it denies them: 'I never saw you.'
See, this is the joy of his way, and out of the dust others will spring up.
See, God does not reject the blameless, nor does he take the hand of evildoers.
He will yet fill your mouth with laughter and your lips with shouts of joy.
Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more."
Then Job answered:
"Truly I know that this is so. But how can a mortal be in the right before God?
If one wished to contend with him, he could not answer him once in a thousand times.
He is wise in heart and mighty in strength. Who has hardened himself against him and come out whole?
He moves mountains, and they do not know it, when he overturns them in his anger.
He shakes the earth from its place, and its pillars tremble.
He commands the sun, and it does not rise. He seals up the stars.
He alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the Sea.
He made the Bear and Orion, the Pleiades and the chambers of the south.
He does great things that cannot be searched out, wonders without number.
Look, he passes by me, and I do not see him. He moves on, and I do not perceive him.
If he snatches away, who can stop him? Who can say to him, 'What are you doing?'
God does not hold back his anger. Beneath him the helpers of Rahab cower.
How then can I answer him, choosing my words with him?
Though I were in the right, I could not answer him. I could only plead for mercy with my judge.
If I summoned him and he answered me, I do not believe he would listen to my voice.
For he crushes me with a tempest and multiplies my wounds for no reason.
He will not let me get my breath, but fills me with bitterness.
If it is a matter of strength, he is the strong one. If it is a matter of justice, who can summon him?
Though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me. Though I am blameless, he would prove me crooked.
I am blameless. I do not care about myself. I despise my life.
It is all one, so I say: he destroys the blameless and the wicked.
When disaster brings sudden death, he mocks at the despair of the innocent.
The earth is given into the hand of the wicked. He covers the faces of its judges. If it is not he, who then is it?
My days are swifter than a runner. They flee away and see no good.
They go by like boats of reed, like an eagle swooping on its prey.
If I say, 'I will forget my complaint, I will put off my sad face and be cheerful,'
I am afraid of all my pains. I know that you will not hold me innocent.
I will be condemned. Why then should I struggle in vain?
If I wash myself with snow and make my hands clean with lye,
you will plunge me into the pit, and my own clothes will abhor me.
For he is not a man as I am, that I might answer him, that we might come to trial together.
There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both.
Let him take his rod away from me, and not let dread of him terrify me.
Then I would speak without fear of him, for I am not so in myself."
"I loathe my life. I will give free rein to my complaint. I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.
I will say to God, 'Do not condemn me. Let me know why you contend with me.
Does it please you to oppress, to despise the work of your hands and to favour the plans of the wicked?
Have you eyes of flesh? Do you see as humans see?
Are your days like the days of a mortal, or your years like human years,
that you seek out my guilt and search for my sin,
although you know that I am not guilty, and there is none who can deliver from your hand?
Your hands shaped me and made me, and now you turn and destroy me.
Remember that you made me like clay. Will you return me to dust?
Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese?
You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews.
You gave me life and kindness, and your care preserved my spirit.
Yet these things you hid in your heart. I know that this was in your mind:
if I sinned, you would watch me and not acquit me of my guilt.
If I am guilty, woe to me. If I am in the right, I cannot lift my head, for I am filled with shame and drunk with my affliction.
And if I lift myself up, you hunt me like a lion and again show your wonders against me.
You renew your witnesses against me and increase your anger towards me. Fresh troops come against me.
Why did you bring me out of the womb? I should have died, and no eye seen me.
I should have been as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave.
Are not my days few? Let me alone, that I may find a little comfort
before I go, and I will not return, to the land of darkness and deep shadow,
the land of gloom like thick darkness, of deep shadow without order, where light is like thick darkness.'"
Then Zophar the Naamathite answered:
"Should a multitude of words go unanswered, and a talker be pronounced right?
Should your babble silence people, and shall you mock and no one shame you?
For you say, 'My teaching is pure, and I am clean in your eyes.'
But oh, that God would speak, and open his lips against you,
and tell you the secrets of wisdom, for sound wisdom has two sides. Know then that God exacts from you less than your guilt deserves.
Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty?
It is higher than heaven. What can you do? Deeper than Sheol. What can you know?
Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.
If he passes through and shuts up, and calls an assembly, who can hinder him?
For he knows worthless men, and when he sees iniquity, will he not consider it?
But a hollow man will get understanding when a wild donkey's colt is born a human.
If you prepare your heart, and stretch out your hands to him,
if iniquity is in your hand, put it far away, and let not injustice dwell in your tents,
then you will lift up your face without blemish. You will be secure and will not fear.
You will forget your misery. You will remember it as waters that have passed away.
And your life will be brighter than noonday. Its darkness will be like the morning.
And you will feel secure, because there is hope. You will look around and take your rest in safety.
You will lie down, and none will make you afraid. Many will court your favour.
But the eyes of the wicked will fail. Escape will be lost to them. Their hope is to breathe their last."
Then Job answered:
"No doubt you are the people, and wisdom will die with you.
But I have a mind as well as you. I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these?
I am a laughingstock to my friends, I who called on God and he answered me, a just and blameless man, a laughingstock.
Those at ease have contempt for misfortune, a shove for those whose feet are unsteady.
The tents of robbers are at peace, and those who provoke God are secure, those who carry their god in their hand.
But ask the animals, and they will teach you, the birds of the air, and they will tell you.
Or speak to the earth, and it will teach you, and the fish of the sea will tell you.
Who among all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this?
In his hand is the life of every living thing, and the breath of every human being.
Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes food?
Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding comes with length of days.
With God are wisdom and might. He has counsel and understanding.
If he tears down, it cannot be rebuilt. If he shuts a person in, there is no opening.
If he holds back the waters, they dry up. If he sends them out, they overwhelm the land.
With him are strength and sound wisdom. The deceived and the deceiver are his.
He leads counsellors away stripped, and makes judges fools.
He loosens the bonds of kings, and binds a waistcloth on their loins.
He leads priests away stripped, and overthrows the long-established.
He deprives trusted advisers of speech, and takes away the discernment of elders.
He pours contempt on nobles, and loosens the belt of the strong.
He uncovers the deep out of darkness, and brings deep shadow into light.
He makes nations great and destroys them. He enlarges nations and leads them away.
He takes away the understanding of the leaders of the people, and makes them wander in a trackless waste.
They grope in the dark without light. He makes them stagger like drunkards.
"See, my eye has seen all this, my ear has heard and understood it.
What you know, I also know. I am not inferior to you.
But I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to argue my case with God.
As for you, you whitewash with lies. You are all worthless physicians.
If only you would keep silent, and it would be your wisdom.
Hear now my argument, and listen to the pleadings of my lips.
Will you speak falsely for God, and speak deceitfully for him?
Will you show partiality towards him? Will you plead the case for God?
Will it be well with you when he searches you out? Or can you deceive him as one deceives a human?
He will surely rebuke you if in secret you show partiality.
Will his majesty not terrify you, and the dread of him fall on you?
Your maxims are proverbs of ashes. Your defences are defences of clay.
Be silent, and I will speak, and let come on me what may.
Why do I take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my hand?
Though he slay me, I will hope in him. Yet I will argue my ways to his face.
This will be my salvation, that the godless cannot come before him.
Listen carefully to my words, and let my declaration be in your ears.
See, I have prepared my case. I know that I shall be in the right.
Who is there who will contend with me? For then I would be silent and die.
Only grant me two things, and then I will not hide from your face:
withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me.
Then call, and I will answer. Or let me speak, and you reply to me.
How many are my iniquities and my sins? Make me know my transgression and my sin.
Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?
Will you frighten a driven leaf? Will you chase dry chaff?
For you write bitter things against me, and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.
You put my feet in the stocks, and watch all my paths. You set a limit for the soles of my feet.
Man wastes away like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten.
"A mortal, born of woman, is short of days and full of trouble.
Like a flower he comes up and withers. He flees like a shadow and does not last.
And do you open your eyes on such a one, and bring me into judgement with you?
Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? No one.
Since his days are determined, and the number of his months is with you, and you have set limits he cannot pass,
look away from him and leave him alone, until he finishes his day like a hired hand.
For there is hope for a tree: if it is cut down, it will sprout again, and its shoots will not fail.
Though its root grows old in the ground and its stump dies in the soil,
at the scent of water it will bud and put out branches like a young plant.
But a man dies and lies helpless. A human being breathes his last, and where is he?
As waters fail from a lake, and a river wastes away and dries up,
so a man lies down and does not rise. Until the heavens are no more, he will not awake or be roused from his sleep.
Oh, that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your anger passes, that you would set me a time and remember me.
If a man dies, will he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, until my relief should come.
You would call, and I would answer you. You would long for the work of your hands.
For then you would number my steps, but you would not keep watch over my sin.
My transgression would be sealed up in a bag, and you would cover over my iniquity.
But the mountain falls and crumbles, and the rock is moved from its place.
The waters wear away the stones. Their torrents wash away the soil of the earth. So you destroy the hope of a person.
You overpower him for ever, and he passes away. You change his face and send him away.
His sons come to honour, and he does not know it. They are brought low, and he does not perceive it.
He feels only the pain of his own flesh, and mourns only for himself."
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
"Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind?
Should he argue with useless talk, or with words that do no good?
But you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering devotion before God.
For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty.
Your own mouth condemns you, not I. Your own lips testify against you.
Were you the first man to be born? Were you brought forth before the hills?
Have you listened in the council of God? And do you limit wisdom to yourself?
What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that is not clear to us?
Both the grey-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father.
Are the consolations of God too small for you, or the word that deals gently with you?
Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash,
that you turn your spirit against God and let such words go out of your mouth?
What is a mortal, that he should be pure? Or one born of woman, that he should be righteous?
See, God puts no trust in his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in his eyes.
How much less one who is vile and corrupt, who drinks injustice like water.
I will show you, listen to me. What I have seen I will declare,
what wise men have told, and their ancestors have not hidden,
to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them.
The wicked writhe in pain all their days, and the ruthless have only a few years stored up.
Terrifying sounds are in their ears. In peacetime the destroyer comes upon them.
They do not believe they will return from darkness, and they are marked for the sword.
They wander about for bread, saying, 'Where is it?' They know that the day of darkness is ready at hand.
Distress and anguish terrify them. They overwhelm them like a king ready for battle,
because they stretched out their hands against God and acted arrogantly against the Almighty,
running stubbornly against him with a thick-bossed shield.
Because they covered their faces with fat and put fat on their loins,
they will live in ruined towns, in houses that no one should live in, which are destined to become heaps of rubble.
They will not be rich, and their wealth will not endure, nor will their possessions spread over the land.
They will not escape from darkness. A flame will dry up their shoots, and by the breath of his mouth they will be carried off.
Let them not trust in emptiness, deceiving themselves, for emptiness will be their reward.
It will be paid in full before their time, and their branch will not be green.
They will shake off their unripe grapes like the vine, and cast off their blossom like the olive tree.
For the company of the godless is barren, and fire consumes the tents of bribery.
They conceive trouble and give birth to evil, and their womb prepares deceit."
Then Job answered:
"I have heard many such things. You are all miserable comforters.
Is there no end to windy words? What provokes you that you answer?
I also could speak as you do, if you were in my place. I could string words together against you and shake my head at you.
I could encourage you with my mouth, and the movement of my lips would bring relief.
If I speak, my pain is not relieved. If I hold back, how much of it leaves me?
Surely now God has worn me out. You have made desolate all my company.
And you have shrivelled me up; it has become a witness. My leanness rises up against me and testifies to my face.
His anger has torn me and hunted me down. He has gnashed his teeth at me. My adversary sharpens his eyes against me.
They have opened their mouths against me. They have struck my cheek with scorn. They have massed themselves together against me.
God gives me up to the ungodly, and tosses me into the hands of the wicked.
I was at ease, and he broke me apart. He seized me by the neck and dashed me to pieces. He set me up as his target.
His archers surround me. He pierces my kidneys without pity. He pours out my gall on the ground.
He breaks me with breach upon breach. He runs at me like a warrior.
I have sewn sackcloth over my skin and laid my strength in the dust.
My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is deep darkness,
although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure.
O earth, do not cover my blood, and let my cry find no resting place.
Even now, see, my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high.
My friends scorn me. My eye pours out tears to God,
that he would argue the case of a man with God, as a person does for a neighbour.
For when a few years have come, I shall go the way from which I shall not return."
"My spirit is broken, my days are extinguished, the graveyard is ready for me.
Surely there are mockers around me, and my eye dwells on their provocation.
Give me a pledge now. Put up security for me with yourself. Who else will put up a pledge for me?
For you have closed their minds to understanding, therefore you will not let them triumph.
He who denounces his friends for a share of their goods, the eyes of his children will fail.
He has made me a byword among the peoples, and I am one in whose face people spit.
My eye has grown dim from grief, and all my limbs are like a shadow.
The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent stirs himself up against the godless.
Yet the righteous holds to his way, and the one with clean hands grows stronger and stronger.
But come back, all of you, and come now. I shall not find a wise man among you.
My days are past, my plans are broken off, the desires of my heart.
They turn night into day. 'The light is near,' they say, in the face of darkness.
If I hope for Sheol as my house, if I make my bed in darkness,
if I say to the pit, 'You are my father,' and to the worm, 'My mother' or 'My sister,'
where then is my hope? Who will see my hope?
Will it go down to the bars of Sheol? Shall we descend together into the dust?"
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
"How long will you hunt for words? Think, and then we will speak.
Why are we counted as cattle? Why are we stupid in your eyes?
You who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be abandoned for your sake, or the rock be moved from its place?
Yes, the light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine.
The light is dark in his tent, and his lamp above him is put out.
His strong steps are shortened, and his own plans throw him down.
For he is thrown into a net by his own feet, and he walks on a mesh.
A trap seizes him by the heel. A snare lays hold of him.
A rope is hidden for him on the ground, and a trap for him on the path.
Terrors frighten him on every side, and chase him at his heels.
His strength is hungry, and calamity is ready at his side.
It eats away parts of his skin. The firstborn of Death eats his limbs.
He is torn from the tent where he felt secure, and is brought to the king of terrors.
Fire lives in his tent that is not his. Sulphur is scattered over his home.
Below, his roots dry up, and above, his branches wither.
His memory perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the street.
He is driven from light into darkness, and chased out of the world.
He has no offspring or descendant among his people, and no survivor where he used to live.
People of the west are appalled at his day, and people of the east are seized with horror.
Surely such are the dwellings of the unjust, such is the place of one who does not know God."
Then Job answered:
"How long will you torment me and crush me with words?
These ten times you have reproached me. You are not ashamed to wrong me.
And if it is true that I have erred, my error stays with me.
If indeed you magnify yourselves against me and make my disgrace an argument against me,
know then that God has put me in the wrong and has closed his net around me.
Look, I cry out, 'Violence!' but I am not answered. I call for help, but there is no justice.
He has walled up my way so that I cannot pass, and he has set darkness on my paths.
He has stripped my honour from me and taken the crown from my head.
He breaks me down on every side, and I am gone. He has uprooted my hope like a tree.
He has kindled his wrath against me and counts me as one of his adversaries.
His troops come on together. They have built up their siege-ramp against me and camp round my tent.
He has put my brothers far from me, and my acquaintances are wholly estranged from me.
My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me.
The guests in my house and my maidservants count me as a stranger. I have become a foreigner in their eyes.
I call to my servant, but he gives no answer, though I plead with him with my mouth.
My breath is strange to my wife, and I am loathsome to my own family.
Even young children despise me. When I rise, they talk against me.
All my intimate friends abhor me, and those whom I loved have turned against me.
My bones cling to my skin and to my flesh, and I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.
Have pity on me, have pity on me, you my friends, for the hand of God has struck me.
Why do you pursue me as God does? Why are you not satisfied with my flesh?
Oh, that my words were written! Oh, that they were inscribed in a book!
Oh, that with an iron pen and with lead they were engraved in the rock for ever!
But I know that my redeemer lives, and that at the last he will stand on the dust.
After my skin has been stripped away, yet from my flesh I will see God,
whom I myself will see, on my side, and my own eyes will behold, and not a stranger. My heart wastes away within me.
If you say, 'How shall we pursue him?' and, 'The root of the matter is found in him,'
be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgement."
Then Zophar the Naamathite answered:
"Therefore my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me.
I hear censure that insults me, and out of my understanding a spirit answers me.
Do you not know this from of old, since man was placed on earth,
that the exulting of the wicked is short, and the joy of the godless is but for a moment?
Though his height mounts up to the heavens, and his head reaches to the clouds,
he will perish for ever like his own dung. Those who have seen him will say, 'Where is he?'
He will fly away like a dream and not be found. He will be chased away like a vision of the night.
The eye that saw him will see him no more, and his place will no longer behold him.
His children will seek favour from the poor, and his hands will give back his wealth.
His bones are full of the vigour of his youth, but it will lie down with him in the dust.
Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue,
though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth,
yet his food is turned in his stomach. It is the venom of cobras within him.
He swallows down riches and vomits them up again. God casts them out of his belly.
He will suck the poison of cobras. The tongue of a viper will kill him.
He will not look upon the rivers, the streams flowing with honey and curds.
He gives back the fruit of his toil and does not swallow it. He does not enjoy the profit of his trading.
For he has crushed and abandoned the poor. He has seized a house that he did not build.
Because he knew no contentment in his belly, he will not save anything he treasures.
There was nothing left after he had eaten. Therefore his prosperity will not last.
In the fullness of his abundance he will be in distress. The hand of everyone in misery will come against him.
To fill his belly to the full, God will send his burning anger into him and rain it down on him as his food.
He will flee from an iron weapon. A bronze arrow will strike him through.
It is drawn forth and comes out of his body. The gleaming point comes out of his gall. Terrors come upon him.
Complete darkness is laid up for his treasures. A fire not fanned will devour him. It will consume what is left in his tent.
The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.
The increase of his house will depart. His goods will flow away on the day of God's anger.
This is the wicked man's portion from God, the heritage appointed for him by God."
Then Job answered:
"Listen carefully to my words, and let this be the consolation you give.
Bear with me, and I will speak, and after I have spoken, mock on.
As for me, is my complaint against a human? Why should I not be impatient?
Look at me and be appalled, and lay your hand on your mouth.
When I remember, I am dismayed, and shuddering seizes my flesh.
Why do the wicked live, grow old, and become mighty in power?
Their offspring are established in their presence, and their descendants before their eyes.
Their houses are safe from fear, and no rod of God is upon them.
Their bull breeds without fail. Their cow calves and does not miscarry.
They send out their little ones like a flock, and their children dance.
They sing to the tambourine and the lyre and rejoice at the sound of the pipe.
They spend their days in prosperity and go down to Sheol in peace.
They say to God, 'Leave us alone. We do not desire to know your ways.
Who is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?'
Look, their prosperity is not in their hand. The counsel of the wicked is far from me.
How often is the lamp of the wicked put out? How often does their calamity come upon them? How often does God distribute pains in his anger?
How often are they like straw before the wind, and like chaff that the storm carries away?
You say, 'God stores up their iniquity for their children.' Let him pay it back to them, so that they know it.
Let their own eyes see their destruction, and let them drink the wrath of the Almighty.
For what do they care for their houses after them, when the number of their months is cut off?
Will anyone teach God knowledge, seeing that he judges those who are on high?
One dies in full prosperity, being wholly at ease and secure,
his pails full of milk and the marrow of his bones moist.
Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted prosperity.
They lie down alike in the dust, and worms cover them.
See, I know your thoughts and the schemes by which you would wrong me.
For you say, 'Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in which the wicked lived?'
Have you not asked those who travel the roads, and do you not accept their testimony
that the evil man is spared in the day of calamity, and rescued in the day of wrath?
Who declares his way to his face, and who repays him for what he has done?
When he is carried to the grave, watch is kept over his tomb.
The clods of the valley are sweet to him. All people follow after him, and those who go before him are without number.
How then will you comfort me with empty nothings? There is nothing left of your answers but falsehood."
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
"Can a man be of use to God? Surely the wise man is of use only to himself.
Is it any pleasure to the Almighty if you are righteous, or is it gain to him if you make your ways blameless?
Is it for your fear of him that he reproves you and enters into judgement with you?
Is not your evil great? There is no end to your iniquities.
For you took pledges from your brothers for no reason and stripped the naked of their clothing.
You gave no water to the weary to drink, and you withheld bread from the hungry.
The man with power possessed the land, and the favoured man lived in it.
You sent widows away empty-handed, and the arms of the fatherless were crushed.
Therefore snares are around you, and sudden terror overwhelms you,
or darkness, so that you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you.
Is not God high in the heavens? See the highest stars, how lofty they are.
But you say, 'What does God know? Can he judge through the deep darkness?
Thick clouds veil him, so that he does not see, and he walks on the vault of heaven.'
Will you keep to the old way that wicked men have trodden?
They were snatched away before their time. Their foundation was washed away like a river.
They said to God, 'Leave us alone,' and 'What can the Almighty do to us?'
Yet he filled their houses with good things, but the counsel of the wicked is far from me.
The righteous see it and are glad, and the innocent laugh them to scorn,
saying, 'Surely our adversaries are cut off, and what they left the fire has consumed.'
Agree with God and be at peace. In this way good will come to you.
Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart.
If you return to the Almighty, you will be built up. If you remove injustice far from your tents,
if you lay gold in the dust, and gold of Ophir among the stones of the brooks,
then the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver.
For then you will delight in the Almighty, and lift up your face to God.
You will pray to him, and he will hear you, and you will pay your vows.
You will decide on a matter, and it will be established for you, and light will shine on your ways.
For when they are brought low, you will say, 'It is pride.' But he saves the humble.
He will deliver even the one who is not innocent, who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands."
Then Job answered:
"Even today my complaint is bitter. His hand is heavy despite my groaning.
Oh, that I knew where I might find him, that I might come to his dwelling.
I would lay my case before him and fill my mouth with arguments.
I would know what he would answer me and understand what he would say to me.
Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? No, he would pay attention to me.
There an upright person could argue with him, and I would be delivered for ever from my judge.
If I go forward, he is not there. If I go backward, I cannot perceive him.
On the left he works, and I cannot see him. He turns to the right, and I cannot find him.
But he knows the way that I take. When he has tested me, I shall come out as gold.
My foot has held fast to his steps. I have kept his way and not turned aside.
I have not departed from the commandment of his lips. I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my daily bread.
But he is unique, and who can turn him back? What he desires, that he does.
For he will complete what he appoints for me, and many such things are with him.
Therefore I am terrified at his presence. When I think of it, I am afraid of him.
God has made my heart faint. The Almighty has terrified me.
Yet I am not silenced by the darkness, nor by the thick darkness that covers my face."
"Why are times not stored up by the Almighty, and why do those who know him never see his days?
The wicked move boundary markers. They seize flocks and pasture them.
They drive away the donkey of the fatherless. They take the widow's ox as a pledge.
They push the needy off the road. The poor of the earth all hide themselves.
Like wild donkeys in the desert, the poor go out to their work, seeking food in the wasteland for their children.
They gather their fodder in the field, and glean in the vineyard of the wicked.
They spend the night naked, without clothing, and have no covering in the cold.
They are wet with the rain of the mountains and hug the rock for lack of shelter.
There are those who snatch the orphan from the breast, and take a pledge from the poor.
They go about naked, without clothing, and, hungry, they carry the sheaves.
Between the rows of olive trees they press oil. They tread the winepresses, but suffer thirst.
From the city the dying groan, and the soul of the wounded cries for help. Yet God does not charge anyone with wrongdoing.
There are those who rebel against the light. They are not acquainted with its ways, and do not stay in its paths.
The murderer rises at dusk to kill the poor and needy, and in the night he is like a thief.
The eye of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, 'No eye will see me.' He covers his face.
In the dark they dig through houses. By day they shut themselves up. They do not know the light.
For deep darkness is morning to all of them. They are friends with the terrors of deep darkness.
They are swift on the face of the waters. Their portion is cursed in the land. No one turns toward their vineyards.
Drought and heat snatch away the snow waters, so does Sheol those who have sinned.
The womb forgets them. The worm finds them sweet. They are no longer remembered. So wickedness is broken like a tree.
They wrong the barren childless woman, and do no good to the widow.
Yet God drags away the mighty by his power. They rise up when they have no assurance of life.
He gives them security, and they are supported, and his eyes are upon their ways.
They are exalted a little while, and then are gone. They are brought low and gathered up like all others. They are cut off like the heads of grain.
If it is not so, who will prove me a liar and show that my words are worth nothing?"
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
"Dominion and dread belong to God. He makes peace in his high places.
Is there any counting of his armies? On whom does his light not rise?
How then can a mortal be righteous before God? How can one born of woman be clean?
See, even the moon is not bright, and the stars are not pure in his eyes.
How much less a human, who is a maggot, a mortal, who is a worm."
Then Job answered:
"How you have helped the one who has no power! How you have saved the arm that has no strength!
How you have counselled one who has no wisdom, and made known sound knowledge in abundance!
With whose help have you uttered these words, and whose spirit has come out of you?
The shades below tremble, the waters and all that live in them.
Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.
He stretches out the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing.
He binds up the waters in his clouds, and the cloud is not torn open under them.
He covers the face of the full moon and spreads his cloud over it.
He has drawn a circle on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness.
The pillars of heaven tremble and are astounded at his rebuke.
By his power he stilled the Sea, and by his understanding he struck down Rahab.
By his breath the heavens were made fair. His hand pierced the fleeing serpent.
See, these are but the outskirts of his ways. How small a whisper do we hear of him. But the thunder of his power, who can understand?"
And Job again took up his poem and said:
"As God lives, who has taken away my right, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter,
as long as my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils,
my lips will not speak falsehood, and my tongue will not utter deceit.
Far be it from me to say that you are right. Until I die I will not put away my integrity from me.
I hold fast my righteousness and will not let it go. My heart does not reproach me for any of my days.
Let my enemy be as the wicked, and let him who rises up against me be as the unjust.
For what is the hope of the godless when he is cut off, when God takes away his life?
Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?
Will he take delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?
I will teach you about the hand of God. What is with the Almighty I will not conceal.
See, all of you have seen it yourselves. Why then have you become altogether vain?
This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage that oppressors receive from the Almighty:
If his children are many, they are for the sword, and his descendants have not enough bread.
Those who survive him the plague buries, and his widows do not weep.
Though he heaps up silver like dust and prepares clothing like clay,
he may prepare it, but the righteous will wear it, and the innocent will divide the silver.
He builds his house like a moth's, like a booth that a watchman makes.
He goes to bed rich, but will do so no more. He opens his eyes, and it is gone.
Terrors overtake him like a flood. A whirlwind carries him off in the night.
The east wind lifts him up and he is gone. It sweeps him out of his place.
It hurls at him without pity. He flees from its power in headlong flight.
It claps its hands at him and hisses him out of his place."
"Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place where gold is refined.
Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted from the ore.
Miners put an end to darkness and search out to the farthest limit the ore in gloom and deep darkness.
They open shafts far from where people live, forgotten by the foot, hanging far away from mortals, they swing.
As for the earth, out of it comes bread, but underneath it is turned up as by fire.
Its stones are the place of sapphires, and it has dust of gold.
That path no bird of prey knows, and the falcon's eye has not seen it.
The proud beasts have not trodden it. The lion has not passed over it.
Miners put their hand to the flint and overturn mountains at the roots.
They cut out channels in the rocks, and their eyes see every precious thing.
They dam up the streams so they do not trickle, and what is hidden they bring out to the light.
But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding?
No human knows the way to it, and it is not found in the land of the living.
The deep says, 'It is not in me,' and the sea says, 'It is not with me.'
It cannot be bought for gold, and silver cannot be weighed out as its price.
It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire.
Gold and glass cannot equal it, nor can it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold.
No mention shall be made of coral or crystal. The price of wisdom is above pearls.
The topaz of Cush cannot equal it, nor can it be valued in pure gold.
From where then does wisdom come? And where is the place of understanding?
