When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and died, and great fear came on everyone who heard of it.
The young men got up, wrapped him up, carried him out and buried him.
About three hours later his wife came in, not knowing what had happened.
Peter said to her, "Tell me, did you sell the land for this amount?" She said, "Yes, for that."
Peter said to her, "Why did you agree together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Look, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out."
At once she fell down at his feet and died. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
Great fear came on the whole assembly and on everyone who heard of these things.
Many signs and wonders were happening among the people through the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon's Colonnade.
None of the rest dared to join them, but the people held them in high honour.
More and more believers were added to the Lord, crowds of both men and women,
so that they even carried the sick out into the streets and laid them on beds and mats, so that when Peter came by, at least his shadow might fall on some of them.
The crowd from the towns around Jerusalem also gathered, bringing the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
Then the high priest and all who were with him (the party of the Sadducees) rose up, filled with jealousy,
and they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison.
But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, led them out and said,
"Go, stand in the temple and tell the people all the words of this life."

When they heard this, they went into the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now the high priest and those with him arrived and called together the council and the whole senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
But the officers who went did not find them in the prison, and they returned and reported,
"We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside."
When the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were perplexed about them, wondering what this could turn into.
Then someone came and reported, "Look, the men you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people."
Then the captain went with the officers and brought them, but without force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people.
When they had brought them, they made them stand before the council. The high priest questioned them,
saying, "We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name, and look, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching and you intend to bring this man's blood on us."
But Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than people.
The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree.
God exalted him at his right hand as leader and Saviour, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins.
And we are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him."
When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them.
But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law respected by all the people, stood up and ordered the men to be put outside for a little while.
And he said to them, "People of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men.
For some time ago Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were scattered and came to nothing.
After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered.
So in the present case I tell you: keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this work is from people, it will be overthrown,
but if it is from God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found fighting against God."
So they were persuaded by him, and they called in the apostles, beat them and ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
They left the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name.
And every day in the temple and from house to house they did not stop teaching and announcing the good news that the Christ is Jesus.

In those days, when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint arose from the Greek-speaking Jews against the Hebrew-speaking Jews because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution.
The twelve called the whole company of the disciples together and said, "It is not right for us to neglect the word of God to serve tables.
So, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, whom we will put in charge of this need.
But we will give ourselves to prayer and to the service of the word."
What they said pleased the whole company, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolaus, a convert from Antioch.
They had them stand before the apostles, and after praying they laid their hands on them.
The word of God kept spreading, and the number of the disciples in Jerusalem increased greatly, and a large crowd of the priests became obedient to the faith.
Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.
But some from the synagogue called the Synagogue of the Freedmen, and of the Cyrenians and the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and argued with Stephen,
but they could not stand against the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.
Then they secretly persuaded some men to say, "We have heard him speaking blasphemous words against Moses and God."
They stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and came upon him, seized him and brought him to the council,
and set up false witnesses who said, "This man never stops saying things against this holy place and the law.
For we have heard him say that this Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place and change the customs that Moses handed down to us."
And all who sat in the council looked intently at him and saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
The high priest asked, "Is this true?"
He said, "Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran,
and said to him: 'Leave your land and your relatives, and go to the land I will show you.'
Then he left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. After his father died, God moved him from there to this land, where you now live.
He gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length, but he promised to give it to him as a possession, and to his descendants after him, though he had no child.
This is what God said: his descendants would be foreigners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and ill-treat them for four hundred years.
'But I will judge the nation they serve,' God said, 'and after that they will come out and worship me in this place.'
He gave him the covenant of circumcision. So Abraham became the father of Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.
The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt. But God was with him
and rescued him from all his troubles, giving him favour and wisdom in the eyes of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who put him in charge of Egypt and of his whole household.
Then a famine came over all Egypt and Canaan, with great hardship, and our fathers could find no food.
When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers there on a first visit.
On the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh.
Joseph sent and summoned his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five people in all.
So Jacob went down to Egypt, and there he died, and our fathers too,
and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.
As the time drew near for the promise that God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt
until another king, who did not know Joseph, rose over Egypt.
He exploited our people with cunning and ill-treated our fathers by making them expose their babies so that they would not live.
At that time Moses was born, and he was beautiful before God. He was brought up for three months in his father's house.
When he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter took him up and brought him up as her own son.
So Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was powerful in his words and deeds.
When he was about forty years old, it came into his mind to visit his brothers, the sons of Israel.
Seeing one of them being wronged, he defended him and avenged the man who was being ill-treated by striking the Egyptian down.
He supposed his brothers would understand that God was giving them rescue through his hand, but they did not understand.
The next day he appeared to two of them as they were fighting and tried to make peace between them, saying, 'Men, you are brothers. Why are you wronging each other?'
But the one who was wronging his neighbour shoved him away, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?
Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'
At this saying Moses fled and became a foreigner in the land of Midian, where he had two sons.
When forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in the flame of a burning bush.
When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight. As he went closer to look, the voice of the Lord came:
'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.' Moses began to shake and did not dare to look.
The Lord said to him, 'Take the sandals off your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.
I have certainly seen the ill-treatment of my people in Egypt and heard their groaning, and I have come down to rescue them. Now come, and I will send you to Egypt.'
This Moses, whom they had refused, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and judge?', God sent as both ruler and liberator, through the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
This man led them out, doing wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years.
This is the Moses who said to the sons of Israel: 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.'
This is the man who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai and with our fathers, and who received living words to pass on to us.
Our fathers were not willing to obey him, but pushed him aside and in their hearts turned back to Egypt,
saying to Aaron, 'Make us gods who will go in front of us. As for this Moses who led us out of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.'
They made a calf in those days, offered a sacrifice to the idol and rejoiced in what their hands had made.

But God turned away and gave them up to worship the army of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: 'Did you bring me victims and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?
You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images you made to worship. So I will deport you beyond Babylon.'
Our fathers had the tent of testimony in the wilderness, made as the one who spoke to Moses ordered, according to the pattern he had seen.
Our fathers received it in turn and brought it in with Joshua when they took over the land of the nations that God drove out in front of our fathers, until the days of David,
who found favour in God's sight and asked to find a dwelling for the God of Jacob.
But it was Solomon who built him a house.
Yet the Most High does not live in what is made by human hands, as the prophet says:
'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool under my feet. What kind of house will you build me, says the Lord, or what is the place where I rest?
Did not my hand make all these things?'
You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you are always resisting the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you.
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who announced in advance the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered,
you who received the law as handed down by angels, and did not keep it."
When they heard this, they were furious in their hearts and gnashed their teeth at him.
But he, full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently up into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at God's right hand,
and said, "Look, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand."
They shouted with a loud voice, held their ears shut and rushed at him all together.
They threw him out of the city and began to stone him, and the witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.
As they stoned Stephen, he called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."
Falling on his knees he shouted with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

And Saul was in full agreement with his killing. That day a great persecution broke out against the assembly in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered across the districts of Judea and Samaria.
Some devout men buried Stephen and mourned loudly over him.
Saul, meanwhile, was devastating the assembly, going from house to house, dragging off men and women and putting them in prison.
So those who had been scattered went about announcing the word.
Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them.
With one mind the crowds listened closely to what Philip said, hearing it and seeing the signs he did.
For unclean spirits came out of many people, shouting with a loud voice, and many who were paralysed or lame were healed.
So there was great joy in that city.
A man named Simon had been practising magic in the city for some time, amazing the Samaritan people and claiming to be someone great.
They all listened to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the power of God called the Great Power."
They listened to him because he had amazed them for a long time with his magic.
But when they believed Philip as he announced the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptised, men and women alike.
Simon himself also believed, and once baptised, he kept close to Philip, and seeing signs and great powers happening, he was astonished.
When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them.
They went down and prayed for them to receive the Holy Spirit,
for it had not yet come down on any of them. They had only been baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus.
Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
When Simon saw that the Spirit was given by the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money
and said, "Give me this power too, so that anyone I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit."
Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could acquire God's gift with money.
You have no part or share in this matter, for your heart is not straight before God.
So repent of this wickedness of yours and ask the Lord whether the intention of your heart may be forgiven you.
For I see that you are poisoned with bitterness and bound with wrongdoing."
Simon answered, "You pray to the Lord for me, so that nothing of what you have said happens to me."
So, after testifying and speaking the word of the Lord, they went back to Jerusalem, announcing the good news in many Samaritan villages on the way.
An angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Get up and go south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." (It is a deserted road.)
He got up and went. And there was an Ethiopian eunuch, a high official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, in charge of her whole treasury. He had come to Jerusalem to worship
and was on his way home, sitting in his chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and stay close to that chariot."
Philip ran up and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah. He asked, "Do you understand what you are reading?"
He said, "How could I, unless someone explains it to me?" And he invited Philip to climb up and sit beside him.
This was the passage of scripture he was reading: "Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb silent in front of its shearer, he does not open his mouth.
In his humiliation justice was taken from him. Who will tell of his generation? For his life is taken from the earth."
The eunuch said to Philip, "Tell me, who is the prophet talking about here? Himself, or someone else?"
Philip opened his mouth and, starting from this scripture, announced the good news of Jesus to him.
As they went along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "Look, water. What is to stop me being baptised?"
\[This verse is not in the critical Greek text. See the footnote.\]
He ordered the chariot to stop, and both of them, Philip and the eunuch, went down into the water, and Philip baptised him.
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing.
Philip found himself at Azotus, and he went through the towns announcing the good news in all of them until he reached Caesarea.
Meanwhile Saul, still breathing out threats and murder against the Lord's disciples, went to the high priest
and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any who belonged to the Way, men or women, he could bring them to Jerusalem in chains.
As he was travelling and getting close to Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him.
He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?"
He said, "Who are you, Lord?" The voice said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do."
The men travelling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one.
Saul got up from the ground, but when his eyes were open he could see nothing. They led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
For three days he could not see, and he neither ate nor drank.
There was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." He said, "Here I am, Lord."
The Lord said to him, "Get up and go to the street called Straight, and at Judas's house ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul. Look, he is praying,
and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay hands on him so that he may see again."
Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many people about this man and all the harm he did to your holy ones in Jerusalem.
And here he has authority from the chief priests to arrest everyone who calls on your name."
But the Lord said to him, "Go, because this man is a vessel I have chosen to carry my name before the nations and kings and the sons of Israel.
For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name."

So Ananias left and went into the house, laid his hands on him and said, "Brother Saul, the Lord has sent me, Jesus, who appeared to you on the road you were travelling, so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit."
At once something like scales fell from his eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptised,
and after he had taken food, he regained strength. He stayed some days with the disciples in Damascus,
and straight away he began proclaiming Jesus in the synagogues: "He is the Son of God."
All who heard him were amazed and said, "Is this not the man who wrecked those in Jerusalem who called on this name? And did he not come here to take them in chains to the chief priests?"
But Saul grew more and more powerful and threw the Jews living in Damascus into confusion by showing that this Jesus is the Christ.
After a good many days, the Jews conspired to kill him,
but their plot became known to Saul. They were even watching the gates day and night to kill him,
but his disciples took him by night and let him down over the wall in a basket.
When he reached Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, because they did not believe he was a disciple.
But Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles, and told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road, and that he spoke to him, and how in Damascus he had spoken boldly in the name of Jesus.
So he moved freely among them in Jerusalem, speaking boldly in the name of the Lord.
He talked and argued with the Greek-speaking Jews, but they kept trying to kill him.
When the brothers found out, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
So the assembly throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria had peace and was built up. Living in the fear of the Lord and in the encouragement of the Holy Spirit, it grew in numbers.
As Peter was travelling through all the regions, he also went down to the holy people living in Lydda.
There he found a man named Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years, paralysed.
Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your own bed." And at once he got up.
All who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha (in Greek, Dorcas). She was full of good deeds and acts of charity that she did.
In those days she fell ill and died. They washed her and laid her in an upstairs room.
Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him with the request, "Please come over to us without delay."

Peter got up and went with them. When he arrived, they took him up to the upstairs room. All the widows stood around him crying, showing the tunics and cloaks that Dorcas had made while she was with them.
Peter sent everyone out, knelt down and prayed, then turned to the body and said, "Tabitha, get up." She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
He gave her his hand and helped her up. Then he called the holy ones and the widows and presented her alive.
This became known all over Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
Peter stayed on in Joppa for a good many days with a man named Simon, a tanner.
There was a man in Caesarea named Cornelius, a centurion in what was called the Italian Cohort,
a devout man who feared God, together with his whole household. He gave generously to the people and prayed to God constantly.
About three in the afternoon he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God come in to him and say, "Cornelius."
He stared at him in terror and said, "What is it, Lord?" The angel said, "Your prayers and your gifts to the poor have gone up as a memorial before God.
Now send men to Joppa and fetch a man named Simon, who is called Peter.
He is staying with Simon the tanner, whose house is beside the sea."
When the angel who spoke to him had gone, he called two of his household slaves and a devout soldier from among those who attended him,
explained everything to them and sent them to Joppa.
Next day, while they were on their way and close to the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray at about noon.
He became hungry and wanted something to eat. While the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance.
He saw heaven opened and something like a large sheet coming down, being lowered to the earth by its four corners.
In it were all the four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth and the birds of the sky.
A voice came to him: "Get up, Peter, kill and eat."
But Peter said, "Certainly not, Lord. I have never eaten anything common or unclean."
The voice came to him again, a second time: "What God has made clean, do not call common."
This happened three times, and then the sheet was taken up into the sky at once.
While Peter was puzzling over what the vision he had seen could mean, suddenly the men sent by Cornelius, having asked their way to Simon's house, were standing at the gate.
They called out to ask whether Simon, who was called Peter, was staying there.
While Peter was still thinking over the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Look, three men are looking for you.
Get up, go down and go with them without hesitation, because I have sent them."
So Peter went down to the men and said, "Look, I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason you have come?"

They said, "Cornelius the centurion, a righteous man who fears God and is well spoken of by the whole nation of the Jews, was instructed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say."
So he invited them in and gave them lodging. Next day he got up and went with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa went along with him.
The following day he arrived in Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends.
When Peter came in, Cornelius met him, fell at his feet and bowed to him.
But Peter raised him up, saying, "Stand up. I too am only a human being."
Talking with him, he went in and found many people gathered.
He said to them, "You know that it is against our law for a Jew to associate with or visit someone of another nation. But God has shown me that I must call no person common or unclean.
So I came without objection when I was sent for. I ask, then, why you sent for me."
Cornelius said, "Four days ago, at this very hour, three in the afternoon, I was praying in my house, and suddenly a man in shining clothing stood in front of me
and said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your gifts have been remembered before God.
So send to Joppa and invite Simon, who is called Peter. He is staying in the house of Simon the tanner, beside the sea.'
So I sent for you at once, and you were kind enough to come. Now we are all here in God's presence to hear everything the Lord has commanded you to say."
Then Peter opened his mouth and said, "I now really understand that God shows no favouritism,
but in every nation the person who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.
He sent his word to the sons of Israel, announcing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ. This one is Lord of all.
You yourselves know the thing that happened throughout all Judea, starting from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed:
how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and how he went about doing good and healing all who were under the power of the devil, because God was with him.
We are witnesses of everything he did, both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They killed him by hanging him on a tree,
but God raised him up on the third day and let him be seen,
not by all the people but by witnesses whom God had chosen beforehand, by us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.
He ordered us to proclaim to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead.
To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name."
While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who were listening to the word.
The believers from the circumcised who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the nations,
for they heard them speaking in other languages and praising God. Then Peter said,
"Can anyone refuse water for baptising these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we did?"
And he ordered them to be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay on for some days.
The apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the nations too had received the word of God.
So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, those who held to circumcision criticised him,
saying, "You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them."
But Peter began and explained it to them point by point:
"I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: something like a large sheet coming down, lowered from heaven by its four corners, and it came right to me.
I looked closely into it and saw four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, reptiles and birds of the sky.
I also heard a voice saying to me, 'Get up, Peter, kill and eat.'
But I said, 'Certainly not, Lord, for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.'
The voice answered a second time from heaven, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.'
This happened three times, and then everything was drawn up again into heaven.
And suddenly, at that very moment, three men arrived at the house where we were staying, sent to me from Caesarea.
The Spirit told me to go with them without hesitation. These six brothers also went with me, and we entered the man's house.
He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house and saying, 'Send to Joppa and fetch Simon, who is called Peter.
He will speak words to you by which you will be saved, you and all your household.'
As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning.
And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he used to say: 'John baptised in water, but you will be baptised in the Holy Spirit.'
If, then, God gave them the same gift that he gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to stand in God's way?"
When they heard this, they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, "So God has given the nations also the repentance that leads to life."
Now those who had been scattered because of the persecution that began over Stephen travelled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, came to Antioch and spoke also to the Greeks, announcing the good news of the Lord Jesus.
The Lord's hand was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.
News about them reached the ears of the assembly in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas as far as Antioch.
When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he encouraged them all to stay with the Lord with firm purpose of heart,
because he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a large crowd was added to the Lord.
Then Barnabas went off to Tarsus to look for Saul,
and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the assembly and taught a large crowd. And it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.
In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
One of them, named Agabus, stood up and announced by the Spirit that a great famine was going to come over the whole inhabited world. (This happened in the time of Claudius.)
The disciples decided that each of them, according to his means, would send help to the brothers living in Judea.
They did this, sending it to the elders through Barnabas and Saul.
About that time King Herod laid violent hands on some who belonged to the assembly.
He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword,
and when he saw that this pleased the Jews, he went on to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread.
After seizing him he put him in prison and handed him over to four squads of four soldiers each to guard him, intending to bring him out to the people after the Passover.
So Peter was kept in prison, but the assembly was praying earnestly to God for him.
On the very night before Herod was going to bring him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and guards in front of the door were watching the prison.
Suddenly an angel of the Lord stood beside him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, "Get up quickly." And the chains fell from his hands.
The angel said to him, "Fasten your belt and put on your sandals." He did so. And the angel said, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me."
He went out and followed him, not knowing that what the angel was doing was real, but thinking he was seeing a vision.

When they had passed the first guard and the second, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them by itself, and they went out and walked along one street, and at once the angel left him.
When Peter came to himself, he said, "Now I know for certain that the Lord sent his angel and rescued me from Herod's hand and from everything the Jewish people were expecting."
Once he realised this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was also called Mark, where many were gathered and praying.
When he knocked at the door of the gateway, a slave girl named Rhoda came to answer.
She recognised Peter's voice and, in her joy, did not open the gate but ran in and announced that Peter was standing at the gate.
They said to her, "You are out of your mind." But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, "It is his angel."
But Peter went on knocking, and when they opened the door they saw him and were astonished.

He motioned to them with his hand to be quiet, and described how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, "Report these things to James and the brothers." Then he left and went to another place.
When day came, there was no small commotion among the soldiers about what had become of Peter.
After Herod had searched for him and not found him, he cross-examined the guards and ordered them to be led away to execution. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

Now Herod was furious with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him in a body. Having won over Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king's country for food.
On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, sat on the throne and made a speech to them.
The people shouted, "The voice of a god, not of a human being."
At once an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give the glory to God, and he was eaten by worms and died.
But the word of God kept growing and multiplying.
Barnabas and Saul returned to Jerusalem when they had completed their service, taking John, who was also called Mark, with them.
In the assembly at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen (who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch) and Saul.
While they were worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them."
Then, after fasting and praying, they laid their hands on them and let them go.
So, sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there sailed to Cyprus.
When they reached Salamis, they announced the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. They also had John with them as an assistant.
They went through the whole island as far as Paphos, and there they found a magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus,
who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man. He summoned Barnabas and Saul and wanted to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the magician (for that is what his name means) opposed them, trying to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
But Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, stared at him
and said, "You son of the devil, full of every kind of deceit and fraud, enemy of everything right, will you never stop twisting the straight ways of the Lord?
Look, the Lord's hand is on you now, and you will be blind, unable to see the sun for a while." At once a mist and darkness fell on him, and he went about looking for people to lead him by the hand.
When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, astonished at the teaching about the Lord.
Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. But John left them and went back to Jerusalem.
They went on from Perga and reached Antioch in Pisidia. On the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders sent them a message: "Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, speak."
So Paul stood up, motioned with his hand and said, "People of Israel, and you who fear God, listen.
The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with a raised arm he led them out of it.
For about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness.
After destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance for about four hundred and fifty years.
After that he gave them judges until the prophet Samuel.
Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
When he had removed him, he raised up David as their king, and he gave this testimony about him: 'I have found David son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do everything I want.'
From this man's descendants God has brought to Israel a Saviour, Jesus, as he promised.
Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel.
As John was completing his course, he said, 'What do you suppose I am? I am not he. But look, one is coming after me, the sandals on whose feet I am not worthy to untie.'
Brothers, children of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, the word of this salvation has been sent to us.
For those living in Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognise him, or the voices of the prophets that are read every Sabbath, and yet they fulfilled them by condemning him.
Though they found no grounds for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have him killed.
When they had carried out all that was written about him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb.
But God raised him from the dead,
and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people.
And we bring you the good news that what God promised to our fathers,
he has fulfilled to us, their children, by raising Jesus, as it is also written in the second psalm: 'You are my Son, today I have become your Father.'
And as for his raising him from the dead, no more to go back to decay, he said it in this way: 'I will give you the holy and faithful promises made to David.'
So he also says in another psalm: 'You will not let your Holy One see decay.'
For David, after serving God's purpose in his own generation, fell asleep, was laid with his fathers and saw decay,
but the one whom God raised did not see decay.
So let it be known to you, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is announced to you,
and that everyone who believes is set free through him from everything from which you could not be set free by the law of Moses.
Beware, then, that what is said in the Prophets does not come upon you:
'Look, you scoffers, be amazed and vanish, for I am doing a work in your days, a work you will never believe, even if someone explains it to you.'"
As they were going out, the people begged that these things be spoken to them again on the next Sabbath.
When the synagogue meeting broke up, many Jews and devout converts followed Paul and Barnabas, who spoke with them and urged them to hold on to the grace of God.
On the next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.
But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what Paul said, abusing him.

Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly: "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. Since you push it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, look, we are turning to the nations.
For this is what the Lord has commanded us: 'I have set you as a light for the nations, to bring salvation to the end of the earth.'"
When the nations heard this, they began to rejoice and to glorify the word of the Lord, and as many as had been appointed to eternal life believed.
And the word of the Lord was being carried through the whole region.
But the Jews stirred up the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, started a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their district.
They shook the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.
And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
At Iconium they went into the Jewish synagogue together and spoke in such a way that a large crowd of both Jews and Greeks believed.
But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the nations and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
So they stayed for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace by granting signs and wonders to happen through their hands.
But the people of the city were divided, some siding with the Jews and some with the apostles.
When a move was made by both the nations and the Jews, together with their rulers, to ill-treat them and stone them,
they found out about it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and the surrounding country,
and there they went on announcing the good news.
In Lystra a man was sitting who could not use his feet. He was lame from birth and had never walked.
He was listening to Paul speak. Paul looked straight at him, saw that he had faith to be made well,
and said in a loud voice, "Stand up on your feet." And he jumped up and began to walk.
When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they shouted in the Lycaonian language, "The gods have come down to us in human form."
They called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, because he was the main speaker.
The priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought bulls and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds.
When the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their clothes and rushed out into the crowd, shouting,

"People, why are you doing this? We too are human beings, with the same nature as you, and we are bringing you good news, that you should turn from these worthless things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them.
In past generations he allowed all the nations to go their own ways.
Yet he did not leave himself without a witness, doing good, giving you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness."
Even with these words they barely stopped the crowds from sacrificing to them.
But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having won over the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, thinking he was dead.
But when the disciples gathered round him, he got up and went into the city, and next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.
When they had announced the good news in that city and made many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch,
strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to remain in the faith, and saying that it is through many hardships that we must enter the kingdom of God.
And when they had appointed elders for them in each assembly, with prayer and fasting they entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had believed.
Then they went through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia.
After speaking the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia,
and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been handed over to the grace of God for the work they had now completed.
When they arrived and gathered the assembly together, they reported everything God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the nations.
And they stayed there no short time with the disciples.
Some people came down from Judea and began to teach the brothers: "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved."

Paul and Barnabas had no small disagreement and debate with them, and it was arranged that Paul and Barnabas and some of the others should go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.
So, sent on their way by the assembly, they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, telling in detail of the turning of the nations, and they brought great joy to all the brothers.
When they arrived in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and they reported everything God had done with them.
But some from the party of the Pharisees who had come to believe stood up and said, "It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses."
The apostles and the elders met to look into this matter.

After a long debate, Peter stood up and said to them, "Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that through my mouth the nations would hear the word of the good news and believe.
And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us,
and he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith.
So why are you now testing God by putting on the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been strong enough to carry?
No, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same way as they are."
The whole company fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul telling of all the signs and wonders that God had done through them among the nations.
When they stopped speaking, James answered, "Brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has explained how God first looked on the nations to take from them a people for his name.
And the words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written:
'After this I will return, and I will rebuild the fallen tent of David. I will rebuild its ruins and set it up again,
so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord, and all the nations over whom my name has been called, says the Lord, who makes these things
known from long ago.'
So my judgement is that we should not make things hard for those of the nations who are turning to God,
but write to them to keep away from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what has been strangled and from blood.
For Moses has had those who proclaim him in every city from ancient generations, since he is read aloud every Sabbath in the synagogues."

Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole assembly, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers,
with this letter: "The apostles and the elders, your brothers, to the brothers from the nations in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia: greetings.
Since we have heard that some went out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, though we gave them no instructions,
it has seemed good to us, having come to one mind, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
So we have sent Judas and Silas, who will themselves tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things:
that you keep away from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell."
So they were sent off and went down to Antioch, and having gathered the company together, they delivered the letter.
When they had read it, they rejoiced at its encouragement.
Judas and Silas, who were prophets themselves, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words.
After they had spent some time there, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them.
\[This verse is not in the critical Greek text. See the footnote.\]
But Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and announcing the word of the Lord, with many others also.
After some days Paul said to Barnabas, "Let us go back and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are doing."
Barnabas wanted to take John called Mark with them also.
But Paul thought it wrong to take along the one who had left them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work.
There was such a sharp disagreement that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and set out, handed over by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.
He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.
He came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who believed, but of a Greek father.
The brothers in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him.
Paul wanted him to go out with him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.
As they went through the cities, they handed on to them for observance the decisions reached by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem.
So the assemblies grew stronger in the faith and increased in numbers every day.
They went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, since they had been prevented by the Holy Spirit from speaking the word in Asia.
When they came opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not allow them.
So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas.
During the night Paul saw a vision: a man of Macedonia was standing there begging him, "Cross over to Macedonia and help us."
As soon as he had seen the vision, we looked for a way to go on to Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to announce the good news to them.
So we put to sea from Troas and ran a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day to Neapolis,
and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We stayed in this city for some days.
On the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the river, where we thought there would be a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had gathered.
One woman, named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a dealer in purple cloth, a worshipper of God, was listening. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what Paul was saying.
When she and her household had been baptised, she urged us: "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come and stay at my house." And she persuaded us.
Once, as we were going to the place of prayer, a slave girl met us who had a spirit of divination and earned her owners a great deal by fortune-telling.
She followed Paul and us, shouting, "These men are slaves of the Most High God, who announce to you the way of salvation."
She did this for many days. Paul, worn out by it, turned and said to the spirit, "I order you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her." And it came out that very moment.
When her owners saw that their hope of profit was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them to the authorities in the marketplace.
They brought them to the magistrates and said, "These men are Jews, and they are throwing our city into confusion.
They are promoting customs that it is not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practise."
The crowd joined in the attack on them, and the magistrates tore the clothes off them and ordered them to be beaten with rods.
After inflicting many blows on them, they threw them into prison and ordered the jailer to guard them securely.
Receiving such an order, he put them in the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them,
when suddenly there was such a great earthquake that the foundations of the prison were shaken. At once all the doors were opened, and everyone's chains came loose.
The jailer woke up and saw the prison doors open. He drew his sword and was about to kill himself, thinking that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul shouted with a loud voice, "Do not harm yourself, for we are all here."
The jailer called for lights and rushed in, and shaking with fear he fell down in front of Paul and Silas.
Then he brought them outside and said, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?"
They said, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household."
They spoke the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his house.
He took them that same hour of the night and washed their wounds, and at once he was baptised, he and all his household.
Then he brought them up into his house and set a meal before them, and he rejoiced with his whole household that he had come to believe in God.
When day came, the magistrates sent the officers with the message, "Let those men go."
The jailer reported these words to Paul: "The magistrates have sent word that you are to be released. So come out now and go in peace."

But Paul said to them, "They beat us in public without a trial, though we are Roman citizens, and threw us into prison. And now do they want to send us away in secret? No. Let them come themselves and take us out."
The officers reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens.
So they came and apologised to them, and they took them out and asked them to leave the city.
After leaving the prison they went to Lydia's house, and when they had seen the brothers they encouraged them and left.
After they had travelled through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews.
Paul went in, as was his custom, and over three Sabbaths he argued with them from the scriptures,
explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, "This is the Christ: Jesus, whom I am announcing to you."
Some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, along with a large number of devout Greeks and quite a few of the leading women.

But the Jews, filled with jealousy, took some worthless men from the marketplace, gathered a mob and set the city in an uproar. They attacked the house of Jason and tried to bring them out to the people.
When they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, "These people who have turned the world upside down have come here too,
and Jason has taken them in. They are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus."
The crowd and the city authorities were alarmed when they heard this.
After taking security from Jason and the others, they let them go.
The brothers at once sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue.
These people were more open-minded than those in Thessalonica. They received the word with great eagerness and examined the scriptures every day to see whether these things were so.
Many of them therefore believed, and so did a number of Greek women of high standing and of men.
But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God had been proclaimed by Paul in Berea also, they came there too, to stir up and agitate the crowds.
Then the brothers at once sent Paul off toward the sea, but Silas and Timothy stayed on there.
Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and, after receiving an instruction for Silas and Timothy to join him as quickly as possible, they left.
While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols.
So he argued in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout people, and every day in the marketplace with those who happened to be there.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also debated with him. Some said, "What is this scrap-collector trying to say?" Others said, "He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities," because he was announcing Jesus and the resurrection.
They took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, "May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?
For you are bringing some strange things to our ears, and we want to know what they mean."
(All the Athenians and the foreigners living there spent their time on nothing except telling or hearing something new.)
So Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said: "People of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious.
For as I walked around and looked at the things you worship, I found an altar with this inscription: 'To an unknown god.' So what you worship without knowing it, this I announce to you.
The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by hands,
nor is he served by human hands as if he needed anything, since he himself gives life and breath and everything to all.
From one he made every nation of humanity to live on the whole face of the earth, having fixed the seasons they were given and the boundaries of where they live,
so that they would seek God, in the hope that they might feel their way to him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us.
For 'In him we live and move and exist,' as some of your own poets have said, 'For we too are his offspring.'
Since we are God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine nature is like gold or silver or stone, shaped by human skill and invention.
God overlooked the times of ignorance, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent,
because he has set a day on which he is going to judge the world with justice by a man whom he has appointed, and he has given proof of this to everyone by raising him from the dead."
When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, but others said, "We will hear you about this again."
So Paul left them.
But some men joined him and believed, among them Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
After this he left Athens and went to Corinth.
There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. He went to them,
and because he practised the same trade, he stayed and worked with them, for they were tentmakers by trade.
He argued in the synagogue every Sabbath, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself fully to the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.
When they opposed him and abused him, he shook out his clothes and said to them, "Your blood be on your own heads. I am clean. From now on I will go to the nations."
He left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshipper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
Crispus, the leader of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with his whole household, and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptised.
One night in a vision the Lord said to Paul, "Do not be afraid, but keep speaking and do not be silent,
for I am with you, and no one will lay a hand on you to harm you, because I have many people in this city."
So he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him to the tribunal,
saying, "This man is persuading people to worship God in a way that is against the law."
Paul was about to open his mouth when Gallio said to the Jews, "If this were a matter of some wrong or vicious crime, I would be justified in accepting your complaint, you Jews.
But since these are questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things."
And he drove them out of the tribunal.
They all seized Sosthenes, the leader of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this.
Paul stayed on many more days, then took leave of the brothers and sailed for Syria, together with Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had his hair cut, because he was under a vow.
They arrived at Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and argued with the Jews.
When they asked him to stay for a longer time, he did not consent,
but taking leave of them he said, "I will come back to you if God wills." And he set sail from Ephesus.
When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the assembly, and then went down to Antioch.
After spending some time there, he left and travelled from place to place through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, powerful in the scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and with a burning spirit he spoke and taught accurately the things about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.
When he wanted to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he was a great help to those who had believed through grace,
for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, showing from the scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul travelled through the inland regions and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples
and said to them, "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?" They said to him, "No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit."
He said, "Into what then were you baptised?" They said, "Into John's baptism."
Paul said, "John baptised with a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was coming after him, that is, in Jesus."
When they heard this, they were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus.
When Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in other languages and prophesying.
There were about twelve men in all.
He went into the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, arguing and persuading about the kingdom of God.
But when some became hardened and refused to believe, speaking evil of the Way in front of the crowd, he left them, took the disciples with him and argued every day in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
This went on for two years, so that all the residents of Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord.
God was doing extraordinary miracles through the hands of Paul,
so that even cloths and aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.
Some of the travelling Jewish exorcists also tried to use the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, "I order you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims."
Seven sons of a Jewish chief priest named Sceva were doing this.
But the evil spirit answered them, "Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?"
And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, overpowered all of them and was so violent against them that they ran out of the house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks, and fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honour.
Many of those who had come to believe came, confessing and declaring their practices.
And a number of those who had practised magic collected their books and burned them in front of everyone. They added up the price of them and found it came to fifty thousand silver coins.
So the word of the Lord kept growing and prevailing with power.
After these events, Paul resolved in the Spirit to go through Macedonia and Achaia and on to Jerusalem, saying, "After I have been there, I must see Rome also."
He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, into Macedonia, while he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
About that time a serious disturbance arose about the Way.
A man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no small profit to the craftsmen.
He gathered them, with the workers in similar trades, and said, "Men, you know that our prosperity comes from this business.
And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost the whole of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great crowd, saying that gods made by hands are not gods.

There is a danger not only that our trade will come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing, and that she whom all Asia and the world worship will be stripped of her greatness."
When they heard this, they were filled with rage and began to shout, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians."
The city was filled with confusion, and they rushed together into the theatre, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's travelling companions.
Paul wanted to go in among the people, but the disciples would not let him.
Even some of the Asiarchs, who were his friends, sent to him and urged him not to venture into the theatre.
Some were shouting one thing and some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together.
Some of the crowd explained the matter to Alexander, whom the Jews had pushed to the front. Alexander motioned with his hand and wanted to make a defence to the people.
But when they recognised that he was a Jew, they all shouted with one voice for about two hours, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians."

When the town clerk had quietened the crowd, he said, "People of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is the keeper of the temple of the great Artemis and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky?
Since these things cannot be denied, you ought to be calm and do nothing rash.
For you have brought these men here who are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
If Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.
But if you seek anything further, it will be settled in the regular assembly.
For we are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no reason we can give to justify this commotion."
And when he had said this, he dismissed the assembly.
After the uproar had ended, Paul sent for the disciples and encouraged them, and after saying goodbye he left for Macedonia.
When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece.
There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.
He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea, by Aristarchus and Secundus from the Thessalonians, by Gaius from Derbe, by Timothy, and by Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia.
These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,
but we sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we joined them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days.
On the first day of the week, when we were gathered to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to leave the next day, and he went on speaking until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we were gathered.
A young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window, was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on. Overcome by sleep, he fell from the third storey and was picked up dead.
But Paul went down, threw himself on him and put his arms around him, and said, "Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him."
Then Paul went back up, broke the bread and ate, and talked with them for a long while, until daybreak, and then left.
They took the boy away alive and were greatly comforted.
We went ahead to the ship and set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul on board there, for he had arranged it this way, intending himself to go by land.
When he met us at Assos, we took him on board and came to Mitylene.
Sailing from there, we came the next day opposite Chios, the day after that we crossed to Samos, and the day after we came to Miletus.
For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he would not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hurrying to be in Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the assembly to come to him.
When they came to him, he said to them: "You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time, from the first day I set foot in Asia,
serving the Lord with complete humility and with tears and with trials that came on me through the plots of the Jews,
how I held back nothing that was helpful, but declared it to you and taught you in public and from house to house,
testifying to both Jews and Greeks of repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
And now, look, I am going to Jerusalem, bound by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there,
except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that chains and hardships are waiting for me.
But I do not count my life of any value or as precious to myself, if only I can finish my course and the service I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the good news of the grace of God.
And now, look, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again.
So I testify to you today that I am clean from the blood of everyone,
for I did not hold back from declaring to you the whole plan of God.
Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of God, which he acquired with his own blood.
I know that after I am gone savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock,
and from among your own selves men will arise speaking twisted things, to draw the disciples away after them.
So be alert, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not stop warning each one of you with tears.
And now I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and give you an inheritance among all those who are sanctified.
I wanted no one's silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands met my needs and the needs of those who were with me.
In everything I showed you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'"
When he had said this, he knelt down and prayed with them all.
There was much weeping among them all; they threw their arms round Paul's neck and kissed him,
grieving most of all over the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they went with him to the ship.
When we had torn ourselves away from them and set sail, we ran a straight course to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
Finding a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went on board and set sail.
We sighted Cyprus and passed it on our left, sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, because the ship was to unload its cargo there.
We looked for the disciples and stayed there seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem.
When our days there were over, we left and went on our way, and all of them, with wives and children, escorted us out of the city. On the beach we knelt down and prayed,
said goodbye to one another, and went on board the ship, and they returned home.
When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for a day.
Next day we left and came to Caesarea, and we went into the house of Philip the evangelist, one of the seven, and stayed with him.
He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
While we were staying there for some days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul's belt, tied his own feet and hands with it and said, "This is what the Holy Spirit says: 'The man who owns this belt will be bound like this by the Jews in Jerusalem and handed over to the nations.'"
When we heard this, we and the people there begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus."
Since he would not be persuaded, we fell silent, saying, "The Lord's will be done."
After these days we packed up and went up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea also went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we were to stay.
When we reached Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us gladly.
The next day Paul went with us to James, and all the elders were present.
After greeting them, he described one by one the things that God had done among the nations through his service.
When they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, "You see, brother, how many thousands of believers there are among the Jews, and they are all zealous for the law.
They have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who live among the nations to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or to live according to the customs.
What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.
So do what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow.

Take these men, purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law.

But as for the nations who have believed, we have sent a letter with our decision that they should keep away from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled and from sexual immorality."

Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice of the completion of the days of purification, when the offering would be made for each of them.
When the seven days were almost over, the Jews from Asia saw him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and seized him,

shouting, "People of Israel, help. This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he has even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place."
For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
Then the whole city was stirred up, and the people rushed together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut.
While they were trying to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion.
He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. When they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He asked who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd shouted one thing, some another. Since he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks.
When he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,
for the mob of the people followed, shouting, "Away with him."
As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, "May I say something to you?" And he said, "Do you know Greek?
Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?"
Paul said, "I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people."
And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people, and when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:
"Brothers and fathers, listen to the defence that I now make to you."
When they heard that he was speaking to them in the Hebrew language, they became even quieter. And he said,
"I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, trained at the feet of Gamaliel in the strict way of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God, just as all of you are today.
I persecuted this Way to the point of death, binding men and women and putting them in prison,

as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear witness. From them I also received letters to the brothers in Damascus, and I was on my way there to bring those who were there to Jerusalem in chains to be punished.
As I was travelling and getting close to Damascus, at about noon a great light from heaven suddenly flashed around me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?'
I answered, 'Who are you, Lord?' He said to me, 'I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.'
Those who were with me saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the one speaking to me.
I said, 'What am I to do, Lord?' The Lord said to me, 'Get up and go into Damascus, and there you will be told about everything that has been assigned to you to do.'
Since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, those with me led me by the hand, and I came into Damascus.
A man named Ananias, a devout man according to the law and well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,
came to me and stood beside me and said, 'Brother Saul, see again.' And at that very hour I could see him.
He said, 'The God of our fathers has appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth,
because you will be a witness for him to all people of what you have seen and heard.
And now, why are you waiting? Get up, be baptised and have your sins washed away, calling on his name.'
When I had come back to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance
and saw him saying to me, 'Hurry and leave Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.'
I said, 'Lord, they themselves know that in synagogue after synagogue I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you.
And when the blood of your witness Stephen was being shed, I myself was standing by, approving, and looking after the clothes of those who killed him.'
And he said to me, 'Go, for I will send you far away to the nations.'"
They listened to him up to this word. Then they raised their voices and said, "Take such a man off the earth. He should not be allowed to live."
As they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and tossing dust into the air,
the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be questioned under the whip, to find out why they were shouting against him like this.
But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion standing by, "Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen who has not been condemned?"
When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and told him, "What are you about to do? This man is a Roman citizen."
The tribune came and said to him, "Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?" He said, "Yes."
The tribune answered, "I bought this citizenship for a large sum." Paul said, "But I was born a citizen."
Those who were about to question him withdrew from him at once, and the tribune too was afraid when he realised that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him.
